title: Claus Guth never thought he'd be a stage director. Now he's among the world's best
summary: Claus Guth never imagined he’d be a stage director
story: Claus Guth never imagined he’d be a stage director
NEW YORK -- Claus Guth never imagined he’d be a stage director.
“My original vision was to be a filmmaker, but I never wanted to do films with talking. I always was dreaming of films with only music,” he said.

Long removed from making movies with friends on a Super 8 camera, the 62-year-old was named stage director of the year for 2025-26 by the magazine Opernwelt. His latest production, Leoš Janáček’s “Jenůfa,” opened at the Metropolitan Opera on Monday after successful runs in London and Chicago. It can be seen through Dec. 4.

“He’s a very mild-mannered dictator as far as directors go, has a great kind of bedside manner, knows how to charm people into doing things that he wants to get his way,” Met general manager Peter Gelb said.
Guth learned piano as a child, and played an electric bass and drums. He studied literature, philosophy and history at the University of Munich.

After a year as an intern at CBS’s production studios in Manhattan, he tried the publishing industry and computer games as he tested vocations. Guth’s breakthrough came when he entered the first class of a directing school in Munich founded by August Everding.

“It was, for me, like an arrival after a long search. Because suddenly in this first moment, I was in a rehearsal room with actors, singers, and I was kind of giving them directions for the first time,” Guth said. “I immediately noticed: Wow, yeah, that’s it. Of course, that’s it.”
His graduation production of Henry Purcell's “Dido and Aeneas” was seen by opera house heads who hired Guth to direct contemporary compositions because he could read music.
“At some point I said: `Hello people, I also can do a classical opera,'" Guth said.
His first staging of a standard was Verdi's “La Traviata” at Mannheim in 1994, which resulted in an audience uproar.

“I was under huge influence at that time from the movies of David Lynch. And the whole thing was like a David Lynch movie, and opera people, especially in Germany, they didn’t know David Lynch,” Guth recalled. “So the result was very bad reviews, a complete 100% booing audience, and they sent me back to the modern opera.”

He waded back into the familiar with Richard Strauss’ “Ariadne auf Naxos” in the northwestern German city of Bremen in 1996 and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s “Le Nozze di Figaro” in Munich the following year.

Guth's career took off when Gerard Mortier hired him to direct the world premiere of Luciano Berio’s “Cronaca del Luogo” at the 1999 Salzburg Festival in Austria. High-profile engagements followed for Wagner's “Der Fliegende Holländer” at the 2003 Bayreuth Festival in Germany and the three Mozart/Lorenzo Da Ponte operas from 2007-09 in Salzburg.
His 2017 staging of “Bohème” in Paris shifted the story to space, sparking fierce jeers. When it returned for two revivals, it became an avant-garde classic.

“It was just a very strange experience to be booed every night because of the set," soprano Sonya Yoncheva, the production's original Mimì, said last month. "And now they love it. He was ahead of the time.”

Guth directs three or four productions annually and took on musical theater with a 2025 staging of “Cabaret” in Munich, where he lives. His 19-year-old daughter, Josephine, is a journalism student in Vienna, and his oldest son, 27-year-old Paul, is studying dramatic theater. When the family travels to the home outside Salzburg that Guth inherited from grandparents, he jams with his 11-year-old son, Felix.

One year ahead of an opera's opening, he spends two weeks with his production team that creates set, costumes, lighting, projections and choreography. Before traveling to the opera house, he spends two weeks studying the score on an iPad, marking likely cues alongside bars of music, which he then brings to six weeks of rehearsals.
“He’s a lot about physical language,” said soprano Nina Stemme, who plays the Kostelnička.
Guth's “Jenůfa" staging premiered at London's Royal Opera in 2021 and won an Olivier Award the next year.
"I trust him, he trusts me,” said soprano Asmik Grigorian, who performs the title role. “It’s really a joy and really somehow smooth, easy. I never feel stressed.”

Guth’s Met debut was in Strauss’ “Salome” in 2025. After his own rehearsals, he rides around New York on a Citi Bike, trying to catch shows and concerts. He’s also been studying the score of John Adams’ “Doctor Atomic” which he will stage in Munich starting Feb. 4.

Guth will direct Lucia Ronchetti’s “Battaglia – Die Frauen von Palermo" in Frankfurt, Germany, in June and Hans Abrahamsen’s “The Dreamers” at the Festival d'Aix-en-Provence in France this summer, when his world premiere production of Brett Dean’s “Of One Blood” travels to the Santa Fe Opera in New Mexico.

Handel’s “Semele,” which opened in 2023 in Munich, will come to the Met in 2028 starring Ying Fang, and Guth is planning a staged version of Franz Joseph Haydn’s “Die Schöpfung” for the Park Avenue Armory on Manhattan's Upper East Side.

“Every piece is my one and only,” Guth said. “Normally I don’t repeat myself, because there are too many new things. It’s different for conductors. They earn a lot of money once they know a piece by heart and then they travel with it. For me that’s boring."
He will stage Georges Bizet's “Carmen” starring Grigorian in Munich, and would like to direct Alban Berg's “Wozzeck” and “Lulu” along with more Baroque operas.
Guth goes on the road with an empty suitcase and fills it with devices that intrigue his youngest son.

“If I’m somewhere in the world and I’m in flea markets, I always buy instruments. Anything, a trumpet, a trombone — just bought an alphorn,” Guth said. “At some point, it’s boring and he picks up one of these instruments and he’s playing around, like, for half an hour. And suddenly, he knows how to play it.”

title: A global National Book Awards lineup, but 2 finalists can't enter the US
summary: Edwidge Danticat, Valeria Luiselli and David Levithan are among the finalists for the 77th annual National Book Awards
story: Edwidge Danticat, Valeria Luiselli and David Levithan are among the finalists for the 77th annual National Book Awards

NEW YORK -- Edwidge Danticat, Valeria Luiselli and David Levithan are among the finalists Wednesday night for the 77th annual National Book Awards, where winners in five competitive categories will be announced and Salman Rushdie will be presented a medal for lifetime achievement.

The nominees and the stories they tell span the globe, from Sicily in Luiselli's novel “Beginning Middle End” to Haiti in Danticat's “Dèy” to the Middle East in fiction finalist Hannah Lillith Assadi’s “Paradiso 17.” Actor-author Kyle MacLachlan will host the dinner ceremony at Cipriani Wall Street and singer Michelle Zauner, author of the bestselling memoir “Crying in H Mart,” is the musical guest.

Not all of the finalists will be in attendance. Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, a nominee for nonfiction, and Samar Yazbek of Syria, a finalist for books in translation, were denied visas to the U.S., according to the National Book Foundation.

“It feels unjust that some, but not all, of our finalists are able to participate in in-person programming to recognize their exceptional books,” reads a statement from the Foundation, which presents the awards.

The State Department declined to comment on any specific cases, but issued a statement saying that “The Trump Administration continues to put America and its interests first by fully enforcing U.S. immigration laws and ensuring lawful travel through our visa process. As Secretary (of State Marco) Rubio said, ‘a visa is a privilege, not a right’.”

Winners for fiction, nonfiction, books in translation, young people's literature and poetry each receive $10,000. Publishers submitted 1,912 books in all, judged by panels of authors, editors, booksellers and others in the literary community.

title: Family of Vince Lombardi grants rights for a feature film about the coaching great's life
summary: The family of Vince Lombardi has granted an exclusive life rights option to Eighteen Worldwide filmmakers James Manera and Massimiliano “Max” Musina for a feature film about the late Green Bay Packers coaching great
story: The family of Vince Lombardi has granted an exclusive life rights option to Eighteen Worldwide filmmakers James Manera and Massimiliano “Max” Musina for a feature film about the late Green Bay Packers coaching great

BEVERLY HILLS, Calif. -- The family of Vince Lombardi has granted an exclusive life rights option to Eighteen Worldwide filmmakers James Manera and Massimiliano “Max” Musina for a feature film about the late Green Bay Packers coaching great.

The option also allows for the possibility of related scripted television and documentary projects. Lombardi’s son, Vince Lombardi Jr., who will serve as an executive producer of the film, reached the agreement on behalf of the family.

The film will have the involvement of former Packers players Dave Robinson, Boyd Dowler, Marv Fleming and Chuck Mercein, who all played for Lombardi. Manera’s screenplay begins with Lombardi’s arrival in Green Bay in 1959. In nine seasons, Lombardi coached the team to five NFL championships, including the first two Super Bowls.
Robert Schmidt, head of the Vincent T. Lombardi Foundation, will be a co-executive producer.
Eighteen Worldwide LLC is a production company founded by Manera and Musina.

title: Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in Manhattan closet sells for $4.8M
summary: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million
story: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million
NEW YORK -- A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been buried in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades sold at auction Tuesday for $4.8 million.

The 1930 landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” is likely the first in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico, according to Christie’s auction house. Its existence was known from a 1931 photograph, but its whereabouts had been kept secret until recently.

A Manhattan woman in her 90s nonchalantly told her niece one day in 2022, “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” Her family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother, who had purchased it in 1963 from a New York gallery for $3,800.

The woman, who died recently, displayed it in her East Village apartment for many years until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. From then on she kept it in her closet, safely hidden behind coats and boxes.

When the family finally unboxed it this year, they discovered it has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her signature marking on the back: a star with her initials scrawled in the middle.

The 10-x-24-inch (25.4-x-61-centimeter) oil painting is among O’Keeffe's early love letters to New Mexico, where she settled and lived for decades. The identity of the winning bidder was not disclosed; it sold for $4,878,000.

Known as the “mother of American modernism,” O’Keeffe maintained a home and studio in Abiquiu and a nearby summer residence tucked between the red-rock cliffs of Ghost Ranch. She died in 1986 at age 98 and is best known for her paintings of flowers and American Southwest landscapes.
The second piece in the “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico” collection is at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.

title: Mexico's Catholic street DJs turn annual pilgrimage into a party
summary: A mix of street DJs and Catholic devotees are taking to the streets in one of Mexico's most important pilgrimages
story: A mix of street DJs and Catholic devotees are taking to the streets in one of Mexico's most important pilgrimages
MEXICO CITY -- A sea of people carrying statues of Mexico's patron saint, the Virgin of Guadalupe, marched along the avenue leading up to the country's most important basilica on Wednesday.
Such pilgrimages are practically embedded in the daily rhythms of the bustling Mexican capital. But the roughly 1,000 pilgrims from across the Latin American nation aren't just Catholic devotees.
They're also Mexican street DJs.
The annual procession and street party known as the “sonidero” pilgrimage is perhaps one of the most Mexico City-esque convergences of celebrations to hit the city.

Sonideros, as they're known, are a particular brand of DJs found primarily in Mexico City, but also in other parts of Mexico and Colombia. The DJs mix rhythmic tunes of cumbia with radio announcements, chanting shout outs that mingle with the music.

The tradition is so important in the city, particularly in working-class neighborhoods, that in 2023 the city government recognized sonidero culture as intangible cultural heritage — a designation UNESCO quickly celebrated. The music has even evolved into its own dance, a derivation of cumbia that has more open steps meant for street parties than the classic two-person cumbia.

Each neighborhood has its own set of sonideros who organize pop-up mobile parties. Wednesday's party-procession on the avenue leading up to the famed Basilica de Guadalupe wasn't so spontaneous, but rather part of an annual celebration now spanning decades.

“The root of faith in Mexico is the Virgin of Guadalupe,” said Christian Castañeda, a musician who joined the throngs of people marching through the gates of the Basilica. “We mix this party with the joy of music and we come to play for the Virgin.”

Nearly 80% of Mexicans identify as Catholic, according to Mexican census data, and Mexicans from as far as northern Baja California flock to the capital each November to give thanks for good luck they've had throughout the year.

Esperanza Rivera, donning a bright gold and neon blue T-shirt with images of different radio sets, said she started preparing for the march before the sun came up. At 4 a.m. the 76-year-old began packing sandwiches and putting the final touches on a massive pink altar her family planned to carry through the streets.

Some families see the march as a way to pass down sonidero and religious traditions to the next generations. Others enjoy the chance to connect with other street DJ communities from across the country.
“Everyone, all of the sonideros, unite on this day,” she said.
They walk for hours, using motorcycles to cart a mix of flower-lined altars like Rivera's and mobile DJ booths.
Rivera and her relatives joined a mass in the Basilica before returning with other sonideros by bus to their neighborhood of Tláhuac in the city's outskirts.
That's where they continue the party.
Megan Janetsky contributed to this report from Mexico City.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Singer Julio Iglesias faces Spanish High Court probe into alleged sexual misconduct
summary: A Spanish High Court judge has opened an investigation into singer Julio Iglesias after two former employees accused him of sexual offenses, degrading treatment and assault
story: A Spanish High Court judge has opened an investigation into singer Julio Iglesias after two former employees accused him of sexual offenses, degrading treatment and assault

MADRID -- A Spanish High Court judge has opened an investigation into singer Julio Iglesias following a complaint filed by two former employees in which they alleged sexual offenses, degrading treatment and assault, a court ruling seen by The Associated Press on Wednesday said.

Rights group Women's Link Worldwide filed the complaint on behalf of the two women, who alleged that Iglesias had sexually and physically assaulted them in 2021 in his Caribbean residences in which they worked. It followed a joint investigation into Iglesias' alleged misconduct by Spanish outlet elDiario.es and U.S. broadcaster Univision.

An email seeking comment from Miami-based entertainment lawyer Russell L. King, whose website lists Iglesias as among his clients, was not immediately answered. Iglesias has previously called the allegations untrue.
The 83-year-old is one of the world’s most successful musical artists, having sold more than 300 million records in more than a dozen languages.

Investigating judge Antonio Piña said the complaint presented sufficient preliminary evidence for the court to open criminal proceedings, the ruling said. By doing so, the court is not making a judgment on the credibility of those allegations, Piña said.
He dismissed portions of the complaint alleging human trafficking and violations of workers’ rights.
After making his start in Spain, Iglesias won immense popularity in the U.S. and wider world in the 1970s and 1980s. He is the father of pop singer Enrique Iglesias.
In 1988, he won a Grammy for Best Latin Pop Performance for his album “Un Hombre Solo.” He also received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Grammys in 2019.
Prosecutors earlier this year said that Spanish courts ​lacked jurisdiction ⁠because the alleged misconduct took place abroad and the complainants did not reside in Spain.
The women later filed a direct complaint with the ⁠High ​Court, which agreed to ​investigate the allegations.
The judge has ordered the two complainants to testify in person on Feb. 3, ​2027.

title: Movie Review: Mason Reeves shines in Beth de Araújo's 'Josephine,' which stars Channing Tatum
summary: An 8-year-old girl witnesses a rape at the beginning of Beth de Araújo’s harrowing family drama “Josephine.”
story: An 8-year-old girl witnesses a rape at the beginning of Beth de Araújo’s harrowing family drama “Josephine.”
While exercising in San Francisco's Golden Gate Park, 8-year-old Josephine runs far ahead of her dad.

Before he catches up, she hears screams coming from a public restroom and hides behind a tree, peeking out to see a woman try to run from an attacker, who pushes her down, bangs her head into the ground and rapes her.

Like the girl, played by newcomer Mason Reeves in Beth de Araujo’s harrowing family drama “Josephine,” we as the audience must bear witness to this horrific act of violence. We must also carry the burden of what we’ve seen for the duration of the film, which won top prizes at the Sundance Film Festival. But, of course, unlike her, we are not 8.

The awful truth of being a parent is that you cannot control when your child will learn about, or experience, the horrors of the world. How do you help a kid navigate the emotional fallout? How do you even know when it will hit, or how it will manifest? We want to protect our children as long as possible, to shield them from realities that are often beyond even our understanding. But nothing ever really goes according to plan, does it? And kids? They have their own internal world of fears and dreams.

Josephine’s parents, Damien ( Channing Tatum ) and Claire (Gemma Chan), are well-meaning, but they are not on the same page. When Josephine asks questions, Damien deflects. Claire tries to engage more directly. But the truth is that they were never going to be able to control or even manage this situation. They can try to explain things as gently as possible, but then there is the chaos of what an 8-year-old who has ears and the passcode to her mother’s phone can find out on her own. She might misspell rape in the search bar, but Google is there to help direct her to the correct definition.

We don't get to know Josephine before the incident. We don’t know if she was a joyful kid or a rebellious one. We don’t know if she was one who lashed out at her parents and schoolmates in anger or frustration. We don’t know if she’d ever wanted to buy a toy gun at the store before or if, when face-painting is on the table, she chooses something scary with monster teeth. What we do know is that she appears to be going through something she doesn’t understand — the world around her no longer seems safe.

When Josephine sees her father being intimate with her mother, she screams at him to get away. Her guard is up with strangers, too, and through Araújo’s lens, you sense danger looming. Then there are the visions — Josephine sees the perpetrator everywhere. Like an imaginary friend, or rather a nightmare, he’s just there, in all her spaces.

This scenario is sadly rooted in the real-life experiences of the filmmaker, who witnessed something in Golden Gate Park as a child and whose family did not talk about it after. Araújo has set her film version in more modern times, with one parent at least, Claire, who tries to talk to Josephine about what happened. But even when you’re being as direct as possible, it’s hard to know what kids are hearing and concluding. You get the feeling that this little girl, and this family, will be forever altered.

Then there are the police, the detectives and the therapists and the stressful possibility of a trial in which Josephine is the only witness and the victim’s only hope. It is all quite agonizing, but Araújo keeps things moving and the camera close on Josephine’s face. It is a marvel of direction that Reeves, who turned 8 during filming, never appears to be performing or reciting lines that an adult has written for her. You really do believe that you’ve dropped in on their lives. Tatum and Chan make their characters feel quite real as well (albeit unusually beautiful).

Because “Josephine” dares to tackle such a challenging and upsetting subject, it won't be for everyone. But those who do take a chance will find a thoughtful and honest film, made with beauty, care and courage.

“Josephine,” a Sumerian Pictures release in theaters Friday, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “rape, graphic nudity, some language and sexual content.” Running time: 120 minutes. Three-and-a-half stars out of four.

title: Movie Review: Andrew Scott stuns in deeply moving biopic of a fallen actor in 'Elsinore'
summary: “Elsinore” captures the final months of Scottish actor Ian Charleson's life as he performs “Hamlet” while dying with AIDS
story: “Elsinore” captures the final months of Scottish actor Ian Charleson's life as he performs “Hamlet” while dying with AIDS

Playing Hamlet has been compared to climbing Mount Everest, a physical and mental feat with no equal. Scottish actor Ian Charleson tackled it in 1989 with a secret: He was dying, the equivalent of ascending to the top of the world without oxygen.

“Elsinore” captures the final months of the actor's life as he delivers show-stopping performances of Shakespeare's Danish prince while his body is succumbing to AIDS. For Andrew Scott, playing Charleson, it has created a likewise career-defining performance.

Struggling actors as movie heroes are having a moment at the multiplex these days — think “Misty Green” and “I Play Rocky.” “Elsinore” is the one in this trio that embraces live theater and its chummy community.

Directed by Simon Stone with a screenplay by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” is not just a portrait of bravery and art in the face of death. It's a reminder of a terrible time when a mysterious illness was ripping through a terrified population, prompting a dreaded daily routine of looking for lesions on your body and hospitals burning the sheets of those who died.
No recording of Charleson's stage feat exists, but his Hamlet, inside the pressure-cooker of the brutalist National Theatre complex on London’s South Bank, is widely regarded as the greatest ever.

Charleson was then a struggling actor trying to shake off his role in “The Chariots of Fire,” noting bitterly that everyone only recalls the film for the music. After Daniel Day-Lewis pulled out of “Hamlet” halfway through its run, Charleson was asked to step in. He knows it may hasten his own death, but he says he's after quality, not quantity, of life.

“Elsinore” shows Scott puking into buckets backstage, collapsing after onstage speeches with his lungs on fire as he pours his life spirit into the role. “I’d rather die of ‘Hamlet’ than AIDS,” he says. “It's glory. It's joy.” He would die just weeks after the run, at age 40.

While that all sounds like a grim viewing prospect, there are plenty of moments of levity — Scott's Charleson has a dry, cutting sense of humor — amid an uplifting community. Charleson finds a queer support team and relies on his deep friendships, like his best friend played by Billie Piper, who cooks and leaves him food.

Another of his angels is Dr. Margaret Johnson, a U.K. pioneer of HIV and AIDS treatment who is trying to keep her patients alive. That means she expects no exertions and certainly no four-hour “Hamlet,” which she calls Charleson's “ridiculous enterprise.” Johnson is played with stern-but-caring perfection by Olivia Colman.

The movie also explores what it was like to be a gay man in the late 1980s, the competing demands of avoiding mainstream prejudice by staying closeted and the urgent need to not stay silent in the face of an extinction-level epidemic.

One of Charleson's colleagues is avant-garde director Derek Jarman, who urges Charleson to go public with his illness. “We cannot survive in a culture of lies,” he tells him. Jarman — played soulfully by David Dawson — is also dying of AIDS. “I'm going blind,” he confesses and your heart breaks. He's a director, after all.

One scene cuts through the gloom when Charleson finds a cassette tape of Ethel Merman singing “There’s No Business Like Show Business” and creates a elaborately choreographed, lip-synced show in a hospital AIDS ward to lift spirits, especially for one young, patient who hoped to be a dancer.

Scott is no stranger to “Hamlet,” of course, having starred in a production at the Almeida Theatre in 2017. In a nice twist, his Gertrude then is his Gertrude now, Juliet Stevenson, and a close Charleson friend, the actor David Rintoul, also has a role.

It's time to talk about Scott, who here clearly strengthens his case for being one of his generation's best actors. To play Charleson with such wit, anger, love, frustration and grace is astonishing. To then play Charleson playing Hamlet is just insane.

The script does a masterful job of connecting Hamlet's plight and the one facing its leading actor. As its director notes about the play: “It’s about being alive and becoming dead.” Knowing that Charleson is dying gives Shakespeare's dialogue even more pathos, like the lines around “There’s a special providence in the fall of a sparrow.”
One nifty bit of filmmaking comes toward the end — the use of crosscuts from the anguished stage performance between Hamlet and Horatio and the anguished interaction between Charleson and his bestie.

So we have to thank Day-Lewis twice. Once for abandoning the stage so that Charleson could shine and again this fall for setting in motion a stunning way for Scott to soar. Join us as we say: “Good night, sweet prince.”
“Elsinore,” a Focus Feature release that's in theaters Friday, is rated PG-13 by the Motion Picture Association for “frightening material.” Running time: 1111 minutes. Four stars out of four.

title: Activist archivists are bringing back old home movies
summary: Archiving activists who roam from town to town in France are making people's forgotten home movies great again by preserving them digitally
story: Archiving activists who roam from town to town in France are making people's forgotten home movies great again by preserving them digitally
ANTIBES, France -- They flicker on a small screen — grainy, almost ghostly images of lives and times that Romain Gimenes has heard about from family for years but is too young to have known himself.

Slowly hand-winding reels of decades-old Super 8 film through a viewing machine — lent to him by archiving activists who have made it their mission to save home movies like these from being tossed out as trash — Gimenes marvels as loved ones and places that his grandfather filmed in the 1970s dance back to life in sepia tones.
“Oh! That’s my grandfather,” the 30-year-old French Riviera school teacher exclaims. He inherited his middle name, Gabriel, from the man whose bearded face appeared fleetingly and whom he never met.

Interspersed among more images — of his mother, his 94-year-old grandmother, even a great-grandmother and others — pops up a prized find: Footage of a service station the family used to own, since demolished and replaced by a bakery, in the Riviera town of Antibes.
Gimenes whips out his phone and snaps a photo, a digital copy of an analog image to show and remind his mother of halcyon days.

“A photograph of a photograph,” he says, reflecting on his Instagram-era reflex gesture. “Today, we film everything and photograph everything. But who takes the time to look at it all? Who takes the time really to see things, really to look?”
“It’s that gesture of our time — the swipe.”

Just 200 years ago, only one human being — also a Frenchman — had the power to freeze time and our world into a photographic image. The father of photography, Nicéphore Niépce, knew back in 1824 that he'd invented something special, writing to his brother that the image he'd taken of the view from a window was “vraiment quelque chose de magique” — really something magical.

The world's fastest cameras today capture trillions of frames per second. Never have so many people been armed with the ability to immortalize children's first steps, to unmask abuses by filming them, to distort truths by altering or inventing images, to edit instances into reels and stories, to sear joys and horrors, beauty and ugliness onto our retinas and our brains.
And never have humans been so addicted — but also, perhaps, so inured — to that power.

On the clouds of Google Photos alone, users have stored more than 9 trillion photos and videos. Images take up so much digital space that it has to be measured in zettabytes, which are mind-blowingly gigantic. Just one zettabyte is equivalent to 250 billion DVDs and if each of its 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes of data were a liter of water, a zettabyte would fill more than 7,000 Pacific Oceans, according to U.S. technology company Cisco Systems, Inc.
Boston-based data research company IDC estimates that photos and moving images will have generated about 144 zettabytes of data worldwide in 2026.

“That includes captured, streamed, broadcast and replicated copies. By 2030, that figure is forecast to reach about 234 zettabytes as higher-resolution smartphone cameras and video-first social platforms put more content in more hands, and as AI-generated images and video add a new source of data on top of what people capture,” says Adam Wright, an IDC senior research manager. He answered questions via email.
But then there are images that make up no zettabytes — yet — and that are, those archiving them say, crying out for rescue.

For Stephanie Ange, Pierre Bouchut and Margot Lestien, who roam from town to town in France, collecting home movies and digitizing them for archives, image preservation is a battle waged reel by reel.

The name that the trio chose for their group, Ofnibus, plays off the French word for UFO. They can never be sure what they might find on the films and video cassettes that people bring them, often without much of a clue of what they show. Rummaged from garages, attics, cupboards and drawers, and often filmed by people who have since died, they are, quite literally, noninventoried cinematic objects until Bouchut runs them through his film-scanner or pops them into his VHS machines.

In their 23 residencies over five years, Bouchut has seen “everything there is to see in life”: Marriages, baptisms and birthdays galore but also an A-to-Z from farmers butchering prized pigs to the forcible shaving of women's heads during World War II to punish and shame them for suspected relations with German soldiers.
He’s had plenty of surprises, not all of them pleasant, including what today might be called sex tapes — or as he more delicately puts it: “Births, and the stage before births.”
“I love picnics,” he says. “And the Tour de France — everyone filmed that.”
The more he watches, the more he's struck by how “everything changes, but nothing changes.”

“Children apparently weren’t better behaved in the past. People enjoyed themselves just as much as they do today,” he says. “There’s a universality that comes through, something that gives you a little faith in humanity.”
But as time passes, so do the people who know what the images show.

“Finding the material, being able to watch it again and digitize it is one thing, but you still need to be able to interpret and understand it,” Lestien says. “That’s where the urgency lies: the people who still remember the events and what’s on the films are dying.”

The introduction in 1965 of Kodak's Super 8 mm format democratized moviemaking with hand-held cameras that whirred through cartridges containing 50 feet (15 meters) of film. But ever-fewer families still have the functioning projectors (followed later by VCRs) that would be fired up occasionally to watch their home movies together. Films that were treasured can, for the generations that inherit them, become unwatchable clutter.
“Eventually they throw it away because it takes up space, it’s starting to smell bad, and they can’t really see what they could do with it,” Lestien says.
The projectors and video-viewing machines that the Ofnibus team carts around France are making forgotten home movies great again.

In Antibes, they digitized 22 hours of images for archiving and reconnected their donors with memories and family histories. They also commissioned an editor who boiled down selected images into a 30-minute movie for a public viewing that 50 townspeople attended. It included rediscovered footage of Brigitte Bardot, the cinema icon who lived on the French Riviera and was filmed with a basket of roses.

Retired 65-year-old travel agent Sophie Roux-Nantas brought 16 reels of film from the 1930s to the '60s that were languishing in her garage. She saw herself as a 3-year-old on a beach “playing just as children play, just as the new generation does. We made sandcastles. That hasn’t changed, and we swam in the same way.”
On one of his 28 videocassettes “that were all sleeping in a box,” 41-year-old physiotherapist Yohan Chabert was transported back to the 1990s and a family game of Monopoly.
He snapped a photo of the screen.
“It’s moving,” he said. “And, I think, it’s something to share. Because having reels at home and leaving them in a cupboard is a bit of a shame.”

title: Willie Nelson on a near-death experience, Dolly Parton, James Talarico and his book, 'The Last Leaf'
summary: Willie Nelson, at 93, continues to embrace life and creativity
story: Willie Nelson, at 93, continues to embrace life and creativity

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Willie Nelson is a lot of things — a 12-time Grammy winner, singer, songwriter, guitarist, actor, activist, architect of outlaw country and an icon inextricable from the American imagination. He's also 93 years old and isn't planning on slowing down anytime soon.

“I really enjoy playing live. I enjoy the fans. I enjoyed the bus rides. It’s just all really a lot of fun, and right now I’m not touring, and I miss it,” he told The Associated Press over the phone from Maui.

His new book, “The Last Leaf: Reflections on Late-Life Creativity — and My Longest Love Affair,” chronicling the last 12 years, is full of reflections and brand-new anecdotes. And of course it is: In that period, the always prolific Nelson has recorded 17 studio albums, written 36 songs and five books, and performed live over 400 times. There's a lot of heart too: Nelson spends considerable time talking about his family and his wife of four decades, Annie Nelson.
So, does wisdom really come with age? “No,” Nelson laughs. “I guess a little bit. A hard head makes a sore ass.”

A lot has been written about Nelson's songwriting, and that continues throughout “The Last Leaf.” “My life has been lived out in two parts,” he writes near the book's end. “The first part is living. The second part is writing and singing about living.”

He says he's still writing, and the process usually begins on the road. “When I write, I usually go riding down the highway,” he says, “And then I’ll get to Trigger later,” referencing his beloved, beat-up Martin N-20, a nylon-string classical guitar — his musical companion since the late '60s.

Trigger and Nelson make a dynamic duo, as does Nelson and Mickey Raphael, his harmonica player and the last surviving member of the classic lineup of his Family band. “He’s been with me since he was 17 years old. He knows my songs as well as I do,” Nelson says of Raphael. “He is a great harmonica player. And he fits in with our group perfectly.”

“The Last Leaf” is named after Nelson's cover of Tom Waits’ “Last Leaf,” a song that perfectly expresses Nelson’s long-held survivor status. (He's outlasted fellow outlaw country artists Waylon Jennings, Johnny Cash, Kris Kristofferson, Merle Haggard and then some.)

“Me and Merle, you know, we're a lot alike. We both enjoyed the same things. Some of it was good for us, some of it wasn’t,” Nelson reflects. “I think I was fortunate enough to live through it, and Merle’s health finally got him.”

Health has long been a priority for Nelson, who gave up drinking decades ago as well as smoking marijuana in 2019 when he was diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). But on the first page of “The Last Leaf” introduction, Nelson reveals something harrowing: He contracted COVID-19 in 2022 and nearly died.

“I wanted to die. It was so bad,” he reflects. “And I felt so bad, and Annie wouldn’t let me, you know. She took care of me for 10 days. She slept in the next room on an ironing board, waiting for me to get better. And she literally saved my life.”
In “The Last Leaf,” Nelson recounts the experience with Annie, who says he asked her to let him die, twice. She says he brought up reincarnation.
Despite the severity of the situation, Nelson says, “I think positive every chance I get.” And that doesn't mean reflecting on his legacy.
When asked how he hopes to be remembered, he says, “Uh, he was sick. No, I’m just kidding. Who knows? There will be all kinds of opinions.”

It's likely they'll remember the songs he wrote and the good he did with events like Farm Aid as well as the causes and politics he supported. Earlier this year, Nelson endorsed Democratic state Rep. James Talarico in his 2026 U.S. Senate race in Texas against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico won, becoming the first Democratic senator in the state since the 1990s.
“I think it was great,” Nelson says. “I think Texas did what Texas wanted to do and they went blue big time.”
Nelson and Dolly Parton shared a decades-long friendship, so her death earlier this year no doubt affected him.

“I go way back to the Porter Wagoner, Dolly Parton shows, and I love those. Those were two of my favorite people doing what they do best. And I saw Dolly recently and I knew she wasn’t feeling well,” he says. “But she was a sweetheart and I loved her.”

After Parton passed, news broke that Nelson had covered her song “I Will Always Love You.” Nelson says he doesn't know when his version will be released, but he hopes soon. Particularly because searching for the cover yields unauthorized, AI-generated videos of him “performing” the song.
“I don't worry about it,” he says of artificial intelligence, adding that “They're a bunch of thieves.”
For now, he's got simple aims for those interested in reading “The Last Leaf.”
“I just want them to read it and enjoy it,” he says.
“And then throw it away,” he says, laughing.

title: Bellagio's annual holiday flower show opens with tens of thousands of blooms
summary: More than 100 people worked around the clock over a six-day span to bring to life the latest display at the Bellagio's Conservatory and Botanical Gardens
story: More than 100 people worked around the clock over a six-day span to bring to life the latest display at the Bellagio's Conservatory and Botanical Gardens

LAS VEGAS -- As giant, silver snowflakes were hoisted toward the high glass ceiling at the Bellagio's Conservatory and Botanical Gardens, tourists snapped photos of the tens of thousands of flowers arranged underneath in one of Las Vegas’ most popular holiday displays.

Visitors over the weekend got a first look at “Postcards From Christmas,” which will be up until Jan. 2 and features holiday snapshots reminiscent of childhood. Trays of poinsettias and chrysanthemums and rows of winter evergreens filled the room with scents of pine and cinnamon.

Every year since the hotel's opening in 1998, the Bellagio showcases five different displays. “Postcards From Christmas” includes snapshots of classic holiday vignettes, from a giant, cozy chair sitting next to a fireplace decked with stockings, to a teddy bear dressed as a drummer boy.

“This feels like a childhood Christmas for me,” said Ed Libby, creative director and conservatory designer for the Bellagio. “But it also feels like a Christmas that I would want to come to as a guest and take as a journey.”

Installing the display was no small feat, with over 100 people working around the clock over a six-day span. More than 25,000 visitors are expected to stroll among the elaborate floral arrangements each day — a peaceful reprieve from the bustling casino floor.

Libby, who has been the brains behind the displays since 2016, said he travels constantly and attends fashion shows to find inspiration. He plans the full experience, from what guests smell and hear to how they should feel as they turn a corner.

The living room scene, where a dog sleeps curled up in front of the hearth, is meant to represent hospitality, Libby said. And a red and green train in the back of the gardens represents the journey to the Bellagio, he said.

In the middle of the room stands a white fir Christmas tree at 45 feet (13.72 meters) tall. The tree is adorned with red and gold ornaments and is surrounded by intricate designs of red preserved roses, hydrangeas and reindeer moss.

This year, guests can pose for holiday photos in a space cut into the garden bed. Libby sees the space as a postcard from the Bellagio to guests and as an opportunity for visitors to create their own postcards.
It is project manager Lea Jonic’s job to make Libby’s visions a reality, and it takes months of planning.

Roughly 20,000 plants from up to 150 different varieties are used in each display, sourced from growers around the world, Jonic said. Growers are contacted about a year in advance so they can get to work in growing many of the plants.
“They were born to be here,” she said.
The Bellagio's holiday exhibit showcases plants grown mostly in California.

The 42 fresh-cut Christmas trees in the display come from Mount Shasta in California. Jonic said the Bellagio works with a company that plants two trees for every one it harvests. The poinsettias are raised indoors in California, Jonic said.
Jonic's goal is to use as much plant material as possible throughout the 14,000-square-foot (1,300-square-meter) display.

Once the designs are approved, Jonic contacts between five and 10 artists and sculptors from around the country to build the structures and decor, which sometimes need to be hand-carved or hand-painted, she said.
After months of planning, a team of gardeners, electricians, carpenters, sculptors and artists spends two days taking down the old exhibit, and four days building the new one, Jonic said.
“It is an enormous effort from so many people,” she said.

In about a month, the display will make way for one celebrating the Lunar New Year. Nine gardeners work full-time to water the plants by hand and keep them fresh, Jonic said. If a plant doesn't look its best, an extra will be swapped in from a small nursery onsite.

When it’s time to dismantle, the plants that are nearing the end of their lives are taken to a composting facility. They’ll also have a plant sale for hotel employees, and that money is donated to the hotel’s foundation, Jonic said.

title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal and accepts sexual assault conviction
summary: French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set
story: French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set

PARIS -- French actor Gérard Depardieu said Monday he was dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set and will accept the 18-month suspended sentence. He also issued an apology.
“I was found guilty," Depardieu said in a written statement, as his appeal trial was scheduled to open Monday in Paris. He added that he “hears it” and accepts the sentence.
“I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered,” he said.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a 54-year-old set decorator and a 34-year-old assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” (“The Green Shutters”) in 2021. He received an 18-month suspended prison sentence in a case that was widely seen as a post-#MeToo test for the country’s film industry.

The court also ordered the 77-year-old Depardieu, one of the most prominent figures in French cinema for decades, to pay both accusers a total of 29,040 euros ($32,350) in fines, and that his name be listed in the national sex offender database.

“On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu wrote.
“I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that no longer exists,” he added. “I have therefore decided to withdraw my appeal.”

The comments contrast with the actors’ statements during the trial last year, when he had strongly denied the accusations. He acknowledged using vulgar and sexual language on the film set and grabbing the set dresser's hips during an argument, but denied that his behavior was sexual.
Depardieu is expected to face other legal proceedings soon.

In 2018, actor Charlotte Arnould accused him of raping her at his home. An investigating judge in August 2025 requested that the case go to trial and a Paris appeals court is to decide next week whether it will proceed.

For more than a half-century, Depardieu was a towering figure in French cinema, known for his commanding physical presence and versatility. In recent years, his behavior toward women has come under renewed scrutiny, including after a documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

title: A look at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame 2026 inductees and how they were honored
summary: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has inducted its 2026 class of 18 musical legends at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles
story: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has inducted its 2026 class of 18 musical legends at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles
LOS ANGELES -- The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has inducted its 2026 class of 18 musical luminaries at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
Artists become eligible for the hall 25 years after their first music release.
Here’s a look at this year's Rock Hall class, a few of their defining songs and who inducted them.

The 75-year-old English singer, songwriter and drummer is already in the hall as a member of Genesis and now gets in again for a solo career that brought some of the biggest hits of the 1980s. Key songs: “Against All Odds,” “One More Night,” “You'll Be in My Heart.”
Collins was inducted by Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker, who also played Collins' famous drum fill as Cynthia Erivo sang “In the Air Tonight” in tribute.

Wu-Tang Clan is an epic hip-hop coalition from Staten Island — made up of RZA, GZA, Method Man, Raekwon, Ghostface Killah, Inspectah Deck, U-God, Masta Killa and previously, the late Ol’ Dirty Bastard. They’ve been hip-hop innovators since their 1993 debut album, “Enter the Wu-Tang.” Key songs: “C.R.E.A.M.,” “Protect Ya Neck,” “Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nuthing Ta F’ Wit.”
The group was inducted by Chris Rock. The many members performed a medley of their hits, including "C.R.E.A.M." and late member Ol' Dirty Bastard's “Shimmy Shimmy Ya,” backed by a big jazz band.

The 56-year-old New Jersey-born Queen Latifah achieved unprecedented success for a female rapper, becoming a star at 19 with the release of her 1989 album “All Hail the Queen” and the single “Ladies First.” Key songs: “Ladies First,” “When You’re Good to Mama.”
She enters the hall as a recipient of the Early Influence Award.
She was inducted by Megan Thee Stallion and accepted in person. She and fellow nominee MC Lyte jointly performed a medley of their hits, including “U.N.I.T.Y.”
Vandross was an R&B singer whose velvet-voiced love songs made him a definitive voice of the 1980s and ’90s. Vandross died in 2005. Key songs: “Never Too Much,” “Dance With My Father,” “I’d Rather.”
He was inducted by Oprah Winfrey. Usher sang a medley of his songs, including “Here and Now” and “So Amazing."
The Brit-pop lords of the 1990s are led by famously feuding brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher. Key Songs: “Wonderwall,” “Live Forever,” “Don’t Look Back in Anger.” They did not appear at the ceremony.
The band was inducted by actor Bob Odenkirk. Singer-songwriter Stephen Wilson Jr. played an acoustic rendition of “Wonderwall.”

A trailblazing Brooklyn rapper in the late 1980s, MC Lyte became the first female rapper to release a full solo album, “Lyte as a Rock.” Her hard-edged rhymes brought a political consciousness that was growing in hip-hop at the time. Key songs: “Keep on Keepin’ On,” “Cold Rock a Party,” “Ruffneck.”
She entered the hall as a recipient of the Early Influence Award and was inducted by rapper Remy Ma. She accepted the honor in person. Her medley with Queen Latifah included her “Ruffneck.”

Sade is a British band most prominent in the 1980s that blended jazz, smooth-and-sultry R&B and sophisti-pop, led by a Nigerian-born singer of the same name. Key songs: “Smooth Operator,” “No Ordinary Love,” “Like a Tattoo,” “Kiss of Life.” She did not appear.
Sade was inducted by singer Andra Day. Singer Sienna Spiro sang their biggest hit, “Smooth Operator.”

Parsons was arguably the most important figure in rock’s turn toward country in the late 1960s and early ’70s. Parsons was a member of the Byrds, co-founded the Flying Burrito Brothers and became a solo artist with Emmylou Harris as his duet partner and backup singer. He died in 1973. He entered the hall as a recipient of the Early Influence Award. Key songs: “Hickory Wind,” “Love Hurts,” “Return of the Grievous Angel.”
Parsons was inducted via video montage. Parsons had a separate tribute on Wednesday at the Troubadour club that featured his duet partner Emmylou Harris, Sheryl Crow and Elvis Costello.

He was honored for bringing the Beatles, Elvis Presley, Buddy Holly, James Brown and the Doors to American living rooms, and for consistently featuring Black artists despite network pressure to keep television segregated. He died in 1974.
Sullivan was inducted via video montage and got into the hall as a recipient of the Ahmet Ertegun Award for non-performers who shaped rock and roll and youth culture.
These artists will be inducted later in the evening:

The 70-year-old punk-coded English rock singer had major hits through the 1980s. He will be inducted along with his longtime guitarist Steve Stevens. Key songs: “Dancing With Myself,” “White Wedding,” “Eyes Without a Face.”

The two British rock bands will get a rare joint induction that makes sense given their members and circumstances. Joy Division was a dark and seminal post-punk band formed in 1976. When their charismatic lead singer, Ian Curtis, died in 1980, the remaining members formed New Order. Key songs: “Love Will Tear Us Apart,” “Blue Monday,” “Bizarre Love Triangle.”
The scorching rock band led the new wave of British heavy metal and became the quintessential metal band of the 1980s. Key songs: “The Trooper,” “Fear of the Dark,” “Run to the Hills.”

The queen of salsa and innovator and spreader of Afro-Cuban sounds and one of the most popular Latin artists of the 20th century, the Havana-born singer Cruz is the first member of the Hall of Fame who sang primarily in Spanish. She died in 2003. Key songs: “Vasos Vacíos,” “La Vida Es Un Carnaval,” “El Último Adiós.”
She enters the hall as a recipient of the Early Influence Award.

The Nigerian saxophonist, bandleader, progenitor and activist was born in 1938 in colonial Nigeria. His music career, which spanned the late 1950s up to the 1990s, was a signature blend of high-octane horn, jazz, and funk with Yoruba rhythms. Kútì, who died in 1997, is the first African-born solo artist to enter the Rock Hall. He gets in as a recipient of the Early Influence Award.
Key songs: “Water No Get Enemy,” “Zombie,” “Let’s Start.”

The 63-year-old producer was instrumental to the popularization of hip-hop in the 1980s through his work with the Beastie Boys, LL Cool J, Run DMC and his Def Jam Recordings label. Rubin went on to work in rock and country, producing Johnny Cash’s haunting final recordings in the 1990s.
He gets into the hall as a recipient of the Musical Excellence Award.

The late songwriter and producer will enter the hall for helping to define the Philadelphia soul sound of the 1970s, penning hits for the Stylistics, Teddy Pendergrass and the Spinners. Creed died in 1986 at 37.
She gets into the hall as a recipient of the Musical Excellence Award.

Mardin gets the honor for his decades of work as a producer for Atlantic Records for his work in helping create the soul sound of Aretha Franklin and his production of Rock Hall of Famers including Hall & Oates, the Bee Gees, Chaka Khan, Diana Ross and Cher. Mardin died in 2006.
He gets into the hall as a recipient of the Musical Excellence Award.

Miller was known for producing rock acts of the 1960s and 1970s, including the Rolling Stones albums considered to represent their artistic peak: “Beggars Banquet,” “Let It Bleed,” “Sticky Fingers” and “Exile on Main St.” He died in 1994.
He gets into the hall as a recipient of the Musical Excellence Award.

title: Rex Ryan is back on ESPN days after arrest in Nashville
summary: Former NFL coach Rex Ryan was back in his role as ESPN analyst on Sunday, a few days after his arrest
story: Former NFL coach Rex Ryan was back in his role as ESPN analyst on Sunday, a few days after his arrest
NEW YORK -- Former NFL coach Rex Ryan was back in his role as ESPN analyst on Sunday, a few days after his arrest.

Ryan turned himself in to Nashville police on Wednesday on misdemeanor charges after he allegedly hit two pedestrians with his truck in a popular area downtown last week and then drove off after an argument, police said.
The former New York Jets and Buffalo Bills head coach was in ESPN's studio for its three-hour “NFL Sunday Countdown" pregame show. Ryan didn't address his arrest.

Ryan was driving a pickup truck when he allegedly ran over the feet of both individuals, who had the right of way crossing a main street in Nashville’s honky-tonk and music tourist district on Nov. 5, police said in a release Wednesday.

The pedestrians involved, who sustained minor injuries, waved Ryan down at another red light and said he stepped out to argue with them, according to police. They took a photo of the driver and the truck’s license plate, police said.
Ryan “immediately surrendered” himself to authorities after learning of the charges, his attorney, David Raybin, said Wednesday.

“From the outset, Coach Ryan has been fully cooperative with law enforcement and he intends to remain cooperative as the case moves forward,” Raybin said. “Because we just received the warrant today, we currently have limited information regarding the allegations.”

Ryan was charged with two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failure to give information or render aid and two counts of failure to obey a traffic control signal, according to court records. All are misdemeanors.

A judicial commissioner set Ryan’s bond at $6,000, but he qualified for pretrial release, according to the Davidson County Sheriff’s Office. That means he was released on non-financial conditions. He is scheduled to appear in court next month.
Ryan led the Jets to the AFC championship game in consecutive years after the 2009 and 2010 seasons.

While with the Jets, Ryan became one of the team’s — and the NFL’s — most popular figures, especially during his first few seasons as coach, because of his brash, colorful approach in news conferences that became must-watch TV.

He has not coached since being fired by the Bills with one game left in the 2016 season, though he has since expressed an interest in coaching and interviewed in 2025 for the Jets’ head coaching vacancy when Aaron Glenn was hired.

His father, the late Buddy Ryan, was an NFL coaching legend who famously coordinated the 1985 Chicago Bears defense that was one of the best in history. Seth Ryan, one of Rex Ryan’s two sons, is currently in his first season as the Jets’ passing game coordinator.
Ryan is best known now for his work at ESPN as one of the analysts on the network’s NFL pregame show.
