title: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction set for Los Angeles, with many big names skipping the stage
summary: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday may feel like an '80s night
story: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday may feel like an '80s night

LOS ANGELES -- It may feel like '80s night at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, with the new members including Billy Idol, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, New Order, Luther Vandross and Iron Maiden.

But it's hard to say exactly what the vibe will be on Saturday at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, with many of the inductees opting out of performing or appearing, and the Hall of Fame revealing next-to-nothing about the show during the run-up.
After streaming the ceremony live the past few years, the Rock Hall is returning to its previous model, where the public won’t see it until an edited version airs on ABC and Disney+ on Dec. 9.
Here's what we do know about the show:
Oasis, youngest of the inductees, won’t be coming. Guitarist Noel Gallagher is playing a gig back home in Britain, and his little brother, Liam Gallagher, just doesn't want to come.
“It’s too far to be going for the night,” he said in a post on the social platform X. He added in another, “I dont like award ceremonies they freak me out I dont know why I just get weird vibes."

Iron Maiden will be on tour in Australia. Sade is opting to sit it out, too. Collins is likely to appear, but he said he has to decline from playing his songs for health reasons. Key members of New Order, getting a joint induction with their previous incarnation Joy Division, will also be out for health reasons. Vandross died in 2005.
But the show will go on, and hip-hop could be the highlight. Wu-Tang Clan will be inducted along with Queen Latifah and MC Lyte, and all are expected to appear and probably perform.
And Idol, being inducted with his longtime guitarist Steve Stevens, will take the stage ready to rock.
Latifah and Lyte enter the hall as recipients of the Early Influence Award along with posthumous nominees Gram Parsons, Fela Kuti  and Celia Cruz.

Parsons, an essential figure at the crossroads of country and rock in the 1960s and '70s, got his own separate tribute Wednesday night at the legendary Troubadour club in West Hollywood, where his duet partner Emmylou Harris along with Rock Hall-of-Famers Elvis Costello and Sheryl Crow sang his songs and saluted his legacy.
Kuti will become the first African-born artist in the hall, and Cruz will become the first member who sang primarily in Spanish.

A group of producers will be inducted via the Musical Excellence Award: Rick Rubin, Linda Creed, Arif Mardin and Jimmy Miller. And TV host Ed Sullivan will get in as the winner of the Ahmet Ertugun award, which goes to nonmusicians who've made rock history.

Many other major stars are likely to appear to induct the new members or to play the absentees' songs in tribute. The past few years, the hall has announced several special guests, though not their roles, the week of the show, but with no live airing this year it has returned to a model of keeping nearly everything secret until it happens.
The show is in Los Angeles for the second straight year, and organizers have said it will be here more often while still rotating to New York and Cleveland, where the actual hall resides.

title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade 100th edition: Which stars are in the lineup?
summary: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade promises a spectacular celebration with Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo among the performers
story: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade promises a spectacular celebration with Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo among the performers

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Megan Moroney,Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo will help celebrate the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade this year, a lineup that includes a record-breaking, very appropriate 100 inflatables in the sky, including Bluey, Mickey Mouse and Hello Kitty.

The parade will begin at 8:30 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day in all time zones and will feature a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer, Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus.

Performances will also include EJAE, Indigo Girls, Natalie Merchant, Baha Men, Natasha Bedingfield, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Feid, Mckenna Grace, Icona Pop, Il Volo, Wyclef Jean, Jamie Miller, Ryan Peter Murphy, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, RIIZE and Smash Mouth.

The familiar TV hosts — Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker from the “Today” show — will return on NBC and Peacock. A Spanish-language simulcast on Telemundo will be hosted by the network’s Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz and Clovis Nienow.

“For our 100th parade, we’re creating a celebration of unprecedented scale and will deliver an unforgettable Thanksgiving for millions across the country,” said Sharon Otterman, Macy’s chief marketing officer, in a statement.

New balloons and inflatable elements include Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, Earl the Squirrel, Hello Kitty Big Apple, Joe Cool & Woodstock from “Peanuts,” Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey, Underdog and a new balloonicle, Fuzzyeti’s Fur Wheel Drive by Levi’s. Macy’s Studios also created Billie Brightpaw for the centennial lineup, described as a cheerful and curious bear.

New floats in the 2026 parade lineup include Dashing All the Way with DoorDash; Hogwarts Holiday with HBO; Mr. Peanut Power Plant with Planters; Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs with Purina Dog Chow; Road Trip to Parade with GEICO; and Macy’s Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes.

There also will be iconic characters from past parades, including Angry Birds’ Red, Arthur, Bugs Bunny, Bullwinkle J. Moose, Curious George, Adventure Time’s Finn & Jake, Jimmy Neutron, Popeye & Olive Oyl & Swee’Pea, Pink Panther, Poppy from “Trolls,” Scooby-Doo, Sonic the Hedgehog, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and Wild Thing.
“Few holiday traditions capture the excitement of Thanksgiving morning quite like Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade,” said Jen Neal, executive vice president at NBC & Peacock, in a statement.

The parade will be preceded by a new documentary, “America’s Parade: 100 Years of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade,” set to air Nov. 20 on NBC and begin streaming the next day on Peacock. The film will be “celebrating the people, artistry and imagination behind the tradition,” blending archival moments with a look at preparations for the milestone march. It will include interviews with previous performers like Billy Porter and Andrew Rannells.

This year’s marching bands will represent schools from Indiana, Tennessee, South Carolina, Hawaii, Texas, Alabama, Connecticut, Illinois, as well as the New York Police Department Marching Band and Macy’s Great American Marching Band, which represents students from all 50 states.
There will also be performances from Maria Verdeja School of the Arts, The Divine Nine Unity Step Team, Native Pride Productions, Spirit of America Cheer and Spirit of America Dance.
Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade made its debut in 1924 and has become an annual tradition and hallmark of the holiday season, with the exception of a three-year break during World War II.

title: Incoming congressman Bobby Pulido was just one political moment at the Latin Grammys
summary: Bobby Pulido is a member-elect for the U.S. House of Representatives who has also recently won the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album
story: Bobby Pulido is a member-elect for the U.S. House of Representatives who has also recently won the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album

Shielded by the shadow of his signature cowboy hat, Bobby Pulido took to the stage of the Latin Grammys to accept the award for best Tejano album. It was his third time accepting a win in the category, but it was his first as a member-elect in the U.S. House of Representatives.

One week earlier, the Democrat won a competitive race to flip Texas’ Republican-held 15th Congressional district. Onstage, he confirmed his retirement from a monumental music career, but underscored his gratitude in representing both the politics and music of the Lone Star State.
“I have so much pride to be from Texas, to be Tejano, and to represent this music,” Pulido told the audience Thursday.

The appearance from the future congressman was one of several long-dormant political references during this year’s ceremony in Las Vegas. From red carpet interviews to main stage performances, emboldened artists called for international unity and representation across the diaspora.

Ten years ago, the Latin Grammys made headlines for restricting journalists for asking political questions on the red carpet. In past performances, artists proudly denounced racism in American politics and brought attention to human rights crises in Mexico. A 2016 policy quieted this advocacy in the years that followed.

After historic milestones for representation in the recent midterm elections, propelled in no small part by Latino voters, Pulido’s double victory matched similar messages championing change across music and politics.
“We have to represent,” Pulido said in his speech. “We have to get to work, to use our voice for something different.”
The Latin Grammys did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press on Friday.

Daddy Yankee opened his crowning performance as the Person of the Year honoree draped in a flowing cape of the Puerto Rican flag. Building on a landmark year of advocacy from Boricua artists, Yankee proclaimed: “Puerto Rico isn’t small. The map is small.”

“Years ago the government even thought that we were criminals, that we had no future,” said Yankee in his acceptance speech. “Once I dreamed of being a baseball player. So I’m grateful that I’m getting hits here in the big leagues, at the Grammys.”
Silvana Estrada, a Mexican folk musician with a legacy of advocating against femicide in her home country, told the AP that the role of a musician today is “super important.”

“Artists should step forward without fear and say what we think, because that’s how we encourage the people who follow us to find that confidence in themselves,” said Estrada, who’s single “Dime” was awarded best singer-songwriter song.

In the most overtly political moment of the night, Brazilian artist Anitta 's victory for best pop contemporary Portuguese album marked the first time an award in the language was handed out during the televised ceremony. Anitta used her platform to call for unity across the different communities of Latin America and in her home country.
“For many years Black culture was erased in Brazil,” Anitta said. “This album comes to help with that, so that Black culture in Brazil is strong forever.”
Getting ready for the red carpet, Anamaria Sayre of NPR’s “Alt.Latino” had one major question on her mind. She asked online: “Are the Latin Grammys going to get political tonight?”

Sayre is a producer of El Tiny, the Latino version of NPR’s Tiny Desk, where she’s followed the shift in alternative musicians being recognized by the Latin Recording Academy, especially ones who, she said, “overtly” center their advocacy in their art.

Sayre attributes this wave of genre-bending creativity to the very reason the Latin Grammys were founded. “We needed a whole other Grammys to fit all of the different types of music that come out of Latin America,” she told the AP.

Political turnover took place across the Western Hemisphere this year, with broader right-wing movements across Latin America matched by progressive shifts in the U.S. and Brazil. “It doesn’t split that cleanly,” Sayre added, which, to her, underscored the correlation between musical and political change-making even more.
“I don’t think you can ever look at music, or how we value music, as independent from a political landscape,” Sayre said.
Associated Press journalist Leslie Ambriz in Los Angeles contributed reporting.

title: 'The Sun Also Rises' at 100: Women are now leaders in Hemingway scholarship
summary: Hilary K
story: Hilary K

NEW YORK -- Hilary K. Justice, an Ernest Hemingway scholar at Boston's John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, remembers having to defend her chosen field of expertise as a graduate student some 30 years ago.

“I was told that studying Hemingway amounted to committing professional suicide — ‘Haven’t we killed him yet?’ was the comment of one professor in my PhD program,” she said in a recent interview. Justice oversees the Hemingway collection at the JFK library, where the author's papers are stored.
“I used to be able to count on being asked ‘How do you, as a woman, justify studying Hemingway?’ at every Q&A session at every public speaking event.”

This year marks the centennial of Hemingway's classic breakout novel, “The Sun Also Rises,” an occasion for scholars and fans to celebrate his work — and express relief that his outsized legend has receded enough that his books can stand or fall on their own. Hemingway died more than 60 years ago, and at least a generation of students has come of age knowing little about the man who for countless predecessors embodied the very ideal — or anti-ideal — of the writing life: the macho adventurer, drinker and womanizer who once famously defined courage as “grace under pressure.”

At a centennial event last month at the 92nd Street Y Unterberg Poetry Center in Manhattan, Maya Hawke, Will Harrison, Sarah Pidgeon and other actors read from “The Sun Also Rises,” and a panel discussion featured “Bright Lights, Big City” novelist Jay McInerney and a handful of Hemingway descendants. Grandson Brendan Hemingway, a teenager during the rise of second-wave feminism in the 1970s, spoke of female classmates approaching him in high school hallways just to tell him how much they despised the author.

“People decided that they'd project on to me whatever they liked or didn't like about Ernest Hemingway and were surprised that wasn't a great experience for me,” said Brendan Hemingway, now 65. “And the big thing for me at 100 (years of “The Sun Also Rises”) is for my daughter's generation that's all gone. We've outlasted the baggage. We've outrun the backlash. For my daughter's generation, you read him or you don't."

Justice and other Hemingway scholars say they generally encounter little resistance these days. Verna Kale, an associate research professor at Penn State, says she recently asked a group of students if they had ever read Hemingway and was told that none of them had. Ross K. Tangedal, an associate professor of English at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point and a member of the Hemingway Letters Project editorial team, said his students usually were “exposed to his work in small doses in high school.”
“So when they come to my college classroom they encounter the work before the myth,” he added.

Hemingway's 1926 novel follows British and American expatriates adrift in Europe, sustaining themselves on sex, alcohol, boxing and bullfights. It was a foundational text for the so-called “Lost Generation” of the post World War I era, and for many aspiring writers after. McInerney, 71, told the audience gathered at the Poetry Center that he first read “The Sun Also Rises” while in college and remembered how the novel “blew me away.”

“I couldn't believe how fresh it was and how it seemed really cool, to me” he said. "When the book was published, it essentially revolutionized English prose. It was a really radical new voice that somehow still spoke directly to me."

“The Sun Also Rises” is still popular, although its numbers fall well short of the book's famous contemporary, F. Scott Fitzgerald's “The Great Gatsby.” According to Circana, which tracks around 85% of the print market, “The Sun Also Rises” has sold just under 40,000 copies this year so far, down from a peak of more than 60,000 for each of several years in the 2010s. Over the past 20 years, sales in the U.S. have topped 1 million copies ("Gatsby" sales over the same time period approached 8 million).

Debra Moddelmog, who serves on the editorial board of The Hemingway Review, acknowledges that many readers familiar with Hemingway's image regard the women in his books as stereotyped and marginalized. But she thinks of Hemingway as a “deceptive” writer whose famously terse prose holds unexpected dimensions. She cites the libertine Lady Brett Ashley of “The Sun Also Rises" as someone whom close reading reveals to be a “complex character rather than the typical femme fatale.”

Justice notes that women hold many of the leading roles in Hemingway scholarship, including Moddelmog; Sandra Spanier, general editor of the Hemingway Letters Project; and Suzanne del Gizzo, editor of The Hemingway Review.

Kale, an associate editor for the Hemingway letters project and the editor of a Norton Library edition of “The Sun Also Rises,” is a self-identified Gen-Xer who started out as a student of medieval literature. She changed her focus after experiencing a Hemingway-esque epiphany as she read “The Sun Also Rises” — on a night train to Spain during a trip to Europe.

“I was just the right age to read it, and I became very interested in the expatriate modernists,” she said. “I’ve never had any misgivings about studying Hemingway whatsoever. I find his writing captivating, and documenting his life through his letters has become my life’s work.”

title: Johnny Depp film ‘Ebenezer’ gets actor first No. 1 opening in 8 years
summary: Depp is back atop the box office with his first studio movie in eight years.
story: Depp is back atop the box office with his first studio movie in eight years.

Johnny Depp is back at the top of the box office with his first studio movie in eight years, and since fallout from a contentious libel trial against ex-wife Amber Heard left his future in Hollywood in jeopardy.

But six years after he was asked to leave the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise, and three years after Depp said that he had “no further need for Hollywood,” “Ebenezer,” a Paramount Pictures release, opened in first place with about $19 million in ticket sales, according to studio estimates on Sunday. Paramount released it in 3,535 theaters.

While it might be a far cry from the heights of the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, which twice opened over $100 million, or even the $62 million opening of “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald” in 2018, it is a solid start for the film, which cost a reported $38 million to produce. Internationally, it made $23 million from 63 markets, adding up to a $42 million global debut.
Outside of his franchise fare, Depp more often had openings in the $20 million range (as with “Black Mass” and “Public Enemies”).

The audience for “Ebenezer” was about 52% female and 81% over the age of 25, according to PostTrak exit polls. About 65% of ticket buyers said they would “definitely” recommend the film to friends. Less than half, or 47%, of the “kid” demographic (ages 12 and under) said they would tell their friends they “must see it right away.”

The Charles Dickens-inspired tale is rated PG-13 and directed by Ti West, who is best known for the horror franchise X. Critics were not as warm as audiences about the film. It’s currently sitting at 52% on Rotten Tomatoes. Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley also star.

The question still remains as to whether this marks a major comeback for Depp, but time might tell. In exit polls, 51% of moviegoers cited Depp as their reason for attending the film. Depp's next film, a revenge thriller called “Day Drinker,” is set for a March release from Lionsgate.

“The personal lives of stars generally don’t impact the box office. It really comes down to the movie,” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “The key now will be its long-term playability.”

Sony's “Ghost Soldier” and Amazon MGM Studios’ “How to Rob a Bank” also opened this weekend to less fanfare. “Ghost Soldier,” an action film starring Jim Caviezel, debuted in sixth place with $5.2 million from 2,558 theaters. “How to Rob a Bank” landed in seventh place with just under $5.2 million from 2,810 theaters. Internationally, it made $5.1 million. The film from “The Fall Guy” director David Leitch had a reported net production budget of $40 million. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, “How to Rob a Bank” did not receive good reviews.

“The Cat in the Hat” landed in second place in its second weekend in theaters with $11.4 million, followed by “Godzilla Minus Zero” in third place with $8.3 million (down a whopping 73% from its opening). Fourth place went to “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” also in its second weekend, with $5.5 million. And the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” rounded out the top five with just under $5.5 million, bringing its domestic total to $89 million.
“The ‘You Can See Everything’ phenomenon continues,” Dergarabedian said. "It has become the ‘have you seen’ movie of the moment."

“Wild Horse Nine” also added 1,075 theaters in its second weekend, where it earned $4.6 million. Jordan Firstman's “Club Kid” had one of the best limited expansions of the year with $756,060 on 27 screens. And James Gray's acclaimed crime thriller “Paper Tiger” opened in six locations in New York and Los Angeles to $215,009 before it expands nationwide next week.

Overall it was a slower weekend than last with around $86 million in total ticket sales from North American theaters. Business should pick up next weekend, however, with the release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Ebenezer,” $19 million.
2. “The Cat in the Hat,” $11.4 million.
3. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” $8.3 million.
4. “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” $5.5 million.
5. “You Can See Everything,” $5.5 million.
6. “Ghost Soldier,” $5.2 million.
7. “How to Rob a Bank,” $5.2 million.
8. “Wild Horse Nine,” $4.6 million.
9. “Wildwood,” $4.5 million.
10. “Clayface,” $3.7 million.

title: After 8 nominations without a win, Glenn Close is 'overwhelmed' by honorary Oscar
summary: Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards
story: Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards
When Glenn Close got the call that she’d been chosen to receive an honorary Oscar, the 79-year-old actor had two somewhat unconventional thoughts.
“My first reaction was I don’t need a consolation prize,” Close told The Associated Press in a recent interview. “And my second reaction was, I don’t know … do I want to end my loss record?”

Close does indeed have an Oscars record going: Over the course of her career, she’s been nominated for acting prizes eight times and never won. It’s a distinction she has worn with grace and humor over the years, and she’s in good company: Peter O’Toole was similarly nominated eight times without a win.

The honorary Oscar, also known as the Academy Honorary Award, is indeed different from a competitive Oscar. Although the golden statuettes are the same, the award is not given for a specific film, but for a body of work and contributions to the motion picture industry. The voters, or rather selection committee, is also much smaller: The film academy’s Board of Governors as opposed to the entire Academy membership. There are no “losers.” And, since 2009, the prizes have been presented not during the Academy Awards but in a separate event in Los Angeles known as the Governors Awards.

Perhaps most importantly, however, with no broadcast television cameras, the Governors Awards have the luxury of time, for touching montages and thoughtful speeches by friends and collaborators, and the honorees themselves. There is space to reflect without the pressure of a ticking clock, or an orchestra ready to play you off.

“I’m still processing it and it means it means a lot, you know, at this point in my life,” Close said. “I’ve been a working actor for over 50 years, I got my first Oscar nomination 43 years ago. So it’s been a life, you know? And it’s overwhelming.”

The occasion has Close thinking about her own history with the Oscars, and how much things have changed over the years. Her first nomination came for her first film role, in George Roy Hill’s “The World According to Garp.” She remembers receiving the news while shooting “The Big Chill,” where her performance as Sarah Cooper, the woman hosting the gathering after the death of their friend, would earn her a second nomination.
“It was the furthest thing from my mind,” Close said. “I never even thought about the possibility of being nominated for an Oscar. I still can remember my absolute astonishment.”

The thing that she remembers most about that first ceremony, held at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in 1983, was what she wore: “The most beautiful little velvet dress,” she said, designed by her friend, costumer Ann Roth.

Some of her memories are about what other people wore, like the one time she sat behind Madonna and marveled at her “fabulous” white fur. Then there was the year she was nominated for “Fatal Attraction,” when there was a whole section of the crowd outside that had styled their hair in tight curls like her character, Alex Forrest.
“That was fabulous,” she said.

What was a little confusing, however, was when she walked out to present an award with her co-star Michael Douglas and the audience laughed. She was eight months pregnant at the time and had to fly to Los Angeles on a private plane, with her OB-GYN as chaperone, because she wasn’t allowed to fly commercial.

“At first, I thought, why are they laughing?” Close said. “And we realized it was because in the movie, I say I’m pregnant with this child and he doesn’t want to have anything to do with it, denies it, and there was always a question whether she really was telling the truth or not. And there I was, hugely pregnant, walking out with Michael. So it was very funny.”

Douglas recently made headlines for saying on The Graham Norton Show that Close deserved to win that year. When asked if she was surprised that he’d said that, Close paused and said: “Publicly, yeah.”
While the phrase “it’s an honor to be nominated” has become a bit of a cliché, it’s also a kind of mantra for Close, who has never done a role thinking that it would lead to awards.

“I have the DNA of an outsider,” Close said. “So because of that, I’ve always felt the greatest honor was to actually be in the room … the winner loser thing — especially in the temperature of our country now — for me, does not apply. The fact that you are in the room with some of the most creative people on the planet is what counts.”

She hasn’t decided where she might put her statuette in her home, but she is already thinking about how she can share it with the people of Bozeman, Montana. Close has been grateful to be able to continue working as much as she does (just this year she’s appeared in the Spanish language epic and presumed Oscar nominee“La Bola Negra,” the latest season of “All's Fair” and a new Hunger Games movie ). But her ability to leave, to go home to a place away from Hollywood, is the thing that allows her to recharge between performances.

“In some ways, I want to share it with the community here,” she said. She wants to find a place where, “for a day, people can go and see what a real Oscar looks like.” And she has an idea for where: A “fantastic bakery called the Wild Crumb.” But, she added, she hasn’t talked to them about it yet.
At the Governors Awards on Sunday, Close will be accompanied by her daughter and son-in-law, and wearing a custom Armani gown, which she’s very excited about.

The honorary Oscar doesn’t negate Close’s competitive Oscars record either. O’Toole also received one, in 2003, after all. Now, she’s just feeling grateful and putting the finishing touches on her speech.
“It’s incredibly special and it’s a huge honor,” Close said. “I don’t know how I’m going to get through it because it’s very emotional for me. But I will somehow.”

title: At Sing Sing prison, incarcerated men get preview of new PBS documentary on nation's justice system
summary: Incarcerated men at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility have previewed a new docuseries on the history of the nation's criminal justice system
story: Incarcerated men at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility have previewed a new docuseries on the history of the nation's criminal justice system

OSSINING, New York -- As the lights dimmed inside the chapel at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility in New York, around 30 incarcerated men sat scattered across the pews, waiting to preview a new docuseries on the history of the nation’s criminal justice system.
Our Lady of Hope chapel was soon abuzz with discussion, as some learned new things about an American institution with which they already have a great deal of personal experience.

The four-part series, “Crime and Punishment in America,” is set to premiere Monday on PBS. It spends eight hours tracing how the justice system evolved, from the colonial period to present day, and viewers get to hear from legal scholars, formerly incarcerated people, victims’ families and corrections officers.

The U.S. maintains the world's largest incarcerated population, with nearly two million people behind bars in prisons and jails. In 2024, each state incarcerated more people per capita than most countries, according to the Prison Policy Initiative.

“What are we hoping to accomplish with this?” film director Lynn Novick said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Digging into the history and revealing it will help us to have a different conversation about what justice means in this country.”

Novick developed the series with frequent collaborator Ken Burns, an acclaimed filmmaker with numerous PBS documentaries to his name. In 2019, the two partnered on “College Behind Bars,” which followed a Bard College program to provide a liberal arts education to incarcerated people.

Sing Sing was Novick’s sixth screening for prison populations in correctional facilities: Maine, Connecticut, California and Washington state prisons, as well as New York City’s Rikers’ jail, have hosted previews of “Crime and Punishment in America.”
Sing Sing prisoners were shown a 47-minute reel from the full series.

“I hope that as people see this documentary, that they are challenged to think about what we have to do differently,” said Michael Shane Hale, 54 and from Kentucky, who has served 32 years of a 50-to-life prison sentence.

Hale said the viewing public should no longer question whether it's possible for prisoners to turn their lives around. The question, he added, should instead be “what do we do with transformed people?”

The conversation at Sing Sing was more animated than Novick had anticipated. Some of the prisoners gathered in the chapel were invigorated by news of California Gov. Gavin Newsom saying he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.

Several prisoners inundated a panel of speakers with concerns about what rehabilitation through incarceration looks like for their families and for victims. Others drew connections between their crimes, mental illness and economic circumstances.

“Nobody is the sum of their worst mistake, right?” said José Colon, 44 and from the Bronx, who entered prison at age 17 and has been incarcerated for nearly 28 years. “No matter where you are in life, there’s always room for growth.”
John Rizzo, another Sing Sing prisoner, asked the panel what “rehabilitation” means to society.
“When we come in here, we’re tainted,” Rizzo said later in an interview with the AP. “When we go back out into society, when is the incarcerated individual going to be acceptable again?”

Rizzo has served 16 years so far on a conviction for conspiracy and attempted murder. He said he spends his time helping peers apply for prison jobs and studying for a bachelor’s degree in behavioral science that he intends to earn while incarcerated.

Reginald Dwayne Betts, a panelist and poet who served eight years for a carjacking at 16, agreed with Rizzo. He said people seemed to focus on his past when he returned to life after prison. “It was always, ‘Can you tell me more about your crime?’” he said.
Betts has created a documentary following his life and became known for his work installing libraries in the nation’s prisons.

Daniel F. Martuscello III, the first former correction officer appointed commissioner of the New York State Department of Correction, said he agreed to screen Novick's film because he sees it as an extension of the prison’s Rehabilitation Through the Arts workshops.

“It’s our obligation, not only as commissioners, but as people running the system, lawmakers, to make sure that we’re telling that story,” Martuscello said. “Because to not do so, it takes away from that transformation, and really, it degrades public safety.”

John J. Lennon is an incarcerated Sing Sing prison journalist and a recipient of a 2026 Guggenheim Fellowship, a prestigious and competitive grant to support scholars, artists and scientists for work “under the freest possible conditions.” In-prison programs, he says, are what allowed him to build a writing career after entering prison with a ninth-grade education.
He said New York, and the nation as a whole, has much more reform work to do.
“If you want accountability in America, then there has to be forgiveness on the table,” Lennon said. “There has to be mercy on the table.”

title: US visa restrictions force some African contestants out of Miss Universe competition
summary: Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico due to visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration
story: Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico due to visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration

HARARE, Zimbabwe -- Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico because of visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration, while two others are struggling to obtain visas.

Representatives from Zambia and the Republic of Congo have withdrawn from the pageant, which takes place this month in the U.S. territory, after failing to secure visas. Contestants from South Sudan and Zimbabwe are still awaiting theirs.
The United States has imposed sweeping travel restrictions affecting dozens of countries, many of them in Africa, under proclamations issued during Trump’s second administration.

Last December, the administration expanded restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while maintaining a full suspension of entry for nationals of the Republic of Congo and South Sudan.

“She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves,” Miss Universe Zambia organizers said in a statement this week announcing the withdrawal of their representative, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka.

In the Republic of Congo, Georgina Kambongo made history when she was crowned the Central African country’s first Miss Universe representative. National organizers say her inability to travel to Puerto Rico is linked solely to Trump’s travel restrictions.

“American visa challenges have delayed that journey, but the fight is not over,” Zimbabwe’s representative, Roseanna Hall, said in a social media post. “After months of preparation, I am not giving up. I remain confident that God who began a good work in me will bring it to completion.”
In South Sudan, organizers said contestant Adut Deng’s participation remained uncertain despite months of efforts to secure the necessary travel documents and approvals.
“South Sudan deserves to be seen, heard, and represented. Our queen carries the hopes, dreams, beauty, and resilience of a nation,” organizers said in a statement.
The competition’s 75th edition is expected to attract up to 120 contestants. Delegates began arriving in Puerto Rico on Sunday for rehearsals and other preliminary activities.
A national costume competition is scheduled for Nov. 21, followed by swimsuit and evening gown segments the following day. The winner will be crowned on Nov. 24.

title: Glenn Close marvels at honorary Oscar as Ridley Scott and indie producers also get statuettes
summary: Glenn Close has finally received her first Oscar, an honorary award at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles
story: Glenn Close has finally received her first Oscar, an honorary award at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles

LOS ANGELES -- LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close paused and leaned back before accepting her first Oscar statuette from her old friend John Malkovich, as if she wanted to prolong the moment. When she took it, she gazed down at it as if it were her child. The award may have been honorary, but it was clear that to her, it was no empty gesture.

Close, 79, whose eight Oscar nominations without a win tie her for the record, received the career achievement Oscar at the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Governors Awards in Los Angeles on Sunday night. She was honored alongside director Ridley Scott, Disney animator Floyd Norman and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler.

“To be in this room tonight embraced by the people who have consistently inspired me, whose work has sustained and challenged me and only made me want to be better is the greatest honor of all,” Close said, on the verge of tears.

Close was nominated for her very first film, “The World According to Garp,” in 1983. She was nominated the following year for “The Big Chill” and the year after that for “The Natural.” In 1988 came a nomination for her best-known role, in “Fatal Attraction,” and in 1989 she was nominated for “Dangerous Liaisons.” Three more losses came in the ensuing decades.
Malkovich, her “Dangerous Liaisons” co-star, presented her with the honor. He said to him, the mark of a great actor was how well they died on screen.

“Glenn has had some of the most marvelous character deaths ever captured,” he said, getting a laugh from the crowd at the Ray Dolby Ballroom, in the same Hollywood complex where the main Oscars ceremony is held.

“Throughout her illustrious 50-year career, she’s been decapitated, stung by scorpions, devoured by hungry, infected children. She died in several car crashes, was strangled, shot at a feminist rally, shot again, emerging from the bathtub in that iconic climax of ‘Fatal Attraction.’”
But, Malkovich said, she was just as compelling in banal moments.
“She simply does the dishes in the ‘Big Chill’ and it’s interesting,” he said.

Matt Damon gave the presentation on Scott, who did not attend. The 88-year-old director of “Alien,” “Blade Runner” and “Gladiator” whose epic decades of work have blended popular success and prestige like few others, has also never won despite four nominations, including best director nods for “Thelma & Louise” and “Black Hawk Down.”
Damon starred in Scott's 2015 film “The Martian” and was alone with the director and the crew for most of the shoot. He said working with Scott was “like getting shot out of a cannon.”
“There is nothing like the feeling of everyone rowing in the same direction when you’ve got a master at the helm,” Damon said.
Scott accepted via recorded video. He paid tribute to his brother Tony Scott, director of films including “Top Gun,” “True Romance” and “Man on Fire,” who died in 2012.
“I'm flattered and proud to receive this award, and I also accept it for Tony,” Scott said. “His great work would certainly have earned him this recognition.”

The Governors Awards — the name refers to the Academy's Board of Governors — often go to artists with extraordinary careers but no competitive Oscar. Some win the honorary version then go on to win a competitive Oscar soon after, as both Henry Fonda and Paul Newman did in the 1980s.
The event is especially star-studded, as it serves as the unofficial kickoff to Hollywood’s awards campaign.
Oscar hopefuls in attendance included Zendaya, Tom Holland, Timothée Chalamet, Pedro Pascal, Julianne Moore, Olivia Wilde, Christopher Nolan, Andrew Garfield and Andrew Scott.
Malkovich (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Damon (“The Odyssey”) are also among the hopefuls, and could be competing for a best actor Oscar soon.
Vachon and Koffler received the Academy's Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award for creative producers.
They are the first female producing team and the first independent producers to receive it, and said in their acceptance speeches that they were also the first dyed-in-the-wool New Yorkers to get it.
The duo founded the New York-based indie production hub Killer Films in 1995, specializing in queer cinema and other films told from outsider perspectives that weren't getting made.

“An ethos emerged in those early years and it has guided the company from day one,” Koffler said. “To champion voices we believe in, stories we love, with a pragmatism that enables them to actually exist.”
They marveled at getting an award whose previous winners have been the very definition of the Hollywood establishment, including David O. Selznick, Walt Disney, Samuel Goldwyn and Cecil B. DeMille.
Midway through their acceptance speeches, Vachon said, “I've just noticed that we're both like, clutching these things. They're not going to take them away.”

Koffler and Vachon have produced over 100 films, and some television too, with their company Killer Films: “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” “One Hour Photo,” “Velvet Goldmine,” “Far from Heaven,” “I’m Not There,” “Carol” and “Past Lives,” for which they received their first best picture nomination.

Norman, 91, began his 65-year career in 1956 when he became the first Black animator for Walt Disney Animation Studios, contributing to “Sleeping Beauty,” “Mary Poppins,” “101 Dalmatians” and “The Jungle Book.”
Mahershala Ali, who presented Norman with the award, said Norman had never even been eligible for one because of how Disney and the Oscars were structured.

Norman recalled his love of drawing and animation as a child growing up in Santa Barbara, California, and his desire to work for Disney, a dream that culminated in getting to working directly with the man himself on “The Jungle Book.”
He thanked his wife and five kids, all in attendance, and said he had led a life remarkably free of drama or strife.
“On occasion, even movies have happy endings,” he said, and held up his Oscar. “Here’s my happy ending.”

title: With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot?
summary: Now that measles is back in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia, some are asking if adults need a booster shot
story: Now that measles is back in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia, some are asking if adults need a booster shot
Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?
Generally, experts say, the answer is no.
“Most people are protected without getting a booster shot” because they’ve either been vaccinated or had measles as kids, said Dr. Richard Martinello at Yale School of Medicine.
The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress. Last year, Canada lost its measles-elimination designation.

Doctors say getting two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is the best way to protect against one of the most contagious viruses in the world. The vaccine usually protects people for life, as does having had the disease. Americans born before 1957 are considered to have “presumptive evidence” of immunity because almost everyone back then got measles during childhood.
But doctors say certain people should consider getting boosters.

One group is healthcare workers born before 1957 without proof of immunity. They’re more likely than the general public to come in contact with people who have measles, so they may get it or even spread it to vulnerable patients.

Adults vaccinated between 1963 and 1967 also might want to think about boosters. During those years, some children received an inactivated vaccine that uses a killed version of the virus, which was less effective than the current vaccine containing live, weakened virus. Doctors said people who know they got the inactivated vaccine or aren’t sure should get at least one dose of the live MMR vaccine. One dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, while two doses are 97% protective.

Until 1989, only a single dose was standard. Now the recommendation is for adults to have at least one documented dose of MMR. Two doses are recommended for certain people in high-risk groups who don’t have other evidence of immunity.

“People who have had no shots should go get vaccinated, if they weren't born before 1957,” said Dr. Joshua Sharfstein at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “If they have had only one shot, they may want to consider whether they’re in a risk group for a second shot.”

That risk group, he said, includes people in school, healthcare workers, international travelers or people living with family members who have compromised immune systems. In places with active measles outbreaks, health officials sometimes recommend that everyone have two shots, Sharfstein said.
For people who have only had one shot, especially in an area where measles is circulating, “it’s always a good idea to talk with your physician about whether another shot is needed,” Martinello said.
But what if you don’t know how many shots you received or even if you’ve been vaccinated?

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests asking your parents or doctor, checking with your high school or college health services or reaching out to previous employers that required immunizations. You can also try contacting your state’s health department; some states have registries that include adult vaccines.

If you’re still unsure about your vaccination status, you can talk with your doctor about an MMR immunity blood test that can show whether you have antibodies against measles. But Martinello said this isn't an ideal measure of how safe you are from the virus. Though the test is accurate, he said, scientists don’t know how to link the result perfectly with the level of protection someone might have.
Regardless, doctors said getting a booster just to be safe won’t harm you unless you’re in a group that is not supposed to get the vaccine at all, such as pregnant women.
Now that measles is circulating in the U.S., doctors said it’s crucial to take measures to protect yourself.

“This is a moment to not just check for yourself, but also encourage others to make sure that they are adequately vaccinated,” Sharfstein said. “Too many people took measles for granted … or just didn’t think about measles. But now it’s something to think about.”

title: Palestinians victims of a third of violations against children worldwide, Save the Children says
summary: Save the Children warns that children in the Gaza Strip face severe dangers after three years of war
story: Save the Children warns that children in the Gaza Strip face severe dangers after three years of war

AMMAN, Jordan -- The children of the Gaza Strip face unmatched dangers after three years of war, a prominent non-governmental organization warned Thursday, as they suffer from repeated displacement, loss of family members, lack of healthcare and education, and abysmal living conditions.

Save the Children said almost one third of the tens of thousands of attacks and violations against children recorded worldwide last year took place in the Palestinian territories. The danger was especially high in Gaza, the tiny enclave with a population of 2 million where at least 20,000 children have been killed, according to local health authorities.
The psychological and physical impact on Palestinian children in Gaza will “live for many years to come,” Save the Children Regional Director Ahmad Alhendawi told The Associated Press.

In its annual global report, Save the Children said that one in four children, some 589 million, lived in conflict zones in 2025, the highest number documented since the end of the Cold War in 1990. The vast majority are in the Middle East and Africa.
The number is expected to increase this year with the ongoing war in Iran and the wider Mideast, and renewed war in Lebanon and Yemen in 2026.

Save the Children reported nearly 12,500 cases of violations against children in the Palestinian territories, mostly attacks on hospitals and schools and deprivation of aid. It said the situation was especially critical in Gaza, where Israel continues strikes despite an October 2025 ceasefire agreement with Hamas.
Although the latest report focused on 2025 figures, Alhendawi said conditions have shown little improvement this year.

“Lots of children who have survived themselves are injured themselves and are without surviving parents,” said Alhendawi. “This report is showing very clearly that what happened and what continues to happen in Gaza are violations at a scale that we haven’t seen and needs to be prioritized by the international community.”

Israel launched its war in Gaza in response to Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. It says its ongoing strikes, including one on a hospital in the southern town of Khan Younis last week, target militants and are responses to Hamas violations of the ceasefire agreement.

While Israel has killed most of Hamas’ senior leadership, the conflict has devastated the territory and taken a heavy toll on Gaza’s civilians. The vast majority of people live in crowded tent camps or in the ruins of their former homes, with little access to food, water, or electricity.

“The children of Gaza are deprived of the bare minimum in life,” said displaced Palestinian Riad Abou Shamel, 65, surrounded by children playing in an open lot in Khan Younis filled with rubble and remains of pancaked buildings hit in airstrikes.
“They go to the market and can barely bring back half a cucumber or half an apple.”
Israel's military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

The report shed light on the surge of cases of abductions, sexual violence, and recruitment of children by armed forces in Africa, in conflict areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nigeria, Sudan, and Somalia, and attacks on hospitals in Ukraine.
The data and figures in Save the Children's report of violations against children and children living in conflict zones come from the United Nations and the Peace Research Institute Oslo.
Chehayeb contributed from Beirut. Associated Press Senior Producer Wafaa Shurafa contributed to this report from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

title: British women to receive automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
summary: The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnancies
story: The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnancies
LONDON -- British women convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will be automatically pardoned Monday, the government said.
The action follows Parliament's passage last year of a landmark vote to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section from the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons and some will be issued posthumously.

“For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police had investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once “dragged from hospital beds to police cells” and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

“This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they’ve always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.
The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy. An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for “compassion, not punishment.”

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious thing with intent to procure a miscarriage. Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant more than 10 weeks.

title: Doctors are raising concerns about US babies born with measles
summary: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles
story: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles
For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.
Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns.

From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday.
“This is a brand new phenomenon,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy.

The condition's emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus’s spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it's had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases.

“We’re now seeing levels of measles that we haven’t seen in 30 years,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' infectious diseases committee. “When you have measles under control,” congenital measles doesn't happen.

The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn't get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community “are important to prevent measles and related complications.” CDC scientists authored the alert.

Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania's health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation.

People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles.

“What’s happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back,” Osterholm said. “Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles.”

Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth.

MMR can’t be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications.

If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there’s a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says.

Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal.

Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. “That's something that sadly we're learning more about,” he said.

Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots.

This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas.

“We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that’s gonna take some doing,” Ratner said. “It’s going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it’s an important thing for us to do.”
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York.

title: Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV says his recent lung cancer surgery hasn't changed his agenda or outlook
story: Pope Leo XIV says his recent lung cancer surgery hasn't changed his agenda or outlook

ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE -- ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE (AP) — Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church.

Leo seemed full of health, energy and jokes during an airborne news conference on Monday while returning to Rome from Peru. The grueling, 12-day trip through three South American countries left several members of the travelling Vatican delegation and press corps sick.
“I’m not 100% but I’m pretty good,” Leo said of his surgical recovery. “Endurance is one of the gifts the Lord gave me.”
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 because of a cancerous tumor. He said it was discovered by chance during an annual checkup and appeared at first as a shadow on his lung.

“The first news was a surprise. There were no symptoms. I felt fine,” he said. Once the cancer was confirmed, he decided to proceed immediately to have it removed, and said he hoped his experience would help others not fear having checkups or pursue preventive care.
Prior to going into surgery, Leo said he saw no need to make provisions for the leadership of the Catholic Church if he were left medically impaired and unable to govern.

He said he hadn’t written any instructions, as his predecessors had done, outlining the criteria under which he would resign, which some legal experts believe is necessary if a pope were to end up in an irreversible coma and unable to articulate his resignation.

“Eventually I will do it, I think, but I don’t see the need now,” Leo said, adding that he never doubted he would be in good enough shape afterward to make the South America trip. He credited good doctors, prayer and what he described as a strong sense of determination to recover.

Leo also showed himself in no hurry to appoint new cardinals who will eventually elect his successor, another sign that he is planning to be around for a while. “I will eventually get around to that,” he said.

The pontiff also seemed in no hurry to get things done, saying he still doesn’t know what trips he’ll be taking next year — aside from his previously confirmed trip to South Korea to attend World Youth Day in August.

Leo made it very clear that his No. 1 priority was “unity” and healing in the church, a reference to the polarization that has always existed but in some ways deepened during Pope Francis’ sometimes turbulent pontificate.

Leo was asked, for example, whether he would consider ordaining married men to ease the priest shortage in the Amazon, where remote Indigenous communities can go months or longer without a priest to celebrate the sacraments. Amazonian bishops had asked Francis to allow for such a change but he declined.
Leo said he had no plans to go down that path, either, saying the issue was too divisive.

While ordaining married men is one solution to the priest shortage, Leo said “it’s a solution which in certain areas of the church can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance.”
“One of my priorities is first to promote unity and communion among us as members in the church,” he said.
“It may be in the future that some things will change. However for right now, for what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together,” he added.

He similarly said he had no plans to change one of Francis’ most divisive decisions restricting the celebration of the old Latin Mass. Traditionalist Catholics had hoped Leo would be more sympathetic to their cause and would reverse Francis’ crackdown.
But Leo said Francis’ decision already allowed for exceptions and that his decision stands.
Where Leo did hint at some change was on the thorny issue of clergy abuse.
He met with abuse survivors in Argentina and in Peru, and said he recognized that the issue of “spiritual abuse” was a problem in the church that needed to be addressed.

For over two years, a Vatican working group has been studying “spiritual abuse,” given the increasing number of cases of people — often adult women — who accuse priests of using their spiritual authority to psychologically, physically or sexually abuse them.

While the Catholic Church has laws punishing priests who sexually abuse minors, priests who use their spiritual authority to take advantage of people under their care rarely are sanctioned since there are no explicit laws criminalizing the practice.
Leo, a canon lawyer, said he was aware of the loophole in the church’s canon law.

“Spiritual abuse is a very serious topic in the church,” and needs to be addressed canonically, Leo said. “In order to exercise justice, you have to have a codification or a juridical expression of how to apply that, and that’s a very vague concept still,” he said.
At the same time, he conceded that “we all probably could describe either specific cases or kinds of instances where that has happened.”

One recent case of alleged spiritual abuse is expected to land soon on Leo’s desk. A Vatican-appointed tribunal is deciding the fate of the Rev. Marko Rupnik, a once-famous Jesuit mosaic artist accused by two dozen women of spiritual, psychological and sexual abuse.

The women began complaining about his behavior in the 1990s, but nothing was ever done until the victims went public, amid suspicions he was protected by his Jesuit superiors, up to and including Francis.

title: Huge crowds, low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as pope visits South America
summary: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
story: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles.
Cases are already surging in the region this year and mass gatherings provide an opportunity for one of the world's most contagious viruses to spread further.

The Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, and officials in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru have been preparing for potential problems to different degrees for months, including mounting vaccination campaigns and increasing surveillance to try to limit spread.

Uruguay, where thousands of people attended a prayer vigil and a Mass celebrated by Leo, implemented a nationwide intensified surveillance monitoring period until Nov. 29, three weeks after Leo’s departure from the country, according to Nataly Rodriguez, director of epidemiology at Uruguay’s health ministry. Uruguay has also taken steps to boost its vaccination rate to among the highest in the region.
“As a preventive strategy, the ministry has been emphasizing the importance of keeping vaccination schedules up to date,” Rodriguez said.

The Nov. 6-17 trip to the continent where around 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics live marks a return home for Leo, who spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop.

Ahead of the visit, PAHO assessed the public health risk of measles in the context of the religious mass gatherings in South America as “very high.” That's in part because there has been a nearly five-fold increase in cases between January and October compared with the same period last year.
“We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized,” said Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO. “It’s a very complex situation.”

Measles spreads easily through the air when an infected person breathes, sneezes or coughs. A person can be contagious even before they show symptoms. The virus first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes and a rash. It most commonly affects children and while it usually isn’t fatal, it can be.

The vaccine for measles is extremely effective, but the first of two doses is not usually recommended for babies until their first birthday. In order to stop the disease from spreading in a community, to protect infants and others who can't get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated with two doses.

As of 2025, only Uruguay had achieved that number, according to data from the World Health Organization. Peru has reached 90% with one dose and 82% with two doses while Argentina has reached only 84% with one dose and 55% with both doses.

PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and the end of October, nearly five times the number recorded during the same period in 2025. At least 81 people have died so far this year due to the disease.
With nearly 3,000 cases, Peru has seen the fourth highest number of cases in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.
In the five Peruvian cities Leo will be visiting including Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa, a total of 170 measles cases have been identified so far in 2026.

Ahead of the Pope’s visit, Salas Peraza said PAHO had supported efforts to encourage vaccination in Peru, including initiatives targeting adolescents, deploying equipment to strengthen vaccine storage and delivery capacity, and intensifying vaccination along the border with Brazil.

In late October, authorities carried out measles vaccination campaigns in areas with the highest rates of transmission. These included a dose for babies aged six to eleven months, as well as vaccination for people up to 29 years old.
By the end of September, 1.2 million vaccine doses had been administered since April in Peru, with more than two million additional doses available.
Still, with vaccination rates so far below the threshold needed for community protection in parts of the region, experts say conditions are ripe for further spread.

In Argentina, authorities issued a warning in late October about the high risk associated with the pope’s visit, after estimating that they expected up to 4 million people in the province of Buenos Aires.

But Argentina President Javier Milei has slashed Argentina’s healthcare budget, eviscerating agencies tasked with planning, financing and tracking immunization campaigns. The cuts coincided with a measles outbreak that in April 2025 led to Argentina’s first measles death in two decades and some are concerned that efforts are falling short.

Marcela Lopez Yunes, a doctor and pediatric infectious disease specialist, said she hadn’t seen what she considered sufficient public communication to encourage vaccination. “We need to do a little more to give diseases such as measles the attention and importance they deserve,” she said.

A spokesperson for Argentina's health ministry said that while the federal government is in charge of purchasing and distributing vaccines, provinces are in charge of administering them to their populations. They also said that there is an ongoing public service announcement speaking to the importance of vaccination in general.
Leo took aim at Milei’s austerity measures as he arrived in Argentina Sunday, insisting that political leaders must put people, not the economy, first.
Associated Press journalists Ramiro Barreiro in Montevideo, Uruguay, and Franklin Briceño in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.

title: US, Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here's what to know
summary: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
story: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
NEW YORK -- International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories — the elimination of measles.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past two years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths.

Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico — that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations' borders.
“It’s a big deal. The decision represents us moving backwards,” said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments.
Here's a look at the meeting's deliberations and why it's important.

In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for one year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024.
“It’s solely based on genetics,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have “eliminated” measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998.

The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said.
A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said this week.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks,” she said in the statement.

But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation's health agencies.

Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule, reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and lauded Trump’s executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups’ recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say.

Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak.

But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine — which is credited with saving millions of lives globally — is possibly “quite lethal.” Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities.

Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah and South Carolina. And the more than 5,100 confirmed cases this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year — more than any year in more than three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed — in 1963, in the U.S. — and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016.

Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected.
As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old.

The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan lost their status.
Associated Press writer Megan Janetsky contributed to this story from Mexico City.
