title: Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living
summary: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head
story: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head

WASHINGTON -- Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.

Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.

The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer’s, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn’t have Alzheimer’s but advanced CTE instead.
The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE.

Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn’t reliably identify early-stage CTE.

It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn’t involved with the research.

Abnormal tau is found in several brain diseases, many of which can overlap in older adults, adding to the difficulty in teasing apart its role in any one disease, including CTE. Sato, who studies such tauopathies, also stressed much more research is needed.
The findings were published late Friday by the medical journal JAMA and presented at a scientific meeting in Japan.

title: Bus crashes into fuel truck in Pakistan and at least 10 people are killed
summary: A bus has rammed into a fuel truck carrying liquefied petroleum gas in southwestern Pakistan, igniting a fire that killed at least 10 people and left several injured
story: A bus has rammed into a fuel truck carrying liquefied petroleum gas in southwestern Pakistan, igniting a fire that killed at least 10 people and left several injured

QUETTA, Pakistan -- A bus rammed into a fuel truck carrying liquefied petroleum gas in southwestern Pakistan on Thursday, igniting a fire that killed at least 10 people and left several injured, police said.
The crash took place on the Makran coastal highway in Balochistan province, senior police officer Muhammad Aslam Bangulzai said.
The victims were taken to a nearby hospital, where some of the injured were listed in critical condition, he said, providing no further details. An investigation was underway.

Deadly traffic accidents are common in Pakistan due to poor road infrastructure and disregard for traffic laws. In August 2022, a passenger bus rammed into a fuel truck in eastern Pakistan, killing 20 people.

title: Mongolia's lawmakers accept president's resignation following corruption accusations
summary: Mongolia’s parliament has accepted President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa's resignation after he was accused of benefiting from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister
story: Mongolia’s parliament has accepted President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa's resignation after he was accused of benefiting from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister

ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- Mongolia’s parliament on Thursday approved the resignation of President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa after recent accusations by another politician in the ruling Mongolian People’s Party that he had benefited financially from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister.
The president's resignation highlights infighting underway between the factions of the ruling party and is seen as a political power play by experts.
The accusation came from Nyambaatar Khishgee, the former mayor of the country's capital, Ulaanbaatar, who is from a different faction of the party. He lives in self-imposed exile in Canada.
Khurelsukh's resignation took immediate effect after 96 out of 104 members of parliament — known as the State Great Khural — voted in favor of it.
According to Mongolian law, an election for his replacement must be held within four months, with the parliament speaker serving as interim president during this period.
Khurelsukh, who was in parliament on Thursday, had a warning for Nyambaatar.

“That individual who has flown away like a ‘bird’ must be brought back and made to answer before the law. I hear he is seeking asylum abroad," Khurelsukh said and accused Nyambaatar of taking bribes related to a different development project.
On Tuesday, Khurelsukh had announced he was resigning and said he would cooperate with any investigation, though he denied corruption allegations.
“I have never stolen from my people or my state,” he said. “I will hand over my duties as president and become an ordinary citizen.”
While Khurelsukh is formally not part of the party, he is still active in its politics and a powerful figure in the country, analysts have said.

Marissa Smith, who served as an elections monitor in Mongolia in 2024, said an early election could be an advantage for both the ruling party and Khurelsukh. His term was originally due to end in June 2027.
Khurelsukh's previous resignations had served to boost his political career, said Julian Dierkes, a Mongolia expert at the University of Mannheim in Germany.

Khurelsukh resigned in January 2021 when he served as prime minister so that he could run for president. He won six months later and his Mongolian People’s Party won a majority in the legislature at the same time.

“I see strong parallels to his resignation as prime minister in early 2021, ostensibly responding to protests the way he is claiming to be responding to corruption allegations, but then turning around merely months later to run for office," Dierkes said.
Associated Press writer Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Danish lawmakers approve a security deal with Greenland and the US, hoping to finally end tensions
summary: Denmark’s parliament has approved an agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic
story: Denmark’s parliament has approved an agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic

COPENHAGEN, Denmark -- Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought deal with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, a final step aimed to defuse months of tensions over the Trump administration's pressure about a possible U.S. takeover of the vast, mineral-rich island.

The trilateral deal — between U.S. President Donald Trump and Danish and Greenlandic leaders — paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark. It also eases tensions in the Atlantic alliance and with the European Union over Trump’s repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the U.S.

The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step: The deal enters into force once the parliaments of Denmark and Greenland have signed on, followed by formal notification of the United States in a diplomatic note.
Greenland’s parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.
“Today is a big day,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen wrote on Facebook. “It hasn’t been an easy process.”
She said the agreement respects Denmark's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the right of Greenlanders to self-determination.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen wrote on Facebook that Thursday's vote proved that Greenlanders can stand firm in their rights while also finding solutions through dialogue and cooperation.

“We have been through a difficult time, during which many people here at home have been concerned about our country and our future,” he said. “I hope that today’s decision will help bring greater calm and a sense of security.”
The U.S. ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the "strong support" in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal “paving the way for it to enter into force.”

"The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO," he wrote on X.
The aim is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the deal in September in New York, after months of quiet, behind-the-scenes negotiations to address his security concerns and Danish and Greenlandic fears of a possible U.S. takeover.

Under the deal, which builds on a defense agreement dating to 1951, the United States can expand its military presence on the island and “modernize and expand” its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest.

The U.S. can also set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east of Greenland, and can establish additional defense areas in the territory and strengthen its military operations or sites.

The three sides expressed support for a stronger NATO engagement in the Arctic, and for allowing the U.S. military access to Greenland to defend the NATO area — including through the " Golden Dome defense system.”

After repeated U.S. warnings about the threat in the region from geo-strategic rivals Russia and China, the agreement says only NATO members can establish manned or unmanned military installations on Greenland.

title: A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia's Kerch Bridge to Crimea
summary: Ukraine has launched a third aerial attack in four days on the Kerch Bridge, a crucial link between Russia and Crimea
story: Ukraine has launched a third aerial attack in four days on the Kerch Bridge, a crucial link between Russia and Crimea

KYIV, Ukraine -- A third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia and illegally annexed Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, a Russian official said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion.

Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it was to be restored starting from around 4 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Thursday, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.

The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.
The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside European leaders.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation and has been a prime target for Ukraine.
A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in this week's attack that was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy.
The latest attack used domestically produced Neptune missiles and damaged the train track, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
It added that Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies overland, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo,” it said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night.
Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations, according to the statement.
At least 10 people were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.

Russia’s bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv’s defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances.

Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine’s resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv’s domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries.
In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy.

Ukrainian officials fear their country’s fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments alarmed by Moscow’s aggression are trying to avoid being sidelined by Washington and Moscow.
The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in the midterm elections.

Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump administration’s stance and that of the American people.

Kushner and Witkoff have led efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough.

Kushner said Thursday on X that Washington’s priority at Thursday's meeting in Berlin is to “further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations.”

The meeting will also explore how Ukraine’s European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements. Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was due to welcome French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham as well as other leaders to the meeting.
Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: South Korea’s top court overturns charges against ex-PM for his role in martial law
summary: South Korea’s Supreme Court has overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for aiding in the declaration of martial law in December 2024
story: South Korea’s Supreme Court has overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for aiding in the declaration of martial law in December 2024

SEOUL, South Korea -- SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea’s Supreme Court on Thursday overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for aiding in the declaration of martial law in December 2024.
Han was convicted for aiding ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol in legitimizing the decree by securing its endorsement at a Cabinet meeting.
The court on Thursday ruled that prosecutors had not sufficiently proven the case.
Han’s case will now be sent back to the Seoul High Court, which sentenced him to 15 years in prison in May.
But the Supreme Court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon’s wife, Kim Keon Hee, on corruption charges including stock price manipulation and bribery.
Han and Kim, both currently imprisoned, did not attend the ruling.

title: Fire set at home of former Bangladesh interim leader as political tensions rise
summary: Authorities in Bangladesh say a fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appears to have been intentionally set
story: Authorities in Bangladesh say a fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appears to have been intentionally set

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- A late-night fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appeared to have been intentionally set, police said, as growing waves of violence and damage have followed a declaration by the ousted former prime minister that she plans to return.

The fire occurred before midnight Wednesday at the home of Muhammad Yunus, who served as interim leader of the country for 18 months following a mass uprising that led to the resignation of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was flown out of the country by the military on Aug. 5, 2024.

The fire in an abandoned, ground-floor room of Yunus' house in Chattogram was spotted by a police patrol that immediately doused the flames, Police Inspector Mozammel Haque told local media Thursday. Police are investigating and additional details were not immediately available.

The possible arson comes during ongoing political tensions following an announcement by Hasina that in December she will end her exile in India. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this month, Hasina said even death cannot prevent her from returning to Bangladesh.

Hasina has requested a passport and national identity card to facilitate her return, but the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman insists she will not receive the documents and must be handed over by India under an extradition treaty.

Police and BNP leaders blamed Hasina’s supporters for attempting to create anarchy ahead of her intended return. Explosions of crude bombs, arson and roadblocks have taken place in the capital Dhaka and other locations throughout Bangladesh in recent weeks.

Yunus governed until February when his interim administration handed over power to an elected government under Rahman. He was given the temporary leadership role following a student-led mass uprising that ended Hasina's 15-year rule.

Hasina was sentenced to death on charges of crimes against humanity involving the deaths of hundreds of protesters in the uprising. Her political party, the Bangladesh Awami League, was banned by the Yunus administration.
The Yunus administration and Rahman’s government requested her extradition from India, which did not respond to the requests.
Rahman on Wednesday urged “democratic forces” to remain united to prevent Hasina’s party from returning to Bangladesh politics.

Protests by Hasina's supporters and violence were reported in at least 22 districts nationwide in recent weeks. On Wednesday, at least two BNP supporters died in a clash with Hasina supporters in the southwestern district of Narail, police and media reports said.

Grameen Bank, a small-credit agency founded by Yunus that shared in the Nobel Prize award, also has come under attack. The bank said in a statement Tuesday that at least 22 branches were targeted by arson attacks and vandalism between Nov. 10 and Nov. 17.

At Hasina's ancestral home in Gopalganj district, protesters have regularly blocked highways leading to the country’s longest bridge connecting Dhaka with southwestern and southern regions. Protesters recently torched a police station and repeatedly clashed with security officials. Hundreds of paramilitary border forces remained deployed in the district to maintain order.
Police in Dhaka on Tuesday arrested former Mayor Mohammad Sayeed Khokon, a Hasina supporter, and on Wednesday arrested former Hasina Cabinet minister and ally Nurul Islam Nahid.
The country’s leading English-language newspaper, Daily Star, reported that the homes of former Hasina administration and party officials Dipu Moni and Sujit Roy Nandy were set on fire Wednesday.

title: Pakistan military says it killed 22 militants in raids on hideouts in northwest
summary: Pakistan's military says security forces have raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants
story: Pakistan's military says security forces have raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistani security forces acting on intelligence raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants, the military said Thursday.

It alleged that the militants killed were backed by neighboring India. There was no immediate comment from New Delhi, but Pakistan often accuses Afghanistan and India of supporting the Pakistani Taliban and other militant groups, allegations both countries deny.
The raids took place over the past 48 hours in the South Waziristan, Bannu and Tank districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the military said in a statement.
The military reported last week that security forces had killed 74 militants over several days in raids on hideouts in the northwest and in southwestern Balochistan province.
The military said troops were searching the areas for any remaining militants and pledged to continue operations against what it described as foreign-backed terrorism.

President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in separate statements praised the security forces for eliminating “Indian-supported” militants and vowed to continue the fight against militancy. Sharif said militants and their supporters would not be allowed to spread unrest in Pakistan and that the nation stood behind the forces fighting them.

Militant attacks targeting Pakistan’s police and security forces have surged in recent years. Authorities have blamed the Pakistani Taliban, who are known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan or TTP, and allied militant groups for most of the violence.

The Pakistani Taliban are a separate group from but allied with Afghanistan’s Taliban, who took power in Kabul in 2021. Many TTP leaders and fighters are believed to operate from sanctuaries across the Afghan border, straining relations between Islamabad and Kabul.

title: In a landmark judgment, top UN court says Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
summary: The United Nations' top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority during a 2017 military operation
story: The United Nations' top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority during a 2017 military operation

THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- In a landmark judgment, the United Nations’ top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home.

International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”

The 15-judge panel of the World Court, which included Navi Pillay, the respected international jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, rejected Myanmar’s defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.

Iwasawa said that “the court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers.”

The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide and comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.
The atmosphere following the hearing was electric, with lawyers and members of the Rohingya, some of whom had traveled thousands of miles (kilometers) to attend the reading, hugging and crying.

“This is a great day for the Rohingya, and it is a great day for all oppressed people, everywhere, who have been told that their suffering does not count and that no one is listening,” said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court’s ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the nearly three-hour reading of the ruling.

The court also ordered Myanmar to commit to reparations including allowing Rohingya “safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence.” It ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings.
The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.

The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.

In a previous judgment in 2007, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.
Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

“The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military. The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.
Associated Press writer Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Wreck of Australia's first warship built at home found 128 years after sinking
summary: The wreck of Australia’s first Australian-built warship, HMCS Spitfire, has been found 128 years to the day after it sank off the country’s north coast
story: The wreck of Australia’s first Australian-built warship, HMCS Spitfire, has been found 128 years to the day after it sank off the country’s north coast

MELBOURNE, Australia -- The wreck of the first Australian warship built in the country, HMCS Spitfire, was found 128 years to the day after it sank off the north coast of what is now Queensland state, officials said Thursday.

The 19-meter (62-foot) schooner was launched in Sydney in 1855 to fight a potential Russian invasion. But Spitfire had been operating as a fishing boat four decades later when it sprung a leak and foundered on Aug. 21, 1898, off Piper Island, documents show.

A Royal Australian Navy mine hunter vessel found and exposed 16 meters (52 feet) of the wreck nearly three months ago, also on Aug. 21, after a monthlong search using a dive team and remotely operated vehicles, a joint statement from multiple agencies said.
“It is remarkable luck that Spitfire was discovered on the 128th anniversary of its sinking,” Queensland heritage officer Celeste Jordan said in the statement.
The discovery was not announced sooner because of reporting processes between government agencies required under laws designed to protect shipwrecks, the Defense Department explained Thursday.

Bearing the designation of HMCS, meaning Her Majesty’s Colonial Schooner, Spitfire was commissioned in 1855 during the Crimean War when the British colonial government of New South Wales in Sydney feared the Russian Pacific Fleet would invade, Australian National Maritime Museum archaeologist James Hunter said.

Britain was at war with Russia in a conflict centered on Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula. Gold had recently been discovered in New South Wales and the neighboring colony of Victoria, making them lucrative targets for conquest.
The Australian colonies then relied on Britain’s navy for defense and British warships were rare in the most distant reaches of the empire.

The Crimean War ended in 1856 without the Australian two-mast sailing vessel ever being used in battle. Spitfire became a pilot vessel in 1857 at Moreton Bay in what would soon become the Colony of Queensland, but was then still part of New South Wales, documents show.
The Queensland government sold Spitfire in 1885 into private ownership for use as a fishing boat.
Shipbuilder John Cuthbert delivered Spitfire two months after winning the contract. The speed suggested the warship’s construction already had been underway for a different purpose, Hunter said.
It was built from native timbers including an ironbark keel, blackbutt frames and kauri planking. The ship had copper sheathing below the waterline.
Russia’s Pacific Fleet at the time was mostly iron-hulled, steam-powered and “armed to the teeth warships,” Hunter told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
Spitfire was armed with a single cannon that fired 32-pound (14.5-kilogram) iron cannonballs.
“Would that have bounced off the side of one of those larger, Russian iron-hulled warships? Probably,” Hunter said.

There are no plans to salvage the wreck, which is largely buried in seabed sand. Authorities have not revealed Spitfire's exact location because it lies at a depth that can be reached by scuba divers. The ship is protected by federal and state law.
Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, chief of the Australian navy, said Spitfire represents the beginning of the service's continuing story.
“Spitfire occupies a unique place in Australia’s naval history as the first warship built in Australia for Australian service,” Buckley said.

title: North Korea is expanding its original uranium enrichment facility, UN nuclear watchdog says
summary: The U.N. nuclear watchdog says that North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at its Yongbyon nuclear complex
story: The U.N. nuclear watchdog says that North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at its Yongbyon nuclear complex

SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the U.N. nuclear watchdog said, in yet another sign that the North is delivering on its vow to bolster its nuclear weapons program.

The assessment by International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi came as U.S. President Donald Trump expressed his eagerness to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un while he was in Asia for a regional forum in China.

“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026,” Grossi said in a statement Wednesday to the IAEA’s board of governors. “The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s uranium enrichment program remains a cause for serious concern.”
DPRK stands for Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.

The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other locations in North Korea since the country kicked out the agency’s inspectors in 2009. The IAEA has said it uses satellite imagery and open source information to monitor developments in North Korea’s nuclear program.

North Korea has called its Yongbyon complex “the heart” of its nuclear program. Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon.

Observers say North Korea has taken steps to build additional uranium enrichment facilities at Yongbyon and elsewhere since Kim’s earlier high-stakes nuclear diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. Last year, South Korea’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

While Trump expressed interest in meeting with Kim, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said no meeting was yet scheduled for Trump’s China visit with Kim but he said the president is prepared to begin a new dialogue with Pyongyang.

North Korea hasn’t responded to Trump’s fresh overture. Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state. Experts say North Korea is eager to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that it could demand the lifting of U.N. economic sanctions.

title: In the land that gave us 'cinema,' activist archivists are bringing back old home movies
summary: Archiving activists who roam from town to town in France are making people's forgotten home movies great again by preserving them digitally
story: Archiving activists who roam from town to town in France are making people's forgotten home movies great again by preserving them digitally
ANTIBES, France -- They flicker on a small screen — grainy, almost ghostly images of lives and times that Romain Gimenes has heard about from family for years but is too young to have known himself.

Slowly hand-winding reels of decades-old Super 8 film through a viewing machine — lent to him by archiving activists who have made it their mission to save home movies like these from being tossed out as trash — Gimenes marvels as loved ones and places that his grandfather filmed in the 1970s dance back to life in sepia tones.
“Oh! That’s my grandfather,” the 30-year-old French Riviera school teacher exclaims. He inherited his middle name, Gabriel, from the man whose bearded face appeared fleetingly and whom he never met.

Interspersed among more images — of his mother, his 94-year-old grandmother, even a great-grandmother and others — pops up a prized find: Footage of a service station the family used to own, since demolished and replaced by a bakery, in the Riviera town of Antibes.
Gimenes whips out his phone and snaps a photo, a digital copy of an analog image to show and remind his mother of halcyon days.

“A photograph of a photograph,” he says, reflecting on his Instagram-era reflex gesture. “Today, we film everything and photograph everything. But who takes the time to look at it all? Who takes the time really to see things, really to look?”
“It’s that gesture of our time — the swipe.”

Just 200 years ago, only one human being — also a Frenchman — had the power to freeze time and our world into a photographic image. The father of photography, Nicéphore Niépce, knew back in 1824 that he'd invented something special, writing to his brother that the image he'd taken of the view from a window was “vraiment quelque chose de magique” — really something magical.

The world's fastest cameras today capture trillions of frames per second. Never have so many people been armed with the ability to immortalize children's first steps, to unmask abuses by filming them, to distort truths by altering or inventing images, to edit instances into reels and stories, to sear joys and horrors, beauty and ugliness onto our retinas and our brains.
And never have humans been so addicted — but also, perhaps, so inured — to that power.

On the clouds of Google Photos alone, users have stored more than 9 trillion photos and videos. Images take up so much digital space that it has to be measured in zettabytes, which are mind-blowingly gigantic. Just one zettabyte is equivalent to 250 billion DVDs and if each of its 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes of data were a liter of water, a zettabyte would fill more than 7,000 Pacific Oceans, according to U.S. technology company Cisco Systems, Inc.
Boston-based data research company IDC estimates that photos and moving images will have generated about 144 zettabytes of data worldwide in 2026.

“That includes captured, streamed, broadcast and replicated copies. By 2030, that figure is forecast to reach about 234 zettabytes as higher-resolution smartphone cameras and video-first social platforms put more content in more hands, and as AI-generated images and video add a new source of data on top of what people capture,” says Adam Wright, an IDC senior research manager. He answered questions via email.
But then there are images that make up no zettabytes — yet — and that are, those archiving them say, crying out for rescue.

For Stephanie Ange, Pierre Bouchut and Margot Lestien, who roam from town to town in France, collecting home movies and digitizing them for archives, image preservation is a battle waged reel by reel.

The name that the trio chose for their group, Ofnibus, plays off the French word for UFO. They can never be sure what they might find on the films and video cassettes that people bring them, often without much of a clue of what they show. Rummaged from garages, attics, cupboards and drawers, and often filmed by people who have since died, they are, quite literally, noninventoried cinematic objects until Bouchut runs them through his film-scanner or pops them into his VHS machines.

In their 23 residencies over five years, Bouchut has seen “everything there is to see in life”: Marriages, baptisms and birthdays galore but also an A-to-Z from farmers butchering prized pigs to the forcible shaving of women's heads during World War II to punish and shame them for suspected relations with German soldiers.
He’s had plenty of surprises, not all of them pleasant, including what today might be called sex tapes — or as he more delicately puts it: “Births, and the stage before births.”
“I love picnics,” he says. “And the Tour de France — everyone filmed that.”
The more he watches, the more he's struck by how “everything changes, but nothing changes.”

“Children apparently weren’t better behaved in the past. People enjoyed themselves just as much as they do today,” he says. “There’s a universality that comes through, something that gives you a little faith in humanity.”
But as time passes, so do the people who know what the images show.

“Finding the material, being able to watch it again and digitize it is one thing, but you still need to be able to interpret and understand it,” Lestien says. “That’s where the urgency lies: the people who still remember the events and what’s on the films are dying.”

The introduction in 1965 of Kodak's Super 8 mm format democratized moviemaking with hand-held cameras that whirred through cartridges containing 50 feet (15 meters) of film. But ever-fewer families still have the functioning projectors (followed later by VCRs) that would be fired up occasionally to watch their home movies together. Films that were treasured can, for the generations that inherit them, become unwatchable clutter.
“Eventually they throw it away because it takes up space, it’s starting to smell bad, and they can’t really see what they could do with it,” Lestien says.
The projectors and video-viewing machines that the Ofnibus team carts around France are making forgotten home movies great again.

In Antibes, they digitized 22 hours of images for archiving and reconnected their donors with memories and family histories. They also commissioned an editor who boiled down selected images into a 30-minute movie for a public viewing that 50 townspeople attended. It included rediscovered footage of Brigitte Bardot, the cinema icon who lived on the French Riviera and was filmed with a basket of roses.

Retired 65-year-old travel agent Sophie Roux-Nantas brought 16 reels of film from the 1930s to the '60s that were languishing in her garage. She saw herself as a 3-year-old on a beach “playing just as children play, just as the new generation does. We made sandcastles. That hasn’t changed, and we swam in the same way.”
On one of his 28 videocassettes “that were all sleeping in a box,” 41-year-old physiotherapist Yohan Chabert was transported back to the 1990s and a family game of Monopoly.
He snapped a photo of the screen.
“It’s moving,” he said. “And, I think, it’s something to share. Because having reels at home and leaving them in a cupboard is a bit of a shame.”

title: China and Russia say they and US agree on UN reforms, boosting fuel supplies, dialogue on nuclear
summary: China, Russia and the U.S. have agreed to seek reforms at the United Nations, increase oil supplies and engage in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks
story: China, Russia and the U.S. have agreed to seek reforms at the United Nations, increase oil supplies and engage in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks

SHENZHEN, China -- China, Russia and the U.S. agreed Thursday to seek reforms at the United Nations, increase oil supplies and engage in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks at a three-way meeting, according to Chinese and Russian officials.

The three countries also took aim at the International Criminal Court, saying state officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions and warning that it should not abuse its jurisdiction. Russian President Vladimir Putin is wanted by the court — and the U.S. has heavily sanctioned it and its officials for recent investigations.

The declaration followed a historic meeting among U.S. President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, a moment that could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op. Experts have kept expectations low for major breakthroughs.
The declaration did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, two issues that U.S. President Donald Trump said he raised with the leaders earlier in the day. The U.S. has not released the document.
Xi later called the meeting positive, constructive and “fruitful.”

The statement said the leaders are committed to advancing U.N. reforms “to more effectively address global challenges," to increase the production and supply of oil products to ensure a stable flow of energy, and to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.

Trump has promoted this first-ever three-way meeting with Xi and Putin — two of America's leading rivals — as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."

Xi, meanwhile, earlier said the meeting would focus on "promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, harkened back to the three countries’ shared history as “victors in World War II,” saying that “we hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at APEC,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”

Before the three-way meeting — which lasted more than an hour on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit — the U.S. president had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.

The U.S. president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.

Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.

Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend."
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin. Their meeting lasted roughly 40 minutes.

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. president also added that the trio would talk about ways to “protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court."

Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

The U.S. president's ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutual — and Trump does not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.

On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.

By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter, Annmarie Hordern, from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session.
Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.

While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world's two largest economies. China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the U.S. has almost equally large trade deficits.

And the race between the U.S. and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks. Trump’s ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose former company is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.
Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China's ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to aggravate relations.

U.S. officials have said that China had not fully honored its commitments made last year in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more U.S. agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics.
The trade truce between the U.S. and China reached last year after dueling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan. 10.
Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the U.S. war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth.
Associated Press writers Darlene Superville and Will Weissert in Washington, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok and Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

title: For Putin, sharing a spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on the global stage
summary: For Russian President Vladimir Putin, the three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping offers a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to demonstrate that he heads a superpower on a par with the United States and China
story: For Russian President Vladimir Putin, the three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping offers a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to demonstrate that he heads a superpower on a par with the United States and China

For Russian President Vladimir Putin, the three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping offers a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to demonstrate that he heads a superpower on a par with the United States and China.

While dealing another blow to Western efforts to isolate Putin, it also gives him an opportunity to try to persuade Trump to lean into Moscow’s demands for a settlement in Ukraine at a time when Washington wants to broker a peace deal.

Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin, Trump and Xi are expected to touch on a broad variety of issues, including Ukraine and other conflicts that "are literally festering now.” Trump and Putin met separately on Thursday ahead of the three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China.

Kyiv and its European allies view the three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with deep suspicion. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another “Anchorage moment,” a reference to a Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska in August 2025 that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners.

Some in the West are comparing the three-way meeting to the 1945 Yalta conference, where the wartime leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union divided Germany and Berlin, carved out zones of influence in Europe, and agreed to establish the United Nations. The Kremlin, which long has courted the concept of a “multipolar world” offering an equal say to all nations, plays down the Yalta comparisons, which are also unwelcome to China for similar reasons.

Fyodor Lukyanov, a pro-Kremlin foreign policy expert, noted that even as Moscow publicly rejects the Yalta analogy, it seems to believe the leaders could “reach agreements and make decisions that will determine global developments.”
Of the three nations, "it seems that only Russia really believes in the possibility of global control,” he told a recent roundtable.

Chatham House director Bronwen Maddox said in a commentary that “standing with Xi and Trump, Putin will look like one of the three main leaders of the world," even though “Russia is no superpower” and its economy, overloaded with military spending, is dwindling. She warned that “the danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force.”

The meeting follows U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine held in Abu Dhabi last week for the first time in nine months. The negotiations produced few visible results as the parties stuck to their sharply divergent demands.

The Kremlin welcomed a U.S. proposal to discuss broader European security as part of a possible settlement, an offer that hews to a longtime Russian demand for the West to take Moscow's security concerns into account. Kyiv and its allies oppose the idea, fearing it could allow Russia to divert attention from a Ukrainian settlement and try to pursue its demands.

Trump’s recent moves have appeared to favor the Kremlin. He has waived tough, new sanctions against Moscow and shocked Ukraine and the Europeans by striking a diesel deal that allowed Russia to resume fuel exports, reversing years of U.S. pressure. He urged Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian refineries, blaming them for spiking diesel prices in the U.S. even though they largely were driven by the Iran war.

Ukraine also has reported a throttling of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, a move that was widely seen as an attempt by the U.S. to force Kyiv into making concessions in negotiations.
Both sides have escalated their long-range aerial attacks on each other, trying to seize the initiative as fighting largely stalls along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line.

In a major embarrassment to Moscow ahead of the Shenzhen meeting, Ukrainian drones and missiles seriously damaged the Kerch Bridge, Putin’s pet project and potent symbol of Moscow’s control over Crimea. Russia, meanwhile, continues to pummel Ukraine’s power grid and bridges in Kyiv.

Putin acknowledges the damage from Ukrainian strikes but argues that Russia has meted out much more punishment. He resists Kyiv’s push for a ceasefire, saying Moscow wants a comprehensive peace deal, not a temporary truce that would allow Ukraine to rest and rearm.
While pursuing its demands, the Kremlin also seeks to unblock U.S.-Russian economic cooperation and to open new business ventures even before a peace deal.

Trump has said he would like to discuss “denuclearization” at the talks. Russia has signaled openness to discussing nuclear arms control but voiced understanding for China’s reluctance to consider any reductions in its atomic arsenals, which are much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow.

Just before the summit, Russia sent a pair of nuclear-capable Tu-95 bombers on a visit to Vietnam in a reminder of its nuclear might. And as Putin arrived in China, Russian TV zeroed in on an officer in his retinue who was carrying a briefcase with the codes for Moscow's nuclear forces.

title: Brazil's Senate approves Lula's $10 billion fiscal package after costly election spending
summary: Brazil’s Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October
story: Brazil’s Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October

SAO PAULO -- SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil 's Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October led market analysts to worry about Brazil’s economy. The 81-year-old leader came back with a series of incentives to voters after losing the first round of voting to Flávio Bolsonaro.

The Brazilian government’s fiscal package, which will also have to be approved by the lower house, introduces new rules to slow down the growth of spending, limits corporate tax breaks and closes loopholes. It seeks to improve the ‌public finances by up to 60 billion reais (about $10 billion) next year.

Lula’s move is laying bare the challenges ahead of his fourth nonconsecutive administration, as it already has many critics left and right. Many of his supporters see the plan as a risk to welfare programs, while his critics among market agents deem it to be too shy.

Many analysts say Lula's fiscal package is too dependent on boosting revenues rather than cutting expenses. That perception has led to the depreciation of Brazilian assets in recent days, including the country's real currency. Lula is yet to announce who will be his finance minister for the new term.
Lula’s victories in 2002 and 2022 also sparked immediate depreciation of Brazilian assets, but stock markets eventually recovered from high losses.

Ahead of the runoff election, Lula rolled out costly initiatives, including a 15% increase in his flagship welfare program Bolsa Família, or Family Grant. That measure alone will cost 5.8 billion reais ($1 billion) this year and around 22 billion reais ($3.7 billion) next year, according to Brazilian government figures.
The minimum monthly benefit per family rose in October to 691 reais ($117) from 600 reais ($102). The average benefit will increase from 675 reais ($115) to 777 reais ($132).

Other major measures of the Lula administration included subsidized credit and debt-relief programs for small businesses and low-income earners, temporary federal fuel tax cuts, and proposed zero-fare weekend public transportation. Additionally, Congress passed legislation shortening the weekly workweek without cutting pay.

Low income voters were key for Lula’s victory. Students, who also led Lula’s charge to keep the presidency, took to Sao Paulo’s Brigadeiro Faria Lima avenue on Tuesday to protest against the government’s fiscal package. That artery of the metropolis hosts many of its banks and brokers.

title: UK's Prince Harry sees 'big separation' between US administration, public on support for Ukraine
summary: Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the U.S. administration’s stance and that of the Ameri...
story: Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the U.S. administration’s stance and that of the Ameri...

LONDON -- Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump Administration’s stance and that of the American people.

Harry, a British Army veteran who returned to his home country last summer after six years in California, also said he believes Britain has been in conflict with Russia for the past decade and that he is ready to serve in the military once again if he is called upon to do so.

The comments came in an interview with The Daily Telegraph that took place last weekend during Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the full-scale Russian invasion. The newspaper published a story about the interview on Wednesday and is scheduled to release the full interview in a podcast that will be posted at midnight London time (0000 GMT).

“I think there’s been a big separation between what American society feel regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in this case an administration, that was perhaps thinking about it differently,” Harry said.

Harry traveled to Ukraine last weekend to meet with athletes who are preparing to take part in the 2027 Invictus Games, the Paralympic-style competition he founded to inspire wounded veterans. Next year’s games will take place in Birmingham, England. The prince is not a working member of the royal family and traveled to Ukraine as a private citizen.

Harry said now is the time for Britain and its allies to double their support for Ukraine to ensure that it defeats Russia at a time when Moscow is trying to stir up divisions within European society.

British intelligence and military officials are increasingly warning about sabotage, disinformation campaigns and other so-called hybrid attacks carried out by Russian operatives to destabilize western societies.

“I think the threat has been there and been consistently there for the last 15 years,” Harry said. “Just because there’s not drones, bullets and rockets flying at us, that doesn’t mean that we’re not at war. I feel like we’ve been at war for the last decade.”
Harry, who was deployed to Afghanistan twice during his military career, said veterans should be ready to serve again.
“If the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel,” he said.

title: Mexico's Catholic street DJs turn annual pilgrimage into a party
summary: A mix of street DJs and Catholic devotees are taking to the streets in one of Mexico's most important pilgrimages
story: A mix of street DJs and Catholic devotees are taking to the streets in one of Mexico's most important pilgrimages
MEXICO CITY -- A sea of people carrying statues of Mexico's patron saint, the Virgin of Guadalupe, marched along the avenue leading up to the country's most important basilica on Wednesday.
Such pilgrimages are practically embedded in the daily rhythms of the bustling Mexican capital. But the roughly 1,000 pilgrims from across the Latin American nation aren't just Catholic devotees.
They're also Mexican street DJs.
The annual procession and street party known as the “sonidero” pilgrimage is perhaps one of the most Mexico City-esque convergences of celebrations to hit the city.

Sonideros, as they're known, are a particular brand of DJs found primarily in Mexico City, but also in other parts of Mexico and Colombia. The DJs mix rhythmic tunes of cumbia with radio announcements, chanting shout outs that mingle with the music.

The tradition is so important in the city, particularly in working-class neighborhoods, that in 2023 the city government recognized sonidero culture as intangible cultural heritage — a designation UNESCO quickly celebrated. The music has even evolved into its own dance, a derivation of cumbia that has more open steps meant for street parties than the classic two-person cumbia.

Each neighborhood has its own set of sonideros who organize pop-up mobile parties. Wednesday's party-procession on the avenue leading up to the famed Basilica de Guadalupe wasn't so spontaneous, but rather part of an annual celebration now spanning decades.

“The root of faith in Mexico is the Virgin of Guadalupe,” said Christian Castañeda, a musician who joined the throngs of people marching through the gates of the Basilica. “We mix this party with the joy of music and we come to play for the Virgin.”

Nearly 80% of Mexicans identify as Catholic, according to Mexican census data, and Mexicans from as far as northern Baja California flock to the capital each November to give thanks for good luck they've had throughout the year.

Esperanza Rivera, donning a bright gold and neon blue T-shirt with images of different radio sets, said she started preparing for the march before the sun came up. At 4 a.m. the 76-year-old began packing sandwiches and putting the final touches on a massive pink altar her family planned to carry through the streets.

Some families see the march as a way to pass down sonidero and religious traditions to the next generations. Others enjoy the chance to connect with other street DJ communities from across the country.
“Everyone, all of the sonideros, unite on this day,” she said.
They walk for hours, using motorcycles to cart a mix of flower-lined altars like Rivera's and mobile DJ booths.
Rivera and her relatives joined a mass in the Basilica before returning with other sonideros by bus to their neighborhood of Tláhuac in the city's outskirts.
That's where they continue the party.
Megan Janetsky contributed to this report from Mexico City.
