title: Inside Greenland’s push for fine dining, from polar night logistics to 'kaffemik' traditions
summary: Greenland's chefs are transforming traditional Inuit ingredients into modern fine-dining experiences
story: Greenland's chefs are transforming traditional Inuit ingredients into modern fine-dining experiences

ILULISSAT, Greenland -- ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — Greenland, a vast Arctic territory of about 56,000 people, is perhaps better known for its icebergs, polar bears, rare minerals and geopolitical tensions than its cuisine.
But a new generation of chefs is working to change that, transforming traditional Inuit ingredients into modern fine-dining experiences.
Greenland’s food culture has long been rooted in hunting and fishing, with local ingredients ranging from ptarmigan, reindeer, musk ox and lamb to capelin, shrimp, snow crab, whale and halibut.

Restaurant Ulo opened two years ago in Hotel Arctic, believed to be the world’s northernmost four-star hotel, in Ilulissat, a town of 5,000 that sits about 300 kilometers (about 186 miles) north of the Arctic Circle.
The restaurant takes its name from the “ulo,” a traditional crescent-shaped knife used by women for hunting and food preparation.

“There is no fine-dining culture here,” said executive chef Sudarshan Sundararaj. “We wanted to do the fine-dining culture here in a modern technique with modern cookery, gastronomy style with mainly Greenlandic items — so that was the challenging part.”
“It’s about creating something to reveal Greenland, to experience Greenland for whoever is coming for a visit,” said Sundararaj, who moved to Greenland from his native Sri Lanka six years ago.
Ulo's 13-course meal puts local produce center stage and — like many things in far-off Greenland — comes at a steep price: 3,900 Danish kroner (about $570) per person with wine included.
The fluffy starter dish known as “rekling” reimagines air-dried halibut as a delicacy distinct from the dried fish familiar to many Greenlanders.
"We thought, ‘okay, what makes Greenland special?’” said Danish sous-chef Esben Staun-Olsen. "There are a lot of things that make Greenland special, but part of it is really, really good protein.”

Running a fine-dining restaurant on the edge of the world comes with unique challenges: Every year, Ilulissat is plunged into 44 days of polar night, fresh ingredients are difficult to grow, and frozen harbors can prevent supply boats from reaching town.
Most vegetables on Ulo’s menu are imported, and supplies are often unreliable because of the weather, said Sundararaj.
Other upscale restaurants are beginning to appear across the Arctic territory.
Restaurant Sarfalik, in the high-rise Hotel Hans Egede in the capital, Nuuk, offers a changing menu of freshly-caught fish with views of the fjord and nearby mountains.
In the southern town of Qaqortoq, newly-opened bistro Tamassa serves reindeer steak, lamb chops and traditional Greenlandic soup.
Ulo’s chefs believe fine dining doesn’t require imported luxuries like caviar or truffles. But understanding Greenlandic food culture means going beyond restaurant kitchens and into people's homes.

At its heart is “kaffemik” — which roughly translates as “with coffee” in Greenlandic — a traditional social gathering centered around coffee, food and community that’s often an all-day affair, bringing people together to celebrate a new baby, a birthday or other special occasion.
For Greenlander Kathrine Johansen, it’s more than just a gathering; it’s a treasured tradition.
“It means a lot to me, because I grew up in a big family where we had a lot of kaffemiks,” she says. “That is our way of living with those traditions.”
One delicacy on the menu is mattak, a traditional Inuit dish made from raw whale skin and blubber.

“It’s a tradition in many years that we have been eating this kind of food. I really like it,” says 24-year-old tour guide Niklas Johansen, savoring the small cubes of raw whale at Johansen's home. “I usually eat it this way, when it’s fresh.”

title: The UK and EU are holding a summit to patch up ties after their bitter Brexit divorce
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is meeting EU officials in Brussels on Friday to discuss closer ties between the UK and the bloc that it left in 2020
story: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is meeting EU officials in Brussels on Friday to discuss closer ties between the UK and the bloc that it left in 2020
LONDON -- Britain and the European Union went through a bitter divorce, then slowly tried to be friends again.
Now they are starting to consider maybe, one day, getting back together.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet the EU’s top officials in Brussels on Friday for a summit that the British leader has called a step toward undoing a decade of damage triggered by the U.K.'s 2016 vote to leave the bloc.

“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” Burnham said this week. He has said that all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc.
Burnham has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and is far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but of a mistrustful EU.
Still, Burnham has broken British governments’ decade-long code of silence on the option of rejoining.

Most economists agree that Brexit has hurt the British economy by erecting barriers to trade with the country's neighbors, but U.K. politicians have been wary of reopening a painful debate. Both sides of the argument remember the anger and divisiveness of the referendum campaign and the acrimonious divorce negotiations that followed before the final split in 2020.

Friday’s EU-U.K. summit is only the second since Britain became the first country ever to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on social media that she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”

The two sides are expected to sign a trade deal for food and drink, an agreement on emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham says that the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain’s economy.

Even closer ties, and a bigger economic boost, would require Burnham to break the pledge made by Keir Starmer, his predecessor as Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market, or to restore free movement for EU nationals to the U.K.
Burnham says he will set out options for the long-term U.K.-EU relationship later this year, but won’t go beyond Starmer’s boundaries before the next national election, which must be held by 2029.
“There’s no rush,” Burnham told Sky News on Tuesday. “The red lines in the Labour manifesto will stand. And the British public will be in charge of whatever comes next.”

But some in the Labour Party are pushing to go further. Lawmaker David Lammy, who served as foreign secretary and deputy prime minister under Starmer, said the government should make rejoining the EU part of its platform for the next election.
Lammy said “the position of the United Kingdom was diminished” when it cut ties with its European neighbors.
“This is the age where middle powers come together to effect change,” he told a meeting at the Chatham House think tank on Wednesday.
“It just doesn’t make sense" for the U.K. to go it alone, he said. “It never did.”
Others worry that the chances of a calm and reasoned national debate about the emotionally loaded topic are slim.

New pro- and anti-EU campaign groups have already sprung up, backed by veterans of the 2016 battles. Former Conservative Cabinet minister Michael Gove, a backer of the “Stay Out” group, said rejoining “would mean handing back control of our laws, borders, money and trade, and paying a good deal more for membership than we did before.”
Pro-Brexit campaigners are cranking out warnings about Brussels meddling, including a claim the new food trade deal will mean a ban on Brits’ beloved smoky bacon flavor potato chips.
In response, the Burnham government assured people that “smoky flavors in crisps, sauces, and soups will remain on U.K. supermarket shelves.”
The EU has welcomed Britain’s warmer tone, and some national leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron, have said they would welcome it back into the fold.

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s undoubted military strength, are drawing the two sides back together, and for the EU the summit provides an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense and the fight against irregular migration.

But feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary after dealing with the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers during the last decade.

Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador in London, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, “there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant.” She said that if Britain wants to reopen negotiations, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants.”

Simon Usherwood, a professor of politics and international studies at the Open University, doubts British politics is ready to have a grown-up discussion about the “slow and painful process” of refashioning the country’s relationship with the EU.

“All of this requires an informed and educated debate about what is involved, what the EU might want and accept, what the costs and benefits will be of any option,” he said. “And I’m not yet sure that we’re at that point. Actually, I’m pretty sure we’re not at that point.”
Associated Press writer Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this story.

title: Ukraine criticizes IAEA plan to appoint sanctioned Russian official to senior post
summary: Ukraine has criticized the proposal by the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official, sanctioned by Kyiv, to a senior position
story: Ukraine has criticized the proposal by the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official, sanctioned by Kyiv, to a senior position

VIENNA -- VIENNA (AP) — Ukraine on Wednesday denounced a proposal by the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official sanctioned by Kyiv to a senior position at the U.N. nuclear watchdog in Vienna.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the proposed appointment of Alexey Ferapontov as deputy director general “categorically unacceptable” and urged IAEA chief Rafael Mariano Grossi to “abandon this appointment" in a post on X.

In a note sent Nov. 16 to all 35 members of the IAEA Board of Governors, which was seen by The Associated Press, Grossi proposed the nomination of Ferapontov to the position of deputy director general in the Department of Nuclear Energy.

The note also proposed a candidate from the United States to the position of deputy director general in the Department of Management, and a candidate from North Macedonia to become director in the Department of Safeguards.

Grossi suggested holding an informal briefing about the senior appointments with members of the board this week. According to the IAEA’s Statute and staff regulations, the IAEA director general has the authority to appoint staff members.

“Ferapontov is subject to Ukrainian sanctions for his involvement in Russia’s attempts to legitimize the illegal seizure of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant,” Sybiha wrote on X. “Officials implicated in such violations should face accountability, not be rewarded with senior positions in international organizations,” he added.

“Appointing a senior official from the Russian authority complicit in legitimizing Russia’s illegal seizure of the plant would be an unacceptable endorsement of impunity and a serious blow to the Agency’s credibility,” Sybiha noted.
Ferapontov is currently deputy head of Rostechnadzor, Russia’s Federal Environmental, Industrial and Nuclear Supervision Service.
The Russian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has been under Russian control since early in Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Although the plant is not operating, it needs reliable external power to cool its six shut-down reactors and spent fuel to avoid any catastrophic nuclear incidents.
The plant is near the front line and has been occupied by Russia since March 2022. Ukraine and Russia have traded blame for shelling close to the plant.

On Nov. 8 the site experienced its 27th complete loss of off-site power since the start of the conflict, according to the IAEA. The external power line has since been restored, but diesel fuel reserves that are necessary for emergency generators have been reduced at the plant, the IAEA warned.
Sybiha also referred to Grossi’s campaign to become the next U.N. Secretary-General, stressing the importance of the “independence and impartiality” of the IAEA.
“There can be no room for political considerations or external influence in decisions of such importance,” he wrote.

Grossi confirmed his plans to appoint Ferapontov as deputy director general in the IAEA’s Department for Nuclear Energy during a news conference on Wednesday on the first day of a regular meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors in Vienna. Grossi said the criteria in making such appointments relate to the “technical experience and the technical capacities” of the appointees.

“When I appoint somebody, I’m not appointing a country, I am not appointing a policy, I am not appointing preferences in this regard,” Grossi said. “We are appointing the person and individual that has the capacities to fulfill that position.”
Grossi added that in the specific case related to Ferapontov, “it’s a very well-known expert in areas like nuclear safety, nuclear security and others.”

The post of deputy director general in the IAEA’s Department for Nuclear Energy became vacant after the IAEA in September suspended the previous incumbent, Mikhail Chudakov, a Russian senior official who had a decades-long career in Russia’s nuclear industry.

Chudakov reportedly promoted a book he published under a pseudonym among a U.N. youth group that allegedly contained degrading comments about feminism and LGBT people and expressed support for authoritarian government. The IAEA never commented publicly on the suspension. Bloomberg first reported about Chudakov’s suspension.
The IAEA has six deputy director-general posts.

title: St. Peter's Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of Roman Catholicism
summary: St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication
story: St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication

VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism whose commanding dome defines the Roman skyline, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication Wednesday, a monument to artistic achievement and perseverance.

Its construction spanned 120 years, 20 pontificates and the work of a succession of 12 architects, enduring the Protestant Reformation and the sack of Rome before Pope Urban VIII dedicated it on Nov. 18, 1626.

“You walk through those doors and you won’t feel the conflicts and the disasters and the setbacks,” said Elizabeth Lev, a Rome-based American art historian. “You walk through those doors and you see continuity and beauty and achievement and triumph.”

A setting for papal ceremonies and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year, the basilica was built over the traditional burial site of the Apostle Peter, replacing a church that had stood for more than a millennium.
Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone on April 18, 1506, launching a project whose architects included Donato Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, who completed its facade.
Even on the day of its dedication, the basilica’s familiar setting was still taking shape.
“The church facade was complete, but the amazing piazza, which is part and parcel of the church we know today, wasn’t there yet,” Lev said.
“As a matter of fact, you would have heard lots of people complaining about the new facade and how it blocked Michelangelo’s dome,” she said.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s sweeping oval piazza was completed in 1667, its curving colonnades conceived as the welcoming arms of the Church. Its 284 columns, arranged in four rows, frame an oval space connected to the basilica by a trapezoidal forecourt.

Inside, the basilica’s architecture draws attention toward its spiritual center: Peter’s tomb beneath the main altar, Bernini’s monumental bronze canopy and Michelangelo’s dome rising overhead. Generations of popes have been entombed in the basilica and the Vatican Grottoes below.
“The inside of St. Peter’s Basilica is marked by unity and magnificence,” Lev said. “So for a church that took 120 years, it’s amazing how each part fits together into something of a unified whole.”

The basilica and its square have witnessed the opening of the Second Vatican Council, papal funerals and the first appearances of newly elected pontiffs. Crowds gather in the square for Sunday blessings, while at Christmas and Easter the pope traditionally delivers his message and “Urbi et Orbi” blessing — Latin for “to the city and to the world” — from the basilica’s central balcony.
In one of the defining images of the coronavirus pandemic, Pope Francis stood before the rain-soaked, deserted square to impart an extraordinary blessing on March 27, 2020.
The basilica also provided the setting for a private meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy before Francis’ funeral on April 26, 2025.
For Lev, the basilica's long history offers a message for another unsettled age.

“I think one of the great lessons about St. Peter’s is that people adapt, the church adapts according to the circumstances,” she said. “And yes indeed, many terrible things happened while they were building that church and they forged onwards and they ended up making something beautiful.”
Barry reported from Milan.

title: Remains of Ecuadorian killed in New York building collapse arrive in Quito
summary: The remains of José Caguana, one of two Ecuadorian construction workers killed in a New York building collapse, have arrived in Ecuador
story: The remains of José Caguana, one of two Ecuadorian construction workers killed in a New York building collapse, have arrived in Ecuador

QUITO, Ecuador -- The remains of one of two Ecuadorian construction workers killed when a building collapsed into an adjacent pit that was being excavated in New York arrived Wednesday in Ecuador’s capital and were turned over to his family.
Relatives said they would take the body of José Caguana, 26, from Mariscal Sucre airport to his central Andean hometown of Quisapincha.

Gabriel Sigüenza, 22, also died in the collapse in Brooklyn, and his remains were expected to arrive Wednesday night in the port city of Guayaquil before being returned to his family in Cañar, in Ecuador's southern Andes region.
The Ecuadorian government paid for the repatriations, a foreign ministry statement said.

Tens of thousands of Ecuadorians have migrated to the United States without authorization in recent years, seeking work as their country struggles with recurring economic and employment crises and rising violence.
New York authorities said the collapse of the three-story building next to an excavation site killed eight people, including some from Ecuador, Mexico, Guatemala and Trinidad.

The collapse remains under investigation. City officials said authorities had determined that the demolition of the previous building lacked adequate safeguards, and court records show the construction company faced two lawsuits accusing it of damaging adjacent buildings in other projects. The building that collapsed also had a record of safety violations.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
summary: A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand
story: A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand

BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.

At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.

The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.

China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.

The court’s action comes after increasing public concern about Chinese influence over local business, especially through the use of Thai citizens as proxies to disguise their real ownership. In some cases, the concern extends to suspicion that such enterprises are fronts for illegal activities, including money laundering and online scams.

The involvement of Chinese companies in the building collapse and other construction-related accidents has drawn considerable attention. The most notable other accident took place in January this year on a line that is part of a Thai-Chinese high-speed railway project linking the capital to northeastern Thailand. At least 32 people were killed and dozens injured when a construction crane crashed onto a moving passenger train, derailing it.
Italian-Thai Development was also the construction contractor for the railway project, and a Chinese company handled design and construction supervision.

After the train accident, China’s ambassador to Thailand, Zhang Jianwei, said that China requires its companies to follow the rules when participating in overseas projects, and that Beijing is willing to “guide Chinese companies to actively cooperate with the Thai authorities’ investigation."

Wednesday’s court case also saw three Thai shareholders found guilty of acting as nominees for China Railway No. 10 (Thailand). Two were sentenced to six years in prison each and fined 2 million baht ($58,900), while the third received a three-year prison term and a 1-million-baht ($29,450) fine. However, the court reduced their sentences and their fines by one-fifth after they confessed to the offenses.

title: El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
summary: El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff
story: El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.

Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.

Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”
He noted that Jeff’s home is very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been very difficult.
Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years.
“In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said.
The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that.

Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on Nov. 8, Salvadoran troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He wasn’t killed in the attack.
Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control.

He noted that Jeff and Lanmò San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue.
Canaan was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there.
The attack comes a day after thousands of Haitians in Port-au-Prince and beyond marched in favor of Bukele, thanking him and his troops for fighting violent gangs.
On Wednesday, Haitians were again celebrating.
“Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesperson in Port-au-Prince. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.”
Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.
Associated Press reporter Evens Sanon in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails weapons produced in the country
summary: Ukraine says it has carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia
story: Ukraine says it has carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia

KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia, officials said Wednesday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the effectiveness of Kyiv’s domestically produced weapons that damaged the key Kerch Bridge between Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Attacks by both sides have continued even as delegations await word on another round of U.S.-mediated talks. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to discuss the nearly five-year war with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia on Thursday during a visit to China.

Ukraine’s General Staff said that storage tanks were hit at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit was struck at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, which were also targeted on Sunday night, can process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the front line in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.
Russian officials reported attacks on two industrial enterprises in the region, but they gave no details.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted refineries as Ukraine seeks to hurt Russia’s oil sector, a mainstay of its economy, and Moscow presses on with its all-out invasion of its neighbor.
“Our technologies and companies are developing very well,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.
Ukraine's cutting-edge long-range drones and missiles were deployed against the Kerch Bridge in a large-scale attack on Monday night that was prepared over weeks, he said.
“Right now, we’re in the top three in the world for tech development. In Europe, I think we’re number one,” Zelenskyy said.
The Pentagon has argued that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive, but Ukraine's European backers don't agree.
The Ukrainian leader said that the Kerch Bridge strike, which could hamper Russian deliveries to its front-line troops, was justified by Russia’s relentless bombardment of Ukraine.
Moscow’s forces have focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before the winter, aiming to erode the morale of civilians.

Attacks last month killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians and wounded 1,981 others — a number 95% higher than in October 2025, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on social media Wednesday.
This year, the war has brought “significantly higher” civilian casualties than in previous years, the agency said.

“The first 10 months of this year have seen more civilian deaths than all of 2025, which in turn was worse than the year before,” said Danielle Bell, who heads the U.N. agency in Kyiv. “The world should not become numb to the deadly toll the war exacts on Ukraine’s civilians.”

Russians attacked energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings in five regions with drones overnight into Wednesday and in the morning, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Four people were killed in a Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa on Wednesday, local officials said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Wednesday that its forces used drones overnight to strike the port of Izmail in the Odesa region.
A Russian drone attack on a market in the Kharkiv region wounded 12 people, including an 11-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Services said.
Barry Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: EU proposes fresh $49 billion loan for Ukraine as war costs mount
summary: The European Commission wants to raise a 45 billion euro loan for Ukraine to support its economy and war effort in 2027
story: The European Commission wants to raise a 45 billion euro loan for Ukraine to support its economy and war effort in 2027

BRUSSELS -- The European Commission announced Wednesday a plan to borrow another 45 billion euros ($49.4 billion) to support Ukraine’s economy and war effort in 2027, as the costs of five years of fighting mount.

Almost a year ago, European Union leaders endorsed an interest-free loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion) to cover most of Ukraine’s military and economic needs for 2026 and 2027. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining the country’s finances.
EU leaders had hoped countries outside the 27-nation bloc would also provide substantial loans, but those contributions have fallen short of expectations.

The commission now estimates that Ukraine will need 70 billion euros ($77 billion) next year. It plans to raise about two-thirds of that amount on capital markets, providing loans of 20 billion euros ($22 billion) for Kyiv’s economy and 25 billion euros ($27 billion) for its armed forces.
“We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

“The budget support will keep essential civilian services running, it will keep schools and hospitals operating, and the military support will give Ukraine the means to defend itself,” von der Leyen told reporters.

The commission plan would use the interest generated from Russian assets frozen under EU sanctions to help pay the loans. The vast majority of the assets — around 204 billion euros ($224 billion) at the end of September — are held in Euroclear, a Belgian financial clearing house.

Euroclear estimates that it has paid out about 8 billion euros ($9 billion) in windfall profits raised from the assets to the EU so far. Belgium has vetoed loaning the assets themselves to help Ukraine.

Again, countries outside the EU with a triple-A credit rating have been urged to make up the rest of the 70 billion euros ($77 billion). Australia, Canada, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland are considered likely candidates.

Ukraine would only have to pay back the loans once Russia has paid hundreds of billions of euros in reparations for the destruction it has caused since launching its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

European leaders broadly view Russia’s war as an existential threat and Ukraine as their first line of defense. But some countries refuse to provide military support. The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia declined to participate in the previous loan and are threatening to do so again.
Von der Leyen said all 27 member states “say very clearly that they want to support Ukraine” and expressed confidence that all would come on board.

She acknowledged that some countries only “want to invest in civilian support; and this is possible, as this loan has two legs.” She said there would be “no problem to indirectly assign their commitments towards the civilian part.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz threatened to hold up agreement on the EU’s next long-term budget if there were no “collective commitment” made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception.”

“Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support,” Merz said in extracts of a letter seen by The Associated Press that he wrote to European Council President António Costa earlier this month.

Costa and many EU leaders want a plan for the 2028-2034 budget approved by the end of the year. The spending package also includes money for Ukraine. The leaders will discuss the budget and loan at a two-day summit in Brussels late next week.
Associated Press writer Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Walmart raises its outlook for the year for the 3rd time after a solid quarter
summary: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices
story: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices

NEW YORK -- Walmart reported solid third quarter sales gains as the retailer continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum that are seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices.

The company topped Wall Street’s profit and sales projections and it raised its annual guidance for the third time this year, but the outlook released Thursday was more conservative than industry analysts had expected.

Comparable sales, which include digital channels and stores, rose 2.9%. That is better than last quarter's 2.6% increase, when Walmart reported its weakest comparable sales growth in six years. But it's still a slowdown from the 4.5% growth registered during the same period last year.
Shares rose nearly 1% before the opening bell Thursday.
“We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” Walmart's CEO John Furner said in prepared remarks.

Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers use its website or visit its stores every week, according to Walmart. Analysts look to the massive retailer for clues about what to expect from the industry as a whole during the critical holiday shopping season.

Consumers in the U.S. have remained resilient in the face of painful inflation, but they have also grown more selective about what they buy. Many rely on retailers like Walmart as a one-stop shop for low-priced household goods, groceries and pharmaceuticals.

The latest U.S. retail sales data revealed that shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as Americans pulled back on a variety of purchases, from cars, clothing and furniture and even their own hobbies.
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to Commerce Department data released this week.
Walmart has been hammering its low price message while refining its store label fashion brands like Scoop and Free Assembly.

Walmart is also trying to increase subscriptions to its shipping programs. During the third quarter, Walmart launched a combined Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus annual membership bundle for $120 per year. The package saves shoppers nearly $100 compared to buying both plans separately, it said.

Walmart, based in Bentonville, Arkansas, has begun to capture a larger share of wealthier consumers. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart have been coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000, the retailer has said.

Walmart’s quarterly net income was $4.94 billion, or 62 cents per share, in the three-month period ended Oct. 31. Adjusted per-share results were 65 cents, higher than the 64 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet. In the year-ago quarter, the company earned $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share.
Sales rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion in the latest quarter. Analysts were predicting $187.38 billion, according to FactSet.

The company said that comparable sales were driven by groceries and general merchandise categories like furniture and toys. But the figure was once again hit by federal legislation that requires pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said.
Global e-commerce sales rose 17%, while U.S. e-commerce sales increased 23% during the latest quarter.
Walmart said that more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders are being fulfilled from stores, including its third party marketplace orders.

For the full year, Walmart now projects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.84 to $2.89, up from the prior guidance of $2.80 to $2.87. Sales should be up anywhere from 4.9% to 5.2%, up from the prior forecast of 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $748.12 billion to $750.25 billion, according to FactSet.
Analysts expected $2.89 per share and sales of $752.68 billion for the year, according to FactSet.

title: Japan's PM Takaichi says Russia and Japan will keep talking as ties remain chilled
summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says that she met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 30 minutes in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years
story: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi says that she met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 30 minutes in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years

SHENZHEN, China -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Thursday that she and Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks and agreed to keep communicating in the first such encounter between the two countries’ leaders in seven years.

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, she said she raised the issue of Moscow’s treatment of Japanese businesses in Russia and urged Putin to release a Japanese journalist detained for alleged spying during their meeting late Wednesday in Shenzhen, China.
“We reached an agreement to maintain communication at various levels, including direct contact between the president and myself,” Takaichi said.
Japan's ties with Russia have long been strained by a territorial dispute dating back decades.

Japan lodged a protest with Russia in October over the arrest of a Japanese journalist working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper on suspicion of spying, demanding that Moscow provide an explanation, consular access and humane treatment.

Moscow recently seized control of some local subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco, the largest cigarette maker in Russia, and the company reported it expects a 724 billion yen ($4.5 billion) loss for this year due to the takeover.

Earlier, Japan Tobacco had forecast a 662 billion yen profit for the financial year ending Dec. 31. The company said it has not given up legal ownership of the Russia-based subsidiaries or withdrawn from operating in Russia.

Tensions rose in August after Putin visited Iturup, one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims. Earlier this month, Tokyo protested after two Russian aircraft briefly violated Japanese airspace off southwestern Japan.

The last bilateral in-person talks between Japanese and Russian leaders were held between then-Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Putin in September 2019, during the Eastern Economic Forum in the Russian city of Vladivostok.

Putin is attending the annual APEC summit for the first time in nine years. He, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump held a summit meeting Thursday after the APEC gathering, an event that seems to underscore Japan's diminished role as a global power.
Takaichi herself was given a very minimal reception on her arrival in Shenzhen, provoking speculation over a deliberate snub by her hosts.
When asked, Takaichi said she did not believe the summit between Xi, Trump and Putin would undermine Japan’s interests.

“We have been maintaining close communication with the United States and other allies while carefully monitoring the impact on the international situation and we will continue to respond appropriately,” Takaichi said. "We do not believe that Japan’s interests will be compromised.”
She did not elaborate on efforts to repair damage to Japan’s ties with China following remarks she made nearly a year ago about Taiwan.
“China is an important neighbor. Given the various issues and challenges that exist between Japan and China, I believe it is essential to engage in dialogue and maintain communication," she said.
Yamaguchi reported from Tokyo. Associated Press journalist Haruka Nuga in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Asian stocks are mixed and US futures climb ahead of Anthropic's blockbuster IPO
summary: Asian shares are mixed and U.S. futures have edged higher ahead of Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering
story: Asian shares are mixed and U.S. futures have edged higher ahead of Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering
HONG KONG -- HONG KONG (AP) — Asian shares were mixed and U.S. futures advanced Thursday as Anthropic is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq with a blockbuster $81 billion offering.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude artificial-intelligence tool priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, higher than its earlier pricing range. Its trading debut is widely watched by investors looking for signs of where the AI boom may be going, and whether growth in adoption of the technology and massive AI spending can translate into sustained profitability for AI companies.

Anthropic’s decision to go public also came at a time of market volatility and rising concerns over an AI slowdown, particularly following the Nvidia fallout and an expectation that the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the U.S. midterms could lead to greater regulation of the industry.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7% to 59,444.21. SoftBank Group, which invests heavily in AI, added 4.6%. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron climbed 2.8%, while memory maker Kioxia Holdings added 3.1%.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index gained 1% to 5,118.96. Memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.1%, while Samsung Electronics was 0.5% higher.
Taiwan’s Taiex dropped 4.4%, with its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., falling 3.5%.

AI-related stocks including semiconductor shares have been losing some steam over the past weeks in what some analysts called a share price correction following strong gains earlier in the year riding on the global AI frenzy.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gave up 1.9% to 22,851.15. The Shanghai Composite index was 0.3% lower at 3,577.62.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 slid 1% to 8,730.40.
India’s Sensex climbed 0.6%.
On Wednesday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 dropped 0.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.1%, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite was up 0.4%.

Nvidia was 2.9% lower following its latest quarterly earnings results announcement, the first after former CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang was ousted following his extramarital affair that raised U.S. national security concerns, even as the company logged stronger-than-expected revenue and profit.
Now all eyes are on Anthropic on Thursday. OpenAI, its main rival, is also expected to go public but said earlier this year it wasn't planning to do so before 2027.

Significant growth is expected from growing AI adoption and from Anthropic’s “position at the frontier of model development, particularly in areas such as coding and cybersecurity,” Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said in a commentary.

However, Anthropic “will need to sustain rapid growth while managing the enormous cost of developing and running its models, and there is still considerable uncertainty around how the competitive landscape and economics of generative AI will evolve,” he added.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September issued a warning over the risks that rapid AI developments could pose to humanity and called for an AI slowdown over safety needs. His call was echoed by AI leaders including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

In commodities trading, oil prices were mostly stable. A recovery in global oil supply has eased some supply concerns surrounding the situation in the Middle East. But the U.S. and Iran have not yet reached a deal and Iran on Wednesday widened its attacks on Gulf neighbors, underscoring risks to the region's energy shipments.
Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.6% to $92.52 per barrel. It was trading at roughly $72 a barrel before the war began in late February.
Benchmark U.S. crude added 0.2% to $83.43 per barrel.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.61 Japanese yen from 159.35 yen. The euro was unchanged at $1.0975.
AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

title: Skydance to combine Warner Bros. TV Group and Paramount Television Studios
summary: Skydance is combining Warner Bros
story: Skydance is combining Warner Bros

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Skydance will combine two of its key TV production units, Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, bringing such shows as "The Pitt,” “Ted Lasso,” “Reacher” and “Landman” under the same roof.

The combined entity will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, with Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell serving as presidents. The merger of the studios will be completed in early 2027, according to a memo released Wednesday.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level," George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV, said in the memo.
It’s the latest move since Skydance-owned Paramount last month closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, ushering in a new Hollywood giant under the leadership of David Ellison.
The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will house more than 120 TV series, including HBO's “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” Netflix's “Emily in Paris” and CBS' “Marshals.”
CBS Studios — another studio that produces shows such as the “NCIS” and “Fire Country” franchises — will continue to operate as a standalone entity under David Stapf.

title: Why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding
summary: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry
story: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry

PARIS -- Russia is responding forcefully to confirmation from France that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine to provide training and maintenance help with some of the weaponry it has supplied for the war.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said: “This is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,' but direct participation in the war.”
France says the soldiers and weapons specialists are noncombatants.
“Since we are not at war with Russia, these, in fact, are not combat units,” French Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said.
Here's a closer look:
Speaking on Wednesday to French broadcaster RMC, Rufo said French personnel are “a very long way from the front line. They come to carry out occasional missions.”

She didn't specify their numbers, but said that they are “a few soldiers, specialists, including armaments engineers, who work — or can come to work — on an occasional basis to maintain complex equipment, such as Mirage aircraft or Caesar howitzers, and provide targeted training on certain equipment.”

France first delivered Mirage 2000-5 fighters last year to Ukraine and trained pilots and mechanics for them. The French Defense Ministry says the aircraft have helped fend off missile and drone attacks.
It also says that with donations from allies and purchases, Ukraine's force of high-precision French-made Caesar howitzers has grown to become the largest in the world.
France has also supplied precision bombs, cruise missiles, air defense systems, light tanks and other equipment.

Rufo told French lawmakers on Tuesday that France is “accelerating” its support in light of Russia's air campaign against Ukrainian targets. She spoke of a “complete absence of any intention to engage in combat” and described as “absurd” Lavrov's accusation that France is directly participating in the war.
Only a “very limited" number of French personnel are engaged in “the extremely limited” missions, Rufo said.

Her comments came after French media, including broadcaster RFI and Le Monde newspaper, reported that small contingents of French military officers stay in Ukraine for short rotations as part of the so-called Operation Volia, since at least this summer.

French military personnel have been operating in Ukraine for more than six months and France isn't alone in providing such support, Lavrov said Tuesday at a news conference in Manila, Philippines, where he was attending a summit of Southeast Asian nations.

“We have conveyed our concern through the available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,’ but direct participation in the war,” he said, without naming the countries.
“This is just like the assistance with target designation, the provision of satellite data and much else,” he said.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that Moscow will regard any foreign troops in Ukraine as legitimate targets and it will be up to the Russian military to determine a response.

The United Kingdom has soldiers in Ukraine, but officials haven't disclosed how many or what their role is. The U.K. Defense Ministry confirmed two deaths of British soldiers in Ukraine in the past year, in both cases in accidents.

Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, dozens of countries have trained more than 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers, at locations outside the country — in France, the U.K., the United States, Poland, Germany and elsewhere — including on Patriot missile batteries, F-16 combat jets and other equipment. They have also trained recruits, officers, medics and other specialists for combat.
Jill Lawless in London, Sylvie Corbet and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report.

title: How three leaders donated the $20 million Melinda French Gates gave them with no strings attached
summary: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b...
story: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b...
Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble says she was shocked when philanthropist Melinda French Gates picked her to receive $20 million to donate however she wanted.

The psychologist, author and founder of The AAKOMA Project, a nonprofit supporting the mental health of young people of color, has long admired French Gates’ work, especially in the diversity of her support initiatives. Breland-Noble just never expected to be the focus of one of those initiatives.

“It really was shock and awe,” she said. “My mom just had a knack and a penchant for finding people that nobody else was helping and she would help them. And so for me, the excitement was I get to honor my mother’s legacy by doing the same thing.”

In 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries, including Breland-Noble, without warning or requirements other than donating the money by the end of 2026. It was part of her plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls at a time when nonprofits focusing on their issues receive only about 2% of all U.S. philanthropic funding.

Now, with nearly all the money donated, Pivotal has seen enough to call the trust-based philanthropy initiative a “huge success” and is looking for ways to replicate it and encourage other donors to do the same.

“There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” French Gates said in a statement to The Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.”
According to Pivotal, the average grant the Global Leaders handed out was approximately $240,000, with 91% of the donations going to organizations that had not received funding from Pivotal before.

Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said a final report on the Global Leaders program will come next year, but that the organization is already looking for ways to build on it. “We did this not just for the impact," Ley said, “but because it was a model that was intriguing to us.”
French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges have made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful.
“For me, this is as much about expanding who gets to make decisions about funding as it is about where funding goes,” she said.
For Breland-Noble, being able to donate to others on a grand scale was a meaningful new experience.

Though she has been working in the mental health field for decades, she is relatively new to running her own nonprofit. Breland-Noble established The AAKOMA Project, which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents, in 1999 as an academic research lab, only turning it into a nonprofit in 2018 so that it could put its research findings into action.

To donate the $20 million that French Gates had given her, Breland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund – short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity, but also named for, and inspired by, her mother Mattie McLeod Breland.

The MATTIE Fund donated to well-established groups like Asian Mental Health Collective. But Breland-Noble made a point of expanding her donations to groups outside her network, searching Google and LinkedIn to find ideas. She asked her Instagram community for recommendations, as well as audiences at her speaking engagements.

Those searches led to her support of BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression.
Breland-Noble said she was thankful to French Gates for the opportunity to give.
“She saw me and supported me and pulled me out – like a needle in a haystack,” said Breland-Noble. “I then had the ability to do that for somebody else.”

Former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern said she is also grateful for the opportunity to make $20 million in donations. And she knows she took the decidedly tougher route by not making large gifts to established organizations.
“I wanted to use this funding to achieve things that otherwise may not have existed were it not for this opportunity,” she said. “That took time.”

She began working with the International Rescue Committee on a program to prevent postpartum hemorrhaging for women in areas affected by war and other humanitarian crises, where 58% of maternal mortality occurs. The resulting Safer Births in Crises Consortium now focuses on preventing the deaths of mothers in South Sudan, Burkina Faso and Papua New Guinea.

What Ardern did not anticipate was that her donations through The Matariki Fund for Women would coincide with funding cuts for international aid. As a former prime minister who previously dispatched such aid, she said she had two distinct reactions to seeing life-saving programs cut.

“One is we’ve just got to get on with it. What do we do? How can we help?” Ardern said. “And then I think about how I can advocate for the restoration. How we can lift the profile of this collective approach to voters? Because ultimately, they’re the ones that demand from their leaders that we keep having this impact.”
Ardern said she has no plans to become a full-time philanthropist. She prefers her new job at the University of Sydney as a professor, announced last month.

“I’ll be working on empathetic leadership, but I’m also attached to the School of Public Health," she said, adding that she intends to continue working on global health issues. “My view is there is absolutely a role for political leadership to rebuild trust, reduce insularity, and reduce the grievance that people feel. Actually, what’s interesting is that the public think that it’s their job too.”
Gary Barker, on the other hand, not only used the $20 million he received from French Gates to expand his philanthropic work, he used it to convince other funders to also support his nonprofit.

Barker is the founder and CEO of the Equimundo Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, which engages men and boys in promoting gender equality, and launched the Caring Masculinity Fund to distribute French Gates’ donation.

“The Minderoo Foundation in Australia looked at what Melinda funded us to do and said, ‘Would you come do the same at the country level in Australia?’,” said Barker. “Her voice saying, ‘This is worth investing in and that this is not taking funds or attention away from women and girls’ is a political boost in addition to boosting our credibility as an organization.”
Barker said the experience has made him seek similar relationships with funders.
“We don’t want to go back to piecemeal fundraising,” he said. “We’re not gonna wanna do it any differently from here on out.”
