title: Xi and Carney call for deeper ties as Canada looks beyond US for trade
summary: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
story: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
SHENZHEN, China -- The leaders of China and Canada  called for deeper ties Tuesday as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.
The meeting came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry.

“Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.”
Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” he said.
Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week
story: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.

Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.

Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.

One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.

“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.

The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.

The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.

“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.

Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.

Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.

But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.

Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.

Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.

“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.

These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.

Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
Wu reported from Bangkok.

title: A top Puerto Rico government official resigns as corruption allegations swirl
summary: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
story: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family announced Monday that she would resign by year’s end as she denied corruption allegations swirling around her.

Lawmakers in the U.S. territory had demanded for months that Suzanne Roig step down over the latest political scandal to hit the administration of Gov. Jenniffer González, which has seen several high-ranking officials resign or be fired in recent years.
Roig is under investigation by Puerto Rico’s Senate, the island’s Justice Department and its Office of the Inspector General.

In recent months, Blanca Medina Díaz, who was dismissed as head of the Administration for the Socioeconomic Development of the Family, which is within the department Roig oversees, publicly accused Roig of pressuring her to approve a nearly $40 million contract that Medina alleges was illegal and would have used federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The alleged push came after Roig and other officials visited Louisiana.
Roig and NOLA Education LLC, a Louisiana-based education company, have said that no contract was signed.
Medina, who has met with U.S. federal authorities, also accused Roig of pressuring her to approve an unrelated contract worth more than $300,000.
Roig has been under fire, as has the governor, who has publicly supported her.
Roig testified before Puerto Rico’s Senate in recent weeks as certain lawmakers who are members of the governor’s pro-statehood party called for her to step down.
Puerto Rico Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz, also a member of the governor’s New Progressive Party, has said that ongoing legislative investigations would continue even if Roig resigned.
As Roig faced increasing scrutiny, she alleged in recent months that she was being stalked and persecuted as she denied all accusations.
In a statement Monday, Roig said that nobody asked her to resign as she thanked the governor for “the time and space that allowed me to defend my reputation against attacks full of falsehoods.”
Her decision to step down on Dec. 31 angered many.

“The resignation should have been immediate,” said Puerto Rico Sen. Juan Oscar Morales, majority whip and a member of the governor’s party. “The Department of the Family needs leadership focused on addressing the agency’s problems and ensuring services for those who depend on it.”

Roig’s announcement came nearly four months after the governor’s chief of staff and deputy chief of staff announced their resignations as they, too, denied corruption allegations. The governor stood by them as she has by Roig.

title: 1.5-hour-long system outage forces United Airlines to delay departing flights
summary: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights
story: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights

A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.

United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane's final weight.

Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft's weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

“It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.”
Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety.

Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers.

In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.
United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.

A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement
story: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement

NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement.

The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers.

In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.”

But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union.
Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already.

Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said.
“We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post.

Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal.
Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely.

Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration.

“We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said.

In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later.
But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court.

title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
story: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
story: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune.

The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts.

The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.”

In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.”
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share.

The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally.

The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation.

The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation, the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile.

title: This marathoner ran 7 races this year. Doing them pregnant was not part of the plan
summary: Deirdre Keane, a 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant, achieved her goal of completing all seven World Marathon Majors
story: Deirdre Keane, a 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant, achieved her goal of completing all seven World Marathon Majors
Deirdre Keane had already run more than 60 marathons when she decided to take on a new challenge of completing the World Marathon Majors. She just didn’t expect to be running them while pregnant.

Earlier this month, the 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant ran the New York City Marathon – her hometown race – in her third trimester. It was the seventh marathon she had finished while pregnant and was the final race she needed to achieve her goal of running all the World Marathon Majors in the same year.

“I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point,” Keane said. “And while it is very unusual, I wasn’t the first woman to have ever done this.”
After getting married last year, Keane and her husband Brian began talking about starting a family. Expecting pregnancy to take a while, Keane made other plans for herself in the interim.
“In my mind, 2026 was going to be my year of bucket list items,” Keane recalled. “I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother.”
She signed up for 11 races: the seven World Marathon Majors, a trail marathon in Ireland, two ultramarathons and an Ironman race.

Keane kicked off her quest by running the Tokyo Marathon in March. But when the Boston and London Marathons rolled around in April, she noticed she was running a bit slower than usual and wasn’t quite feeling like herself. So, she took a pregnancy test.
It was positive, but she wasn’t going to let that get in the way of her goals.

She promised her husband she would take the next marathon in Ireland slowly. She also agreed to forgo the Ironman and the second ultramarathon – she had already completed the first before finding out she was pregnant.

“Brian was understandably skeptical and worried at first. Neither of us fully understood the physical limitations of pregnancy and why. The research we found was surprisingly limited and frustrating,” Keane said. “So, we decided to take it one marathon at a time, with me not pushing the pace and keeping walking in my back pocket.”
Keane was initially nervous to tell her OB-GYN about her marathon plans but was relieved when she got the go-ahead.

“I don’t think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at New York. But I am very stubborn and determined,” Keane said. “Plus I got lucky, I was feeling good. So I was able to do it.”

Exercise is generally considered safe and beneficial during most healthy pregnancies. Experts recommend that pregnant women who were physically active before pregnancy or regularly engaged in vigorous aerobic exercise can continue those activities with approval from their doctor. There is limited research on intensive exercise beyond the recommended amount.

With the approval of her doctor, Keane flew to Australia in August to compete in the Sydney Marathon at 25 weeks pregnant, followed by Berlin at 29 weeks. She then completed the Chicago Marathon at 31 weeks in just under 4 hours and finished with the New York City Marathon at 34 weeks in 4:06.55.

Keane was more worried about the race in New York “because I was starting to look heavily pregnant and feel it too." But she had friends along the course while her husband appeared at multiple spots with water to keep her hydrated.

“The marathon passed a block away from Weill Cornell at mile 16, where I’m delivering, so there were plenty of jokes about just pulling off there to have the baby or testing the medical volunteers’ training on the course with an unusual medical intervention of a delivery,” she said.
Keane’s determination was modeled for her at an early age by her father, John, an Irish immigrant who ran marathons in the 1980s and 1990s.
He died of cancer when she was 13, but continued to run in his final months, completing his final New York City Marathon one day before undergoing surgery to have a tumor removed, Keane said.
Years later, when Keane went to college, she was inspired to run a marathon in her dad’s honor. That’s when she caught the bug.

“I loved marathons from the beginning, because it really shows me what the human body is capable of, not only from a physical standpoint, but from a mental standpoint,” she said. “I realized how much grit I have and how capable I am to overcome hard things.”

Since then, running has become a constant in Keane’s life. She says it helped her cope with the emotional toll of working as a nurse practitioner at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During the pandemic, feeling isolated and needing something to look forward to, Keane signed up for the World Marathon Challenge: Running 7 marathons on 7 different continents in just 7 days. She completed the challenge in 2023 and was the fastest woman to do so that year.

Now, with the World Majors in her rearview, Keane says she’s taking time to reflect on the past 8 months. Just as she learned from her father’s example, she hopes to pass the lessons running has taught her on to her son.

“I want to teach my son resilience and that he can do hard things,” she said. “And that when life inevitably gets tough and throws challenges at him, he will push through them and see the other side of them, whether we elect to do them like a marathon or some things that are way beyond our control.”

title: South Africa beats Bangladesh on Day 5 of first cricket test after Harmer shines again
summary: Simon Harmer has run through Bangladesh’s tail and South Africa has knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first test in Johannesburg
story: Simon Harmer has run through Bangladesh’s tail and South Africa has knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first test in Johannesburg

JOHANNESBURG -- Simon Harmer ran through Bangladesh's tail and South Africa knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first test by nine wickets on Thursday, taking a 1-0 lead in the teams' two-match cricket test series.

Resuming on 100-5 at the Wanderers, Bangladesh's lower-order batters couldn't handle the off-spin of Harmer, who took four of the remaining five wickets to help dismiss the tourists for 168 and have figures of 6-51.
It revived memories of Harmer taking 6-16 on Day 5 of the series-clinching victory over Australia last month.

The Proteas lost first-innings century-maker Marques Ackerman — for a second-ball duck — on the way to reaching their target before lunch, at 12-1. Soon after getting bowled off a no-ball, Aiden Markram (8 not out) scored the winning run.
South Africa dethroned Australia for the top spot in the ICC test team rankings with that series win last month and is the reigning world test champion.

In Harmer it has a 37-year-old player enjoying a renaissance in a test career that was drifting until a year ago, when he returned after a two-and-a-half-year absence and is now a reliable match-winner.

Having already removed Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mahfijul Islam late in Day 4, Harmer took the final four wickets of the match in his brilliant four-over burst that came after overnight batter Litton Das got an inside edge and played onto his own stumps off Kagiso Rabada (3-46).
Mushfiqur Rahim added 34 runs to his overnight 5 before gloving Harmer to a close fielder, for a dismissal that was only given after the Proteas reviewed a not-out call.
In his next over, Harmer had Mehidy Hasan Miraz stumped for 4, before removing Hasan Mahmud (4) and Ebadot Hossain (0) in consecutive balls to wrap up the innings.
Despite making 400 in the first innings after winning the toss, Bangladesh barely avoided an innings defeat.
The second test is at Centurion starting on Monday, and South Africa will head into it atop the points table in the World Test Championship for 2025-27.

title: Sri Lanka reaches 167-5, still trails Pakistan by 60 runs in 2nd cricket test
summary: Pakistan seamers picked up two more wickets despite losing Saqib Khan due to a hamstring strain as Sri Lanka reached 167-5 on Day 3 of the second cricket test
story: Pakistan seamers picked up two more wickets despite losing Saqib Khan due to a hamstring strain as Sri Lanka reached 167-5 on Day 3 of the second cricket test
RAWALPINDI, Pakistan -- Pakistan seamers picked up two more wickets despite losing Saqib Khan due to a hamstring strain as Sri Lanka reached 167-5 at lunch on Day 3 of the second cricket test.
Saqib, who took a seven-wicket haul on debut last week, was ruled out for the remainder of the match after pulling up with injury in the final session on Day 2.
The Pakistan Cricket Board said Saqib was undergoing treatment under the supervision of the team’s medical staff.
Resuming on 74-3, Sri Lanka lost both the overnight batters Pasindu Sooriyabandara (38) and Dhananjaya de Silva (37) in the morning session to trail by 60 runs at the interval.
Sri Lanka’s last recognized batters Kusal Mendis (32) with Sonal Dinusha (19) were unbeaten on a green wicket where seamers still have plenty of assistance.

Sooriyabandara survived an early lbw review against Abbas and extended the partnership to 60 runs with de Silva as the pair survived the opening spell of express fast bowler Razaullah and as Abbas beat the outside edges of both batters.
Allrounder Aamer Jamal brought Pakistan a breakthrough in his first over when he had de Silva trapped lbw off a delivery that nipped back off the wicket and struck the batter on the front pad.

Jamal could have dismissed Sooriyabandara on 31 but Mohammad Talha spilled a regulation catch at first slip. Sooriyabandara couldn’t capitalize on the chance as Razaullah switched ends and had him caught behind down the leg side.
Mendis completed 5,000 career test runs with an edged boundary off Razaullah and thwarted Pakistan’s bid to run into the tailenders by adding 33 runs with Dinusha during the hour before lunch.

title: Luka Doncic calls his play 'unacceptable' as Lakers' 9-game winning streak ends
summary: Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers’ nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz
story: Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers’ nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz
LOS ANGELES -- Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers' nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz on Wednesday night.
Doncic wasn't great despite his 29 points in the Lakers' 109-97 defeat, missing 10 of his 12 3-point attempts and committing nine turnovers. His streak of 11 straight 30-point games also ended.

Although the ugly game was the culmination of a punishing stretch played mostly at less than full strength by Los Angeles, the Slovenian superstar still feels a personal responsibility when he can't will the Lakers to victory.

“Honestly, I've just got to do way better than this,” Doncic said. “This is unacceptable for my part. I've got to lead the team in better ways. Got to look at this game, got to move on and learn from this.”
The Lakers are still 13-3 and atop the Western Conference after their first loss of November was handed to them by a two-win opponent that only ended a 12-game losing streak one night earlier.

Playing without injured second-leading scorer Austin Reaves, the Lakers made only 38.2% of their shots and 27.3% of their 3-point attempts against the Jazz, both season lows. LA managed only nine 3-pointers, tying its season low.
Doncic claimed the blame, but his teammates and coaches weren’t having it.

“Of course he’s going to say that,” Jake LaRavia said. “It’s obviously not on him. It’s a team game. He’s been carrying the offensive load, so if there’s ever bad shooting nights, it’s on the rest of the team to help be better.”
All of the Lakers had an off night, but they rely heavily on Doncic, the league's top scorer during one of the best starts to a season in NBA history.

Doncic's usage rate — a statistic that estimates a player's involvement on offense — is at 40.6%, the highest in the league and the highest of his career. Doncic took 28 shots against the Jazz, and that was only tied for his fourth-highest total this season.
Lakers coach JJ Redick says he's confident Doncic's current preeminence to the Lakers' offense won't prove to be unsustainable.
“The shot creation that is required from him, I think it takes its toll,” Redick said. “That's part of it when Austin is out, for sure.”
Fatigue isn’t allowed to be a factor, Doncic said.

“All NBA teams play 82 games, so that can’t be an excuse,” Doncic said. “I’ve got to do way better, I know that. I feel like we had some open shots we didn’t make. But it’s one game. We’ve got to move on.”
Yet the culprit in this stinker against Utah was most likely the game accumulation that drags down every NBA team at times.

The loss came on the back half of a back-to-back set after the Lakers had to rally from an 18-point deficit late in the third quarter to beat Charlotte on Tuesday night. Doncic scored 37 points, but Quentin Grimes dramatically stepped up with a career-high 47, even forcing overtime with his 10th 3-pointer.

The loss to Utah was the Lakers' third game in four days without the high-scoring Reaves, who has a bruised heel, and it was their 10th game already in November. No team has played more games this season than the Lakers' 16 in the first 29 days, and their top three scorers have all missed games due to injury already.

“Frankly, if you’re playing 82 games, you’re going to have some horrible shooting nights,” Redick said. “My belief in the group and who we are, I’m not going to overreact to a bad offensive night for us.”
The Lakers host Sacramento (1-13) on Friday.

title: UConn coach Dan Hurley gets bucket-list game, but No. 12 Arizona earns 85-79 win
summary: Dan Hurley called UConn’s trip to McKale Center a bucket-list game
story: Dan Hurley called UConn’s trip to McKale Center a bucket-list game
TUCSON, Ariz. -- Dan Hurley called UConn's trip to McKale Center a bucket-list game.
It nearly turned into a Husky house of horrors.

Overwhelmed early by Arizona and the atmosphere, the third-ranked Huskies sputtered through an ugly first half that had the showdown between two of last season's Final Four teams looking like a beatdown.
Down 18 at halftime, the Huskies got back to playing UConn basketball in the second, pulling within eight before No. 12 Arizona pulled out an 85-79 victory in a game that felt like late March.
“Obviously, really disappointed, particularly the first half, just getting hit in the mouth like that. It rarely happens to us,” Hurley said. “We're usually the hammer, not the nail.”

Arizona’s student section was full 90 minutes before tipoff, cascading boos upon Hurley the moment he stepped onto the floor and giving him a dose of what makes McKale Center one of college basketball's toughest road venues.
It’s not the first time a Hurley has heard the vitriol inside this arena.
Dan’s brother, Bobby, was rival Arizona State’s coach from 2015-26 and drew the fans' ire every time he stepped on the floor or became apoplectic at a call he didn’t like.
Bobby was the better player of the brothers, winning two national championships at Duke before playing five NBA seasons.
Dan is the more accomplished coach. He won consecutive NCAA crowns and led the Huskies to last season’s title game.
Tommy Lloyd is building his own foundation at Arizona.

The longtime assistant to Gonzaga’s Mark Few led the Wildcats to at least the Sweet 16 in four of his first five seasons in Tucson, punctuated by last season's first-in-25-years run to the Final Four.
“Obviously, they’re out ahead of us with what they’ve accomplished,” Lloyd said. “That’s a program we’re looking to see if we can kind of get in their shadow a little bit, maybe, follow their lead.”

The early showdown between power programs was a rematch in a home-and-home series that started in Storrs, Connecticut, last season. Arizona won that game 71-67, though the Huskies were without big man Tarris Reed Jr.
Both teams were short-handed for the rematch.

Arizona had hoped to have forward RJ Godfrey in the lineup for the first time this season after a Pima County judge ruled him eligible for a fifth season. Instead, the drawn-out process strung out even more when the NCAA said it wouldn’t comply with the judge’s order.
UConn was without guard Solo Ball (wrist) and forward Nik Khamenia (foot).
There was still plenty of star power for UConn’s first trip to McKale Center since 2017 with Kevin Ollie as coach.
Ivan Kharchenkov and Motiejus Krivas, key cogs in Arizona's Final Four run, were the tone setters.
Kharchenkov showed off his all-around game, bullying his way into the paint and hounding UConn players with physical-without-fouling defense.
Krivas, all 7-foot-2 of him, caused UConn problems at both ends, scoring at the rim, blocking shots, pinballing Huskies in the lane.
“The guy's nasty. He's mean,” Hurley said of Krivas. “I told the guys he's like Godzilla. He ruins everything for you.”

Derek Dixon, a North Carolina transfer, added to UConn's woes by going 3 of 5 from behind the 3-point arc. The combination gave Arizona a 47-29 halftime lead and the students added insult to Hurley's injury, serenading him with an R-rated chant.
Once the second half began, the Huskies were able to silence them — some.
UConn got back to playing physical defense, a Hurley hallmark, and held Arizona without a field goal for 6 1/2 minutes.

Braylon Mullins, a Huskies hero for his game-winning shot against Duke that sent UConn to the Final Four, handled the offensive end. Running defenders ragged off screens, he pulled up for 3-pointers and repeatedly got into the lane, scoring 19 of his 29 points in the second half.
Arizona ended up pulling it out, but UConn made it much harder than expected after getting dominated in the first half.
“It was crazy, it was hectic, it was chaotic,” said Arizona freshman Caleb Holt, who had 19 points. “It was everything you dream as a kid playing a top-three team in the country.”
The brutal-but-beautiful game gave Hurley a checkmark on his bucket list. He just wishes it would have ended better.

title: Trent Perry rallies No. 7 UCLA past Cal State Fullerton 75-71 in final minutes at Pauley Pavilion
summary: Trent Perry scored 27 points, including five straight in the final two minutes to put No. 7 UCLA ahead for good, and the unbeaten Bruins escaped with a 75-71 comeback win over Cal State Fullerton
story: Trent Perry scored 27 points, including five straight in the final two minutes to put No. 7 UCLA ahead for good, and the unbeaten Bruins escaped with a 75-71 comeback win over Cal State Fullerton

LOS ANGELES -- Trent Perry scored 27 points, including five straight in the final two minutes to put No. 7 UCLA ahead for good, and the Bruins escaped with a 75-71 comeback win over Cal State Fullerton on Wednesday night.
Perry added seven rebounds and six assists in 37 minutes to carry the ailing Bruins (5-0), who were favored by more than 30 points at Pauley Pavilion.
UCLA coach Mick Cronin said several of his players were ill, including top freshman Nikola Kusturica. He was limited to seven points, eight rebounds and five assists in 29 minutes.

After opening the season with a neutral-site victory over then-No. 5 Arizona and winning their first four games by an average of 42 points, the Bruins got all they could handle from the fast and feisty Titans (2-2).
UCLA shot just 37% from the field, including 4 for 28 (14%) on 3-pointers.
Christian Williams scored 23 points and Anthony Ponga added 18 for Cal State Fullerton, which went 12 of 33 (36%) from beyond the arc. Joshua Ward had 15 points, seven rebounds and five assists.
Cal State Fullerton led 70-66 before Perry drained a 3 with 1:38 remaining and then scored on a driving layup with 1:09 left to put the Bruins in front by one.
Williams missed a 3 at the other end and Ward came up short on a contested fast-break layup attempt with 8 seconds to go.
Jaylen Petty sank two free throws for UCLA before Williams made one of two, and Perry sealed it with a pair of foul shots.
Eric Dailey Jr. finished with 10 points for the Bruins, who led 40-35 at halftime.
Cal State Fullerton, from the Big West Conference, has two wins over UCLA. The most recent one came in 2019, Cronin’s first season in Westwood.
Cal State Fullerton plays Sunday at Portland State.
UCLA hosts Delaware on Sunday, its fourth consecutive home game.

title: Mullin, appearing before Congress, defends his flight to LSU-Texas game after nationwide ground stop
summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is defending his flight to a football game during a nationwide flight grounding
story: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is defending his flight to a football game during a nationwide flight grounding

WASHINGTON -- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended before a House committee Wednesday his flight to a weekend LSU-Texas football game as travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights, saying canceling it could have caused confusion.

Mullin spoke at a congressional hearing about threats facing the country at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the college football game.

The hearing in front of the House Homeland Security Committee is a standard yearly opportunity for members of Congress to grill top administration officials over national security threats. But it comes as the U.S. has faced a series of cyber and technology problems that have left Americans feeling vulnerable.

The hearing is also the first opportunity for Democrats after their midterm drubbing of Republicans to grill the Cabinet official who is key to President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. Two others facing questioning are FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton.
The secretary has faced scrutiny over his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday to watch the LSU-Texas game.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.
Mullin said the trip had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and that there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin had said Tuesday and reiterated Wednesday that he is required to fly on government planes and that he personally paid for the trip.

Mullin, whose department includes the agency tasked with protecting the country's cyber infrastructure, was front and center in the Republican administration's response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The Trump administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.
At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn't giving the American public clear answers.

“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success," Mullin said.

During a news conference Friday with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at the White House, he pushed for more funding for the aging air traffic control system while also assuring the public that the government was not seeing any signs of a deliberate cyberattack.

The Trump administration has been attempting to offer reassurances about a spate of outages over the last week that have affected everything from Microsoft and the Federal Aviation Administration to the banking industry, United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration national security officials have said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.

Clayton told the committee Wednesday that the outages are “not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Instead, they appear to be “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

Mullin's sprawling Department of Homeland Security also includes an agency designed to play a central role in the federal government's response to cyber incidents. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

But CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump's original pick to lead the agency withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it languished for months in the Senate.
CISA also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the federal government.

Mullin, whose department includes Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, faced questions over the Republican president's immigration agenda at a time when Democrats are vowing rigorous oversight of everything from immigration detention contracts to the use of force by ICE officers.

Trump has indicated he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions over how easily compromise could be reached on the issue.

Mullin took over from ousted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March after the killing of two American citizen protesters in Minneapolis at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies across the country.
Associated Press writers Eric Tucker in Washington, Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pennsylvania and Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed to this report.

title: Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
summary: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence
story: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen "human" as its word of the year, reflecting concerns about artificial intelligence
LONDON -- Fears of artificial intelligence inspired the Cambridge Dictionary to flip back to the 15th century for the word that best captures the 2026 cultural zeitgeist.
“Human,” the dictionary's word of the year, is not just a throwback but also a backlash of sorts that reflects the debate over how AI has blurred the lines between machines and people.

“AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children."

The adjective derived from the Latin “humanus” and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”
Dictionaries typically choose a novel word — sometimes slang that has crossed into the mainstream — or an existing word that has taken on a new meaning.
Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years.

“AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to the tendency of AI to fabricate information. Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its word of the year for low quality content produced by AI while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method.

“AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has promoted the smart use of AI, said in a comment on the Cambridge Dictionary selection. "The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”

Other word contenders for 2026 included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.
