Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on issues such as AI safety and the company's broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said.

The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company," he said. "If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.”

As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly.
The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic's corporate structure, Gadinis said.

“I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community," he said.

title: Fans cheer as popular online platform for spinoff stories nears full return after security incident
summary: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29
story: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29

In a comeback tale like one from Harry Potter battling back his nemesis or a “Heated Rivalry” hockey hero rebounding from injury, a top global fandom site that was sidelined by a security incident is now on the mend.

The activist group behind the popular Archive of Our Own, or AO3, platform, a collaborative online space which serves up fans’ spinoff narratives derived from well-known published stories, says it’s undergoing a limited return after a shutdown on Oct. 29.
“AO3 is now up!” said a status page for the Organization for Transformative Works, an activist group behind the platform, on Sunday.

The outage sent fans of the platform — readers and authors alike — into a desperate void for the past two weeks with a “Bad Gateway” message stirring frustration. The return drew many expressions of joy Sunday.

The organization, in a summary it posted on Instagram of its 2025 results, said nearly 2.6 million AO3 works were created, with nearly 40 billion page views. Nearly 2 million accounts have been created, it said.
AO3 hasn't been without its critics, who have warned about sexual content that could be available to minors and fandom racism through the platform.

The group said some features like user icons have been disabled and importing of external work isn’t available, while downloads are currently only possible in the web-language HTML format. It promised those features will ultimately return.

The team predicted that the security incident would take up to four weeks for AO3 to get back up, while floating the prospect of a partial revival “in a degraded state” — which appears to be what was taking place on Sunday.

The organization said contributors’ “works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are still safe” and that no drafts were deleted during the outage — but it couldn’t rule out that the user database might have been compromised.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the status update said.

AO3 is a hub of content from fans who have produced content that riffs off fiction, art and other culture and entertainment: Imagine a repository of sequels, prequels and derivatives dreamt up by adoring aficionados of some of the world’s best-known titles.
The result is catchy products like “fanfic” — fiction from fans — and similar fanart, as well as “podfics,” readings of narratives shared in audio form.

A recent listing of “ship stats” — or the number of references to relationships of stars from literature — shows that pairings of characters featured in the Harry Potter, Heated Rivalry and anime fandoms were the most prominent this summer.
The reaction from fans of the fandom platform was swift and exuberant.
“So, we've all agreed we don't need to sleep tonight, now that AO3 is finally back, right? Right!?” quipped yet.another.loon on the Threads social media site.
User Verkielos gushed: “Just got email from AO3 about a fic update. The world is healing!”
Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025, company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout
summary: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.
story: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.
Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn't matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. He said his concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.

“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel's “Sunday Morning Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”
Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”
Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.
An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.
As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.
In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
story: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.

Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.

The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.

Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.

The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”

The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.

At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.

Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.

Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

title: Southeast Asian leaders, with US and Chinese counterparts, will renew alarm over online scams
summary: Southeast Asian leaders and key counterparts, including from the U.S. and China, are raising alarms over online scams
story: Southeast Asian leaders and key counterparts, including from the U.S. and China, are raising alarms over online scams

MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders and their key counterparts, including from the United States and China, will renew their alarm over the escalating threat of online scams, according to a draft statement seen by The Associated Press on Friday.

Such transnational crimes, which have swindled billions of dollars from people in Asia to the United States and elsewhere, will be high in the agenda when leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gather in an annual summit with their Asian and Western counterparts on Tuesday in the Philippine capital.

The Philippines currently holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, an 11-nation bloc in a poverty-stricken region where criminal groups have used technology and resorted to human trafficking to expand their illicit and lucrative operations to other parts of the world.

The leaders of the expanded ASEAN bloc, called the East Asia Summit, will express their “grave concern over the escalating threat posed by transnational criminal organizations inflicting harm through online scams, including those originating from scam center operations and associated criminal conduct such as human trafficking,” according to a draft of their joint statement to be issued after their summit.

They acknowledged “the exploitation of digital and other advanced technologies and digital financial platforms, by increasingly sophisticated criminal actors and the need to strengthen financial and digital systems, as well as the severe human consequences associated with scam centers.”

Authorities in Southeast Asia have reported in recent years how large numbers of workers, who were lured by recruitment syndicates into working in online scam centers, including in the Philippines and Cambodia, have been subjected to threats and even torture when they tried to escape or defy orders.

Aside from sharing of information and strengthening law enforcement coordination, the leaders will encourage “the sharing of threat assessments and best practices" as well as strengthening cooperation between relevant authorities in dismantling scam centers, the leaders said in their draft statement, without elaborating.

In July, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime reported how Southeast Asia-based criminal groups have increasingly used integrated networks and technology to expand to other regions. The scams caused estimated combined losses of $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025, according to the report.
Criminals are using new technologies to launder money through global financial systems and using artificial intelligence to steal from victims worldwide, the U.N. report said.

East Asian crime syndicates are running businesses that use malware, generative AI and deepfakes for sexual extortion and exploitation in a trend that increases the risks of in-person as well as livestreamed abuse. Apart from outright trafficking for the sex industry, victims can be sold into domestic servitude, forced begging and forced labor, among other forms of exploitation, the report said.

The East Asia Summit leaders meeting in Manila will underscore “the need to address underlying drivers and other related factors of online scams," such as poverty, lack of social protection interventions, outdated domestic laws, private and public coordination gaps, corruption and limited economic opportunities.
They will stress that government responses to online scams must be consistent with international law and respect human rights.

title: Trump-Putin-Xi meeting updates: Leaders at historic summit chart 'different course'
summary: Trump participated on Thursday in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
story: Trump participated Thursday in a first-ever trilateral talk with Putin and Xi.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
ABC News will have special coverage of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting led by "World News Tonight" anchor David Muir, who will be anchoring from Shenzhen, China, across programs and platforms.
Muir will anchor "World News Tonight" from China on Thursday, Nov. 19.
Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce and White House correspondent Karen Travers will also be reporting from China.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

1 hour and 6 minutes agoXi says China-US-Russia meeting was 'fruitful'2 hours and 2 minutes agoTrump departs China aboard Air Force One2 hours and 7 minutes ago'Good' Trump-Putin bilateral meeting focused on Ukraine, Kremlin aide says2 hours and 21 minutes agoXi says US must do 'the right thing' on Taiwan to avoid 'turbulence'2 hours and 33 minutes agoTrump-Xi-Putin talks conclude
1 hour and 6 minutes agoXi says China-US-Russia meeting was 'fruitful'
2 hours and 2 minutes agoTrump departs China aboard Air Force One
2 hours and 7 minutes ago'Good' Trump-Putin bilateral meeting focused on Ukraine, Kremlin aide says
2 hours and 21 minutes agoXi says US must do 'the right thing' on Taiwan to avoid 'turbulence'
2 hours and 33 minutes agoTrump-Xi-Putin talks conclude
Xi says China-US-Russia meeting was 'fruitful'
China's state-run Xinhua News Agency said President Xi Jinping described Thursday's meeting with President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin as "positive, constructive and fruitful."
The outlet characterized Xi's description, but did not directly quote him.
-ABC News' Karson Yiu
Trump departs China aboard Air Force One

President Donald Trump received a send-off from China full of fanfare after his historic trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the first such sit-down between the leaders of the three nations.

The red carpet was rolled out on the tarmac, flanked by an honor guard and a live band playing. The president shook hands and conversed briefly with officials before boarding Air Force One at 5:35 a.m. ET. He turned to give a wave and fist-pumps before disappearing into the cabin.
Xi did not personally go to the airport to say farewell. The Chinese leader greeted Trump on his arrival on Wednesday.
-ABC News’ Emily Chang and Fritz Farrow
'Good' Trump-Putin bilateral meeting focused on Ukraine, Kremlin aide says

President Donald Trump on Thursday met with Russian President Vladimir Putin for a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, prior to the two leaders' trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As the trilateral meeting began, Trump said he and Putin had had a "long discussion today," including talking about Russia's war with Ukraine.
"I think things are happening. I think that he -- and I hope the other side -- would like to see an end to that war," Trump said.
Trump later met privately with Xi, before the three leaders sat down together.
Entering the room with Putin earlier, Trump said, "Who is he? He is my friend," in reference to Putin. The two leaders then shook hands.

"We look forward to our meeting," Trump told reporters in the room. "We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this or at least start, but I think they’ll come out of this."

Speaking to Russian state media after the meeting, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the talks lasted around 40 minutes. "It was a good meeting. We discussed preparations for the trilateral summit, as well as some issues concerning our bilateral relations. And, of course, we directly addressed the settlement of the Ukrainian conflict," Ushakov said.
Asked whether Ukraine was the main topic of the meeting, Ushakov said, "You could say that, yes."
-ABC News' Charlotte Gardiner, Tanya Stukalova and Anna Sergeeva
Xi says US must do 'the right thing' on Taiwan to avoid 'turbulence'

Chinese President Xi Jinping used his meeting with President Donald Trump in Shenzhen to urge bilateral cooperation on issues including AI, but also warned against the creation of "turbulence" over the issue of Taiwan.
Xi talked up cooperation on AI, saying the two countries should coordinate on AI safety and to keep the technology "under human control."

On Taiwan -- the independent island nation that Beijing considers a wayward Chinese province and that Chinese leaders, Xi among them, have vowed to take control of -- Xi said the U.S. should avoid anything that might cause setbacks in bilateral ties.

"On the Taiwan issue, the United States must keep doing the right thing to avoid the emergence of great turbulence in the China-U.S. relationship," Xi said, as quoted by the state-run Xinhua News Agency.
-ABC News’ Britt Clennett

title: Crimean bridge attacked for 3rd time in a week, officials say
summary: The Crimean bridge came under attack again overnight, according to Russian-aligned officials on the occupied peninsula, prompting the closure of the bridge to traffic.
story: An attack earlier this week collapsed part of the structure, Kyiv said.
LONDON -- The Crimean bridge came under attack again overnight, according to Russian-aligned officials on the occupied peninsula, prompting the closure of the structure to traffic.

The latest strike was the third attack on the bridge in the past week. The structure -- which consists of a roadway and railway -- connects Crimea to the southwestern Russian region of Krasnodar Krai and stands as the prime symbol of Russia's control of the peninsula, which it seized from Ukraine in 2014.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed in a statement that its forces struck the bridge with Neptune missiles on Wednesday night, claiming to have inflicted damage to the railway tracks spanning the structure.

Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian-appointed head of Crimea, said in a post to Telegram, "As a result of another attack on the Crimean bridge, traffic has been temporarily suspended. All responsible services are at their workstations. An assessment of the damage caused is underway."

Russia's Transport Ministry said in a statement on Thursday morning that train traffic across the bridge was "temporarily suspended" due to "last night's drone attack." It added, "There are no casualties as a result of the incident. Specialists are assessing the damage."

Earlier this week, a combined Ukrainian drone and missile attack collapsed part of the bridge, according to Ukrainian officials and the military in Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as "unprecedented" and retaliation for Moscow's targeting of bridges in Ukraine.

The latest Ukrainian attack on the bridge came just before the trilateral meeting of President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

Ukrainian forces have regularly attacked the structure since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Beyond its potent symbolic value, the structure also forms a key supply route for Russian forces stationed in Crimea.
A Ukrainian attack was also reported in the Republic of Tatarstan overnight, where regional officials told the state-run Tass news agency that oil storage tanks near the city of Almetyevsk were hit.

Russia's Defense Ministry said Thursday morning that its forces shot down at least 53 Ukrainian drones overnight, with craft intercepted over the Belgorod, Voronezh, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk and Tula regions, plus the Republic of Tatarstan.

Ukraine's air force, meanwhile, said Russia launched 98 drones, of which 61 were jet-powered, into the country overnight, along with an unspecified number of anti-ship missiles. Defenders downed or suppressed 69 drones, of which 48 were jet-powered, the air force said. Impacts were reported across 18 locations, it added.

title: Walmart raises its outlook for the year for the 3rd time after a solid quarter
summary: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices
story: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices

NEW YORK -- Walmart reported solid third quarter sales gains as the retailer continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum that are seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices.

The company topped Wall Street’s profit and sales projections and it raised its annual guidance for the third time this year, but the outlook released Thursday was more conservative than industry analysts had expected.

Comparable sales, which include digital channels and stores, rose 2.9%. That is better than last quarter's 2.6% increase, when Walmart reported its weakest comparable sales growth in six years. But it's still a slowdown from the 4.5% growth registered during the same period last year.
Shares rose nearly 1% before the opening bell Thursday.
“We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” Walmart's CEO John Furner said in prepared remarks.

Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers use its website or visit its stores every week, according to Walmart. Analysts look to the massive retailer for clues about what to expect from the industry as a whole during the critical holiday shopping season.

Consumers in the U.S. have remained resilient in the face of painful inflation, but they have also grown more selective about what they buy. Many rely on retailers like Walmart as a one-stop shop for low-priced household goods, groceries and pharmaceuticals.

The latest U.S. retail sales data revealed that shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as Americans pulled back on a variety of purchases, from cars, clothing and furniture and even their own hobbies.
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to Commerce Department data released this week.
Walmart has been hammering its low price message while refining its store label fashion brands like Scoop and Free Assembly.

Walmart is also trying to increase subscriptions to its shipping programs. During the third quarter, Walmart launched a combined Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus annual membership bundle for $120 per year. The package saves shoppers nearly $100 compared to buying both plans separately, it said.

Walmart, based in Bentonville, Arkansas, has begun to capture a larger share of wealthier consumers. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart have been coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000, the retailer has said.

Walmart’s quarterly net income was $4.94 billion, or 62 cents per share, in the three-month period ended Oct. 31. Adjusted per-share results were 65 cents, higher than the 64 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet. In the year-ago quarter, the company earned $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share.
Sales rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion in the latest quarter. Analysts were predicting $187.38 billion, according to FactSet.

The company said that comparable sales were driven by groceries and general merchandise categories like furniture and toys. But the figure was once again hit by federal legislation that requires pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said.
Global e-commerce sales rose 17%, while U.S. e-commerce sales increased 23% during the latest quarter.
Walmart said that more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders are being fulfilled from stores, including its third party marketplace orders.

For the full year, Walmart now projects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.84 to $2.89, up from the prior guidance of $2.80 to $2.87. Sales should be up anywhere from 4.9% to 5.2%, up from the prior forecast of 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $748.12 billion to $750.25 billion, according to FactSet.
Analysts expected $2.89 per share and sales of $752.68 billion for the year, according to FactSet.

title: In historic move, House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
summary: Hakeem Jeffries is set to become the first Black speaker of the House.
story: Hakeem Jeffries is set to become the first Black speaker of the House.
Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is set to make history after House Democrats on Wednesday nominated him to become the first Black speaker of the House.

Jeffries is poised to take Speaker Mike Johnson's gavel after a blue wave swept Jeffries' party to majority control of both chambers of Congress. The Brooklyn native, 56, has served as House minority leader since 2023.

House Democrats voted Wednesday behind closed doors. Jeffries requested a recorded vote -- though it was a secret ballot. Multiple sources in the room say that 262 ballots were cast for Jeffries: 251 yes votes and 11 no votes.

Seven of the 11 no votes came from progressive Democrats: Reps. Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez. The group said in a statement that "there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."

Democratic member-elect Don Leonard confirmed on social media that he is one of the 11 Democrats who voted no for Jeffries, saying he would "continue fighting for our anti-corruption agenda." Leonard shared a screenshot of a "no" vote in the mobile app used in the elections. Another member-elect, Angela Gonzales-Torres said in a social media post that she also voted no on Jeffries during the closed-door leadership elections because she said her constituents are “demanding transformative change."
Jeffries is one step closer to clinching the gavel. To become speaker, Jeffries still needs to secure 218 votes on the House floor in January when Democrats are set to hold the majority.
It's also not yet clear whether the no votes on Wednesday will vote against Jeffries for speaker during the floor vote in January.

House Democrats made other historic leadership choices on Wednesday. House Democrats posted on social media that Rep. Katherine Clark was elected to serve as the majority leader, making her the first woman to fill the role; Rep. Pete Aguilar was elected to serve as the next majority whip, becoming the first Latino majority whip in American history; Rep. Ted Lieu was elected as caucus chair, making him the highest-ranking Asian American House member ever.
Jeffries said the economy would be a central focus for House Democrats under his leadership.

"Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one: We hear you. We see you. We feel you -- and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," Jeffries said at a press conference Wednesday afternoon.
He said that House Democrats would fight for every American and that they would challenge the status quo.

"We're committed to delivering in a meaningful way the type of change that the American people deserve so that everyone in this country can live an affordable life, a comfortable life, and a good life," Jeffries added.
Upon securing the nomination, Jeffries posted a photo of himself as a child and thanked his House colleagues.

Asked by ABC News what he would tell the young boy in that photo, Jeffries, who doesn't often talk about his upcoming place in history, spoke about "trailblazer" Rep. Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman elected to Congress.

"I was raised in a working-class neighborhood in Crown Heights during the first 12 years of my life. My congresswoman, though I never met her, was Shirley Chisholm, a trailblazer extraordinaire, and part of the journey that all of us are on is that we recognize we stand on the shoulders of so many giants, and that young man was someone who was being so effectively represented by Shirley Chisholm, and now he has an opportunity, all of us, to try to do the same for the children of America at such a time as this," Jeffries said.

A descendant of enslaved people, Jeffries was born in Brooklyn and attended New York City public schools. He earned a bachelor's degree in political science from the State University of New York at Binghamton and a Master's in public policy from Georgetown University. He earned his law degree from the New York University School of Law.

After clerking for Judge Harold Baer Jr. in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, he practiced law for several years at Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP and served as counsel in the litigation department of Viacom Inc. and CBS.

With Democrats having delivered historic midterm victories, Jeffries now faces heightened expectations from voters and newly elected Democratic representatives to swiftly address the country's affordability crisis -- and to hold the Trump administration accountable.
Jeffries will take the gavel with a more than-80-seat margin.

"In the new Congress, we will aggressively fight for an affordable America. Life is way too expensive, and millions of hardworking taxpayers are drowning in this failed economy," Jeffries wrote in a letter announcing his bid for 57th speaker on Nov. 4, the day after the election. "The era of MAGA extremism is coming to a crashing end."

As speaker, Jeffries will hold near-historic power over the House, with a far greater majority than the two-vote one Johnson had to work with for the past two years. On Tuesday, Jeffries said Democrats will "take nothing for granted" ahead of the leadership elections.

Jeffries succeeded former Speaker Nancy Pelosi as leader of the caucus in January 2023, making him the first Black to lead either party in Congress after Republicans took control of the House in the 2022 midterms.
Pelosi congratulated Jeffries on winning the nomination on Wednesday, posting a photo of them on the House floor together.
On election night, Jeffries centered his celebratory remarks on a list of legislative ambitions to make life more affordable, saying that "today begins the great American comeback."

"The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption," Jeffries said. "They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January."
ABC News' Sarah Beth Hensley contributed to this report.

title: Trump admin says it's weighing new penalties against China over jailed Americans
summary: Beijing has shut down attempts to open negotiations, officials say.
story: Beijing has shut down attempts to open negotiations, officials say.

As President Donald Trump makes a high-stakes visit to China, U.S. officials told ABC News his administration says it's evaluating options aimed at pressuring Beijing to free two American citizens wrongfully detained in the country on allegations of espionage.

Trump has raised the cases of Youlin Chen, a Boston-based seismologist, and Min Zin, a doctoral candidate at University of California, Berkeley, in previous engagements with China’s President Xi Jinping, but the Chinese government has not seriously engaged in any negotiations for their release, according to the officials.

A likely next move would be elevating the State Department’s travel advisory level for China, a diplomatic consequence that can have chilling effect on travel and tourism, U.S. officials told ABC News.

A significantly more severe penalty would be designating China as a State Sponsor of Wrongful Detention, a measure that opens up a range of punitive measures the U.S. government can opt to employ, including financial sanctions and visa restrictions. The officials did not indicate the administration was ready to take that step yet, but said the option remains on the table.
The officials also said the administration would likely wait to take any action until sometime after the president returns from Asia, in order to give talks space to progress.

“We do not preview potential designations or changes to travel advisories,” a State Department spokesman said. “We will continue to evaluate the risks facing Americans in China and take appropriate steps to protect U.S. citizens.”

The president indicated earlier this month he intended to talk to Xi about Americans detained in China during their meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China on Thursday.
“I do talk to him about that a lot. And we've done well,” Trump told reporters on Nov. 6 in West Palm Beach, Florida.

The State Department added a wrongful detention risk indicator to its travel advisory for mainland China in October, a move one official said was intended to both alert Americans to potential danger and warn Beijing that additional repercussions were on the horizon.

China’s foreign ministry has repeatedly rejected the State Department’s determination that Chen and Zin and wrongfully detained and maintains that Chinese judicial authorities are handling the cases in accordance with the country’s laws.

Under China’s sweeping national security laws, routine research and data collection may be interpreted as a threat to the country’s interests – putting academics at greater risk of wrongful detention, according to the State Department.
Critics of the Chinese government also say that its national security laws enable the Chinese Communist Party to target foreign nationals involved with topics it deems politically sensitive.

The policy is seemingly at odds with Beijing’s push to expand tourism and academic exchanges with foreign institutions, including those in the U.S. Following a visit to Washington in September, Xi announced a new initiative to invite 100,000 young Americans to study in China over five years.
The U.S. government has determined that the allegations against both Chen and Zin are meritless and classified both men as wrongfully detained.
Chen was detained in 2024 by state security agents during a trip to visit family members in China. Authorities charged him with espionage and are currently holding him in pre-trial detention.
Zin traveled to China to attend an academic conference at Beijing’s invitation in June. Upon his arrival, he was arrested on suspicion of engaging in espionage. He has not yet been formally charged.

While Chen and Zin are the only Americans officially labeled as wrongfully detained by the Chinese government, experts estimate that dozens of Americans in China are subject to exit bans or other coercive measures that limit their ability to leave the country.
Trump is expected to meet face-to-face with Xi at least one more time this year when G20 leaders gather in Miami for the group’s annual summit in December.

“I’ve been assured that President Trump remains firmly committed to securing Youlin’s freedom and that he intends to raise Youlin’s case with President Xi at both the APEC meeting and, if needed, the G20,” Chen’s wife, Yufang Chen, said in a statement to ABC News.
“We all know that when President Trump gets involved, Americans come home,” she added.
Sylvia Zin, Min Zin’s wife, told ABC News she recently learned her husband was hospitalized last month for severe dehydration and that there is no heat at the location where he is being held.

"My worry for my husband's health and wellbeing increases with each passing day,” she said in a statement. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays."
An ABC News request to the Chinese Embassy for comment on Zin’s status and medical condition did not immediately receive a response.

title: House Dems' bill would establish a 10-year expiration on final orders of removal
summary: House Democrats told ABC News they will introduce legislation that would provide relief to some immigrants who have final orders of removal but no criminal record.
story: The legislation would also create a pathway to lawful permanent residency.

House Democrats will introduce legislation on Thursday that would provide relief to some immigrants who have final orders of removal but no criminal record, and create a pathway for them to obtain legal permanent residency.

This comes after President Trump told CBS News’ “60 Minutes” that he would “love to do something on immigration” with Democrats, who will take control of both houses of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections.

A final order of removal is issued by an immigration judge or immigration authorities and requires a noncitizen to leave the country or be deported. It becomes final once the person’s administrative appeals are exhausted or the deadline to appeal has passed.
The bill, titled the “Protect Our Neighbors Act," was shared first with ABC News and will be introduced by California Democratic Rep. Lateefah Simon.

Under this proposal, final orders of removal would expire 10 years after they were issued for individuals who have been continuously present in the U.S. and have not been convicted of a crime. As of now, there is no expiration on final orders of removal.

The bill would allow an immigration judge to renew an expired final order of removal if it was established by "clear and convincing evidence" that there was significant cause for the delay in executing a final order unrelated to administrative or funding delays and renewal of the order is in the public interest based on new evidence, according to the bill's text.

While a final removal order gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement the legal authority to deport an individual, it does not mean deportation happens instantly or automatically -- removal can be delayed or suspended through the government deferring action, a stay of removal, ongoing litigation or other circumstances.
Former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons told lawmakers in February that there were about 1.6  million people in the U.S. who have final deportation orders.

The legislation would also create a pathway to lawful permanent residency for individuals with expired orders of removal. It's co-sponsored by California Democratic Reps. John Garamendi, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas.

While Democrats are introducing the bill during the lame-duck session, it is unlikely that this bill will be taken up before the end of the year. But it could reemerge on the agenda next year after Democrats take control and are empowered to send legislation to the floor for votes.
Trump’s openness to an immigration deal, however, doesn’t guarantee he would back this measure.
The bill was inspired by the case of Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old grandmother who had lived in the San Francisco Bay Area for three decades before she was deported to India.

In September 2025, Kaur was unexpectedly detained during a routine check-in with ICE. Her attorney said then that she had been checking in with ICE regularly while under a final order of removal and had received authorization to work legally in the U.S.
ICE has said that an immigration judge ordered her removed in 2005.

Kaur worked as a seamstress in Simon's district. In an interview with ABC News, the freshman congresswoman expressed optimism in bipartisan support for her bill and said she has spoken to Democratic leadership about it.

"If you have deportation orders that have been in place for over 10 years, and you continue to do everything right, those deportation orders need to be again turned off, and you need to be able to be in line with other folks to get your green card to continue being a hardworking resident of these communities and hopefully a citizen," Simon said.

Garamendi worked on Kaur's case when she was detained, and after she was deported to India, he dedicated his guest seat to her at Trump's State of the Union address last February and left it empty in protest.

"President Trump promised to go after the 'worst of the worst' in his immigration policy. Yet his administration has repeatedly decided to cruelly deport residents who have been working, paying taxes, and raising families in their communities for decades," Garamendi told ABC News in a statement.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE have expanded enforcement in Trump's second administration against individuals with final orders of removal, including through deportations to third countries. Individuals who have routinely appeared for required immigration check-ins now face renewed risk of detention and deportation.

Kaur's family told ABC News in a statement, "The pain that we still feel today remains with the knowledge that Harjit is one of thousands who've experienced the same situation. We thank the members of Congress for their continued advocacy, and we hope that some good could come from Harjit's story with this bill and others like it."

title: Judge extends temporary restraining order that blocks construction of Trump's arch
summary: The original order was set to expire on Thursday.
story: The original order was set to expire on Thursday.

A federal judge on Wednesday extended for 14 days her temporary restraining order that blocks construction of the Trump administration’s planned 250-foot-high triumphal arch in front of Arlington National Cemetery.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan’s original 14-day order was set to expire on Thursday.

Chutkan had granted the Washington, D.C., and Virginia’s request to delay the project earlier this month just hours after a federal panel led by Trump appointees voted to give final approval to the 250-foot-high arch.
In her Wednesday order extending the construction pause for two more weeks, Chutkan indicated she needed more time to consider the plaintiffs’ ask for a preliminary injunction.
ABC News has reached out to the White House for comment.

The president said in September on his social media platform that the arch was being built for national security purposes at the Pentagon's request, claiming that it would also be used as a "top-grade Military Complex." The Pentagon declined to comment at the time on the president's claim in response to an ABC News request.
Chutkan in her opinion earlier this month for the original order questioned the administration’s arguments for the arch, including its proposed national security uses.

"The court appreciates the government’s significant interest in national security," Chutkan wrote. "But these recent and unsupported attestations of security aspects of a structure that has been extensively discussed over the last year appear nowhere in the planning documents on which the project was reviewed and approved. Indeed, they materialized, for the first time, when Defendants filed their opposition brief last week."

Nine members of the Kennedy family sued in federal court last week to block the arch, which already faced lawsuits from the D.C. and Virginia attorneys general, three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian.
The Kennedy family’s suit argues in part that the arch would cast shadows over Kennedy family gravesites, including that of former President John F. Kennedy.
"This action is about protecting sacred spaces that belong to the American people," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement released on behalf of the family.

The family's lawsuit centers around their concerns that construction of the proposed arch -- which they note would be as tall as a 25-story office building -- would obstruct sight-lines of the family gravesite as well as "permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women" in the cemetery.
The proposed arch would be more than twice as tall as the 99-foot-high Lincoln Memorial and taller than France's Arc de Triomphe.

title: Hochul demands information from ICE about new immigration tent facility for women
summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul is demanding information from ICE and a Virginia-based construction company about a new tent immigration detention facility set to house women.
story: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul is demanding information from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and a Virginia-based construction company about a new tent immigration detention facility set to house women.
In letters released Wednesday by Hochul, two New York state agencies are pressing for information on the soft-sided facility in Batavia, New York.
The site is an addition to the Buffalo Service Processing Center, which is the largest immigration detention center in New York and currently only holds men.

According to the letters released by Hochul, the tent facility in New York is set to house up to 100 women. The detention center is being constructed by the firm Akima Infrastructure Protection amid the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown.

In the letter, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and the state's Department of Health pointed to federal laws to argue that ICE failed to coordinate or conduct proper environmental consultations and public notifications before construction began.
The New York state agencies requested a response by next week to questions about facility conditions, medical care, food and construction.
In a statement to ABC News, a spokesperson for DHS said it "should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space."

"ICE is targeting criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, gang members and more," the spokesperson said. "Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, ICE has new funding to expand detention space to keep these criminals off American streets before they are removed for good from our communities."

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony on Capitol Hill Wednesday, was pressed by Democratic Rep. Timothy Kennedy about the expansion of the Batavia facility, which is located in Kennedy's district.

"Over 70% of the detainees at the Batavia Federal Detention Facility have never been convicted of a crime, yet they’re detained," Kennedy said. "This is not a facility in need of a billion-and-a-half-dollar facelift."

Mullin responded that "we could save all that money" if the administration could house immigrant detainees in the state's prison and jails -- "but because of your sanctuary policies, you're not allowed to work with us," Mullin said, referring to state policy that limits cooperation with federal authorities on immigration enforcement.

In documents previously released by New York lawmakers last month, Mullin said in a letter that the contract supports the Buffalo area through "the expansion and provision of detention services for illegal aliens."
Mullin said in his letter that the tent facility is expected to cost about $8.7 million.
The letters released by Hochul on Wednesday follow concerns raised by lawmakers and immigrant advocates about conditions at other soft-sided facilities.

The facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," a soft-sided detention center in Florida, was closed earlier this year following lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers. When the closure was announced, Florida and ICE officials said the facility was meant to be temporary.
An inspector general report in September found that some detainees at the Florida facility were confined to small metal enclosures, presenting "significant risks" to their health and safety.

The largest immigration detention center in the U.S., Camp East Montana in Texas, is also a soft-sided facility. Human rights organizations and advocacy groups have raised concerns and have filed lawsuits alleging detainees face medical neglect, a lack of adequate food and water, and prolonged confinement in windowless tents.

"Federal oversight agencies have documented unsanitary conditions, gaps in medical services, and deficiencies with clean water access at tent immigration detention facilities in Texas and Florida," wrote the commissioners of the two New York agencies.

title: Congressional Republicans push Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia
summary: Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee
story: GOP Sen. Tim Scott sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify.

House and Senate Republican leaders are demanding answers from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and whether that relationship may have influenced business dealings involving Nvidia and China.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee. It comes after Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," said Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer.
It's not yet clear when Lutnick will appear before the committee.
The committee is requesting Huang to appear on Dec. 3 with Chairman Scott threatening to subpoena Huang if he fails to voluntarily appear in front of the committee.
Meanwhile, top House Republicans have asked Huang to come in for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 as the two sides have been in active negotiations.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford and Select Committee on Chairman John Moolenaar requested a written confirmation of Huang’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, under threat of subpoena.

"Failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing. Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony,” Thursday’s letter to Huang states.

Mast, Crawford and Moolenaar wrote in a statement that as "reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and Megaspeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately."

The three chairmen also asked Nvidia’s General Counsel Tim Teter to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 2 "regarding AI chip smuggling, adversary military use of NVIDIA products, and recent public reporters regarding NVIDIA’s interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving Megaspeed." Republicans requested a written confirmation of Teter’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, saying they will issue a subpoena if they do not.

The requests for both men to testify come amid growing concern over potential Chinese espionage and whether any protocols at the Commerce Department were broken in their oversight of Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

Lutnick is being accused of delaying placing Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia and Alice Huang's employer, on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, even as U.S. intelligence indicated that Megaspeed may have been diverting purchased Nvidia chips to China, something the company denies.

"Well, I want to wait and see if the allegations are true and what he has to say about it. But I'd be concerned. You know, the rumors are very concerning. The reporting is very concerning about it,” Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer told reporters on Thursday.
Republican Sen. John Curtis said "we need answers and accountability" from Huang and Lutnick "immediately."

"Jensen Huang's gross negligence exposed cracks in our national security, but Secretary Lutnick's reported stalling on export controls raises the question of whether the Commerce Department is acting in the best interests of the American people," Curtis wrote in a social media post.

House Republicans are seeking testimony on Dec. 3 from Jeff Kessler, the under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security "for a hearing on chip smuggling, adversary use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations, and Megaspeed."

title: Democratic wave upends battle over Ten Commandments in Texas classrooms
summary: Sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm elections raise questions about the future of laws mandating Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.
story: Critics hope for lax enforcement as legal battles reach the Supreme Court.

HOUSTON -- When Texas lawmakers last year mandated that the Ten Commandments be prominently posted in every classroom of every public school, Rebecca Smith Nash got to work raising money to print thousands of posters of the biblical text and assembling dozens of volunteers to deliver them.
"We know that we have God on our side. So, we put on our armor," said Nash, a mother of two and devout Christian, of the campaign that has sharply divided the Lone Star State.

After years of momentum, winning enactment of classroom mandates in 4 states and inspiring more than a dozen others to consider similar laws, advocates of the Ten Commandments displays now say their success could hang in the balance.
Sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm election -- from statehouses to state legislatures to full control of Congress -- signal a sea change in political priorities, for now.
"The pendulum has swung," said Martin Siegel, a constitutional law scholar and First Amendment expert at the South Texas College of Law.

"The cultural and religious conservative wing of the Republican Party pushed its advantage pretty far, maybe to the outer reaches of what the public will support," Siegel said. "I don't think we're going to see a lot more attempts to infuse religion into school curriculum now that we have a divided legislature and a Democratic governor."
Texas' governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has not yet said how she will handle enforcement of the law or public calls to attempt its repeal, but as a Democratic state legislator she was strongly opposed.

Incoming Texas Democratic leaders will also need to address multiple ongoing legal challenges to the state law and decide whether to continue defending it in court. Under Republican Texas Governor Greg Abbott, the state vigorously defended the Ten Commandments law -- known as SB10 -- against all lawsuits.
The dispute over the Commandments has already reached the U.S. Supreme Court, where the justices are expected to decide in the coming weeks whether to take up the case and decide it next year.

"The Ten Commandments help shape the legal and moral foundations of our nation, and you know, the ideas of respect and truthfulness and responsibility -- these are all essential to a free society," said Jonathan Covey, policy director for Texas Values, a conservative advocacy group that has championed the classroom displays. "Students really deserve to understand about that heritage."

Emily Roth, a Houston mother of two elementary school children who is suing the state over the Commandments, says she shares respect for the biblical values but that it is her right as a parent to present those concepts to her kids.

"We are not able to now introduce faith and religion and Christianity in ways that we want and ways that we control," Roth said. "I'm no longer in control of bringing religion into my child's life because the state is leading it. The state doesn't own my child. My child is mine."
Audrey Nath, a mother of two who has joined Roth in the Texas lawsuit, says she also objects to the concepts presented in the Commandments as inappropriate for elementary school.

"The not coveting thy neighbor's manservant -- that means slave. And I don't think it's OK to say, yeah, sure, don't covet your neighbor's slave," Nath said. "No, if your neighbor is a slave, you should help them escape. None of that is okay for me and what I teach my children."
"The law is still on the books and the poster is still up," she said of the change in state political leadership. "So we're gonna keep fighting until it's gone."
Outside of Texas, the displays may be on firmer footing.

In Louisiana, Alabama, and Arkansas, Republicans retained control of state legislatures and governorships in last month's election, meaning no immediate change is expected in how their respective Ten Commandments mandates are enforced.

New Orleans public school teacher Chris Dier, who was awarded Louisiana teacher of the year in 2020 and opposes posting the biblical imperatives in his classroom, says it will likely take a federal court ruling to get states to back down.
Dier's lawsuit against Louisiana is now pending consideration by the U.S. Supreme Court.

"The fight against having the Ten Commandments in the classroom is not a fight against Christianity itself," said Dier, who identifies as Christian. "We want to make sure we are very clear that we respect all religions."
"I firmly believe it is time for the Supreme Court to step in and make a ruling," he said.

In a landmark decision 46 years ago, the high court struck down a near-identical Kentucky law that had mandated Ten Commandments displays in classrooms, concluding it was a violation of the First Amendment's Establishment Clause, which prohibits government promotion of a particular faith.
That precedent -- Stone v. Graham from 1980 -- may be revisited if the justices agree to take up the Louisiana or Texas cases.

"I think this is the most important First Amendment issue the court has considered really in this century. We're talking millions of kids, millions of families," said Siegel. A decision from the court on whether to wade into the dispute is expected by early next year.
Meanwhile, families in Texas on opposing ends of the political spectrum and Ten Commandments debate are holding firm to their principles.

"I hope that taking the Ten Commandments down off the walls is not a top priority for the Democrats as they come in and take office," said Smith Nash. "If they were to remove it, I would probably stand up and speak out, because it's almost ... I don't know, almost kind of hateful."

title: Trump administration continues to insist tech outages not cyberattacks
summary: Sec. of State Rubio also sought to assuage fears over recent outages.
story: Sec. of State Rubio also sought to assuage fears over recent outages.

Trump administration officials continue to insist that recent technical issues impacting the National Security Agency and other areas are not the result of a cyberattack or state-sponsored activity, after Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also sought to assuage fears over recent high-profile technology failures and service disruptions.

“We have no indication that this is a cyberattack, that these incidents are some kind of cyberattack, that these incidents are connected to a particular actor or groups of actors, or that there's any type of state sponsorship here,” a senior administration official said during a background call with reporters Wednesday.
“We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the results of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied,” the official added.
Clayton echoed those comments Wednesday morning in testimony before the House Homeland Security Committee's Worldwide Threats hearing.

"I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should," Clayton said in his opening comments. "The American people should ask us these questions. But based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

"We have no indication that these events are related," Clayton said later, during questioning by Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.). "But let me let me answer something that the American people should know, which is the speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially, which means legacy systems that were old six months ago in a year are a lot older."

Clayton’s comments came the day after Secretary of State Marco Rubio also sought to assuage fears over recent high-profile technology failures and service disruptions, giving the Trump administration’s clearest declaration that the events are “completely unrelated” and had "nothing to do with a cybercriminal has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country.”
"We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio told reporters.
The secretary acknowledged that the failures were “unsettling,” but said they could be blamed on run-of-the-mill computer errors.
"Each of them are distinct, and they're different in their causation,” he said.
In another interview on Fox Business on Tuesday, Clayton said he was "fairly confident" in his assertion because "we know those things exist and we have been looking for them in the past."

Clayton's comments come after an internal communications system used by NSA employees to share classified information temporarily went down on Tuesday. The NSA said the network issues occurred during "scheduled routine maintenance" and that "mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues."

Clayton told Fox Business that what the administration is fairly confident has been happening is that technology systems across institutions are upgrading and "patching" where vulnerabilities have been found, including at the NSA.
"As you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happened," he told CNBC.
"We will have other patches going forward as we upgrade our infrastructure. But this is not something that is a coordinated cyberattack or a state-sponsored effort against the U.S.," he continued.

Clayton, who also chairs the White House Super Intelligence Force (the Trump administration's term for artificial intelligence), told Fox Business that AI is able to scan systems "more quickly," and as a result, "the ability to identify vulnerabilities has increased."
"That is why it is so incumbent upon all of us to work together, to patch, to report vulnerabilities," he said.
Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, echoed Clayton's remarks in a statement on Tuesday.

"I understand why Americans are concerned about the widespread outages we've seen in recent days, affecting everything from banks and major technology companies to critical government systems. At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort," he said.

Warner also pointed to artificial intelligence, saying AI is "making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change."
"While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity," he said.

title: Mullin grilled about nationwide ground stop as FAA administrator says 'blame me'
summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin was in the hot seat in Congress Wednesday, following last week's air ground stop and several outages of critical online services.
story: The committee's focus is on worldwide threats since the Sept. 11 attacks.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went to Capitol Hill on Wednesday to talk about worldwide threats since Sept. 11, 2001, but he was in the hot seat over questions about technology issues that disrupted millions of Americans over the last week and the Trump Administration's immigration policies.
Meanwhile, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration took blame upon himself for last week's nationwide ground stop that disrupted millions of air travelers.

Mullin testified before the House Committee on Homeland Security for a hearing underway titled "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" along with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia.

However, the hearing immediately shifted to other areas that DHS has come under heavy criticism over the last few weeks. The hearing started with congressmembers bringing up last Friday's rare nationwide ground stop, the second since 9/11, which stranded thousands of passengers going into last weekend.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., had his staff shuffle through several large placards as he cited multiple quotes from Mullin in the wake of the outage including his attendance Saturday at an LSU-Texas football game.
Mullin used his opening statement to rebuke Thompson for the remarks, contending the congressman was "making political points by holding up posters that are completely inaccurate."

Mullin defended his attendance at the LSU-Texas game, saying he "wanted to be a good uncle" in taking the trip that was scheduled weeks earlier and committed to reimbursing the government as required by law.
'Separate service outages'
Mullin, Clayton and Raia were also questioned about the cyber outages that have affected airlines, Microsoft Outlook, banks and other services.

In his opening remarks, Clayton reaffirmed that recent cyber incidents causing disruptions for multiple companies and networks do not appear to be the result of coordinated cyberattacks -- despite widespread speculation among the public.

"I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions. But based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton said.

Mullin has repeatedly assured the public that Friday's air traffic incident, in which flights were grounded for four hours, was not nefarious and echoed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on what caused the disruption.

Duffy told ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that work was being performed to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred.

The ground stop was issued after the installation of a Juniper router at the Arkansas facility flooded the network with data, overwhelming an older system and resulting in telecommunications issues, according to officials.
A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said Sunday "based on what we know, they were working exactly as designed" on Friday.
Duffy told reporters on Tuesday that the FAA had spent a year testing the routers and that the issue occurred on the 69th installation.
'Blame me'

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford took full responsibility for the router issue and insisted that Duffy should not be blamed for it. Bedford previously apologized to the public for the disruptions during a press conference on Saturday.

"I'm the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me. If we need to blame somebody, blame me," Bedford said on Wednesday. "We are going to continue to power through this. We'll learn the lesson. We'll have a transparent accounting on the forensics that we get from the router failure."
Other Democratic House members criticized Mullin over potential cybersecurity threats.

Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Va., questioned the secretary over drastic staffing reductions to the nation's top cybersecurity defense agency, CISA, during the first two years of the second Trump administration.

"The Trump administration inherited a sizable workforce of 3,400 people. They fired and pushed out more than a thousand cyber defenders at precisely the moment the cyber threat was exploding," Walkinshaw said.
"Was it a mistake for them to have been fired and pushed out? Yes or no?" the congressman asked.
"I wasn't there when that was made. I don't know the reasoning behind it," Mullin responded. "So I'm not going to talk about why someone was let go when I wasn't involved in it."
'We're not killing people'
The hearing shifted to immigration, where Mullin was asked by several congressmembers about the administration's controversial increase in immigration related arrests and deportations.
Mullin got into a combative back-and-forth with Rep. Lamonica McIver, D-N.J., as he sought to defend the administration's actions.
"Do you have any regrets or reservations for the leading role you are playing in this administration's immigration agenda?" McIver asked.
"I'll never apologize about enforcing our nation's laws," Mullin responded.
"Not about even killing people? No apologies for that?" the congresswoman asked.
"We're not killing people," Mullin said.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
story: U.S. air travel operations are still recovering after the nationwide ground stop
Officials said they expect airline schedules to fully recover by the end of the day Sunday after a nationwide ground stop that was initiated out of caution caused massive travel disruptions.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,600 were canceled, according to FlightAware. Just over 1,300 of the more than 26,000 flights scheduled for Sunday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. That amounts to about 5.2% of scheduled flights. Prior to Friday, the average cancellation rate for U.S. departures was 3.4%.
But officials said the U.S. airspace was safe and operational and would recover well ahead of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack and no lives were at risk.
Here’s what to know:

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the system was stable Saturday. Several thousand flights were able to fly after the ground stop, but ultimately, some 12,000 scheduled flights were unable to take off Friday, he said.
Officials acknowledged the disruption but said safety was paramount.

Bedford offered an apology for stranded travelers and thanked air traffic controllers, pilots and flight attendants for managing the fallout. He said officials were confident the system is operating safely or else they would keep airplanes on the ground.

American Airlines said in a statement Saturday night that some individual flights might still be canceled as it continued working to fully restore its operations. It urged travelers to check their flight statuses.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight or a full refund if a flight is canceled.
Bedford said the administration was working closely with airlines and said they were waiving all terms and conditions.
Some airlines were allowing passengers to rebook if they had travel scheduled Friday or Saturday. Others extended the offer to people with reservations for Sunday or even Monday.
Bedford advised passengers to contact their airlines.

A contractor was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fiber wire in a remote location Friday afternoon, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Saturday. That kind of work has been happening across the country and across industries for decades, he said.

But on Friday, the router in that location started overloading the air traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds. When officials couldn’t quickly locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.
“We did that out of an abundance of caution,” Bedford said. “I’m sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons.”

Officials stressed that the ground stop was not the result of a system outage or nefarious activity by a foreign actor. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was the cause.

The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. About 70% of copper wire has been switched to fiber already, officials said Saturday.

Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after its own massive outage. There was no indication the FAA ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Microsoft services offline Thursday, according to federal officials and a company spokesperson.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Users reported Microsoft 365 services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were interrupted.

title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
