story: The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop, allowing some domestic flights to depart from U.S. airports
A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.
However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.
Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
Here’s what to know.
The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.
The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.
International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport from Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.
Europe’s aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.
Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.
New technology being hooked up to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.
That caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.
Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said.
The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.
Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.
“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."
The ground stop was enacted “out of an abundance of caution,” he said.

title: Trump administration blames ‘overloaded’ systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems
story: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems

WASHINGTON -- Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.

Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.

A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.

Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: Fed minutes: Higher interest rates needed in December as inflation worries mount
summary: Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-poin...
story: Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-poin...

WASHINGTON -- Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-point increase next month.

The minutes, released three weeks after the Oct. 27-28 meeting of the Fed's rate-setting committee, also said a “vast majority” of the 19 members of the Fed's policymaking committee worried that inflation could persist even if gas prices kept declining and the impact of tariffs and the buildout of AI infrastructure faded.

The minutes will solidify expectations for a rate hike not only in December but likely early next year as well. Wall Street investors already see the odds of a December rate hike at nearly 95%, according to CME Fedwatch. When the Fed lifts its key rate, over time it can also raise borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards. Home sales have withered as mortgage rates have topped 7% in recent months.

The Fed kept its key rate unchanged at 3.9% in October after raising it for the first time in three years in September. Chairman Kevin Warsh at a news conference Oct. 28 gave little guidance on the central bank's next moves, but the statement issued after the Fed's meeting acknowledged that “inflation remains elevated.”

The minutes said “some" policymakers supported lifting rates in October. Two of them, Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, formally dissented in favor of higher rates. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook, but the Supreme Court ruled in June she could keep her position while the case is litigated.

Inflation has accelerated this fall and is showing signs of broadening beyond industries directly affected by higher oil and gas prices or tariffs, a trend that has raised alarm among many policymakers. Several have spoken out in favor of more rate hikes in the past week.

Fed governor Christopher Waller said in an interview on CNBC early Wednesday that inflation is “headed in the wrong direction and it’s spreading out ″ into more goods and services. Waller is one of the Fed's seven governors and a member of its rate-setting committee.

“If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” Waller said. He reiterated his support for a half-point rate increase at the Fed’s December meeting, double the usual hike. He also said that several more hikes — not just the two that many economists forecast — might be needed to tame inflation.

The minutes suggested that one other official also agreed that a half-point increase should be considered in December, though it’s not clear that the official is a voting member. Twelve of the 19 members of the committee vote on rate decisions, though all participate in the debates. The minutes don’t identify which officials took which positions.

Waller noted that in the past three months, core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy categories, has run at about a 3.5% annual rate, far above the Fed’s target of 2%. Businesses increasingly appear willing to pass on their own rising costs and also believe their customers can handle price increases of about 3%, he added.
“That’s the kind of psychology I think we need to start breaking,” Waller said.

Waller also took a shot at Warsh by arguing that one reason he supported a half-point hike is that without greater communication, financial markets won’t know whether a quarter-point increase in December will be followed by a similar move in January. If investors do have a sense of further hikes in the pipeline, they’ll push up market rates in anticipation and help the Fed cool inflation, Waller said.
Yet Warsh has steadily refrained from providing such guidance, which he has said locks the Fed to a predetermined path.

Separately, John Williams, president of the New York Fed and vice chair of the Fed's rate-setting committee, has pushed back against the potential for a half-point increase. He told Axios Tuesday, “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.”

Other Fed officials have suggested many more hikes are likely necessary. Alberto Musalem, president of the St. Louis Fed, said Tuesday in a speech in Buenos Aires that “the economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027” to bring inflation down.

The economy is expanding at a healthy pace, he added, and interest rates aren’t high enough to restrain borrowing and spending sufficiently to cool inflation. Musalem does not have a vote on rates this year.

Mary Daly, president of the San Francisco Fed, said last week that she is leaning toward supporting further rate hikes, and added that she also worries that companies are increasingly willing to pass on higher costs to consumers.
“That’s the inflationary impulse that we want to avoid,” Daly said.

title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo can't undergo surgery after swallowing a hat
summary: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat
story: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat

Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure.
The zoo's animal care team borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract, the zoo said Wednesday.
Video released by the zoo Wednesday shows Fiona snorting and moving about her indoor enclosure.
Veterinarians sedated her Tuesday for a second time to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.
An ultrasound showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she is still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy, using a 9-foot scope, he said.
Specialists have told the zoo that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, he said.

Fiona, who became a global sensation as a tiny newborn after her premature birth in 2017, has inspired books, a line of beer and a bobblehead. During her first year, the zoo recorded her progress while fans worldwide followed her growth online.
She initially couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms) at birth, 25 pounds (11.3 kilograms) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The beloved hippo swallowed the hat just over a week ago. A visitor tossed it into the air, and a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Zoo staff are now monitoring her around the clock, trying to keep her hydrated and giving Fiona her favorite foods to help her pass the knit cap, the zoo said.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked,” Curley said Wednesday. “And they were happy to see her respond.”

title: From pop stars to poets to politicians, hundreds gathering for joyful tribute to Gloria Steinem
summary: Luminaries from political figures to pop stars were gathering in Manhattan for a joyful tribute to the trailblazing activist and feminist Gloria Steinem
story: Luminaries from political figures to pop stars were gathering in Manhattan for a joyful tribute to the trailblazing activist and feminist Gloria Steinem

NEW YORK -- Luminaries from political figures to pop stars to poets were gathering Wednesday in Manhattan for a joyful and music-filled tribute to Gloria Steinem, the trailblazing activist, prolific author and most visible symbol of American feminism.
“It’s Steinemite!” declared the invitation received by about 1,000 guests, an indication of the buoyant mood that organizers say Steinem, who died in September at 92, had wanted for her memorial.

In a way, the late afternoon celebration promised to mirror the spirit of Steinem's famed talking circles, which she hosted at her Upper East Side home for more than 50 years: a vibrant mix of people from near and far, reflecting Steinem’s extensive travels and eclectic tastes in art and music.

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton was expected to be one of the main speakers. There were performances planned from pop star Cyndi Lauper and actor-singer Cynthia Erivo, as well as poetry and choral presentations. Organizers requested that the location not be disclosed ahead of time for security reasons.

“Gloria wanted a true celebration filled with laughter and friends across generations,” said Jill Heller, director of programs at Gloria's Foundation, which is working to preserve Steinem's home as a center to further her work. The presenters “reflect how expansive a life Gloria lived but also just the spirit of community, celebration and hopefulness that she wanted for this moment,” Heller said.
Close friend Amy Richards, a chief organizer of the event, said Steinem “definitely wanted people to have a good time. She hoped that new people will meet each other, and there will be laughter.”

Steinem became an activist after an early career as a journalist. She has said she might have remained a journalist had editors been willing to let her write about social issues of importance, like the nascent women’s movement — but they weren’t interested. It was at a meeting where women spoke out about illegal abortions that she decided to change paths.

“That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me,” Steinem told The Associated Press in 2022. “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.”

Steinem went on to co-found Ms. Magazine and the National Women’s Political Caucus. She traveled constantly, to campuses and rallies and protests, despite an early fear of public speaking. And when she was at home in New York, her living room was a constant gathering place, where groups and movements were born as women gathered from across the country and around the globe.
Steinem, a prolific author, died just weeks before the release of her final memoir, “An Unexpected Life.”

“As I write this, I’m both older than I ever imagined I would become and happier than I ever imagined I could be,” she wrote in the introduction. “I’ve been rewarded with friends who are my chosen family. I have trusted friends in other countries, and we strive to be safe and free, and share hopes for a peaceful democracy in the world.”
Steinem added that she planned to live to 100.

title: Helicopter that crashed, killing 1 and injuring 2, was flying 'extremely' low: NTSB
summary: Investigators say a helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn
story: Investigators say a helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn

MIAMI -- A helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay, killing one person and critically injuring two others, had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn, the National Transportation Safety Board said Wednesday.

The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down Nov. 4 near Bill Baggs State Park off Key Biscayne while on a trip to film a powerboating event offshore, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said. The pilot died, and a photographer and videographer on board were injured.

The helicopter was making low-altitude turns “extremely” close to the surface of the water, according to the safety board's preliminary report. Some of the helicopter's doors had been removed to facilitate photography and videography. On one turn, the rotor blades hit the water and brought down the aircraft.

The photographer told investigators the helicopter flew low and parallel to a boat's right side, then turned and got ahead of it for a “good shot” as the boat passed underneath, according to the report. Then the videographer observed the rotor blades strike the water.

Television news video of the crash showed the helicopter upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.

Witnesses in nearby boats made distress calls, and a good Samaritan tried to help one of the victims, Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said. Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.

title: Fishermen from Ecuador sue Trump administration over boat strike
summary: A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers
story: A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers

WASHINGTON -- A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers.

The fishermen allege American drones struck their boat, the La Negra Francesca Duarte II, in the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ecuador on March 17, according to a federal lawsuit filed Monday.

The vessel was engulfed in flames, with two of the men suffering serious burns, the lawsuit says. The men allege they were held against their will by the U.S. for around 24 hours and treated in cruel and inhumane ways.

“The foregoing attack, kidnapping and torture took place despite the fact that the government of Ecuador, after a three-hour inspection, had just cleared the ship and its crew of any illicit activity,” according to the lawsuit, which was filed in U.S. District Court in Pittsburgh and reported earlier by The New York Times.

The lawsuit is the second against the Trump administration over U.S. military attacks on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narco-terrorists” in September 2025.

U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims that the vessels have been carrying drugs. Democratic lawmakers and some legal experts also say the attacks amount to extrajudicial killings on the high seas.

The Pentagon and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. The Trump administration has justified the strikes in general by declaring drug cartels to be “ unlawful combatants ” and said the U.S. is now in an “armed conflict” with them.

The lawsuit was filed under a U.S. admiralty law that allows for claims against severe injuries inflicted on the high seas as well as unlawful attacks, kidnapping and torture. The fishermen's U.S. attorney, Daniel Kovalik, said he sued in Pittsburgh because of the maritime law expertise in the court's jurisdiction in western Pennsylvania, which includes the three rivers that flow through the city and a port on Lake Erie.

After their ship was attacked, the men jumped into the ocean before using small emergency boats that were on the larger vessel, the lawsuit says. They approached a ship marked with U.S. flags where men in uniforms spoke English.

The lawsuit alleges that the fishermen's hands were tied, hoods were placed on their heads and they were given little water and no food. One of them, Jordy Alexander Flores Lucas, was told through a translator that the men on the boat were the ones who launched the attack.
“They laughed about what they had done and about how they had destroyed the fishing vessel — a vessel which provided the livelihood of all of the plaintiffs," the lawsuit alleges.

The fishermen spent seven days on a Salvadoran ship that took them to El Salvador, the lawsuit says. Most were held in a comprehensive care center for migrants, while two injured men were brought to a hospital. All of the men were eventually flown back to Ecuador by the end of March.

title: Ex-boxer Goran Gogic pleads guilty to drug charge, faces at least 10 years in prison
summary: Former heavyweight boxer Goran Gogic has pleaded guilty to a drug charge and likely faces 10-20 years in prison
story: Former heavyweight boxer Goran Gogic has pleaded guilty to a drug charge and likely faces 10-20 years in prison

NEW YORK -- Former heavyweight boxer Goran Gogic pleaded guilty to a drug charge Wednesday, a year after his trial was upended when it was revealed that a juror had been offered a $100,000 bribe to return a not guilty verdict.

Shackled at the ankles, Gogic, 47, spoke through an interpreter as he admitted conspiring to smuggle 20 tons (18.1 metric tons) of cocaine to Europe from Colombia through U.S. ports using commercial cargo ships.

He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn federal court to conspiracy to violate the Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act, a charge that carries a mandatory minimum penalty of 10 years in prison and a maximum of life.
Under the plea agreement Gogic signed with prosecutors, the boxer agreed to forfeit $1 million associated with his crimes.

Prosecutors said they plan to ask at a sentencing scheduled for Feb. 16 that Gogic be ordered to serve 23 years in prison. His lawyer said the former athlete, who is from Montenegro, is likely to be deported when he is released from prison.
Gogic has been described by law enforcement officials as a “major drug trafficker” who operated on a “mammoth scale.”

He fought professionally in Germany from 2001 to 2012, compiling a 21-4-2 record, according to boxing website Sport & Note. He was listed as 6-foot-5 (1.96 meters) and weighed in at anywhere from 227 pounds (103 kilograms) to 250 pounds (113 kilograms).
“Gogic stepped outside the ring and into the drug trade, and today justice delivered a knockout blow,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a news release.
Alan Futerfas, Gogic's lawyer, said he had no comment Wednesday.

A year ago, law enforcement authorities arrested three people in a jury tampering plot and alleged one of them called a juror in Gogic's trial multiple times on his cellphone before the juror agreed to meet him on Staten Island.
During the meeting, the man told the juror that associates in the Bronx were willing to pay him to return a not guilty verdict, according to a criminal complaint.
When word of the bribery attempt was reported to court officials, a federal judge abruptly dismissed the jury just as it was about to hear opening statements.

title: Charges dismissed against boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. over bad check in Las Vegas
summary: A Las Vegas court has dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. related to allegations that the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch
story: A Las Vegas court has dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. related to allegations that the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch

LAS VEGAS -- A Las Vegas court dismissed felony charges against Floyd Mayweather Jr. on Wednesday at the request of prosecutors, following allegations the boxer wrote a bad check to purchase a watch, according to court records.
A hearing in the case that had been scheduled for Thursday was canceled.
Mayweather, 49, was charged in April with theft and passing a check without sufficient funds with intent to defraud.

Prosecutors in Clark County had alleged Mayweather wrote the $200,000 check to Las Vegas designer resale store Gold and Beyond in December 2024 despite having insufficient funds in his account, according to the criminal complaint.
The Associated Press left emails, voice and text messages this week seeking comment with Mayweather’s attorney, Clark County prosecutors and an attorney for Gold and Beyond.

Mayweather, a former five-division world champion, announced his retirement in 2017 with a 50-0 record. After saying earlier this year that he was coming out of retirement, he was scheduled to be in Athens, Greece, for the “Battle of the Legends” boxing match in June. The event was canceled due to a legal dispute with CSI Sports.

CSI sued Mayweather in the Southern District of New York district court alleging breach of contract for allegedly failing to fight Mike Tyson in a separate event. Mayweather denied the allegations in court documents.
Earlier this year, Mayweather was sued in New York over his alleged failure to pay rent at a Manhattan apartment and was in financial disputes with multiple jewelers.
He also filed a lawsuit in New York against his former business manager, alleging a yearslong fraud scheme.

title: What investors should know about Anthropic's unusual IPO
summary: When the stock of Anthropic begins trading for the first time later this week, it will be a big test not only for the company behind the Claude AI chatbot but also for the entire artificial-intelligence industry and for the U.S. stock market itself
story: When the stock of Anthropic begins trading for the first time later this week, it will be a big test not only for the company behind the Claude AI chatbot but also for the entire artificial-intelligence industry and for the U.S. stock market itself

NEW YORK -- When Anthropic's stock begins trading for the first time later this week, it will be a big test not only for the company behind the Claude AI chatbot but also for the entire artificial-intelligence industry and the U.S. stock market itself.

Anthropic's initial public offering will reverberate far beyond anyone geeky enough to understand what its business structure as a “public benefit corporation” means. It will likely affect even people who make no changes to their 401(k) accounts.
Here's a look at what investors should know ahead of the highly anticipated IPO:
Anthropic is planning to sell shares of its stock for between $70 and $78 apiece, which would likely give it a total value of more than $1 trillion.

Such a size would rival Walmart, which has more than 10,900 stores around the world, and JPMorgan Chase, whose roots go back to 1799. It would also be more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors — combined.
At that size, Anthropic could quickly join indexes that track wide swaths of the stock market, which in turn could bring in even more investment.

Anthropic could join the Nasdaq 100 index within just a few weeks, for example. The index tracks the 100 largest nonfinancial companies trading on the Nasdaq, and it's a popular way for investors to get a quick read on how tech stocks are doing generally.

The index is so popular that an exchange-traded fund that mimics it, Invesco's QQQ ETF, has roughly $457 billion invested in it. If Anthropic joins the index, QQQ and other funds tracking the Nasdaq 100 would automatically buy Anthropic stock.
It would take longer for Anthropic to join the more widely followed S&P 500 index, though. To enter that index, a stock needs to have traded for at least 12 months, among other criteria.
The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners. Usually, that means making profits and growing, both in the short and long terms.

Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal: “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

As part of that, Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company's board of directors. This trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors in the long term.
It's not just the long-term benefit trust that will have an outsized voice on company matters. So will the company's founders.

As part of the IPO, Anthropic is creating a special class of stock that it's giving to CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders. This special class of stock will control 50.1% of the voting power of all the company's outstanding shares.
That means the founders as a group could overshadow every other shareholder and single-handedly dictate issues put before all shareholders, such as how to vote on a potential sale of the company.

The company expects up to 20% of its Class A shares in the IPO to go to what are called “retail investors.” These are regular investors going through a brokerage rather than big institutions getting shares through their connections with Wall Street underwriters.
Most IPOs offer only 5% to 10% of the total offering to retail investors, and Anthropic expects to reach such investors through Charles Schwab, Fidelity and others.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $104 billion for the first nine months of this year. Compare that with the nearly $53 billion in profit that JPMorgan Chase made over the same period.

But most of that loss does not reflect cash running out the door. Instead, it had to do with losses accountants said it had to record because of the shifting value of some of its debt that can be converted into shares.

Anthropic reported an operating loss of $1.26 billion for the first nine months of the year on $33.24 billion in revenue. That's an improvement from its operating loss of $5.22 billion on less than $2.55 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2025.
The U.S. stock market could use a boost. It's been shaky since the summer because of several worries hitting the AI industry, which has become the market's most influential.

At first, it was longstanding concerns that prices for AI-related stocks had shot too high in the frenzy around the technology and inflated into a bubble. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry's growth. Then came this month's sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI.
Most recently, it was the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, the company that's been both supplying chips to AI labs and helping to fund the growth of the broader industry.

All these worries raised questions about whether Anthropic could delay its IPO to wait for a less turbulent time. But market watchers said such a move could also raise more doubts about AI stocks and drive the industry even lower.
How Anthropic's IPO performs could help clarify Wall Street's questions about whether the recent struggles for AI stocks are a temporary setback or the beginning of the end for a potential bubble.

title: US military returns to 2 aircraft carriers in the Middle East
summary: The U.S. military has gone back to having two aircraft carriers supporting Iran war operations after the USS George Washington departed the Middle East
story: The U.S. military has gone back to having two aircraft carriers supporting Iran war operations after the USS George Washington departed the Middle East
WASHINGTON -- The U.S. military has gone back to having two aircraft carriers supporting Iran war operations after the USS George Washington departed the Middle East.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Pacific Fleet, Cmdr. Katie Koenig, said Wednesday that the Japan-based USS George Washington was now under its control and “conducting routine operations” in the Asia-Pacific region.

The development is the latest in a shuffling of aircraft carriers in the Middle East. During the Iran war, the carriers have served as the linchpin of a U.S. flotilla that has blockaded all merchant shipping to and from the Islamic Republic as the Trump administration looks to keep squeezing Tehran's economy by preventing its oil from reaching global markets.

The George Washington departed the Middle East in the same week that the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived, briefly bringing the number of carriers in the waters off Iran to the unusually high amount of three.
The USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in the region in April, and the Roosevelt are now the two carriers in the region as well more than a dozen destroyers, cruisers and a littoral combat ship.

The naval presence is helping maintain the blockade on Iran, while the U.S. also has carried out some limited strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway where nearly a third of the world's oil passed through before the war began Feb. 28. The disruptions to shipping through the strait have raised global energy prices.
The unpopularity of the Iran war and the resulting economic effects contributed to major losses for President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in this month's midterm elections.
Trump has offered mixed signals on whether he plans to return to major combat with Iran, but any negotiated deal to end the fighting appears to be a long way off.

Trump recently has warned Iran that the U.S. military is “locked and loaded” and that the U.S. was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
He also has said it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over.”

The USS George Washington departed the Middle East following its arrival in August. It had been pulled from a patrol in the South China Sea shortly after reports of mental health and supply issues emerged aboard another long-deployed aircraft carrier in the Middle East — the USS Abraham Lincoln. The Lincoln set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, at more than 240 days.

title: Iowa residents brace for a lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
summary: Residents are raising concerns about plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals at an ammunition plant in southeast Iowa
story: Residents are raising concerns about plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals at an ammunition plant in southeast Iowa

DES MOINES, Iowa -- Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.

The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that residents of a neighborhood in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they can’t leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed.

“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure.”
Officials also have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north toward other communities. Some schools in the path of the plume have canceled classes.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the track of the plume.
The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said.
While the Army recommends washing cars and cleaning windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered.

"The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production.

The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency on Nov. 13 approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday's detonation.

That permit required the Army to track the potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday's notification to communities as far as 100 miles (160 kilometers) away.

Less than 20 miles (32 kilometers) northeast in Mediapolis, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure from the planned detonation Sunday, when the map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area.

Mediapolis Community School District announced Tuesday that the “uncontrollable variables” prompted the decision to close school Friday, with no events or sports practices. The public library also is set to close, and the local fire department will hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles.

The EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample the air, soil and water during and after the detonation, according to city officials. But the city will do its own testing as well to try to assure concerned residents.
“This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” said Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.”
Even Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office was first briefed Monday on the public advisory, her office said.

News of the planned blasts also caught the attention of environmental and public health officials in Illinois. They urged the U.S. military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state following the detonations.

The barrels of lead azide had been stored at the ammunition plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, public affairs specialist at the Army Sustainment Command.

During a routine check earlier this year, they found that some of the water had evaporated, causing the lead azide to crystallize. That makes it more sensitive to friction and shock, thus “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the EPA.
Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, officials said. Barati said that possibility increases in cold weather.
“We’re really concerned about the weather situation,” Barati said on moving forward with Friday’s detonation. “We’re really concerned that it will detonate on its own.”
The Army said it put together a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with the detonation plan.
The barrels are surrounded above, below and on all sides with concrete, which is buried under soil. Sand barriers are stacked two stories high around the soil.
During the detonation, the soil will be sprayed with water and the air will be misted to try to keep the majority of lead on Army property, Barati said.

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it is encouraging to see that the Army and the EPA are doing all they can to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.

Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.
Hill reported from Las Vegas and Montoya Bryan from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump's memorial arch in DC
summary: A federal judge has temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation’s capital
story: A federal judge has temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation’s capital
WASHINGTON -- A federal judge on Wednesday temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation's capital.

The temporary restraining order was due to expire on Thursday, but U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended it by 14 days. That would keep President Donald Trump's construction project on hold until Dec. 3 or until Chutkan rules on a pending request for a more permanent preliminary injunction.

The decision followed a Nov. 5 order Chutkan issued shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy commission giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction.

The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.

In issuing the latest delay, Chutkan granted a request by plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch construction. The case has grown more complicated as separate groups have filed lawsuits asking that the project not be allowed to go forward.

District of Columbia and Virginia filed suit Oct. 31. Chutkan consolidated that suit with the original, filed by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit Nov. 10, citing the impact the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would have on family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

Chutkan said the 14-day extension of the order is warranted because nothing has significantly changed in the litigation in the two weeks since she issued it. She decided to maintain the status quo pending her ruling on the injunction request.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats gained control of Congress.

Many of those plans are being challenged in the courts, and four have been filed opposing Trump’s proposed memorial arch. Three of the suits have been consolidated with Chutkan overseeing them. The other was filed in the Eastern District of Virginia.

The original plaintiffs in the District of Columbia — three veterans and a retired architectural historian — had asked Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service “from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation.”

Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue the administration must seek congressional approval for the arch and say that, once built, it will disrupt the sightlines connecting historic landmarks in the nation’s capital. The administration has argued that Congress decades ago cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle.

title: Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force votes on human rights consequences of US policies in Russia
summary: Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia says he will force a vote on the Senate floor to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia
story: Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia says he will force a vote on the Senate floor to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia

WASHINGTON -- Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force a vote on the Senate floor in the coming weeks to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia.

Kaine is introducing the resolution on Thursday under an arcane provision of a foreign policy law that allows any senator to trigger a vote requiring a report on a country’s human rights practices. His measure would request more information about the effects of a diesel deal with Russia that was struck by the Republican president in October and that waived sanctions against Moscow and allowed for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel.

The measure would also require the State Department to report on the consequences of other U.S. policies as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the Pentagon delayed the delivery of Patriot air defense interceptors and that U.S. intelligence that warns of incoming Russian attacks against his country had been interrupted.

Trump said in announcing the deal on Oct. 9 that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote on social media. He did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.”

If passed, the resolution would ask the State Department to calculate how Trump's policies have affected Russia’s ability to wage war in Ukraine and if they have caused or worsened human rights abuses. It also asks for an update on the current status of negotiations to end the war, which Russia launched in February 2022.
Kaine says he hopes the resolution, which he calls a “test of good faith,” can pass with bipartisan votes.

“If they were to give us a nonstarter human rights report that whitewashes Russia’s record, that will tell us a lot and that will tell the American public a lot," the Virginia senator said in an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday.

The resolution — coming as Trump had just wrapped up a meeting in China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping — is part of Senate Democrats’ strategy since the beginning of Trump's second term to force votes on reversing parts of his agenda. Kaine has led efforts to force multiple war powers votes, including several on the war in Iran.

Kaine also triggered a vote last year on a resolution to require more transparency from the Trump administration about the human rights effects of deportations to El Salvador. The Senate, controlled by Republicans, voted along party lines to block it.

The strategy has proven effective for Democrats as they have taken floor time from majority Republicans and forced them to go on record on the Iran war and other issues ahead of this year’s midterm elections, in which Democrats ultimately won control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington.

Kaine said he will continue to find ways to trigger votes even when Democrats take the Senate majority next year. Unlike most bills, the privileged resolutions he has introduced under the Foreign Assistance Act, the War Powers Act and other foreign policy laws prompt a quick vote within weeks and bypass committees.
Getting past a presidential veto will be hard, Kaine concedes, but, “I want to make everybody here own what’s going on” and be accountable for their votes.
“We have to put bills on the president’s desk,” Kaine said.

title: The Latest: Trump arrives in China, seeking to reinforce US's status as world’s leading tech power
summary: President Donald Trump has landed in China, aiming to reinforce the United States' status as a leading technology power
story: President Donald Trump has landed in China, aiming to reinforce the United States' status as a leading technology power

President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the United States' status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public. The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump on Wednesday reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, who is known for her vast shoe collection. The brief meeting took place in the Philippine capital, Manila, at the Malacañang Presidential Palace, where Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who received him with a red-carpet welcome and full military honors, said Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is set to appear Wednesday at a congressional hearing about threats facing the U.S. at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game as travelers across the country were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.
Here's the latest:

The Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, says recent computer systems service disruptions in the government and private sector are “not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”
Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages instead appear to be separate and “associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

The testimony was the latest effort by the Trump administration to offer reassurances after technical outages that have affected everything from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration, the banking industry to United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
Clayton said in interviews Tuesday that the outages appeared to be connected to recent efforts to upgrade systems and patch vulnerabilities.
The Homeland Security Secretary offered a new defense Wednesday for his weekend flight to the LSU-Texas college football game, saying canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Markwayne Mullin, speaking at the House Homeland Security Committee’s worldwide threats hearing, said the trip had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and there was discussion beforehand about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin said Tuesday and reiterated Wednesday that he is required to fly on government planes and that he personally paid for the trip.

His comments, delivered in a forceful tone, came after Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson faulted him for the trip while others were stranded because of the nationwide ground stop, which had been lifted before his flight.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that when the FAA ordered the ground stop, the entire cabinet worked together.
“The whole of government went to work — every aspect of it,” he said.
More than 4,000 planes landed safely and the response was a great success, Mullin added.
Mullin said the government was able to get planes back in the air safely within a matter of hours.

The top ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee criticized Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin for taking a government flight to a college football game shortly after a nationwide ground stop.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, speaking during a committee hearing on worldwide threats, addressed Mullin’s weekend travel at the start of the meeting.

“While Americans were stranded in airports across the country, with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game and visited the private suite of a company that DHS had awarded a $2.2 billion contract for the secretary of Homeland Security,” Thompson said.
Thompson said the Trump administration was failing to take responsibility for that and other recent technological disruptions.
Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black American with the gavel.
Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.

He ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.
Jeffries will face a separate roll call of the whole House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino, a New York Republican and chairperson of the House Homeland Security Committee, said the panel had made repeated efforts to line up FBI Director Kash Patel’s appearance at Wednesday’s worldwide threats hearing but that he made it clear “he had no intention” of being present.
Garbarino said Patel’s absence marked a significant departure from committee precedent. He said the committee has been clear about its expectation that the FBI director appear in person to testify.
The committee’s top Democrat, Rep. Bennie Thompson, also joined in the criticism.
The FBI sent Deputy Director Christopher Raia in Patel’s place.
Also testifying were Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, who chairs the Senate health committee, said they would not consider Jim O’Neill, the White House’s pick to lead the science organization.

Cassidy said O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science” during his time as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, raising concerns about how he might lead the National Science Foundation.
It’s not yet clear why the vote did not happen. In an email, the White House confirmed it has not pulled O’Neill’s nomination.
O’Neill does not have an advanced science degree or research experience.

Earlier this year, around 50 scientific institutions and groups signed an open letter urging the Senate to hold a confirmation hearing for O’Neill so they could learn more about his vision for NSF prior to a vote.
The science foundation’s staff has been gutted over the past year, and more than $1 billion of its allotted funding sat unused when the fiscal year ended last month.
Democrats are voting in a closed-door meeting nominating Jeffries to become the House speaker when the new Congress convenes.
If nominated by his colleagues, Jeffries would face a vote of the whole House on Jan. 3, 2027.
The New York Times said that Vice President JD Vance has canceled his scheduled Wednesday appearance at the news organization’s DealBook Summit.
Vance’s office declined to directly address his decision to skip the event and instead referred to DealBook’s “tweets on the matter.”
The Times reported Vance has been called to stay in Washington to take part in meetings to address tech outages that have impacted airlines and banks.
Five Democrats essentially representing all corners of the caucus will nominate Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.
Among them is Rep. James Clyburn, the legendary lawmaker from South Carolina.
Democrats are meeting to elect their leaders for the new Congress in January.
A congressional hearing on worldwide threats is underway in Washington, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin set to testify.
The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee is aimed at assessing threats 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.
It also comes amid disruptive technological outages, including a rare nationwide ground stop of flights last week.
Also appearing are FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
Mullin, along with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, took the lead briefing the public after the outage, which the Trump administration has said likely is not the result of an attack.
Mullin has also been in the news because he took a government flight — which he said he personally paid for — to an LSU-Texas college football match Saturday, hours after the upheaval at airports.
House Democrats are gathering behind closed doors to nominate the House speaker and choose other top leadership positions.

Leader Hakeem Jeffries faces a key test on his path to becoming House speaker, and is expected to easily clear the majority threshold from Democrats during the private caucus election. He and the other top leaders are running unopposed.
In first voting, Rep. Ted Lieu of California has been elected the caucus chairman.
The House elects its speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. Jeffries would make history as the nation’s first Black American to become speaker of the House.

Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to his already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time the pair have sat down since they met in 2025 in Alaska, conducting talks that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.

The distressing series of technical outages back home has put the Trump administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with Xi and Putin.
Trump on Wednesday reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, who is known for her vast shoe collection.

The brief meeting took place in the Philippine capital, Manila, at the Malacañang presidential palace, where Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who received him with a red-carpet welcome and full military honors, Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez said.

Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday night to join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in their annual summit meetings with major Asian and Western counterparts. In a speech before ASEAN and other Asian leaders over dinner Tuesday, Trump praised Marcos and his parents.
“I just don’t wanna date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” Trump said, addressing the Philippine president. “They were great. I believe in genetics, and they did a good job.”
▶ Read more
Before leaders got into position for the traditional summit family photo, Russian President Vladimir Putin approached President Donald Trump, and they shook hands and exchanged greetings.
Trump had said before departing Washington that he was open to a formal one-on-one meeting with Putin, but it appeared that it might not come to pass while both are in China.
Instead, Trump, Putin and Xi will meet as a group on Thursday on the summit sidelines.
Marcos said he sent Trump a Jollibee delivery so he could have a “taste of Manila” during his short stay in the capital.
Marcos said it was intended as a pick-me-up of sorts for a president who works hard.

“Jollibee … is a very, very popular chain. And one of their main products is fried chicken. And we are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity,” Marcos said at their palace meeting.
“Oh wow,” Trump said upon hearing the claim. “Fantastic.”

“You have been working very hard, Mr. President, so just think of it as providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do that you have done and continue to do, and that is in front of you,” Marcos said.
Trump, who enjoys McDonald’s, didn’t say whether he had tried the chicken. Neither did the White House.
Trump was led by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on a rather lengthy red-carpet stroll around the lush grounds of the Malacañang presidential palace after they reviewed the troops.
They stopped at one point to listen as musicians using bamboo instruments played Elvis Presley’s “It’s Now or Never” and a Filipino folk song.
For a few seconds, Trump moved his forearms from side to side in a windshield-wiper-type motion.
Once seated inside the sprawling palace for their meeting, Trump told Marcos their countries’ people have a lot in common and stressed “architectural tastes.”
“I love what you’ve done here,” Trump said, referring to the palace. “You’ve done a fantastic job.”
Trump is a former real estate developer and builder who has been putting those skills to work on numerous renovations at the White House.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday said that Canada ’s growing trade relations with China are not a top priority for Trump, pointing out that Canada primarily exports commodities to China rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.

“In my conversation with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen, ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”

Carney’s comments came amid criticism from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro over Canada’s willingness to pursue closer economic relations with Beijing, including potentially bringing Chinese automakers to Canada.

Canada and the U.S. have one of the world’s largest trading relationships, but Trump’s tariffs have strained ties and pushed Ottawa to seek other markets. After negotiations collapsed in August, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa.
▶ Read more

The Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic, Chinese President Xi Jinping told business executives gathered Wednesday in the southern Chinese technology and financial hub of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Trump’s “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone. U.S. limits on Chinese access to leading-edge American technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.
Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticizing the U.S. shift toward protecting its own markets.
Xi faces pressure at home from slowing growth as retail spending and investment have dragged as China endures a prolonged property market slump.
Still, Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may lead to an extension of the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.
▶ Read more
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed Trump to Shenzhen at an airport, a rare courtesy for Xi that highlights the importance Beijing attaches to its relationship with Washington.
During Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Trump had also taken the unusual step of greeting Xi on the tarmac.
Chinese official news agency Xinhua reported that Xi recalled Trump’s gesture and said: “China is a nation of etiquette, with a tradition of reciprocating courtesy.”
Xi and Trump greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs and shared a brief hug as an ensemble of young people chanted, “Welcome! Welcome! Warmly welcome!”
Xi said he looked forward to talking with Trump on major issues concerning China-U.S. relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape to advance “strategic stability,” Xinhua said.

President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.

The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.

But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.

title: Misinformation about a FEMA test leveraged distrust in Spanish-speaking communities
summary: On Tuesday, radios and TVs across the U.S. flashed a simulated emergency alert from FEMA
story: On Tuesday, radios and TVs across the U.S. flashed a simulated emergency alert from FEMA

For approximately one minute on Tuesday, radios and televisions across the United States flashed a simulated emergency alert from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. And then, despite dire predictions, it was over.

The week preceding the FEMA drill saw significant communication and service outages that disabled Outlook and other Microsoft programs, grounded thousands of flights, blocked access to JPMorgan Chase, and halted internal communications at the National Security Agency. The test, scheduled every three years to identify issues in the system, has previously become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories and misinformation. This year, even more so.

Online, false and misleading claims questioned the cause of the outages, or connected them to threats of international blackouts caused by rogue or mysterious actors. The narratives spread across borders and in different languages, with particular implications and cultural connections tied to Spanish-language claims that circulated throughout global Latino communities.

Although the misinformation was not limited to Latino or Spanish-language communities, experts warned that these online conversations show how growing distrust in elites and institutions uniquely influences Latino media consumption.

“This sense of general distrust within many communities, but especially including the Latino community in the United States, will then feed into and be amplified by the online discourse around it,” said Dr. Arthur Soto-Vásquez, who teaches ethnic and equity studies at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

In the days leading up to the scheduled FEMA test, conspiracy theories wove together real events to push false theories. The timing of the previous sequence of service outages was cited as supposed evidence of a greater international catastrophe people needed to prepare for.

Social media posts questioned whether the test was really part of greater preparedness efforts as concerns grow about the impact of climate change and growing reliance on technology. They referenced programs including Fortress America, a Defense Department initiative to heighten preparedness efforts on U.S. military bases, and the U.K.’s “Be Ready” campaign that urges the public to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours.
“The success in virality of these rumors is because it’s anchored in things that are real,” said Rafael Olavarría, a research consultant with the Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas.

The DDIA analyzed over 2,200 Spanish-language posts and articles uploaded between Nov. 11 and Nov. 17 to track the spread of claims forecasting a “worldwide outage.” The content, which amassed over 95 million views and 6 million interactions, traveled furthest when pushed by “mainstream and clickbait-style outlets” using “alarmist headlines” that were often debunked inside of their own articles.

Misinformation in English centered mostly on the possibility of prolonged nationwide blackouts, some of which originated with a fabricated video of President Donald Trump warning that “a 90-day blackout is going to happen before the end of the year.” In Spanish, erroneous claims cited real events occurring abroad, distorting them as “proof” of rumored blackouts in their own countries.

“The rumors, according to the data we gathered, exploded online after what we saw with airports and banks going offline,” Olavarría told the AP. “Misinformation, when it gets a grain of truth, has a way of becoming more effective.”

What set the Spanish-language misinformation apart, according to Roberta Braga, founder and executive director of Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas, was the motivations of bad actors to leverage “levels of mistrust among Latinos about elites and institutions.”
The DDIA’s own research shows that most Latinos do not trust tech company CEOs, AI companies, politicians, or government institutions to keep them safe as technology develops.
“I think this all gets at a discomfort that people feel about the digitalization of their lives,” Braga said. “A lot of aspects of their day to day and security are dependent on digital systems.”

Or, “damn, another blackout,” as Bad Bunny laments in his track “El Apagón,” which captures some Latinos’ sentiments of widespread power outages as more than just viral threats. Blackouts, or “apagones,” are increasingly ubiquitous hardships from the islands of the Caribbean to nations across Central and South America.

These outages are rarely ever seen as conspiracies, though. Their increased frequencies stem from rising temperatures and catastrophic climate change, burdening grids that, in some countries, have been neglected for years due to economic constraints or government inefficiency and corruption.

For populations that “grew up distrusting people in power,” this vulnerability becomes something misinformation campaigns are able to exploit when targeting global Latino communities and their distrust of institutions.

“The fear and the mobilization of what’s happening is maybe based off of the distrust of previous experiences with other forms of panic or fear,” said Dr. Soto-Vásquez. “The consistent moderating factor is just this general sense of distrust.”
Though no widespread “apagón” came with the test alert on Tuesday, the false narratives offered an opportunity for people to examine the sources of online information they are using.
“If the apagon doesn’t happen today, now you know that that influencer, that account, shared something that didn’t happen,” Olavarría said on Tuesday.
AP writer Melissa Goldin in New York contributed to this report.
Rincon has participated in the Latinos Media and Democracy Program at the Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas.
