title: School districts have fewer students, but some are delaying painful budget decisions
summary: Seattle Public Schools faces a recurring budget crisis due to declining enrollment
story: Seattle Public Schools faces a recurring budget crisis due to declining enrollment
SEATTLE -- Nearly four decades ago, state auditors delivered a stark warning to Seattle Public Schools.

The district needed to close several campuses with low enrollment to avert a deepening budget crisis. But the recommendations generated a fierce neighborhood outcry, so Seattle officials set the audit aside.

Then, 34 years later, history repeated itself. In 2024, Seattle’s then-superintendent proposed shuttering up to a fifth of its schools because there weren’t enough students to fill them, but again scrapped the plan after community resistance.
Now, the district’s back in the same financial bind, with opposition already building against a new plan to shutter nearly a dozen campuses.

The cycle in Seattle reflects what some education experts call a national paralysis in school district boardrooms. Public school enrollment has plummeted by more than 1.4 million students since the pandemic, according to a recent study by Stanford University researchers Thomas Dee and Jaymes Pyne. That’s primarily due to declining birth rates and expanding school choice. Yet, rather than downsize to match their new financial reality, district leaders throughout the country have largely hesitated.
AP is covering school closures in partnership with The Hechinger Report and Big Local News at Stanford University.

One out of every 4 public schools in the U.S. has lost 15% or more of its student population since 2019, according to the study. (In Seattle, enrollment has fallen by roughly 8% since that year, to below 49,000 students.) Despite these empty desks, the overall number of schools in operation remains virtually unchanged — and teacher headcounts have actually grown by 1% nationwide.
“School districts have been playing Hamlet on this for a while now and dithering on this question,” Dee said. “We’ve never had more teachers per student in our nation’s history.”

Today’s budget woes can be attributed, at least in part, to more than $190 billion in federal pandemic relief aid. The one-time cash allowed superintendents to maintain staffing levels in spite of shrinking student bodies. With those federal funds exhausted, many districts now must confront painful structural deficits. And the needs remain acute. Disability diagnoses are rising — and they’re costly, adding to the financial strain. Many students also haven’t caught up academically after the pandemic.
Research from Arkansas, California, Chicago and elsewhere suggests closing a school yields only modest and temporary budget relief.

“The conversation really should be about the educational experience: How do we better serve the students with the resources we have left?” said Liza Rankin, a Seattle school board member since 2019, noting that employee pay and benefits account for roughly 80% of a district’s budget. “Closing schools doesn’t save much money to begin with. Payroll is where the big money is.”
Instead, leaders have preferred to rely on one-time reserves or small administrative cuts.

In San Francisco, where enrollment fell 10% since 2019, a $100 million-plus deficit prompted a chaotic proposal from the district in late 2024 to shutter more than a dozen schools. That plan was shelved following the superintendent’s resignation. And earlier this year, a new superintendent reached a $183 million contract with the United Educators of San Francisco, or UESF.

In its most recent budget, the district projects it will close its structural deficit next school year, mostly relying on early retirements and cuts to central office to avert closures. The current budget also projects, however, a $26 million deficit by the following year.
Labor leaders insist any panic is unwarranted.

A UESF spokesperson argued the district’s substantial cash reserves could stabilize the budget. Its rainy day fund stood at nearly $139 million last year, according to the district, though it expects to draw down its reserves to just $52 million over the next two years.
Experts strongly warned against tapping rainy day funds to cover ongoing expenses, like salary.

“That could buy them more time, maybe provide another year of planning, but it doesn’t come close to resolving the structural issues that San Francisco has,” said Jason Willis, a school finance expert with research group WestEd who trains K-12 budget officers.

There are no easy solutions — and students could pay the price. Closing schools can set students back academically, research shows, and teacher layoffs may be even more disruptive to student learning.

Still, Dee, the Stanford researcher, warned that if local leadership fails to act, other political actors might. State takeovers of school districts have been rising, with at least 21 happening since 2023, according to a tally from nonprofit news outlet Chalkbeat.
Under state takeovers, school board members and superintendents often have much less flexibility to determine how to cut budgets — or whom to lay off.
Said Dee: “If they don’t manage their finances well, there’s always the specter of some really disruptive state oversight.” ____
Sharon Lurye of The Associated Press contributed reporting.

title: Government lawyers again being assigned in Seattle-area immigration detention cases
summary: The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Seattle says it is once again assigning lawyers to represent the federal government in all cases where people challenge their detention by immigration authorities
story: The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Seattle says it is once again assigning lawyers to represent the federal government in all cases where people challenge their detention by immigration authorities

SEATTLE -- The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington says it is once again assigning lawyers to represent the federal government in all cases where people challenge their detention by immigration authorities.

Late last month, amid the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd wrote that his office had been swamped by such cases — to the point that he didn't have enough staff to handle them.

The challenges, brought as habeas corpus petitions in federal court, typically prompt litigation that can include numerous hearings, motions and responses. Floyd, a former immigration judge himself, wrote in a letter to Chief U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that his office intended to no longer assign attorneys except in cases it considered a priority.

That was a concern for the court, with judges worried there might be no federal government attorneys present to ensure their orders to release certain detainees were communicated to the Department of Homeland Security and carried out.
On Tuesday, Floyd issued a statement saying his office would once again assign staff to appear in court on behalf of the federal government in all immigration habeas cases.

"After collaborative meetings with the judges of the Western District of Washington, we have agreed on new procedures which will result in a more streamlined process for immigration Habeas petitions,” he said.

He did not detail what those new procedures are. But in one such case Wednesday, his office filed what it called an “abbreviated return,” acknowledging the petition from the detainee and making clear that the federal government did not intend to contest it, instead asking the court to rule on the basis of the detainee's petition and any related filings.

“The Court is pleased that the U.S. Attorney’s Office will be appearing in every immigration habeas case and facilitating communications with the parties it represents,” U.S. District Court Clerk Joshua Lewis said in an emailed statement.

Judges across the country have frequently ruled against the Trump administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being illegally held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. U.S. border czar Tom Homan recently told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases.

In western Washington, judges have ruled hundreds of times against the administration in such cases, finding that it was unlawful for ICE to re-arrest immigrants who had previously been detained and then released pending deportation or other proceedings, noted Matt Adams, legal director for the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project.

“These are people who are in the middle of immigration proceedings, who showed up for their appointment and then were arrested at their appointment,” Adams said Wednesday. “It's just caused a tremendous amount of hardship — families are being torn apart, people are losing jobs, people don't have money to pay the rent. The bottom line is the government is digging in its heels and continuing to unlawfully arrest our clients, and the courts are doing what they can to provide relief.”

With cases not being contested by the U.S. attorney's office, Adams said, his clients could be released more quickly than they otherwise would have. It typically has taken a month or more for detainees to be released after filing habeas petitions, he said.

The question of whether detainees who have been living in the U.S. are entitled to a hearing challenging their detention in immigration court while they contest deportation is currently before the Supreme Court.

Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

title: Mental competency at issue in US criminal case against Meghan's father
summary: A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex
story: A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex

TAMPA, Fla. -- A judge scheduled a mental competency hearing Thursday for the 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, two weeks after he was arrested in Florida and charged with storing child sexual abuse material in California.

Thomas Markle was released after his arrest at a senior care center but was ordered to jail four days later, on Nov. 10, when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor. A judge also ordered him to be examined by a mental health professional.
A hearing was set for Thursday afternoon in federal court in Tampa, Florida. Prosecutors declined to comment Wednesday. Markle's lawyer did not reply to an email seeking comment.

Markle’s arrest in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, the FBI said in a court filing.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. and settle in Florida.

The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine National Police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig. Gen. Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.

The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.

Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”

title: Trump faces GOP pushback to his order to use steam to launch jets from aircraft carriers
summary: Senators are pushing back against President Donald Trump's order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults
story: Senators are pushing back against President Donald Trump's order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults

WASHINGTON -- Senators want to scuttle President Donald Trump's order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults to launch fighter jets, a directive that would cost billions of taxpayer dollars and could even blunt the lethality of America's most advanced warships.

Sen. Roger Wicker, the Mississippi Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, put it plainly at a hearing Tuesday: "Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everybody needs to understand that."

Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee also made clear their opposition to Trump’s steam catapult directive in the 2027 defense appropriations bill, which was released Monday. The bill would direct the Navy to provide a report on the effectiveness of the new, magnetically powered catapult system that shoots fighter jets off the deck of carriers versus the old steam-powered one.

“The Committee is concerned that such a major redesign would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in program schedule delays,” Republican lawmakers wrote in an explanatory statement about Trump's order.

The pushback in the waning days of the Republican-controlled Congress is a notable rebuke to one of Trump's pet issues. He claimed that the magnetic catapults “didn’t work” during remarks in the Oval Office last year, issued the memo in August directing a return to the old steam system and has a long history of railing against the technology.

It comes as the Republican president tries to convince Congress to pass his $1.5 trillion defense budget before the end of the year. Democrats will take control of the House and Senate on Jan. 3, setting the stage for battles over spending in Washington.

In a statement accompanying the defense spending bill, Republicans on the Appropriations Committee targeted Trump's steam catapult order and warned against "such significant programmatic shifts without substantive analysis, justification, and Congressional approval.”

The statement also noted what lawmakers and experts have been saying: The fighting in Iran appeared to show that the new electromagnetic system on the nation's most advanced aircraft carrier, the USS Gerald R. Ford, launched more planes in less time and with fewer sailors than the steam catapults of older carriers.
The new technology also appeared to demonstrate greater “combat lethality than previous generation carriers,” the GOP lawmakers said.

The steam catapult issue came up Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering Trump’s nomination of acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to permanently take the top civilian job.

Under questioning from Sen. Tim Kaine, a Democrat from Virginia, Cao appeared to stand behind Trump's directive, arguing that including the new system, along with electromagnetically driven elevators, was “delaying our carriers by seven years.”
“I’m trying to accelerate that,” he added.

While the new systems experienced development delays during the USS Ford’s construction, Navy leaders have praised their performance and maintenance following the carrier’s recent deployment to the Middle East.

Imposing changes to the Ford-class design appears to continue what the administration’s own assessment found to be one of the issues facing American shipbuilding. Trump’s August memo noted that the Navy’s constant design changes “have resulted in cost growth, delays, and cancellations.”
“The Navy shall not impose iterative design changes upon the original mature parent designs,” the memo declared.

When asked about the pushback to the directive, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said: “President Trump has revitalized America’s shipbuilding industry, which is essential to the national security and economic prosperity of the United States. President Trump has fixed critical long-term issues in Navy shipbuilding, and will continue to restore American maritime dominance.”

Cao's support for Trump's order seemed in contrast to the acting Navy secretary's arguments earlier in the hearing, when he touted his decision to halt all engineering changes to the Navy's new frigates to keep that program on track.

When asked about the contradicting testimony, Lt. Cmdr. Adagray Willis, a spokeswoman for Cao, said Cao would work with the White House, Pentagon, Congress and the defense industry "to ensure ours remains the fiercest Navy in the world.”

At the hearing, Kaine spoke out against Trump’s steam directive and noted his conversations with sailors on the flight deck of the USS Ford who spoke “very highly” of the new system. Kaine represents the Ford’s homeport of Norfolk as well as the city headquartering the only company building U.S. aircraft carriers, Newport News Shipbuilding.

“I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches on the Ford before you decide to go down on a path that will be more expensive and less capable,” Kaine told Cao.

Trump's August directive to remove the electromagnetic system and return to steam raised concerns about costs as well as the difficulty of maintaining the older systems, which need more sailors to operate them.
His ire with the new technology goes back to at least 2017 in his first term, when he claimed the new system is “not good” and “doesn’t have the power” of the older, steam systems.
“You’re going to goddamned steam,” Trump said in an interview with Time magazine. The topic has frequently come up since then at rallies and other events.

In April, Cao's predecessor, Secretary John Phelan, announced the Navy was reviewing the design and costs of the Ford-class aircraft carrier and was not ruling out canceling future versions of its design.
The newest Chinese aircraft carriers employ electromagnetic catapults, and France said it plans to use the system on its new carrier.

title: Deep-sea mining auctions spark environmental concerns
summary: The Trump administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor
story: The Trump administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor

PAGO PAGO, American Samoa -- Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka sat in the shallows at Fatumafuti Beach as her 4-year-old daughter, Erhys, splashed through the clear water on a Little Mermaid kickboard. Below, iridescent blue and rainbow-streaked fish wove through fields of coral.

It was a rare moment of calm before a long journey. Soon, Suluai-Mahuka would travel from American Samoa to California to protest the Trump administration’s efforts to lease areas near her island for deep-sea mining. She planned to pack a bottle of seawater that would give members of the Samoan diaspora a chance to touch and connect with the waters she’s fighting to protect.

The administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor. The first waters it is targeting are some of the most pristine areas of the Pacific Ocean near American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, two U.S. territories thousands of miles from where decisions for their islands are being made.

Despite its status as an experimental and controversial industry, deep-sea mining has become a pillar of President Donald Trump’s campaign to expand U.S. control over minerals critical to the technology and defense industries. In April last year, the president directed his administration to expedite the search for those metals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. Auctions for the seabed near Virginia and Alaska could take place next year, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters.

The minerals companies are after include nickel, cobalt, manganese and copper — useful to making everything from smartphones to electric vehicles — that have concentrated over millions of years along the ocean floor and the volcanic crusts of seamounts. It’s unclear how abundant they are near American Samoa and the Northern Marianas.

In granting a lease, the U.S. would be joining a handful of other countries that have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals. Most mining techniques involve deploying underwater vehicles thousands of feet deep to vacuum up rocks and sediment from the ocean floor. Under most proposals, those rocks are filtered and returned to a mining ship, with unwanted debris released back into the ocean.

Suluai-Mahuka and other opponents have tried to stall the auctions of the nearby ocean, rallying public comments criticizing the move. They are prepared to work against the obstacles that come with living in territories dependent on federal aid, where residents have neither a voting representative in Congress nor the right to vote for president.

“When they ask us for public comments, it always feels like we’re just screaming at a moving train,” said David Cabrera, who leads a group seeking to revive Indigenous forms of fishing in Saipan, the main island of the Northern Marianas.

Located in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and Australia, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are two separate chains of volcanic islands that both endured occupations by colonial powers before becoming U.S. territories.

Despite economic challenges and a diaspora that is slowly shrinking their populations of 50,000 people, the territories have kept alive traditions that tie them to the ocean and remain sacred to the Indigenous peoples who first made the region’s islands home.

The U.S. waters surrounding American Samoa include Rose Atoll, an uninhabited island named for the pinkish hue of its coral reefs that is an important habitat for seabirds. The U.S. waters around the Northern Marianas include parts of the Mariana Trench, the deepest place on earth. Both are protected by marine monuments that now border the proposed mining areas.

If a lease is granted, it will be difficult to undo under a different administration, said former Bureau of Ocean Energy Management Director Elizabeth Klein. The government would have to justify the cancellation at a hearing and face potential litigation.

In response to the mounting opposition, the newly formed Marine Minerals Administration has emphasized that the upcoming auctions will only grant companies the right to take initial steps to explore for seafloor minerals. Any testing or commercial mining proposals will go through further public comment and a more intensive environmental review.

“It’s cold comfort,” said Zeno Camacho Deleon Guerrero Jr., a resident of the Northern Mariana Islands and a board member of the Micronesia Climate Change Alliance, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region’s environment and people. “Once you find what you want, you’re going to get it. You’re going to start mining.”
The first auction for deep-sea mining - in waters near American Samoa - was scheduled to take place Thursday in the Southern California city of Thousand Oaks.

Suluai-Mahuka had decided to be in California, despite the long hours it would take to get there. She and her team at Finafinau, the environmental group she founded, were working to bring people from across the Pacific community to protest alongside them.
“If these people are going to be selling our ocean, they’re going to see our faces when they do these bids,” she said.

A legal battle now makes it unclear whether the auction will proceed. On Monday, a judge ruled the government violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to consider the full impacts of a deep-sea mining lease. By Wednesday morning, the Trump administration had yet to delay the auction. Two other lawsuits are pending.

For an opening bid of $3 million, the administration was offering companies the chance to vie for 20-year leases granting them the exclusive right to mine commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. Two areas of the seafloor, each more than 15 million acres in size, were available for bidding.
The administration has proposed another auction for five parcels of the seafloor near the Northern Mariana Islands in December.

Deep-sea mining goes against everything Suluai-Mahuka stands for, she said, and against the Samoan way of life that revolves around the ocean — whether it’s diving among corals, swimming and relaxing, fishing for local delicacies, or the commercial tuna industry that sustains the local economy. All of that, to her, is at risk.
“We would be giving up a piece of ourselves that we cannot get back,” she said. Her group, Finafinau, takes its name from the Samoan word for resilience.
In Samoan legend, the world began as only the heavens and the ocean. “The ocean is life. It’s sacred to us,” said Malouamaua Tuiolosega. “We lose the ocean, we lose life.”

Tuiolosega represents the ancient governing council of Manu’a, a district of American Samoa that makes up the closest inhabited areas to where deep-sea mining leases could be granted, about 100 nautical miles from its shores. Populated by just 800 people across three islands, and isolated by infrequent transportation to the capital city of Pago Pago, Manu’a residents depend even more heavily on the environment for survival.
Since long before American Samoa became part of the United States, the council’s chiefs have overseen the islands’ resources, which they understand are in delicate balance with people.
If more is taken from the islands than is needed to survive, Tuiolosega said, “you violate the relationship and the trust between the people and its resource, and then it disappears.”

He sees the same push toward exploiting the oceans behind deep-sea mining as he does the Trump administration’s efforts to open up marine monuments in the Pacific Ocean to commercial fishing. The governing council, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, has joined one of the lawsuits against the Trump administration over the upcoming lease sale.

“President Trump recognizes the enormous potential of America’s offshore critical minerals to drive technological innovation, economic prosperity, and national security,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to The Associated Press.
“A lease sale is not a mandate to mine. Any future extraction would require additional environmental review and regulatory approvals, informed by engagement with local communities,” Rogers said.

Although no company worldwide has started commercial mining operations in the deep sea, a crop of U.S. startups, buoyed by the president’s policies, hopes to soon change that. Some supporters believe deep-sea mining could be an important income stream for American Samoa if it were to become an industry hub.

“If we don’t look for some kind of manufacturing process, something that people will buy, we’re going to be destitute. We’re going to be broke,” said John Wasko, executive director of the American Samoa Economic Development Council, a group promoting industry on the islands.
The deep-sea mining startup Impossible Metals, which has signaled interest in the upcoming auction, has offered to share 1% of any future profits with the American Samoan community.
Suluai-Mahuka and others don’t buy the promises of jobs and investments.

The leases offered by the Marine Minerals Administration will ask companies to “make every reasonable effort” to hire employees from the territories and support “community well-being,” but the regulations don’t include any binding requirements or numeric targets.

There is also no guarantee of economic gains. While the federal government would collect the winning bid amount, along with regular rent payments and royalties over the life of the lease, there are no mandates for the government to share earnings from deep-sea mining with local territories or states. That’s different from offshore oil and gas drilling, where Gulf states receive 37.5% of revenue.

A major question for local government is whether a deep-sea mining lease will hurt American Samoa’s tuna fishery and force the closure of the last remaining cannery. Purse seine and longline fleets supply tuna for the local StarKist plant, with the longline fleet fishing entirely in U.S. waters — including the areas up for leasing.

Nathan Ilaoa, director of the American Samoa Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, said his agency was hoping for a “more exhaustive” review of the potential impacts to the fishery before the auction. He said he doesn’t yet have answers on whether contaminants or sediment plumes from disrupting the ocean floor will alter the tuna’s migratory patterns.
“We’re extremely concerned that the disappearance of our longline fleet could translate into the cannery leaving American Samoa, which would be an economic disaster for the territory,” Ilaoa said.

American Samoa’s leadership opposed deep-sea mining when word of company interest started reaching its shores. In 2024, the territory issued a moratorium on deep-sea mining in the waters it controls, which extend from shore out to 3 nautical miles (5.5 kms). But the territory has little say over the activities that take place in federal waters beyond that line.

When the auction was proposed last year, American Samoa Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, wrote to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management that he and all chambers of local government unanimously opposed deep-sea mining, as did the vast majority of residents. But the governor now welcomes the auction, according to a Monday statement.
“This is a historic moment for American Samoa and for our nation,” he said.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said it has carefully considered feedback from the governor of American Samoa, and will incorporate it into the agency's process “to the maximum extent practicable,” including sharing the locations of deep-sea mining ships, coordinating with fishing vessels, and reviewing any impacts to fish habitat.

The agency said it supports sharing deep-sea mining revenues with territories, and is working with lawmakers and Department of the Interior leadership to support changes that would grant it the authority to do so.
It did not respond to questions about why the auction was arranged to be thousands of miles from American Samoa, or how it factored in local opposition to its policies on deep-sea mining.

Residents of the Northern Mariana Islands are closely watching the events in American Samoa as they brace for a potential auction of the seabed near their islands. The proposal has come at a challenging time for the territory, which was battered by two super typhoons in April and July.

The territory’s government is in fiscal crisis, with Gov. David M. Apatang warning of austerity measures after a five-day shutdown in October. Many public schools suffered broken windows and damaged roofs from the storms, while residents face rising electricity costs from the territory’s sole energy provider.

“It’s very overwhelming for everybody here in this region right now,” said Cabrera, the advocate for traditional fishing. “You just want to worry about keeping your lights on and putting food on the table, so it’s a challenge to get support for anything other than that.”

Born and raised in Saipan, and descended from the Indigenous Carolinian and Chamorro peoples, Cabrera served in the U.S. Navy for seven years and worked in the United States mainland before returning home. He founded his group, Talaya Club, to teach people on the island how to fish with traditional fishing nets known as talayas that are cast out in the ocean surf.

His long-term goal is to help island families become less dependent on imported food through traditional fishing. Sediment plumes from deep-sea mining near the Northern Mariana Islands could endanger that mission, he said.
“That will inevitably impact our fisheries and the health of our fisheries, and thus the health of our people,” Cabrera said.

Residents of Saipan have already waged many fights against the U.S. government. Most recently, islanders objected to U.S. Navy plans to turn the territory’s beloved island of Pagan into a firing range for thousands of troops. The agency formally abandoned those plans in July after more than a decade of community pushback.

When the deep-sea mining auction was proposed, the Northern Marianas government initially reacted with a measured tone. Both Apatang, an independent, and Kimberlyn King-Hinds, the Republican nonvoting congressional delegate, said they neither supported nor opposed deep-sea mining.

But after the federal government doubled the leasing area in March to include waters both east and west of the territory, Apatang opposed the auction, according to Henry Hofschneider, the governor’s chief of staff. The expanded leasing area is just 57 miles from Saipan and 46 miles from the U.S. territory of Guam.

Still, the governor said in a statement to the AP that he has faith in the rule of law and believes federal regulations will protect the marine environment from harm. He has asked the Marine Minerals Administration to consider pausing the auction until the various lawsuits have been heard and decided. In September, King-Hinds introduced a bill in the U.S. House that seeks to distribute 50% of federal deep-sea mining revenues to the nearest territories.
Cecilio Raiukiulipiy worries that deep-sea mining threatens another tradition in the Northern Marianas — navigation by the sea and stars.

Raiukiulipiy was granted the title of navigator in a special ceremony in 2018. Once you accept the title, he said, “it’s your responsibility to keep the knowledge, to pass it on, and to take care of your people, all the people in the islands and also the environment.”

Several times per year, his voyages take him across the Mariana Trench, adjacent to where the Trump administration could green-light seabed mining. On the western side of the trench, he said, the water is colder and the waves churn like a washing machine. It’s an area home to “all kinds of whales,” and where seafood come to spawn, he said. He has seen baby eels swimming north toward the waters of Japan.
“Those are indicators that we are on the right course,” he said. Known as seamarks, or living waypoints, they are derived from a deep-seated knowledge of the seaways in his part of the world.
Raiukiulipiy belongs to one of the groups suing the Trump administration to try to stop the auction off the Northern Marianas next month.

“They don’t understand how we live,” Raiukiulipiy said of the federal government in Washington. “They’re looking at it with a dollar sign. Us, we look at how we’re going to survive, how we are going to live, how we are going to eat.”
Like many around him, the ocean is also sacred to Raiukiulipiy. His community believes their ancestors come from deep in the ocean.
“We usually do our burials in the ocean,” he said. “We bury them back.”
Wieffering reported from Washington, D.C.

title: Cornyn blocks top Justice Department official nominated for judicial vacancy in Texas
summary: A senior outgoing Republican senator says he will block one of President Donald Trump’s final judicial picks for a Texas court vacancy
story: A senior outgoing Republican senator says he will block one of President Donald Trump’s final judicial picks for a Texas court vacancy

WASHINGTON -- A senior outgoing Republican senator said Wednesday that he will block one of President Donald Trump’s final judicial picks for a court vacancy in Texas, as the GOP-led Senate scrambles to fill all the remaining vacancies in the federal courts before Democrats assume power in January.

Texas Sen. John Cornyn told The Associated Press that he has not returned the “blue slip” for Elliot Gaiser, a top official at the Justice Department who was nominated for the Dallas-area vacancy earlier this month, nor does he plan to. A “blue slip” is effectively a permission slip from home-state senators that allows judicial nominees to advance in their confirmation process, and it gives senators tremendous veto power over a president's court picks.

“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn said in an interview on Wednesday. “This is part, of course, of the constitutional responsibility of senators in the Senate to provide advice and consent. But it’s hard to provide advice and consent when there’s zero consultation, which happened in that case.”
Cornyn also said the White House has requested information about his preferred candidate, Fort Worth lawyer Steve Fahey. The senator said he did not know whether Gaiser would be formally withdrawn.
“He's a very bright young man, and I think has a very bright future,” Cornyn said of Gaiser. “I kind of feel bad that he’s been used basically as a pawn in this process.”

The senator stressed that he did not want to leave the court seat vacant. Fahey served in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas from 2003 until 2021, and was a partner at Kirkland and Ellis until starting his own firm in 2024.

Gaiser, who leads the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, was first contacted by Texas Sen. Ted Cruz’s staff about becoming a federal judge on Nov. 4, the day after the election, according to his nominee questionnaire sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee. Cornyn has repeatedly raised concerns about his nomination process, noting that he has not been vetted by a bipartisan federal judicial evaluation committee that is traditionally used in Texas.

title: Rainfall supercharged by El Niño causes road flooding in Florida
summary: A slow-moving storm system has flooded portions of southern Florida
story: A slow-moving storm system has flooded portions of southern Florida

PLANTATION, Fla. -- A slow-moving storm system dumped heavy rains that prompted an emergency declaration Wednesday in South Florida where the roof of a synagogue collapsed and cars were submerged along roads, authorities said.
On the West Coast, heavy rain and high winds grounded planes at San Francisco’s airport, disrupted ferry service and flooded roads in Napa County and other wine country areas north of the city.

Preliminary figures for Florida showed up to a foot (30.5 centimeters) of rain fell in a 24-hour period ending Wednesday morning in parts of Broward County, said Alejandra Garcia, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Miami.
The threat was expected to last through Friday along Florida's Atlantic Coast with additional rainfall amounts of 12 inches (30 centimeters) possible, the weather service said.

The Florida Division of Emergency Management said in an advisory Tuesday night that "potentially catastrophic” amounts of rainfall could cause flash flooding, life-threatening rip tides and expected minor beach erosion due to high surf.

On top of all that, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, a low-pressure system is expected to form near the northern Bahamas. It could become a subtropical or tropical storm over parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts into early next week, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami.

Garcia said the natural warming cycle called El Niño has disrupted Florida’s typical dry season that runs from October to May and is “helping bring these low pressure systems down toward the southeastern United States, which in turn is causing these heavy precipitation events.”

In Florida, the city of Hollywood declared a state of emergency Wednesday and Mayor Josh Levy urged motorists to stay off roads and avoid unnecessary travel. Portions of the Florida Turnpike and Interstate 95 in Hollywood were closed due to high water and stalled vehicles.
The city said it received more than 300 calls for service overnight.
“It’s a historically significant rainfall event in the city,” Levy said.
Some residents complained that motorists who were driving too fast caused a wake that pushed floodwaters into their homes, he said.
Heavy rains caused the roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood to collapse. No injuries were reported.

The highest rainfall amount was recorded in Plantation, where resident Jade Jaime said the storm just kept going all day "and then by the time we went to sleep at night, still just pouring down like it was never going to end.”
In Fort Lauderdale, the 5.72 inches (14.5 centimeters) of rain that fell in a downpour ending early Wednesday broke the daily record of 1.8 inches (4.5 centimeters) set in 1959, Garcia said.
In northern Florida, a warning was issued for minor flooding along the St. Johns River.

The Los Angeles County Fire Department issued an evacuation warning Wednesday for the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas, saying there was a risk of debris flows as a storm approaches. The warning is in effect from Wednesday evening through Friday morning.

In San Francisco, areas along the Embarcadero were flooded Wednesday morning as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm.
Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties, according to the California Department of Transportation and the California Highway Patrol.
Heavy rain that began falling north of San Francisco was expected to spread south to the Central Coast later Wednesday, the weather service said.
Wind gusts of up to 50 mph (80 kph) were forecast for San Francisco's East Bay and up to 70 mph (113 kph) for the Altamont Pass, which connects Bay Area highways to I-5 in the Central Valley.
Snow accumulations of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada Mountains.
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. Associated Press reporter Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco contributed to this report.

title: Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, Farm Bureau says
summary: Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday
story: Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday
Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday.

The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it's the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a high of $64.05 in 2022.
High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes, frozen peas and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said.

And turkey prices have risen sharply as more Americans seek out protein even as the industry continues to recover from bird flu cases. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has forecast the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year.

title: Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035
summary: The Pew Research Center has released new projections that show that Islam will surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035
story: The Pew Research Center has released new projections that show that Islam will surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035
NEW YORK -- Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released Wednesday by the Pew Research Center.

Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity are growing, but Islam is growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, is that Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups.
“It's the babies,” said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity are much smaller factors than fertility rates.

During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that's considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.

According to Pew's latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew's new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.

The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration.

Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62% of U.S. adults, according to Pew, and will fall below 50% by 2065.
In neighboring Canada, Christians are expected to drop below 50% by 2030, Pew said.

In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41% of the U.S. population and to outnumber Christians in Canada.

The world’s population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070, Pew said. Of the religious groups it analyzed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%.

Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew said. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan.

Over the coming decades, Pew said, most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted.

By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world’s Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing more than threefold to 299 million.
The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline.

For example, the number of people living in Europe will shrink by 17% by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there will drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe's population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6% to 13%.
In the U.S., Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070.

Several mainline Protestant denominations in the U.S. have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations.

By Pew’s estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020-2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers.

Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline.
If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia — which currently has the most Muslims.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations are “extremely important” in light of the evolving trends.

“The ‘clash of civilization’ theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides,” she said via email. “Many Christians are not happy to see that Islam will be the world’s largest religion and it’s causing even more angst.”

“I hope people seek opportunities for greater interreligious education,” she added. “Personal contact is important — when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanizes’ the ‘other’ in fruitful ways.”

Alan Cooperman, Pew's director of religion research, noted that most of the projected proliferation of Muslims and Christians was occurring in countries where they already are the majority — with conversion playing only a minor role.

“I don’t think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians,” he added. “I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims.”
Many countries have seen a steady proliferation of the “nones” — people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of “nones” but faces a sharp decline in overall population, the ranks of “nones” elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070, Pew said.

The “nones” already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.
This version corrects the number of projected Christians in Congo by 2070 to 299 million, instead of 270 million.

title: Florida pastor convicted of US charges related to assassination of Haitian president
summary: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship has been convicted of U.S. charges related to the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse
story: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship has been convicted of U.S. charges related to the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse
MIAMI -- A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted Wednesday of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on all charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges, the most serious one conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
Sanon, who faces up to life in prison at sentencing, showed little reaction as the verdict was announced in a federal courtroom in Miami.

Federal prosecutors said at trial that South Florida was a hub for planning and financing a plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The prosecutors said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. They also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

Sanon had acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the U.S. as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the Midwest.

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a nighttime raid at their home on July 7, 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.

Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from U.S. government programs that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to court records. U.S. prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies — Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU — for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian Supreme Court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

title: Grand jury indicts Illinois man on terrorism and weapons charges in foiled Hindu temple shooting
summary: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in a Chicago suburb faces new charges of terrorism and armed violence
story: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in a Chicago suburb faces new charges of terrorism and armed violence
CHICAGO -- A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in a Chicago suburb faces new charges of terrorism and armed violence, police said Wednesday.

Authorities allege Alexandros Paporakis planned to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Oct. 11, the first day of the Hindu holiday of Navaratri. Paporakis' co-workers at a Taco Bell reported to authorities that he told them he planned to “kill Indian people” and police arrested him that afternoon. He was initially charged with making a terrorist threat and illegally possessing a rifle.

Prosecutors have said Paporakis, of Palatine, Illinois, calls himself a white supremacist and neo-Nazi, and that he wrote a document detailing his fantasies about murdering non-white people. Police have said they recovered a rifle, ammunition, a tactical vest and a patch “displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism” from his house.

A grand jury indicted Paporakis on Nov. 5 on six counts of terrorism, two counts of armed violence and two counts of attempted terrorism, all felonies, according to police. The jury also added nine more counts of making a terrorist threat.
The indictment also included new weapons-related charges, including possession of a firearm without a serial number and not having a police-issued identification card, police said.
It is not clear why police delayed releasing information about the grand jury indictment.
A judge ordered Paporakis to be detained, declaring him a threat to the community. He is due to be arraigned in court on Thursday morning.
Fedor Kozlov, an attorney for Paporakis, told The Associated Press in a text message Wednesday that his client is still planning to plead not guilty to the charges.

The thwarted shooting sparked alarm among members of Chicago's Hindu community and South Asian leaders, who said an uptick in racist rhetoric against their community had fueled the threat. U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was at the temple that was targeted on the day of the planned attack, urged authorities to charge Paporakis with a hate crime. Authorities have not announced any such charge.

The FBI's Chicago field office said Wednesday there was no additional information about possible federal charges. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois has not responded to a request for comment.

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need either a PlayStation5 or Xbox Series X or S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

While the game has yet to officially launch, it has already racked up impressive sales. Nearly 16 million pre-order copies of the game have been sold, generating $1.5 billion in revenue, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, sold more than 200 million copies. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says "it was obvious" to him and others that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond.
story: Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."

On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."
Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown."
The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies.
"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.

Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

title: New James Bond is announced after rampant speculation
summary: After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced who the new 007 will be.
story: Robert Pattinson is the new 007. After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced Monday that Pattinson will be the next James Bond.
He will be the seventh actor to play the role since the first Bond film, "Dr. No," was released in 1962.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The naming of Pattinson comes five years after the beloved franchise's last film, 2021's "No Time to Die," which marked the first time in Bond's 64-year history on the silver screen to end with the character's death.
But 007 will be reborn in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve. It will be the first since Amazon MGM took over the franchise.
For months, fans had been debating the merits of other potential 007s, including names like Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
Pattinson only entered the rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role, the Associated Press reported, along with a few other finalists.

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Pattinson is already associated with three mega-franchises: "The Batman," "Twilight" and "Harry Potter."

Since his breakthrough in "Twilight," Pattinson has also worked in more independent films such as "Good Time," "The Lighthouse" and "Mickey 17." Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
The British royal family responded to the news on social media, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Now in the Bond role, Pattinson follows in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig.

title: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations. See the list.
summary: English singer-songwriter Raye is up for 11 awards at the 2027 Grammys, followed by Spanish singer Rosalía​ with nine nominations.
story: English singer-songwriter Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video.
Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category.

Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award.

Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video.

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.
Taylor Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.

Only recordings commercially released in the U.S. between Aug. 31, 2025, and Aug. 28, 2026, were eligible for nominations. The final round of Grammy voting, which determines the winners, will take place between Dec. 10 and Jan. 7.
The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 at 7 p.m. Eastern, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

title: 4 NFL officials work 2 games each due to ground stop, a rarity
summary: Four NFL officials worked two games Sunday — a rarity stemming from Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA that threw airlines' schedules into complete disarray.
story: Cincinnati — Don Willard did something on Sunday that the NFL hopes doesn't ever have to be duplicated — refereeing two games in one day.

Willard was the referee Sunday afternoon for the Miami Dolphins' game against the Indianapolis Colts in Indianapolis before he and three other members of the crew made the 114-mile trip to work the prime-time contest between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals.

The reshuffling happened after the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop Friday. The stop caused consternation and chaos for professional and college teams throughout the country and even resulted in moving at least one college football game from Saturday to Sunday.

NFL officials audibled by reassigning game officials for this week's matchups to stadiums closer to cities where they reside so they could drive, and Willard was asked to take over as the lead ref for the two games.

Willard usually works NFL games as a side judge. About an hour before kickoff in Indianapolis, he did the traditional microphone check and then he handled the coin toss duties typically reserved for referees.
Willard wasn't the only one doing double duty Sunday.

Umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew also jumped in a minibus and made the two-hour drive down I-74 to work the game in Cincinnati. It's the first time this officiating crew has worked together.
The four officials arrived in Cincinnati at 6:39 p.m., giving them some time to prepare before the 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

There were two instant replay reversals during the first half. A 23-yard completion to Pittsburgh's Germie Bernard was overturned when replay saw Bernard's toe was just out of bounds. An interception by Cincinnati's Jordan Battle was also reversed when a second look showed the ball hit the ground.
However, the crew called only 12 penalties in a game that usually sees a lot of flags because of the intensity of the Steelers-Bengals rivalry.

"I thought they did a great job managing a very difficult game, very testy game, obviously by both sides. So hats off to those guys for what they pulled off today. I know it was a long day for them," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said.
League officials didn't make any of the four officials who did double duty available to the media for either of Sunday's games.
NBC Sports rules analyst Terry McAulay, who worked three Super Bowls, said during Sunday night's "Football Night in America" pregame show that what the crew did was extraordinarily challenging.

"At a high level, it's a brand-new crew working together to work this game tonight that did not have at all the normal preparation - studying tendencies, studying formation style of play, and especially for this game, studying matchups on both sides of the ball. AFC North divisional games are brutal to officiate," he said. "Just working one NFL football game for three hours is incredibly mentally exhausting. When it's done, you're mentally drained. These guys have to do it now twice in one day. They don't have the normal recovery time. I know when I did it, my recovery time was never less than four hours."
The Dolphins didn't have any travel issues, a team spokesman said.
