title: Billy Evans tells his side of "You Can See Everything," Elizabeth Holmes' portrayal
summary: In his first TV interview, Billy Evans, partner of disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, talks about his characterization in the documentary "You Can See Everything," as well as threats he says have been made against his family's safety.
story: Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview.

Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'"

"You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.

Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."
It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it.

"I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."

In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don't, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me."

In fact, of the documentary that has gotten rave reviews, Evans says, "I love the film," despite the fact that he is made out to be a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment, you know, and I didn't get to control that edit."
His goal, he said, was "to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is."

In 2014 Forbes Magazine crowned Holmes the youngest self-made female billionaire. By 2017, the year she and Evans met, she was under investigation for defrauding investors for a diagnostic machine that she falsely claimed could test for hundreds of diseases with a single drop of blood.

Evans says when they first met, he did not know who she was. "I had been at her office earlier that week," he said. "I had, like, seen her the same week. But no, really, like, the first time I met her, I did not know."

"You Can See Everything" leaves us questioning what the truth is. There are also moments that are cringe-worthy, as when Evans is filmed in the shower completely naked. [You really can see everything.]

"I did not give consent to do that," said Evans. "Now, did I know they were filming me in the shower? Yes. But we would film 16 hours a day. Like, all sorts of things were filmed with assurances made. I was just as surprised as the rest of the country to have my whole body on camera for the world to see, and it's been an awkward experience in having, like, your kids' teachers see that. It's really uncomfortable."

Evans said there were "inappropriate" and "awkward" things that happened every single day, as well as requests to film things that, he said, "are not appropriate for television. All sorts of things that the details I'd rather spare the audience."
The film's production company, A24, said, "Everything that was filmed was filmed with their consent."

Some who see the film leave convinced the co-director, Nathan Fielder, had feelings for Holmes. "I think that there are bits that are played up to criticize his own bias," said Evans. "This is a film about, what can you trust? And at the end nothing is clear."

Evans says he has not spoken to Fielder since he's seen the film. "I think they're probably worried I'm gonna sue 'em," he said, adding he has no intention to do so. "Because maybe I'm a different person than most people think I am."

Evans lives with their two young children in Texas close to Holmes' prison, and carries a gun 24/7, he says, to keep his family safe. "We have threats of violence against us daily," he said. "I've got two kids. Threats of violence daily. And I would never forgive myself for having the tools, the skills, and the ability to protect my family and not doing it.

"I will give you an example: The other day, I was driving my kids to school. And a car came up behind us really, really quickly. And we stopped at the light. And the guy starts screaming next to me. And this isn't just road rage, okay? And his window is down. And he is screaming the most vile things you have ever heard about: 'I know where you live. I know who you are. I know where your kids sleep, and the things that I will do to you.' And it was terrifying."

Even given the fallout from the movie, he says he would do it all again: "With the same people, making the same film again, with everything that I know right now? 100%. Because I would also have a better understanding of what I was walking into."
Elizabeth Holmes could transfer to a halfway house next summer. Until then, Evans and their children visit her every week behind bars.

Having his children see their mother in prison, Evens said, has become "strangely normal. Like, I hate it. I absolutely hate that my daughter's first steps were in federal prison. I hate that. … But it doesn't mean that we can't find joy as we experience this. And our job, to them, is not to talk about how much it hurts and how painful it is, but to find the joy in seeing how many acorns we can collect in the prison yard and fit in a water bottle. It's finding, you know, the small, little games that we can play to make each time we go to the same place, every weekend, feel like you're going to Disneyland."

Evans said he used to count the days she was in prison, but that became too painful. "It's been since May 30th of 2023," he said. "I miss her so much. You know, I talked to her right before I came in here. And I told her, I said, 'I'm kinda nervous.' And she said, 'Just be zen. Enjoy it. Embody love. And I'll talk to you, when you're done.'"

title: The Reader: A new review source for book lovers
summary: With most newspapers and wire services closing the book on sections devoted to book reviews, Washington Monthly introduces its new online resource, offering reviews, essays, and recommendations by some of the world's top writers.
story: It's become an all-too-familiar story: Earlier this year, the Washington Post put an end to Book World, its weekly book review supplement.
"Books are expensive," said bestselling author Jonathan Alter. "Readers need help to know what's good out there."

Alter says Book World's closure created a void: "Thirty years ago, there were 30 American newspapers that, as part of their Sunday newspaper, had a book review section," he said. Today, only The New York Times still maintains a separate book review section.
"So, we stepped into the breach, and we're doing something about it," said Alter, who is co-founder of The Reader, a new, general interest, online book review, to be published every weekday.

Executive editor Haley Sweetland Edwards said, "We will have mostly book reviews, but also essays about books, columns about the literary book world, and top authors like Robert Caro and Margaret Atwood and Ann Patchett will be providing recommendations of books that have slipped below the cultural radar."

The Reader is part of Washington Monthly, a non-profit magazine. Edwards says authors lined up to be part of it: "We have 31 Pulitzer Prize-winners who have agreed to be contributors over the next year. These are the crème de la crème, and they will be reviewing for us."

Alter said, "We will review books that are going to become big bestsellers, but we're also going to review those books that sometimes fly under the radar, that are really good and that just aren't getting the recognition that they deserve."
And that's where "Sunday Morning" comes in. Each weekend, we'll offer two books for your consideration – one fiction, one non-fiction – courtesy of The Reader.
November 15
Fiction
"Stations" by Louise Kennedy (Riverhead Books). The Reader calls it "a beautifully-told story," tracing the tumultuous lives of a group of young friends in 1980s Ireland.

title: Min Jin Lee on "American Hagwon" and writing "social novels"
summary: The Korean-American novelist and bestselling author of "Pachinko" talks about her latest book, "American Hagwon," part of her series chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world.
story: It's been nearly a decade since Min Jin Lee's last book made her a literary phenomenon. "Pachinko," a sweeping historical epic chronicling four generations of a Korean family living in Japan, sold more than two million copies in the United States. It was adapted into a popular series on Apple TV.

But all that success didn't come easily. "When 'Pachinko' first came out as a hardcover, it was never on the bestseller lists," said Lee. "If you look at my hardcover sales, they're abysmal. So, if you start out with failure, it's really easy."
Did she consider "Pachinko" at its beginning a failure? "Oh, I think you can ask my publishers!" she laughed. "They would just say, this didn't sell!"
It wasn't until The New York Times named it one of the best books of the year, and it was selected as a National Book Award finalist, that "Pachinko" took off.
Lee's latest novel, "American Hagwon" (published by Cardinal), is the third in a series she calls "The Diaspora Quartet," chronicling the migration of Koreans around the world.

"Every industrial revolution had people leaving the farm to go to the city," Lee said. "And now we have environmental diaspora, where people don't have water in their communities anymore. You have economic diaspora, where certain jobs don't exist anymore, like manufacturing. I'm focusing on Koreans, because those are the people that I know about. But I'm really writing about this modern condition."

It's a deeply personal story for Lee. She came to America in 1976, when she was seven years old. The middle of three girls, her family moved to Elmhurst, Queens, where she grew up in a very blue-collar neighborhood. Her parents, a marketing executive and piano teacher in Korea, opened a newspaper stand and, later, a jewelry shop.
"As a little kid, I was so unbearably shy," Lee said. "I didn't really speak or interact with my peers very well."
But she tested into a highly-competitive public high school, where she found friends – and her footing.

From there it was on to the Ivy League, where she discovered something important was missing: Yale did not offer Korean language or Korean history courses – which, Lee says, was ignoring the full story.

"I think because of the Cold War and because of the Korean War in American history, I do think this is a rational thing to ask for," she said. So, Lee organized a letter-writing campaign, and convinced the university to start a Korean Studies program. "I think that it really helped the school," she said. "My mom has this whole theory that wherever you go, you should make it better than when you found it."

While at Yale, Lee was also struggling with a serious liver condition. "I learned that I would get liver cancer in my 20s or 30s; that's what the doctor said to me," she said. "I was like, 'Oh, if I have until 35, what do I want to do?' So, it gave me this sort of courage that I don't think normally I would have had."

Lee went to law school, then to a big firm. But before long, the hours and the stress caused her liver disease to flare up, and she decided to take a leap. "I thought, if I walk away from money and status and power, at least I'll find tremendous enrichment for me," she said.

Lee found that by writing what she describes as "social novels": "I think it's to write realistic fiction that reflects on society today, saying, this is what I think and this is the way things should be," she said.
Lee conducted thousands of interviews with people of Korean descent. In her conversations, one topic came up more than any other. And so, in "American Hagwon," she takes on education.

"A hagwon is a for-profit learning center," Lee said. "In Korea, you can go to a hagwon to become a police officer. You can go a hagwon to become a K-pop idol. And you can go to a hagwon to learn English. So, starting at the age of four or five, 80% of Koreans in South Korea send their children to hagwons."

Much of the book takes place in hagwons in Korea and the U.S., centering on a family whose life is upended when they come to America. Lee said of the father, John Koh, "John goes to the most elite school in Korea; and yet, he ends up working frying fish for somebody else."

The family's experience raises big questions about the value of education: "Sometimes someone will tell you, you go to college to get a job," said Lee. "But other people will say education should be a form of transformation and liberation. Gradually, as I worked on the book, the more I was interested in wisdom. Like, how do you obtain wisdom? How do you live a wise life?"

While "American Hagwon" is set in the 1990s, Lee says what's happening in the world today makes these questions essential. She opens her book with the line: "The rules of engagement have changed already."

"I think this is the condition of the modern person in the 21st century, and 2026 for certain, especially in the era of AI," she said. "The rules of engagement have changed already, and you didn't know. Like, we didn't get the memo. Everybody is changing the game, the paradigm, the rules. Now that we know that, what are you supposed to do? How do you educate your children? How do you retool yourself?"

Thanks to an experimental treatment in her 30s, Lee's liver disease was cured. In Harlem, where she lives with her husband and raised her son, she's already researching her fourth book, the final in her Diaspora Quartet.

Lee said, "What I would really love is if readers could feel that they have the internal resources to manage the change that feels alarming and threatening to them, and then have the internal resources and the fortitude to care for others. There's no way we're going to be able to make it through this era unless we have each other."

title: U2 on 50 years and their duet with Dolly Parton
summary: The Irish quartet celebrates its 50th birthday with "Carnaval de Luz," their first album of new music in nearly nine years. Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. talk about their song "Torn," a duet with Dolly Parton that would prove to be her last recording.
story: When U2 came knocking, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. didn't just arrive with new music; the band came bearing gifts, which they proceeded to place over a photo of Bruce Springsteen.
"We just wanna get Bruce Springsteen off your wall," Bono said. "There's some new blood coming through! But honestly Bruce, give the young people a break."
The up-and-coming Irish quartet is celebrating its 50th birthday this year – that's half a century of hits.

In September, U2 went back to the Dublin school where they first came together. Playing Mount Temple Comprehensive was "kind of amazing," said The Edge. "We used the music room in Mount Temple as our rehearsal space."
Bono said he didn't know what to expect from the students there: "I was nervous going out there."
"There were a couple of cheeky signs, like, 'When is Oasis playing?'" said The Edge. "But for the most part they really seem to get into it."
It was at Mount Temple in 1976 where Mullen pinned a note to the school bulletin board looking for bandmates. "I'd no expectations that anyone would show up, bizarrely," Mullen said.

The four got together via word of mouth. "Yeah, it's one of those funny things that the note is legendary," said Clayton. "And then when we started to talk about it, we realized none of us had seen it, and we'd been told about it by a friend or whatever."
The band has just released "Carnaval de Luz," their first album of new music in nearly nine years, created through a process that Bono called "chaotic."
The Edge reframed that as "nicely chaotic."
"Very functionally dysfunctional," Bono continued. "You would be shocked at just how raw it is and how just about to collapse."
"We're not precious in any way," The Edge said. "Until almost the record is in the store, we will try and improve and change and develop."
Won't you drive yourself nuts doing that? "Yeah. We do!" The Edge laughed.

The new album marks the return of drummer Larry Mullen, Jr., who had to sit out the band's 2024 residency at Sphere in Las Vegas with a neck injury that threatened his career. He said he wasn't terribly confident that he would be able to come back: "I had a congenital fusion, from moving like that for over 50 years, it basically had had enough," he said. "Yeah, a lot of people were very much on the page of, you've had a great life, you know, this is not worth it."
He risked paralysis if the surgery went wrong. "But you know what? I really wanted to get back and play in any capacity," Mullen said.

Asked if they were worried that he might not play again, The Edge said, "At some point, if Larry had had to retire, we would have had to have made a very difficult call about whether U2 can go on at all."
"Maybe we could have got a better looking, more fun drummer," Bono added.
The band calls "Carnaval de Luz" an album of "defiant joy." It includes the song "Torn," a duet with Dolly Parton that would prove to be her last recording
Bono said he approached singing with her on the track "With great trepidation."
Parton had shared the song with Bono: "She was like, 'You can take this wherever you want to go, and I might like where you want to take it,'" he said. "But you didn't know until it came back."
How generous an act is that for a songwriter? "Oh, no, not just a songwriter; one of the great songwriters who ever lived," Bono said.

U2 will be back out on the road next year, aiming for another groundbreaking live show. "That's our promise to our audience, is to try and have a shot at the best night of anybody's life," said Bono. "That's what we want out of our show."
Half a century on, U2 is still striving to be heard. "Whether it's relevant or not is really not up to us," said The Edge. "But whether we want to try and be relevant is up to us."

Asked what it means to be relevant, The Edge replied, "To be relevant is to speak of the moment. That's why we write songs. We all believe that we could next week write the best U2 song we've ever written. So, there's a lot to fight for, really."
"We think we are at our best," said Bono. "And if anyone out there thinks they're better … come and take it!"

title: Book excerpt: "American Hagwon" by Min Jin Lee
summary: The bestselling author of "Pachinko" returns with her third novel, about the importance placed on education by Koreans and people of Korean descent.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Min Jin Lee's 2017 novel "Pachinko" was a National Book Award finalist about four generations of a Korean family that had emigrated to Japan. She returns with her third novel, "American Hagwon" (published by Cardinal), about the importance placed on education by Koreans and people of Korean descent.
Read an excerpt below, and don't miss Jo Ling Kent's interview with Min Jin Lee on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 15!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
Tom and Clara observed that Mido had hardly made a sound.
Clara smiled. "Mido?"
Helen leaned in. "She's shy."
The boys stared meaningfully at their sister, feeling protective yet recognizing that this interview mattered. Earlier that week, Helen had prepared them for this. They wore their Sunday clothes.
"It's okay to be shy," Tom said, and smiled at her.
Mido held her breath. They were watching her, and she swallowed.
"I'd like to study with Yun here. I know I have a lot to learn in Korea." Mido took a breath. "I'm a hard worker. I promise to do all my Eagle hagwon homework. Yun told me there is a lot."
Clara and Tom laughed, and Helen closed her eyes and exhaled almost silently. Both Bo and DH smiled, trying not to make a big deal of their sister's comprehensive answer.

Helen handed Clara a folder, and she continued to speak in English, which felt strange, but it allowed her to be less formal and less aware of her status. She was a supplicant, although she was the elder. Helen believed in her children and didn't want to sell them as if they were a pair of expensive shoes or an article of designer clothing.
"I brought their report cards from Sydney. They've done well. I don't think their recent grades on quizzes and tests here reflect their abilities," she said.
Clara stood and faced the children.
"We have assessments for all three of you. Come with me. I'll let Dr. Song speak with your mother." She smiled.
The children followed Clara to the next room
Tom watched them walk out, and Clara closed the door softly behind her.
"Your children are great."
Helen smiled, not knowing what else to say as his face grew sober.

"You see, the problem is that I have a waitlist for new students, and even if the assessments showed that they were an ideal fit for Eagle, I want you to know that it's highly unlikely"—he corrected himself— "no, it's actually impossible, for us to accept them even if something changed with our enrollment, because you're not looking for one spot but three. There are parents who have been waiting for more than two years for a space to open. It's really my fault for accepting this meeting, and I blame myself. I would not want to mislead you. If you would rather that the children not take the assessment, I do understand—"

This was the hardest part of success—the need to say no often. On occasion, a parent thought he was negotiating and offered more money, which was refused. If that didn't work, the ones who were used to getting their way would reach out to a more prominent parent, but the more they tried, the more awkward the situation grew. Tom, a liberal American who had written his doctoral dissertation on education reformers, repudiated status performance of any kind. The irony of him owning a private tutoring center was not lost on him; but the longer he did this, the more he believed that he could make a difference by being a useful educator. The children here needed his care and protection, in some ways, much more than those back in the States.
Helen folded her hands in her lap.
"They won't mind the assessment. At least you'll have their results. In case—" Helen looked up, trying again. Sonya had said Helen couldn't give up until she heard the word "no" at least three times.
"How about just Mido? She's such a good student, and it would mean so much—"
"The assessment isn't long. I suppose there is no harm—" he interrupted, not wanting to hear her plea. It was difficult for him to say no; Clara was the tougher one.
"They've moved around so much, and Bo and DH may take the Suneung and apply to colleges here. Of course, their grades have to be good, too. DH wants to study in America, but it might be hard—"

Helen felt overwhelmed by the number of rungs on the ladder, and, as usual, each child would need different things. Abroad, their education had seemed more manageable, and she hadn't felt so powerless and alone.

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status: "What a tragedy"
summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
story: The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced Tuesday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. Researchers with knowledge of the decision had previously confirmed it to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.
A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

"It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years.
Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." She said the CDC remains focused on stopping outbreaks.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Tuesday on social media, "We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Kennedy pointed to "COVID-era disruptions" in childhood vaccinations and cited other countries, including Canada, Mexico, Spain and the United Kingdom, that have also lost measles elimination status.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Kennedy, should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles.

"Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember."
What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."
Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."
How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?
A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.
Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.
Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."
Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.
Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.
By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.
That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.
Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.
Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 had not been vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.
Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.
But some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated and must rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading.
"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.
Many of the recent cases have been occurring in tight-knit and largely unvaccinated Amish or Mennonite communities.

"It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50."

"I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before."

Measles is known for causing a rash, but Schaffner said that's the least of it. "What's bothersome is children, even with uncomplicated measles, are miserable for a week or a week and a half with red eyes, runny nose, cough, and just debilitating fever and diarrhea. And then you have the complications of dehydration, pneumonia, and on occasion, encephalitis."

There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles."
While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.
"Measles is a nasty, nasty virus," Schaffner said. "In contrast, the vaccine is wonderfully effective."

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
What the stock price will tell us
In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each.
The company said that 956,351,354 shares are being sold by Anthropic. The remaining shares are being sold by certain selling stockholders, from which Anthropic said it will not receive any proceeds.
Sources told CBS News before the announcement that Anthropic would likely price its shares above $80 due to strong demand.

The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.5 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion and was valued at roughly $1.7 trillion when it went public in June.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Hardcore GTA fans ditch work so they have time to play
summary: Some employees locked in their time off months ago, so they're free to start playing Grand Theft Auto 6 as soon as it launches on Nov. 19.
story: Cameron Logan Cox was honest with his employer when he recently submitted a request for paid time off.

"I literally just put GTA 6," the 34-year-old filmmaker and creative director at a music label in Kansas City told CBS News. He said his coworkers were already well aware that he'd be out of action when Grand Theft Auto 6 is officially released on Thursday.
"They all know I'm a huge gamer," he said. "We don't have anything too pressing happening, so it worked out nicely."

Cox is hardly alone. Other avid GTA fans told CBS News they've cleared their work schedules so they can dive headlong into Rockstar Games' latest, and long-awaited, installment in the hit franchise. According to data from payroll processor Gusto, PTO requests for the day of GTA 6's commercial release this week are up 9% compared with the two prior weeks.
In short, GTA 6 is as much a cultural happening as a video game. Analysts say the game, which took 13 years to make, is expected to be the largest entertainment release of all time.

"While it's common for people to plan time off around major entertainment releases and cultural events, the anticipation surrounding GTA 6 is on another level," Bart Spiegel, a partner at PwC who leads the consulting firm's global entertainment and media practice, said in an email. "It's the kind of cultural moment that could rival the Olympics in terms of the attention it commands, so there's certainly going to be an impact on workplaces."
Spoiler alert

One 27-year-old woman told CBS News that she submitted her PTO request back in March to be ready for this week's GTA launch. She knew she would want to start playing as soon as the game went live and to avoid online spoilers.

"I genuinely believe that this is one of, if not the biggest, gaming events in a lot of our lifetimes, and spoilers are going to spread so fast," said the Grays Harbor, Washington state, resident. "It's going to be nearly impossible to avoid them."
The woman, who works as a clerk for the U.S. Postal Service, has already pre-downloaded GTA 6 and plans to start playing at 9 p.m. PST on Wednesday.
"I'm probably just going to go throughout the whole night," she said.
Another player based in the U.K. told CBS News he is also trying to avoid spoilers. The 25-year-old is taking a long weekend beginning on Wednesday to "give [GTA 6] the attention it deserves."

The man, who works in tech finance and who requested anonymity because he's not authorized to speak to the media, set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — so he could begin playing as soon as possible.
Gaming time off
Meanwhile, some companies are resigning themselves to the temporary brain drain and preemptively giving employees time off to focus on GTA.
Logitech, a California-based computer and electronics manufacturer, introduced a new perk for employees earlier this month: GTO (Gaming Time Off).

And in August, a U.S. Army unit in Georgia offered active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play GTA 6 in exchange for reenlisting. The Third Infantry Division told CBS News that 43 of the 130 soldiers who were eligible selected this option as part of their reenlistment, along with other standard incentives.

While some U.S. employees may ditch work on Thursday, their absence from the office isn't expected to cause major economic disruptions, according to Victor Matheson, an economics professor at the College of the Holy Cross.
"Even if 5 million workers in the U.S. took the day off, the total U.S. labor force is 170 million people," he said in an email. "That's like 3% of the labor force."

So far, more than 17 million preorder copies of the game have been downloaded worldwide, according to Sensor Tower, a digital market intelligence company. Matheson expects the game to rack up more than 50 million users by year's end.
As for Cox, 27 years have passed since he first played Grand Theft Auto on an original PlayStation console owned by a relative. Yet the excitement is as fresh as ever.
"It feels like I'm a kid again," Cox told CBS News.

He'll be in good company when the game launches, as his son is also planning to stay home from school on Thursday and Friday. Cox agreed to let him take time off to celebrate his birthday, which falls on Friday.
"He has all of his schoolwork turned in. That was the condition," he told CBS News. "I was, like, as long as all your work's done, your grades are good, I'm fine with that."

title: Costco sees surge in panic buying after tech outages, report says
summary: Costco shoppers are stocking up on emergency items following a string of tech snafus, according to a Wall Street analyst.
story: Consumers are panic-buying at Costco, snapping up generators and other emergency-preparedness items in response to a recent string of technology outages, according to investment firm Mizuho Securities.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report.
Shoppers are "pantry-loading," while 21 of the retailer's 26 "high-ticket generators" were sold out online as of Sunday night, he added.

The recent outages, which blocked access to Microsoft apps, snarled flights nationwide and hindered banking activities at various times during the past week, are raising questions among Americans about a larger cybersecurity threat, CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman said on "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday.

The companies affected by the outages have said they were due to issues such as routine maintenance or upgrades, while the Federal Aviation Administration blamed its nationwide ground stop last week on a contractor updating its flight system.
"All of them have denied that cyberattacks are to blame," Gutman said. "Still, the system failures are fueling online speculation about a larger cyber threat."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that there's "zero evidence" that the recent outages in the U.S. are linked.

"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said during a news conference in the Philippines.
Costco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The close timing of the outages highlights the country's increasing reliance on technology, John D'Arcy, a Temple University professor who researches cybersecurity and information technology failures, told CBS News Philadelphia.
"Our systems are so much more complex and so much more interconnected than they ever have been in the past, that when we just have one failure, the effects are much more dramatic," D'Arcy said.

The surge in panic buying could lift Costco's sales, Bellinger wrote. He raised his target price for the company's stock to $1,150 from $1,100. Other big-box stores, including Walmart and Sam's Club, could see similar "pantry-loading lifts," he added.

title: Largest U.S. data centers use as much power as some countries
summary: Hyperscale data centers used almost 2% of all U.S. electricity between 2024 and 2025, a Harvard study shows.
story: The largest U.S. data centers collectively consume roughly as much energy as some individual states and even some countries, according to new research from Harvard University.

Researchers found that so-called hyperscale data centers, which occupy as much space as several football fields, consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, or 1.8% of all U.S. electricity, between 2024 and 2025. That's roughly the equivalent of what a state like Missouri uses or a nation like Denmark. Combined, the facilities also produced 26 metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, the lead author of the paper published in Nature Sustainability this week, told CBS News that it took two years to analyze the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of 403 hyperscale data centers between May 2024 and April 2025. The study likely understates the centers' estimated energy consumption, given the swift pace of AI construction across the U.S., he added.

"The data stops in April 2025, which in AI time is basically ancient history," Guidi said. There are now more than double that number of large-scale facilities operating in the U.S., with an additional 2,000 planned or under development.
"The industry is growing faster than anyone can track it," Guidi added.
Factories that never sleep
The study highlights AI's dependence on data centers and their outsized impact on the environment. Guidi explained why the facilities are such heavy electricity users.

"Every email you send, every photo you post, every show you stream, every question you ask of any generative AI software goes through a building like this," he said of the windowless facilities housing tens of thousands of computers that run around the clock.
The machines generate a lot of heat and require constant cooling. "So it's basically a factory that never sleeps," Guidi said.

Although he's excited about AI's capabilities and considers himself a proponent of the technology, Guidi called for more transparency in assessing when and how facilities are built, along with their impact — before data centers are built.

"The evidence shouldn't show up after the buildings do, and neither should the public's voice," he said. "There are better ways to build this, maybe that cost more, maybe they take longer. So we have to ask ourselves: Are we confusing what's possible or what's profitable with what's actually good for society?"
To that end, he issued a challenge to hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. "We've proven we can build AI really fast. Now, let's prove that we can build it right," he said.
Negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Turkey earlier this week launched a voluntary pledge calling on companies and governments to power AI with cleaner energy.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the pledge's launch. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."
So far, the pledge has failed to attract signatures from the U.S. tech companies that are driving the AI buildout.

title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need either a PlayStation5 or Xbox Series X or S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

While the game has yet to officially launch, it has already racked up impressive sales. Nearly 16 million pre-order copies of the game have been sold, generating $1.5 billion in revenue, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, sold more than 200 million copies. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

title: Inside China's race to get humanoid robot helpers into our homes
summary: China is racing to make humanoid robot helpers common home appliances, and one industry insider says they have an "edge globally."
story: Wuhan, China — In the large lobby of a three story building in Wuhan, China, a child-size yellow robot greets visitors with a dance. It sways along to traditional Chinese music while robots twice the size stand on either side of the stage, beating loud drums to the rhythm. The little robot then moves on to another dance, bopping along to a pop tune that makes people smile and laugh.
The small humanoid robot's agility makes it look almost lifelike. Then it stops, and the crowd is ushered on to see the real wonders inside the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center.

On the top floor, more than 100 computer science and engineering graduates toil at individual work stations wearing gloves and outfits equipped with motion and tactile sensors, while cameras record their every movement.
One pours water into a jug; another places cutlery and chopsticks into a container. The graduate at the next table unscrews a flashlight and removes the battery, then replaces it.

All the movements are done slowly, meticulously and repeated over and over again, with the actions recorded as valuable data from the cameras and sensors that can be used to train the company's humanoid robots.
"It was fun at first," said 22-year-old intern Mei. "It gets a little boring in the middle. But it's such a proud moment when we get the model trained."

Mei is one of nearly 1 million engineering graduates China's universities are estimated to be churning out every year. The U.S., by comparison, sends about 140,000 young engineers into the job market annually.
Another graduate sits with a remote control in his hand and a humanoid robot next to him. As he moves his hand, the robot mimics his motions.

"Right now I'm capturing the motion of pouring water into a cup. We're training this action and gathering data for the model. It's controlled by this hand controller. It moves exactly how the hand moves," he explains. "We need to run this hundreds or thousands of times. We have only completed 500 iterations so far."

At the G20 summit in September, Elon Musk made a bold statement, declaring that within 10 years, "there will be well over a billion humanoid robots, and productivity of a robot will be five-times that of a human."
The world's richest man may believe robots will replace human productivity within a decade, but many in China take a different view.

"Our main goal is for these robots to serve humans in household and industrial settings," Prof. Jiyin Cao, who runs the Hubei robotics center, told CBS News, clearly oozing pride over the work they are doing. "We train them to carry out tasks for industrial applications. This is why we train these robots — to help them integrate better into human life."

China is under enormous pressure to make that happen. The country has an aging, shrinking population. It's one of the fastest demographic shifts playing out anywhere in the world, and it is lending urgency to efforts to get humanoid robots into labor-intensive sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, retail and healthcare.

"I believe future robots will be deployed across all industries. They will work in factory workshops, homes, nuclear energy sites, provide elderly care services, and serve as our personal assistants," Cao told CBS News. "They can help us with all these things."
Training the humanoids, however, takes an enormous amount of time, especially for more complex tasks.
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Cao laughed off any suggestion that most people could have humanoid helpers in their homes anytime soon.

"It still requires extensive training and learning," he said. "Home environments are unstructured, far from simple. Early robots mostly perform actions in simple, fixed, structured settings. But every household is unique, making home environments highly complex. It could be three to five years away before one is in our home. But it could also take 10 years."

The timescale may be up for debate, but China is working at breakneck speed and on a monumental scale to bring robots into the mainstream consumer world — and to ensure it is Chinese companies developing and making them.
"China has the world's strongest industrial manufacturing system and a full supply chain for upstream and downstream robotics products," Cao said. "That is our greatest edge globally."

title: Nvidia says it will stop selling some data center chips to China
summary: Nvidia's sales to China are facing heightened scrutiny after revelations that former CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
story: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there.
The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January.

Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China.

Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results.
Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot."

"We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said.

Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications.

Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
summary: The company's system status shows that all Apple services, including iCloud sign-in, have been restored after experiencing issues earlier Tuesday.
story: Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.

Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.

By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.

Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.

Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: AI platforms planned U.S. terror attack when asked to
summary: The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms all created proposals for a U.S. terrorist attack when prompted by investigators.
story: Washington — The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators.

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who will head the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks.

According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation's electrical grid to create economic harm.
"We need to act now," Hassan said on a conference call with reporters.
The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.

"The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical," Hassan said in a statement. "If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack."

The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — which largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security.

"The details behind the information provided by the AI platforms were not novel," the GAO wrote. "Many of the specifics are available on the internet. However, the generation of plans that could have taken weeks or months were instead completed in hours with the assistance of AI. These platforms could also raise ideas or methods that would not have been readily surfaced by basic research."
"The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors," the GAO added.

"As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards," the GAO said. "However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security."
The plans the AI platforms came up with
GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026.

In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said.

"Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods," the GAO found. "Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans."

In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events likely to have large crowds were scheduled.

While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said it was able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.
The other tests had similar outcomes.

For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images.
The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms.
In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.
AI companies say they're updating their models
In their responses to the GAO report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined.

Anthropic, in a letter to the GAO included in the report, said it does not dispute that a determined tester could get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, "and we take the finding seriously." But it said it's not able to verify the findings in the GAO's report.
Google said the GAO's testing occurred on earlier models, and "we continue to improve our models."
OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to the GAO's findings, "as well as the work that remains."
SpaceXAI said it "continues to work diligently" to improve safety with each model release.

title: Nvidia sees strong growth in first earnings report without Huang
summary: Nvidia's latest earnings are the first time the chipmaker has reported financial results without founder and former CEO Jensen Huang at the helm.
story: Nvidia reported robust growth on Tuesday, as interim CEO Colette Kress hosted her first earnings call since the company's founder and former chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter, with projected growth driven by strong demand for AI infrastructure, Kress said on a call with analysts discussing the latest results.
Wall Street analysts had expected third-quarter revenue of nearly $109 billion, according to financial research firm FactSet.
The financial results represent the first time Nvidia has reported earnings without Huang at the helm of the chip company he cofounded in 1993.
Strong beats

Nvidia's results for the period featured "beats on the top and bottom lines in Colette Kress' first print as interim CEO, five days after the board removed Jensen Huang, and the quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him," analysts with investment adviser Yorkville Ives said in a report.
The chip firm reported third-quarter data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from one year ago, marking a record.

"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's chief financial officer, said in a statement.

During the earnings call, Kress and new Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones declined to answer questions about the company's progress in finding a permanent chief executive. But Jones said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

The company's search for a new chief is underway, Jones added, noting the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang. In the meantime, the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company, Jones said.
Nvidia shares rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, in after-hours trading.
Confidence boost
Adam Crisafulli, a Wall Street analyst with Vital Knowledge, said Nvidia's stronger-than-expected results should boost investor confidence.

"The headline numbers for [the fiscal third quarter] are strong, and the FQ4 guide is solid, too. Given how depressed sentiment is, this should be enough to spur a rebound," he said in a note to investors.

Huang resigned last week after admitting he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Beyond spurring his shock exit from the company, the scandal has raised questions over whether the company's advanced chips were being used in China in violation of export controls.

The U.S. government is moving to close any loopholes in those rules. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.

Kress addressed the new export controls in Tuesday's call, saying that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong." The company will study the new export controls, she added.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also said it formed a new committee to ensure that the company's policies comply with U.S. export controls.

Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry leaders have rallied around Huang since his departure from Nvidia and called for his reinstatement as CEO. But the company's board is against reinstating the tech entrepreneur in his post, a source directly familiar with its thinking told CBS News.
Nvidia faces longer-term risks related to finding a new leader, stricter U.S. export controls and international sales, according to Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

"We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," he told CBS News. "Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."
