title: Democrats set to intensify probe of Trump's Obamacare purge
summary: The Trump administration canceled healthcare coverage for 760,000 enrollees in Affordable Care Act insurance plans, saying the enrollments were unauthorized.
story: A week before the midterm elections, a dozen Democratic senators sent harshly critical letters to 10 health insurance company CEOs.

Why, the letters asked, had those insurers cooperated with what they called a "potentially unlawful" Trump administration effort that resulted in the rapid cancellation of coverage for 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees in late August?

Then came the Democrats' stunning electoral sweep that, come January, will put them in control of both the House and Senate. The power shift lends new weight to the insurance investigation, led by Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who is expected to chair the powerful Finance Committee starting next year, and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

"Some insurers might view this inquiry as more high-stakes than before given that Democrats will have the power to subpoena documents, hold hearings, and otherwise investigate perceived abuses or missteps," said Katie Keith, a director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at the Georgetown University Law Center.

"Senator Wyden will continue investigating the secret arrangement between corporate interests and the Trump administration that has deprived Americans of their health care," Wyden spokesperson Taylor Harvey said in an email. "Senate Democrats will use every tool at their disposal to get answers."
New oversight muscle

For months, the administration has promoted the idea that fraud is rampant in government health programs — from the ACA to Medicaid and hospice — and that the Republican Party is the one to thwart it. The White House and some GOP candidates used this talking point to try to counter Democrats' campaign messages about affordability.

The Trump administration's anti-fraud efforts are ongoing. The August cancellations are part of a larger initiative by the administration to remove from Obamacare plans people who have other coverage and more strictly scrutinize the information people provide to qualify for premium subsidies. Courts blocked some of the administration's new rules, including heightened income verification for certain low-income enrollees and a moratorium that would have kept up to 19,000 new agents from helping people sign up during the current annual open enrollment period. Ongoing, however, is scrutiny of an additional 419,000 ACA enrollments in a second phase of the cancellation operation.

Also, new Trump administration requirements compel some people signing up during open enrollment to undergo additional online identity proofing. Insurers were sent guidance in October asking them to look for suspicious patterns among agents and brokers and take action, including cutting commissions, if they found problems. It's unclear if any insurers have taken those voluntary steps.
The letters from the Democratic senators to insurers provide a look at what the new majority could pursue in its ongoing inquiry into the administration's ACA actions.

Were proper procedures followed for removing people? How many legitimate enrollees were kicked off the rolls? Did the criteria used to target those enrollments —lack of Social Security number or other key data, not having used medical coverage, a full subsidy without a response to outreach efforts — serve as reliable proxies for determining fraud?
"The tone of these letters underscores just how much of a black box this process was," said Keith at Georgetown.
Administration officials, however, have defended the cancellation effort.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz was asked about the initial round of cancellations in late August.

"That is fraud, we believe," Oz said. "That is insurance brokers creating, manufacturing accounts without putting Social Security numbers in and has resulted, we have already determined, in 760,000 phantom accounts that we can't even get in touch with. We call, we write, we send carrier pigeons — like, no one answers."

After some of their executives were grilled early in the year over rising healthcare costs, the insurers were given until Nov. 6 to respond to 28 questions from the senators about the cancellation effort, which began in June when they were asked to try to reach more than a million enrollees the administration targeted as suspicious. They handed back to CMS the names of policyholders who did not respond to emails, phone calls, or letters within 30 days.

The senators sent letters to Elevance Health, Cigna, Oscar Health, AmeriHealth Caritas, Centene, Florida Blue, Health Care Service Corporation, Imperial Insurance Companies, Molina Healthcare, and UnitedHealthcare.
By Nov. 10, Harvey in Wyden's office reported "varying levels of responsiveness" from the insurers.
What happens next?

Few dispute that there are problems with improper ACA enrollment. This category includes, the administration says, sign-ups with missing or incorrect data; people who fudge their income estimates to get subsidies; "phantom" enrollees, meaning people who either don't exist or don't know they have coverage; and those signed up by rogue call centers or agents to garner commissions.
But there are questions about the relative scale of those problems and the steps by regulators to thwart them.

"The question is whether they overreached and set up a situation that led to many people who are eligible losing their coverage," said Chip Kahn, a visiting fellow at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, and the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank. "They will be pushed hard by the new Congress to come up with the goods in terms of making it crystal clear what's been done, who has been dropped." Kahn is also the former president and CEO of the Federation of American Hospitals, a trade association of for-profit hospitals.

The Democratic senators left no doubt about where they stand, saying in their letters that "Republicans are weaponizing fraud falsehoods in order to undercut the ACA Marketplace and kick even more Americans off their health care."
But Democrats will face limits if they try to interfere with the purge.

"Because the cancellation of ACA policies came via executive authority from the Trump administration rather than legislation, they cannot stop the administration from invoking fraud to cancel ACA policies — unless they can find a legislative solution that can survive a presidential veto or is part of a broader budget agreement," said Jonathan Oberlander, who teaches health policy at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.

Democrats have said they will move quickly to try to restore the more generous ACA subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, an effort that will face headwinds. But even a failed attempt might play politically with voters as a move to address affordability concerns. The subsidies were designed to make ACA premiums more affordable.
Marketplace enrollment for 2026 is about 19 million people, down sharply from nearly 22 million in 2025.

Conservative policy groups maintain that the additional subsidies, put in place during the COVID-19 era, fueled fraud by allowing many more people to qualify for fully subsidized plans and encouraging them to fudge income estimates to qualify for the largest credits. Large subsidies that reduced monthly premium payments to $0, they argue, also provided cover for unauthorized sign-ups by rogue brokers.

"If the subsidies go up and there are more people in zero-premium plans, then absolutely there will be more fraud," said Brian Blase, president of the conservative Paragon Health Institute, whose reports assert widespread improper enrollments, sometimes basing that on data it says shows that a growing percentage of enrollees don't use their insurance.

He's critical of the Democrats' letter and expects Congress will ultimately conclude that the administration's cancellation effort included enough checks to ensure that legitimate enrollees were not caught up or, if they were, could be reinstated.

Very few people — fewer than 0.01% of those purged — have contacted the federal marketplace to request reinstatement, the CMS press office said in an unsigned email to KFF Health News. The agency has not released further details about the cancellations, including whether everyone who lost coverage is aware.
Blase is convinced that, eventually, "the Democrats will realize it was commonsense good governance and move on to something else."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Musk says he's "not MAGA," feels "foolish" about midterm spending
summary: After opening his wallet to assist GOP candidates in the 2026 midterms, billionaire Elon Musk said Wednesday he feels "pretty foolish" about spending hundreds of millions of dollars in the race.
story: After opening his wallet to assist Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms, billionaire Elon Musk said Wednesday he feels "pretty foolish" about spending hundreds of millions of dollars.

The world's richest man — who served in President Trump's administration in 2025 — also argued he is "not MAGA" and described his political beliefs as "quite moderate" during an interview at The New York Times' DealBook Summit.

Musk donated vast sums of money to super PACs backing House and Senate Republicans. One of his largest investments was in Texas, where over $150 million of his fortune was transferred to a group supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Those bets largely did not pay off. Democrats won large majorities in the House and Senate, with Paxton losing to Democratic candidate James Talarico, who made Musk's support of his GOP opponent part of his pitch to voters. Democrats also won the Texas governor's office, a notable shift for the state where Musk has based many of SpaceX and Tesla's operations.

Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin his objective in the midterms was to help Republicans hold on to their Senate majority in order to prevent either party from controlling the presidency and both houses of Congress in 2029 — a goal he said "failed."

"Obviously, the Republicans were routed in this election, and … I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that," the billionaire said, adding that "probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money."
Musk later said his goal was to preserve some "checks and balances," calling himself "ideologically quite moderate" and saying he doesn't have any "extreme political views."
Sorkin noted that Musk has made controversial statements on immigration and "MAGA stuff."

Musk responded: "I'm not MAGA. ... I'm not sure what MAGA means, but I don't think I'm, like, if it means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties."

It's a change in tone for Musk, who has donned MAGA hats in the past, and joked at one 2024 Trump rally: "I'm not just MAGA, I'm dark MAGA." Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars assisting the Trump campaign and other GOP candidates that year, and later led the Trump administration's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. Musk and Mr. Trump had a brief falling-out last year, but Musk has appeared to maintain a close relationship with the president since then.
Musk also traveled to China this week for Mr. Trump's trip to the country.

Musk's alliance with Mr. Trump has drawn scrutiny from Democrats, who have vowed to aggressively investigate the Trump administration when they take the House and Senate next year. Musk is expected to be one focus of their oversight probes.

In Wednesday's interview, Musk said he is not worried that Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa could pose problems to his businesses, saying, "Based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."
"The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate," Musk said. "I don't think she's sort of a far-left governor."
He also said some Democrats' comments accusing him of illegality are "a little over the top," telling The Times, "There are definitely a few people grumpy about ... my funding in this past election."
"Hopefully in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison. Aspirationally, that should be how it works," he said.
Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona suggested he was unmoved by Musk's MAGA about-face.
"You are still getting a subpoena," Gallego wrote on X.

title: What to know about Trump's meeting with Xi in China
summary: President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday against the backdrop of a widening scandal.
story: Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.

The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.
The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.
Jensen Huang, Alice Huang and Nvidia

Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.
The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.

"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.

"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."
China and chips
Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.

The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."

"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."

Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote  the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.

"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."

The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.
AI safety

Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.

But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.

Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.
"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.
Taiwan
Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."
David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.

"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.

A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."

"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"
The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting

Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.

"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."
Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.

"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."

They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.

The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.

title: Thune: "Open question" whether Senate GOP can pass massive defense bill
summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Wednesday it's still an "open question" whether Republicans have the votes to approve a massive new defense package sought by the Trump administration.
story: Washington — Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Wednesday it's still an "open question" whether Republicans have the votes to approve a massive new defense package along party lines by the end of the year, following calls from the Trump administration for an infusion of money before Democrats take control.

Senate Republicans have been considering using the reconciliation process for a third time under the second Trump administration to approve the Pentagon's request for $350 billion in new funding. The push has taken on new urgency in recent days, with some Republicans warning that Democrats would abandon defense funds due to their opposition to the war with Iran.

But after a series of GOP conference meetings on Wednesday, Thune said Republicans are still considering their options, pointing to the possibility of approving the funds with the help of Democrats through the normal appropriations process.

The reconciliation process would allow Republicans to pass new funding without Democratic support, but it opens the door to a marathon series of votes on amendments that can stretch overnight. The Senate is only scheduled to be in session for another three weeks before the chamber recesses for the winter holidays, with Democrats set to take control of the chamber in the new year.

GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee that would kick-start the reconciliation process, told reporters that Republicans probably wouldn't move forward on reconciliation this week, but "we're not taking it off the table at all."

Thune said "there is a window in which we could still do [a reconciliation package] if we don't get on it before Thanksgiving holiday." Asked if Republicans could start the process this week, he laughed and said, "Let's just say it's an option."

Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg met with Senate Republicans during a closed-door lunch meeting earlier Wednesday. Ahead of the meeting, Thune told CBS News that Feinberg needed to make the case to his conference, including by confirming the Pentagon's top-line funding number and explaining why the funds are necessary.

"And I think to confirm, obviously, what a lot of our defense hawks have been saying, and that is that we're running out of everything, and that if we're to defend the country, we need a significant amount of funding for defense, which probably isn't going to happen through the normal appropriations process of the Democrats," Thune said. "He's got to make that argument and persuade enough Republicans to get to 50."

Asked after the meeting Wednesday why he thinks Democrats may be willing to help fund defense, Thune said, "I don't know that they will, but we think that we ought to at least explore that possibility."
"I think that's kind of a consensus view that our members have at the moment, and there are multiple ways in which we can do that," he said. "So we're working through it."

Republicans have also been considering moving additional funding for the Federal Aviation Administration through the budget reconciliation process, after an outage last week prompted a rare nationwide ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy met with Senate Republicans on Tuesday, where he sought $50 billion to overhaul the system. But Republicans appeared largely skeptical of the figure leaving the meeting.

The decision comes after Republicans approved President Trump's massive defense, policy and tax agenda through budget reconciliation last year. Republicans also approved a second reconciliation measure to fund the Department of Homeland Security's immigration enforcement agencies earlier this year, after Democrats refused for months, seeking reforms to the enforcement after federal agents fatally shot two American citizens in Minneapolis earlier in the year.

title: NSA network outage linked to software vulnerability
summary: The director of national intelligence and multiple sources said the National Security Agency's network outage stemmed from the patching of vulnerabilities in the programming language, PHP.
story: The National Security Agency's network outage Tuesday has been linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News.

The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline Tuesday, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
Artificial intelligence helped uncover a pair of critical security vulnerabilities, triggering a global scramble last month to update software used by much of the internet, including the NSA.

The flaws, collectively known as PHP2Shell, affect PHP, which is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. The race to patch vulnerable systems may help explain some of the recent technology disruptions.

The PHP2Shell threat was so serious that the FBI, NSA and CISA issued urgent warnings just under a month ago, on Oct. 21, directing organizations to immediately patch vulnerable systems. The three agencies also advised those unable to install the fixes to take affected systems offline altogether until they could be secured.

Speaking on Fox Business Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton directly linked the NSA's classified network outage to urgent software updates following the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP.

"If you go back about 10 days ago, we had what was labeled as PHP, an update to a web interface system," Clayton said. "And the patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today."

According to two sources familiar with the system, NSA Net as of right now is back up and running. Nonetheless, staggered arrival is continuing as fears persist that the system might not be able to handle everyone signing on at the same time. There is no word yet on how long the agency will continue the staggered arrival schedule, known as "Code Gray."

NSA maintains that mission critical information sharing has not been impacted, while it asks personnel to delay nonessential tasks, according to sources. The NSA said Tuesday the agency had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," adding that its mission/critical capabilities were still fully operational. The NSA is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats and protecting U.S. government communications.
The agency has not yet responded to a CBS News request for an update on Wednesday.

One U.S. intelligence official described the broader challenge of updating infrastructure that was originally designed for an earlier internet era. The volume and speed of changes can overwhelm aging equipment. The official's assessment reflects a growing concern among intelligence and Homeland Security officials that modern technology is advancing faster than the systems that support it.

Speaking about PHP vulnerabilities, Clayton also pointed to the growing role of AI in speeding up both those kinds of discoveries and the pressure to respond. He described PHP as a "legacy vulnerability" that has been successfully patched across systems globally, adding, "This type of identification of vulnerabilities and patching goes on all the time."

Unlike the NSA outage, Friday's FAA nationwide ground stop involved a hardware problem, rather than a software vulnerability. Routine telecommunications maintenance triggered excessive network traffic that overwhelmed older routers, creating a cascading disruption across much of the air traffic control system. It is not yet clear whether the banking, airline or technology companies' outages shared the same cause.

title: Cornyn blocks Trump's nominee to federal district court in Texas
summary: President Trump nominated T. Elliot Gaiser, who heads the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, to serve on the U.S. district court in the Dallas area.
story: Washington — Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas has blocked President Trump's nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, a top Justice Department official, for a seat on the federal district court in the Dallas area.
Cornyn told CBS News on Capitol Hill that he declined to return a so-called blue slip for Gaiser, effectively derailing his nomination in the Senate Judiciary Committee.

"I think his nomination is no longer viable," the senator said. Pressed on why he opposes Gaiser's candidacy for the U.S. district court in the Northern District of Texas, Cornyn said, "He's not a Texan, has no trial experience, and the White House tried to jam the Senate and wouldn't allow us to do our due diligence that we need to do on lifetime appointments."

Gaiser was initially expected to appear before the Judiciary Committee for a confirmation hearing on Wednesday. But he ultimately was not among the seven candidates for federal judgeships to testify before the committee.
Asked about Gaiser during an appearance at The Atlantic Summit on Tuesday, Cornyn said, "He's not from Texas."

"That's a basic problem," he said. "The Constitution provides for advice and consent, but there was no consultation whatsoever, no attempt to try to work with the Senate. I've offered an alternative, but we'll see whether they take us up on it. But I think the Senate's not supposed to be a rubber stamp and … we have been too often."

The Judiciary Committee's blue-slip process is designed to generate consultation between the White House and two senators who represent a nominee's home state, which for the vacancy on the Dallas-area district court would be Cornyn and GOP Sen. Ted Cruz. After the president selects a candidate, the home-state senators receive a blue slip of paper to denote their approval or opposition to the nominee. A senator can also withhold the blue slip, as Cornyn has done, which is considered a sign of disapproval for the candidate.
A district court nominee may only proceed and receive a hearing before the Judiciary Committee if both home-state senators return positive blue slips.

Mr. Trump has pushed Sen. Chuck Grassley, the current chair of the panel, to get rid of the blue-slip policy, but the Iowa Republican has kept the longstanding tradition in place for district court and U.S. attorney nominations.

With Congress now convening for the lame-duck session following the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the Judiciary Committee is rushing to confirm the rest of Mr. Trump's nominees to the federal bench before the new Congress begins in January and control of the Senate changes hands. Democrats are poised to hold 56 seats in the Senate, so few — if any — of the president's picks to the federal appeals and district courts are expected to win confirmation.
Mr. Trump announced last week that he would be nominating Gaiser to serve on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas. His nomination was formally sent to the Senate on Monday.

As Cornyn has pointed out, Gaiser does not live in Texas, and his only tie to the state appears to be a one-year clerkship in Houston for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. A native of Ohio who served as its solicitor general, he lived in the Buckeye State before joining the Trump administration last year as head of the Office of Legal Counsel at the Justice Department.

Gaiser said in a questionnaire to the Judiciary Committee that he was first contacted about the vacancy on the district court by Cruz's staff on Nov. 4, one day after Democrats' sweeping victories over Republicans in the midterm elections. He said he discussed a possible nomination with Cornyn's office on Nov. 6 and was informed by the White House Counsel's Office that same day that the president was considering him for the position.
Gaiser's questionnaire to the committee is dated Nov. 7, though it wasn't until Nov. 10 that Mr. Trump announced he would be nominating him to serve on the district court.

As associate attorney general for the Office of Legal Counsel, Gaiser has come under criticism for several memorandum opinions he has issued, which provide the president and federal agencies with advice on legal questions and are considered binding on the executive branch.

Gaiser authored the controversial opinion providing justification for the U.S. military's strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea. He also said in an April opinion that the Presidential Records Act, which requires the president preserve certain documents and turn them over to the National Archives at the end of his administration, is unconstitutional.

An August opinion from Gaiser concluded that Mr. Trump's outside advisers, which are those who are not employed by the federal government, are protected from future congressional and legal investigations. Gaiser found that presidential communications with private outsiders are generally covered by executive privilege.

title: Jeffries wins Democratic nomination for House speaker
summary: Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday.
story: Washington — Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday, paving the way for his election when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Jeffries' current and incoming Democratic colleagues voted 251 to 11 to back his nomination for the gavel during a closed-door meeting where members were also choosing the rest of the House Democratic leadership. The caucus also voted to elevate Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as the next majority leader, the first woman to hold that position.

The speaker is ultimately elected by the full House chamber, a vote that will occur at the beginning of the new Congress. With Democrats on track to control more than 250 seats, Jeffries' path to gaining the 218 votes needed for the speakership is all but secured. Jeffries would be the first Black House speaker in U.S. history.

The New York Democrat faced some hesitance from new progressive members heading into Wednesday's leadership vote. Six incoming progressives who voted against him said in a statement that they were hoping to secure policy commitments from Jeffries on a number of fronts.

"Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," the new members said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."

The members who released the statement were Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York. A spokesperson for a seventh member who was included on the statement, Frederick Haynes of Texas, said in a follow-up statement that he had "narrowly missed the vote" because he woke up ill.

Another incoming member, Don Leonard of Ohio, said he did not support Jeffries because he did not see a strong enough commitment from him on ending Citizens United — a Supreme Court ruling that allowed corporations and other outside groups to spend unlimited money on elections — or a vow to hold a vote on ending U.S. military aid to Israel.
"He does those two things. He's got my vote," Leonard said.
But no other Democrat put their name forward to directly challenge Jeffries' bid. And with the wide Democratic majority, individual members have limited leverage to push for concessions.

"The results of today's election speak for themselves," Jeffries said at a news conference after the election about those who opposed him. "We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people."
Asked whether he would move in the direction of those who opposed him on several policy issues, Jeffries said the caucus has different perspectives and "we embrace that."
"We're going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people," he said.

Jeffries said he wanted a tallied vote during the internal election rather than ask for a vote by acclamation. He told reporters Tuesday that it was the same approach Democrats used in their leadership elections in 2018, when they transitioned from the minority to the majority.

"Certainly seems to me it would be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned based on track record, experience, vision," Jeffries said.
House Democrats also voted Wednesday to fill the roles of whip, assistant leader and caucus chair in the new Congress.
Rep. Pete Aguilar of California was elected whip, Joe Neguse of Colorado won assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu of California won the vote for chair of the Democratic caucus.

House Democrats' leadership election was far less contentious than that of their colleagues in the Senate, where longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Schumer has expressed confidence that he has the votes to be elected majority leader in elections early next month.
Olivia Ardito contributed reporting.

title: Alleged Russian agent accused of spying on U.S. defense firm
summary: A Russian man was indicted for allegedly surveilling and collecting information about employees of a Silicon Valley defense company.
story: Washington — A Russian man was indicted by a federal grand jury on Tuesday for allegedly acting as a foreign agent of Moscow and surveilling and collecting information about employees of a technology and defense company in Silicon Valley.

The Justice Department alleges that Igor D'iu was recruited by unidentified co-conspirators through the encrypted messaging app Telegram to carry out covert assignments that targeted employees of the unnamed technology and defense company. Prosecutors said he crossed the border from Mexico into the United States in July.

While the company is not identified in court documents, context from the charging papers suggests it could be Palantir Technologies. Prosecutors said the company has an office in Palo Alto, California, and had ties to the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine, including Ukraine's use of its software during the war. Palantir has said publicly that it has deployed its technology in Ukraine, and its CEO Alex Karp said in 2023 that the company is "responsible for most of the targeting in Ukraine."
A spokesperson from Palantir did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether it was the company D'iu targeted.

D'iu is charged with two counts related to his alleged work as an agent of the Russian government, one count of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud in connection with allegedly falsified identification documents. If convicted on all charges, he faces up to 16 years in prison and steep fines.

Prosecutors said that as part of the scheme, D'iu received instructions, equipment and financial support from his alleged co-conspirators, who told him he was working for "the Motherland." They also directed D'iu to collect information about the technology company because it was providing resources used by Ukraine, according to the indictment.

Court records allege that D'iu researched, followed and surveilled employees of the company to gather information about it, including by visiting a coffee shop near the company's Palo Alto office, and was told to take photos of employees' laptop screens while they worked. The Justice  Department said the Russian man's co-conspirators instructed him to position his own computer at specific locations near the unidentified company, which would allow them to remotely access it and attempt to collect information from employees nearby.
The Justice Department released the photos D'iu allegedly took of the employees' laptops, as well as images of a Russian passport and forged U.S. passport:
The indictment also alleges that D'iu followed company employees and conducted online searches for several workers' home addresses, including of a senior company executive.

In one instance on Sept. 3, the Justice Department said that D'iu followed a female employee for nearly 30 miles while she drove from Palo Alto toward San Francisco. The employee attempted to evade D'iu by "making irregular turns, taking back roads, and entering a grocery store parking lot." But D'iu continued to follow her, making U-turns, illegal left turns and running a red light, according to prosecutors. The employee called 911 and was instructed to drive to a San Francisco Police Department station, the Justice Department said.

After that incident, the Justice Department said Palo Alto police contacted D'iu. He then allegedly changed vehicles, got a new phone number and traveled to Reno, Nevada, at the direction of his handlers before returning to Northern California to continue his assignments.

After the FBI searched his belongings, it found about $18,000 in cash, a fake U.S. passport and a California identification card with the name Hugo Landry Johns. It also discovered Social Security cards, a notebook containing the addresses of 10 employees who worked for the unnamed tech company and three personal profiles of employees, including personally identifiable information, family information and work history.

The FBI also found messages between D'iu and his alleged co-conspirators, which included photos of at least four company employees and their addresses with instructions to impersonate a food delivery driver and verify that they lived there.
While D'iu was indicted on Tuesday, the Justice Department said in a press release that he made his initial appearance in federal court on Nov. 2 and remains in federal custody.

title: Trump expected to press Xi on Americans detained in China
summary: President Trump is expected to again press Chinese President Xi Jinping to release two Americans wrongfully detained in China when the leaders meet, their families say.
story: President Trump is expected to again press Chinese President Xi Jinping to release two Americans wrongfully detained in China when the leaders meet, their families say, as Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

Mr. Trump previously raised the detention of American scholar Youlin Chen with Xi during a meeting in Beijing in May, and confirmed discussing detained Americans with the Chinese leader again during his September visit to Washington. The leaders' upcoming bilateral meeting would mark the third time Mr. Trump has raised Chen's case and the second time he is expected to raise that of Min Zin, another American scholar who was detained in June.

Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or APEC. He is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday, ahead of a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The families of the detained Americans say they have been assured Mr. Trump intends to raise the cases, though it remains unclear whether the issue will ultimately figure in his discussions with Xi, which are expected to cover a range of trade and national security matters.

Asked whether the president would raise the cases with Xi, the White House pointed to remarks he made earlier this month, when he said he discussed detained Americans with Xi "a lot" and cited the administration's record of freeing Americans. The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Sylvia Zin, whose husband Min Zin has been detained for nearly six months, said he is being held in solitary confinement at an undisclosed location, without access to legal counsel. She said the family recently learned he had been hospitalized last month for severe dehydration following a stomach illness and that the facility where he is being held has no heat.
"My worry for my husband's health and wellbeing increases with each passing day," she said.

"I am grateful for the President's commitment in continuing to raise my husband's wrongful detention, yet again," Sylvia Zin said. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays."

The other American, Youlin Chen, has been detained in China since November 2024. He faces espionage charges stemming from U.S. government-funded research on detecting North Korean nuclear tests. His family denies the allegations, noting that his work relied on publicly available data and was conducted in collaboration with Chinese scientists.
His wife, Yufang Rong, said she has also received assurances that Mr. Trump intends to raise his case directly with Xi.

"I've been assured that President Trump remains firmly committed to securing Youlin's freedom and that he intends to raise Youlin's case with President Xi at both the APEC meeting and, if needed, the G20," she told CBS News.
The next G20 summit is scheduled for December at the president's golf resort in Doral, Florida. Xi is expected to attend, although Beijing has not confirmed his participation.

Min Zin is a naturalized American citizen who fled his native Myanmar during the pro-democracy movement of the 1980s. He was detained by Chinese authorities on June 3 after traveling from Thailand to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference at the invitation of a Chinese professor. He runs a think tank that studies China's role in neighboring Myanmar, and his organization previously received U.S. government funding — which may have been a factor in attracting the scrutiny of Chinese intelligence authorities, U.S. officials have said.
Sylvia Zin previously told CBS News she believes he was lured to China and arrested on false charges. The State Department formally designated him as wrongfully detained in August.

Min Zin is being held by China's Ministry of State Security under a system known as Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location, or RSDL, which human rights groups describe as a form of secret detention. U.S. consular officials have been permitted brief, closely monitored monthly visits with him at a nearby hotel, according to his wife, but his family has not been allowed to see or speak directly with him.

Chinese authorities have accused Min Zin of activities endangering national security, including suspected espionage, allegations his family vehemently denies. Beijing has rejected the U.S. government's wrongful detention designation, maintaining that its authorities are acting in accordance with Chinese law.

The administration has repeatedly touted its record of bringing detained Americans home, including teacher Marc Fogel and ballet dancer Ksenia Karelina from Russia, and academic Dennis Coyle from Afghanistan. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said more than 100 detained Americans have been freed during Mr. Trump's second term.

Most recently, Mr. Trump said he personally appealed to Putin to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, the last American formally designated as wrongfully detained in Russia, who was freed in October without a prisoner swap. There are roughly 20 Americans imprisoned in Russia, and some of them are under review for potential designation by Rubio as wrongfully detained. Mr. Trump and Putin are also expected to meet one-on-one in China on Thursday.
But despite the president's personal interventions, neither of the two Americans held in China has been released.

Their cases have prompted scrutiny of the risks facing Americans traveling to China. In October, the State Department reinstated a "D" risk indicator on its China travel advisory, warning that Americans face a serious risk of wrongful detention there. The designation, also applied to six other countries including Russia, North Korea, Iran and Afghanistan, had been removed from China's advisory in November 2024 following a prisoner exchange. China's overall travel advisory remains at Level 2, with the State Department advising Americans to exercise increased caution.

Eric Lebson of Global Reach, an advocate for the detained Americans, said the administration is considering raising China's overall advisory to Level 3, which would advise Americans to reconsider travel. Such a move would be separate from the wrongful detention designation and could significantly affect academic exchanges, business travel and international conferences in China, Lebson said.

"It is uncharacteristic of the Chinese government to not engage on resolving matters of this type after two discussions about them at the presidential level," Lebson said, suggesting there may be disagreements within the Chinese government over how to handle the cases.

The potential push to secure the Americans' release comes as senior Trump administration officials have publicly disagreed over how aggressively to confront Beijing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, have pressed for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced American technology, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has resisted some of those measures, warning they could jeopardize relations with Beijing.

The disagreement has centered on efforts to prevent sensitive Nvidia chips from reaching China through third countries. Bessent publicly criticized the Commerce Department for delaying restrictions, while Mr. Trump defended Lutnick on Monday, saying he understood the concern that tougher measures could provoke a confrontation with Beijing. The president has at times favored a more accommodating approach to China, even as he has reportedly authorized tighter export controls.

title: FAA contractor struggled to find location of outage during ground stop
summary: It took several hours for contractor L3Harris to pinpoint the source of an outage that caused last Friday's nationwide ground stop​.
story: The contractor that owns the network running the nation's air traffic control system took several hours to pinpoint the source of an outage that caused Friday's nationwide ground stop, forcing a delay in lifting it, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

L3Harris' network operations center is located in Melbourne, Florida, and provides real-time updates to network outages in the ATC system. On Friday, however, sources say the company was not immediately able to identify the IP address where the issue was originating. Where the outage had occurred should have been immediately apparent, given the sophistication of the system that tracks outages, another source said.

The FAA's Federal Telecommunications Infrastructure network, known as FTI, became unstable as data flooded the network, attempting to connect 1,000 times every 4 to 5 seconds, the FAA said. This resulted in a disruption of the system and "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds."

The FAA's initial investigation identified two possible sources, one in Amarillo, Texas, and the other in El Dorado, Arkansas. The agency and L3Harris ultimately concluded that the Arkansas site, where a new router was being deployed, had caused the outage.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters on Tuesday that L3Harris needs to perform better amid concerns about its ability to monitor the network.
"They didn't identify and isolate. That concerns me," Duffy said on Capitol Hill Tuesday.
L3Harris says that its network operations center is monitored 24/7 to identify latency issues and outages.
The company referred CBS News to its statement from Saturday afternoon, in response to inquiries.

In that statement, L3Harris said it has worked "in close coordination with the FAA" on modernizing the National Airspace System and has completed more than 70% of the conversion from legacy copper wires to fiber optics.
The company said it supports the FAA's investigation into the conditions that caused the nationwide ground stop.
In:
Federal Aviation Administration
Federal Aviation Administration

title: "No indication" outages are related to cyberattacks, officials say
summary: Officials are testifying at a House committee hearing on worldwide threats as a series of network outages, including Microsoft Outlook and several banking institutions, have rattled Americans.
story: Washington — Top U.S. national security officials told Congress they have found no evidence that a string of technology outages affecting airlines, banks, Microsoft services and national security communications systems were connected or caused by malicious cyberattacks, even as lawmakers pressed for answers about an outage at the National Security Agency and reports of potential Iranian attacks on U.S. soil.

At Wednesday's House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia attempted to reassure lawmakers that federal agencies were investigating the disruptions and monitoring possible threats.
"We have seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Mullin said, adding that DHS had contacted private industry while reviewing the outages.

Mullin said later in the hearing that he is "98% confident" that recent outages are not the result of malicious activity from foreign adversaries, but did admit that he had "absolutely not" seen this many outages in this amount of time.
Clayton said intelligence officials had reached a similar assessment after reviewing the incidents with government agencies and cybersecurity experts in the private sector.
"These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack," Clayton said.
Raia said FBI cybersecurity specialists had been involved in examining the incidents from the beginning.

"At this point, there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents," Raia said. He added that the FBI would continue working with private-sector partners "in an abundance of caution."

Wednesday's hearing came as many Americans are on edge after the outages affected banks, Microsoft services, banks and the NSA internal network, as well as an hourslong nationwide FAA ground stop on Friday that led to chaos at the nation's airports all weekend. The ground stop was only the second of its kind since Sept. 11, 2001.

Officials said FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris Technologies had performed maintenance updates at a remote facility to replace aging copper communications lines with fiber optic connections. And as the router was being switched, it started flooding other routers and overloaded the system.

Rep. Dan Goldman, a New York Democrat, challenged Clayton's characterization of the recent NSA outage, repeatedly asking whether the disruption had resulted from internal software updates or other technical work.
"It's your testimony today that the technological problems that the NSA faced on Monday were from internal software and technological upgrades," Goldman said.
Clayton responded that officials had found no evidence of outside interference.
"We have no indication that they have come from external threat actors," Clayton said.
Goldman pressed for a more definitive explanation.
"It's a pretty binary. It's either external or internal, right?" Goldman asked.
Clayton described routine maintenance procedures, including software patches, system upgrades and hardware replacement, which can require systems to be taken offline and restarted.
Goldman accused Clayton of avoiding the question.
"You're a very smart person, and you're clearly not answering my direct questions," Goldman rebutted.
Clayton separately warned that advances in computing power and increasingly capable software were placing new demands on older government technology systems.
"The speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially," Clayton said.

He warned that the accelerating pace of technological development was making legacy systems obsolete more quickly, suggesting that infrastructure considered outdated only months earlier could fall even further behind as computing capabilities advance.

Mullin has already faced significant backlash for taking a government plane to a college football game one day after a FAA ground stop while the nation's airports remained chaotic. Mullin said Wednesday that it would have shown "distrust" in the nation's airspace if he had not flown.

Lawmakers also raised concerns about reports that Iranian-linked actors could be developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials using a radiological weapon, commonly called a dirty bomb, or chemical weapons.

Rep. Michael Guest, a Mississippi Republican, raised concerns about the possibility of Iranian sleeper cells operating within the United States and asked whether federal authorities were equipped to identify and disrupt potential attacks.
"Are we concerned about the possibility of sleeper cells?" Guest asked Mullin.
"Is it a concern? Of course. Are we fighting it and stomping it down every single day? Absolutely," Mullin responded.
Mullin said DHS personnel were working closely with intelligence and Justice Department officials to identify threats and prevent attacks.
Clayton also emphasized the danger posed by online radicalization, describing how foreign extremist networks can influence individuals already living inside the United States.
"That's not theoretical; it's real. We saw it in New York. We've seen it in other cases," Clayton said.
Raia cautioned that intelligence reporting about possible plots does not necessarily mean attackers possess the capability to carry them out.
"A lot of the reporting is largely aspirational," Raia said. "But that does not mean that does not mean we do not take it seriously."

He said authorities had revamped their Iranian threat mission center to strengthen efforts against potential attacks, pointing to previously disclosed investigations involving plots against dissidents.
The officials did not publicly confirm that Iranian sleeper cells were preparing attacks within the United States or that the reported dirty bomb or chemical weapons plans were operational.
Clayton said Iranian threats inside and outside of the U.S. have "dramatically increased."

"We remain committed to detecting, deterring and combatting the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said. "These threats have dramatically increased."

title: Top Dem sends letters to people close to Trump ahead of probes
summary: Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, sent letters to 12 people close to President Trump ahead of expected investigations into his second term.
story: Washington — The top Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee sent letters Wednesday to a dozen people close to President Trump ahead of expected investigations into alleged corruption, misconduct by the Department of Homeland Security and the White House's handling of files from the investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The letters from Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to chair the Oversight Committee when Democrats take control of the House in January, went to members of the president's family, as well as former and current administration officials, and instructed them to preserve documents relevant to Democrats' future investigations.

Garcia sent notices to Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Homeland Security senior adviser Corey Lewandowski, Vice President J.D. Vance, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Bureau of Prisons Director WIlliam Marshall.

"Voters gave Congressional Democrats a sweeping mandate to root out corruption and ensure that the government is accountable to the people," Garcia said in the letters. "We intend to act on that mandate in the 120th Congress by conducting the critically important oversight essential for legislative reform."

Garcia told Donald Trump Jr., and Eric Trump that the committee will investigate alleged conflicts of interest and their stakes in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto business. He told Trump Jr. that the Oversight panel is also interested in a Russian oligarch's funding of his post-wedding festivities at a private island in the Bahamas in May.

The letter to Kushner focuses on his personal business dealings and role representing the U.S. government as a negotiator in talks in the Middle East and Russia, which Garcia said raise concerns about "transparency, conflicts of interest and the abuse of" a government position for personal profit.

His document preservation notices to Vance, Wiles, Blanche and Marshall all center around the Trump administration's handling of the release of files from the federal investigation into Epstein, or the transfer of Ghislaine Maxwell, his longtime associate, to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas last year.

Letters to Miller, Noem and Lewandowski indicate that the committee will focus on immigration enforcement operations, and for Noem and Lewandowski, specifically, allegations of corruption and pay-to-play schemes at the department.

Garcia told Guilfoyle that the committee will be investigating alleged pay-to-play schemes surrounding her ambassadorship, and notified Townsend he will be examining private donations to fund construction of the new White House ballroom.

"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse. These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning," the California Democrat said in a statement.

Garcia and congressional Democrats are poised to launch investigations into numerous matters arising during Mr. Trump's second term once they officially take control of the House and Senate in January and will have subpoena power.
But the White House has indicated it intends to fight back against the probes.

White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Garcia last week warning that their investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality," and said any investigative acts by Congress must support a legitimate legislative purpose.
But Garcia dismissed Scharf's threat and said Congress has "wide latitude" to conduct investigations and oversight.

In addition to Scharf's letter, a U.S. attorney in southern Texas, Aaron Reitz, has sent notices to at least five House and Senate Democrats about remarks they've made about forthcoming investigations and ordered them to preserve documents.

title: China's Xi greets Trump at airport ahead of planned summit with Putin
summary: President Trump arrived Wednesday in China, where the Kremlin said he had an informal meeting with Vladimir Putin.
story: President Trump arrived in China on Wednesday after starting a multiday Asia swing in the Philippines. He's scheduled to meet in Shenzhen, a hub of China's tech industry, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit on Thursday.
Mr. Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying such a meeting "may not be possible" but the president is "prepared" for one.
Xi greeted Mr. Trump on a red carpet as he walked off Air Force One in Shenzhen.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Mr. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting Wednesday ahead of the planned trilateral summit. Peskov also said Putin had already held a meeting with Xi, during which they discussed the war in Ukraine. Mr. Trump and Putin may also discuss Ukraine, Peskov said.
Putin mentioned his recent discussions in Moscow with Mr. Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during his meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Peskov said.

"The three leaders have a lot to discuss, given the unstable situation in the world," Putin's senior aide Yury Ushakov told reporters in Shenzhen, according to Russian state broadcaster Vesti. He did not confirm the plan for an initial bilateral meeting between Putin and Mr. Trump on Wednesday, but said they might meet during a formal dinner.
It "will not be a single event," Ushakov said of the possibility of Trump-Putin encounters on Wednesday. "It will take place both standing, on the steps, and while seated."

In Manila, Mr. Trump visited the Malacañang Presidential Palace on Wednesday and met with his Philippine counterpart, Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., before his flight to China. In a public bilateral meeting, the two leaders lauded the U.S.-Philippine relationship, which Mr. Trump called "one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific." The U.S. president suggested the two countries could cooperate further on technology, energy and defense.

In a banquet luncheon before departing for China, Mr. Trump announced that he and Marcos "just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, and it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that. And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly, and it's a magnificent deal for both."
Later, in a social media post, Mr. Trump said the deal "will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of Energy."

A day earlier, after landing in the Philippine capital of Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia-Pacific region. The president described the relationship with the Quad — made up of the U.S., Australia, India and Japan — as "very special."
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korea's Kim in China. After arriving in the Philippines, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia board of directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

title: AI platforms planned U.S. terror attack when asked to
summary: The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms all created proposals for a U.S. terrorist attack when prompted by investigators.
story: Washington — The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators.

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who will head the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks.

According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation's electrical grid to create economic harm.
"We need to act now," Hassan said on a conference call with reporters.
The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.

"The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical," Hassan said in a statement. "If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack."

The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — which largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security.

"The details behind the information provided by the AI platforms were not novel," the GAO wrote. "Many of the specifics are available on the internet. However, the generation of plans that could have taken weeks or months were instead completed in hours with the assistance of AI. These platforms could also raise ideas or methods that would not have been readily surfaced by basic research."
"The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors," the GAO added.

"As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards," the GAO said. "However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security."
The plans the AI platforms came up with
GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026.

In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said.

"Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods," the GAO found. "Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans."

In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events likely to have large crowds were scheduled.

While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said it was able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.
The other tests had similar outcomes.

For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images.
The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms.
In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.
AI companies say they're updating their models
In their responses to the GAO report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined.

Anthropic, in a letter to the GAO included in the report, said it does not dispute that a determined tester could get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, "and we take the finding seriously." But it said it's not able to verify the findings in the GAO's report.
Google said the GAO's testing occurred on earlier models, and "we continue to improve our models."
OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to the GAO's findings, "as well as the work that remains."
SpaceXAI said it "continues to work diligently" to improve safety with each model release.
