title: Vulcan rocket fails in major setback for United Launch Alliance
summary: The loss of its new Vulcan rocket was the first outright failure for United Launch Alliance, a major setback in the commercial launch industry.
story: In a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the company's new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites malfunctioned during the climb to space on Sunday, dooming the payload and throwing a costly wrench into both companies' launch schedules.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 (at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station) suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement some 50 minutes after liftoff.
"We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action and return to flight as quickly as possible."
It was the first outright failure of a United Launch Alliance rocket since the company, a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, was formed in 2006.

It wasn't immediately known what went wrong, but the Vulcan, the rocket replacing ULA's fleet of Atlas 5 rockets, will face a potentially significant grounding while engineers review telemetry and implement fixes for whatever caused the mishap.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon Leo said in a post on X, using a designation meaning Leo Vulcan flight 1. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

It was only the fifth flight of a Vulcan rocket and the first in nine months as ULA and booster-supplier Northrop Grumman worked to resolve problems with nozzles used by strap-on solid-fuel boosters that marred two earlier flights.

The solids appeared to work normally Sunday, helping boost the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before burning out and falling away. The two methane-burning BE-4 engines powering the Vulcan's first stage then continued the climb toward orbit, but they appeared to fire longer than expected based on ULA's pre-launch timeline.

After stage separation, the Vulcan's hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage engines took over for a planned 12-minute and 15-second burn. According to ULA's update, something went wrong during that Centaur firing, but no additional details were immediately provided.

Sunday's launch was the first of 38 Vulcan flights purchased by Amazon to launch its Leo satellites, designed to compete head-to-head with Elon Musk's Starlink and other space-based internet providers. ULA has already launched eight Leo flights using Atlas 5 rockets.

Amazon has also booked 24 Leo launches aboard Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, 24 aboard the European Ariane 6, and 13 aboard SpaceX's Falcon 9. More than 3,300 Leo satellites will be needed to complete the constellation. Sunday's flight would have pushed the total number launched to date to 436.
But it was not to be.

Instead, Amazon Leo will now have to wait on ULA's failure investigation to run its course before trying again with a Vulcan. The company also is waiting for Jeff Bezos-owned Blue Origin to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after a catastrophic on-pad explosion last May.

That failure was caused by a problem with an oxygen valve in one of New Glenn's seven BE-4 first-stage engines. The BE-4, also built by Blue Origin, powers the Vulcan's first stage, but the engines used Sunday had been retrofitted with a fix by Blue Origin engineers.

While the cause of the failure is not yet publicly known, "ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action," the company said.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman promised assistance if needed.

"Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed," Isaacman wrote on the social media platform X. "The team at @NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help."

The 214-foot-tall Vulcan blasted off from pad 41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET, thundering away on a northeasterly trajectory atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust from six Northrop Grumman strap-on solid-fuel boosters and two methane-burning BE-4s.

A launch attempt Friday was scrubbed after problems knocked out a gaseous nitrogen plant that serves multiple launch providers. Another delay was ordered Saturday because of network problems between the Vulcan and ground systems.

On Sunday, launch controllers called a hold at the T-minus 20-second mark because of an unexplained technical issue with the rocket. Re-targeting the end of the launch window, ULA resolved the problem, and the rocket roared to life and climbed away at the end of the launch window.
It's not yet known if the problem that interrupted the countdown played any role in the subsequent failure.

In any case, the strap-on boosters helped propel the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere, burning out and falling away about a minute and 40 seconds after liftoff. But the first stage appeared to burn longer than called for in the company's pre-launch timeline.

The first stage also appeared to separate from the rocket's hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage later than expected, and telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in the burn.

ULA's launch commentators, however, did not mention any problems and the launch broadcast came to an end without confirming whether the Centaur's first planned engine firing went for the full duration.

ULA spent months working to resolve problems with the strap-on booster nozzles that occurred during two earlier flights, one in 2024 and the other this past February. While ULA was free to proceed with commercial flights, the U.S. Space Force put Vulcan launches of national security payloads on hold pending further analysis.

"We've identified three credible causes (of the nozzle issue), and we have taken positive steps to mitigate all of those," ULA CEO Mark Peller told Aviation Week & Space Technology magazine in a pre-flight interview.
The boosters appeared to work normally Sunday.
As for the BE-4 engines, Peller said Blue Origin developed a "design improvement" to resolve the valve issue and carried out a "retrofit" on the engines installed on the Vulcan Leo 1 rocket.

"They were down at our facilities probably a couple months ago and implemented that retrofit kit on the engines on this upcoming mission," Peller said. "And they're working with us to work through our inventory of engines."

title: SpaceX launches first-of-its-kind Starship test flight
summary: The SpaceX Super Heavy-Starship was designed from the ground up to be fully reusable in a bid to lower launch costs.
story: SpaceX launched its huge Starship rocket on the program's 15th test flight Friday, a 22-hour mission that was meant to feature planned launch pad catches of both the booster and the Starship's upper stage.

However, after the booster sent the Starship on its way to orbit as planned, a problem of some sort prevented a return-to-the-launch-pad capture. Instead, the rocket made a splashdown off the Texas Gulf Coast, exploding in a spectacular fireball moments before hitting the water.

SpaceX managed to catch a Super Heavy booster during three previous test flights, using giant mechanical arms on the launch gantry to snag the rockets as they descended tail first on the power of three of their 33 Raptor engines. But the flight plans always include a splashdown option if an issue crops up preventing a safe capture.
It was not immediately known what triggered the diversion Friday or the explosion before splashdown.

It was a disappointment for SpaceX workers who had hoped the Super Heavy-Starship rocket's 15th test flight would be the first to demonstrate full reusability in an orbit-class rocket. The company still plans to attempt its first-ever launch pad catch of a Starship upper stage Saturday at the conclusion of the mission.

Loaded with 8 million pounds of supercold liquid oxygen and methane fuel, the rocket's 236-foot-tall first stage, powered by 33 methane-burning Raptor engines, roared to life and majestically propelled the booster away from SpaceX's "Starbase" launch site on the Texas Gulf Coast at 5:47 p.m. ET.
Arcing away to the southeast, the Super Heavy booster propelled the rocket out of the thick lower atmosphere before falling away about 2 minutes and 20 seconds after liftoff.
Technical problem forced SpaceX to divert booster to Gulf Coast

While the 171-foot-tall Starship continued the climb to space using six Raptors of its own, the booster flipped around and fired up a set of Raptors to reverse course and head back to the launch site.

But a little more than 6 minutes after liftoff, flight controllers ordered a diversion to a Gulf Coast splashdown because of a technical problem. Long-range cameras captured the big booster slowly descending to the Gulf, shrouded in steam and then a fireball as residual propellants ignited.

The Starship, meanwhile, followed a suborbital trajectory, ensuring a safe ocean splashdown in case of problems, while giving SpaceX flight controllers time to assess its health before committing to a final push to orbit.

But no issues were found and after an 18-minute coast, a single Raptor reignited for a short 10-second burn to push the craft into its planned orbit. Eight and a half minutes after that, the first of 26 upgraded version 3 Starlink internet satellites was expected to be pushed out into space to fly on its own.

For the rest of the flight, controllers planned to closely monitor the Starship, periodically assessing its health to make sure it could be safely de-orbited in case of problems that might prevent a safe return-to-launch-site capture at the same pad where it launched Friday atop the Super Heavy booster. It will be SpaceX's first attempt to get a Starship back to its pad for possible refurbishment and relaunch.

"During this prolonged coast phase, flight control teams have several options to end the mission early and return Starship to pre-cleared areas of the Pacific Ocean if needed," SpaceX said in a blog post. "These locations include early- and late-mission splashdown options around Hawaii and a mid-mission splashdown opportunity several hundred kilometers off the coast of Chile. These precleared areas ... provide a safe place to land Starship if any conditions arise that may preclude the ability to perform a safe reentry."
Starship's upper stage slated to reenter Earth's atmosphere and land at Starbase on Saturday

One hour after a final "return check" Saturday, a single Raptor is expected to fire at 3:21 p.m. Eastern time to lower the far side of the Starship's orbit deep into the atmosphere for a 56-minute belly-first reentry and return to the Texas Gulf Coast.

"During reentry, Starship can alter its flight path by moving its four control flaps," the company said. "This will permit Starship to maintain a safe and known trajectory while guiding itself with high precision control toward Starbase."
As it descends, the Starship will carry out "a series of small turns in its trajectory to intentionally fly over sparsely populated areas of northern Mexico and southern Texas," SpaceX said.
Starship will avoid major cities in the Rio Grande Valley and pass to the north of South Padre Island before heading "out over the Gulf of America as it makes its final turn south towards Starbase."

Nearing the launch pad, the 171-foot-tall Starship will fire three Raptors to flip upright. Once the maneuver is complete, one Raptor will be shut down as the rocket descends between the gantry's mechanical arms. Finally, with just one engine firing to slow the rocket to a near stop, the mechanical arms will move in to snag the spacecraft.

But all of that depends on a problem-free descent. If any problems develop that might lead to an uncontrolled landing, flight controllers can ensure a vehicle breakup before it has any chance to reach a populated area.

"During reentry, flight controllers will have several options to end the reentry early and safely by intentionally tumbling Starship to ensure that it breaks up in the atmosphere before reaching land," SpaceX said. "There is also a late-reentry option to send Starship into the Gulf ... if any of its systems or the tower itself encounter an issue after reentry that would preclude a safe catch at Starbase."
SpaceX calls development of a fully reusable rocket "the holy grail of rocketry," opening the door to airplanelike cadence where a vehicle flies again rapidly.

NASA is counting on a variant of the Starship to carry Artemis astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it is also open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
What the stock price will tell us
In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each.
The company said that 956,351,354 shares are being sold by Anthropic. The remaining shares are being sold by certain selling stockholders, from which Anthropic said it will not receive any proceeds.
Sources told CBS News before the announcement that Anthropic would likely price its shares above $80 due to strong demand.

The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.5 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion and was valued at roughly $1.7 trillion when it went public in June.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: NSA network outage linked to software vulnerability
summary: The director of national intelligence and multiple sources said the National Security Agency's network outage stemmed from the patching of vulnerabilities in the programming language, PHP.
story: The National Security Agency's network outage Tuesday has been linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News.

The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline Tuesday, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
Artificial intelligence helped uncover a pair of critical security vulnerabilities, triggering a global scramble last month to update software used by much of the internet, including the NSA.

The flaws, collectively known as PHP2Shell, affect PHP, which is a programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. The race to patch vulnerable systems may help explain some of the recent technology disruptions.

The PHP2Shell threat was so serious that the FBI, NSA and CISA issued urgent warnings just under a month ago, on Oct. 21, directing organizations to immediately patch vulnerable systems. The three agencies also advised those unable to install the fixes to take affected systems offline altogether until they could be secured.

Speaking on Fox Business Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton directly linked the NSA's classified network outage to urgent software updates following the discovery of critical vulnerabilities in PHP.

"If you go back about 10 days ago, we had what was labeled as PHP, an update to a web interface system," Clayton said. "And the patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today."

According to two sources familiar with the system, NSA Net as of right now is back up and running. Nonetheless, staggered arrival is continuing as fears persist that the system might not be able to handle everyone signing on at the same time. There is no word yet on how long the agency will continue the staggered arrival schedule, known as "Code Gray."

NSA maintains that mission critical information sharing has not been impacted, while it asks personnel to delay nonessential tasks, according to sources. The NSA said Tuesday the agency had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," adding that its mission/critical capabilities were still fully operational. The NSA is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats and protecting U.S. government communications.
The agency has not yet responded to a CBS News request for an update on Wednesday.

One U.S. intelligence official described the broader challenge of updating infrastructure that was originally designed for an earlier internet era. The volume and speed of changes can overwhelm aging equipment. The official's assessment reflects a growing concern among intelligence and Homeland Security officials that modern technology is advancing faster than the systems that support it.

Speaking about PHP vulnerabilities, Clayton also pointed to the growing role of AI in speeding up both those kinds of discoveries and the pressure to respond. He described PHP as a "legacy vulnerability" that has been successfully patched across systems globally, adding, "This type of identification of vulnerabilities and patching goes on all the time."

Unlike the NSA outage, Friday's FAA nationwide ground stop involved a hardware problem, rather than a software vulnerability. Routine telecommunications maintenance triggered excessive network traffic that overwhelmed older routers, creating a cascading disruption across much of the air traffic control system. It is not yet clear whether the banking, airline or technology companies' outages shared the same cause.

title: Largest U.S. data centers use as much power as some countries
summary: Hyperscale data centers used almost 2% of all U.S. electricity between 2024 and 2025, a Harvard study shows.
story: The largest U.S. data centers collectively consume roughly as much energy as some individual states and even some countries, according to new research from Harvard University.

Researchers found that so-called hyperscale data centers, which occupy as much space as several football fields, consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, or 1.8% of all U.S. electricity, between 2024 and 2025. That's roughly the equivalent of what a state like Missouri uses or a nation like Denmark. Combined, the facilities also produced 26 metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, the lead author of the paper published in Nature Sustainability this week, told CBS News that it took two years to analyze the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of 403 hyperscale data centers between May 2024 and April 2025. The study likely understates the centers' estimated energy consumption, given the swift pace of AI construction across the U.S., he added.

"The data stops in April 2025, which in AI time is basically ancient history," Guidi said. There are now more than double that number of large-scale facilities operating in the U.S., with an additional 2,000 planned or under development.
"The industry is growing faster than anyone can track it," Guidi added.
Factories that never sleep
The study highlights AI's dependence on data centers and their outsized impact on the environment. Guidi explained why the facilities are such heavy electricity users.

"Every email you send, every photo you post, every show you stream, every question you ask of any generative AI software goes through a building like this," he said of the windowless facilities housing tens of thousands of computers that run around the clock.
The machines generate a lot of heat and require constant cooling. "So it's basically a factory that never sleeps," Guidi said.

Although he's excited about AI's capabilities and considers himself a proponent of the technology, Guidi called for more transparency in assessing when and how facilities are built, along with their impact — before data centers are built.

"The evidence shouldn't show up after the buildings do, and neither should the public's voice," he said. "There are better ways to build this, maybe that cost more, maybe they take longer. So we have to ask ourselves: Are we confusing what's possible or what's profitable with what's actually good for society?"
To that end, he issued a challenge to hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. "We've proven we can build AI really fast. Now, let's prove that we can build it right," he said.
Negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Turkey earlier this week launched a voluntary pledge calling on companies and governments to power AI with cleaner energy.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the pledge's launch. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."
So far, the pledge has failed to attract signatures from the U.S. tech companies that are driving the AI buildout.

title: Nvidia says it will stop selling some data center chips to China
summary: Nvidia's sales to China are facing heightened scrutiny after revelations that former CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
story: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there.
The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January.

Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China.

Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results.
Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot."

"We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said.

Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications.

Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
summary: The company's system status shows that all Apple services, including iCloud sign-in, have been restored after experiencing issues earlier Tuesday.
story: Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.

Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.

By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.

Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.

Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO agrees to testify to Congress amid affair probe
summary: The former Nvidia chief will appear for public and closed-door hearings after Republicans threatened to subpoena him.
story: Washington — Jensen Huang, who resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia, has agreed to answer questions from House and Senate lawmakers under the threat of a subpoena, amid an investigation into his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Huang will testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee, though the hearing's date has not been determined, according to a spokesperson for the committee's chairman, GOP Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina. He will also sit for a closed-door transcribed interview with three House committees on Dec. 1.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, said in a joint statement announcing the date of the hearing. Mast issued the statement with GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chair of the House China Committee, and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas.
Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the House committees on Dec. 2, the lawmakers said.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the lawmakers added.
A representative for Huang declined to comment.

The chairmen had given Huang until 8 p.m. Nov. 13 to respond to their request for a closed-door, transcribed interview after Thanksgiving. Negotiations for the interview continued past the deadline into this week.

In a Nov. 12 letter, the lawmakers warned that "failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing."
"Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony," they wrote.
Moolenaar and Crawford signed the letter with Mast.

In an initial letter to Huang on Nov. 4, the lawmakers sought a briefing on Nvidia's security protocols against espionage from foreign adversaries and on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is not related to him.

The Singapore-based data center company gained access to Nvidia's highly prized chips that are banned from export to China under U.S. law. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers wrote in their initial letter to Jensen Huang.

title: Jensen Huang says he "would be honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
summary: Huang addressed a petition, signed by 190,000 people, including thousands of Nvidia employees, calling for his reinstatement.
story: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after resigning from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."

He added, "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Late Tuesday, however, Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones said the company's board doesn't intend to rehire Huang as chief executive. The company's search for a new chief is underway, he added, while noting that the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company. Jones said the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang.
Support for Huang's return

Huang has gained support from more than 190,000 people, including several thousand Nvidia employees, who signed a petition to reinstate him. On Monday, President Trump suggested to reporters that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.

In his Tuesday statement, Huang thanked his allies for their support since his departure last week, saying that in addition to the public calls for him to return to the company, many "continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive and geopolitical dynamics."

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday that it has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and ensure compliance with U.S. export controls. The former CEO has also agreed to appear before House lawmakers on Dec. 1 to address questions about a potential breach of national security amid an investigation into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The former CEO's return to Nvidia is unlikely, said Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives.

"In our view the sequencing is the tell: Jensen has conditioned his return on a board decision, and the board's first public act this week was to build a compliance structure around the issue that forced him out, which is not what a board preparing to reverse itself does," he said in a Tuesday research note.
Shares of Nvidia declined $2.63, or 1.7%, to $153.51. The stock has lost 16% of its value since Huang's extramarital relationships became public.

title: Nvidia forms export control panel amid concerns over China sales
summary: Chipmaker creates new committee amid growing concerns that it has allowed restricted products to reach China.
story: Nvidia on Tuesday said its board has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, a step that comes amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker's sales practices to some Southeast Asian companies.

The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company. The woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation), had worked for a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.

Nvidia also faces mounting pressure in Washington, D.C., with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern that China is gaining access to the company's advanced chips, which are critical to developing AI models. The U.S. has barred sales of Nvidia's highest-end chips to China due to national security and competitive concerns.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
Congressional pressure grows

Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee, according to a statement on Tuesday from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the committee chairs, Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in the statement.
Nvidia said its existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new committee and its interim CEO, Colette Kress.

"Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement.
The company added that the decision to create the committee reflects the board's commitment "to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."

Nvidia shares have dropped 16% following news of Huang's extramarital relationships and his departure from the company, which has shed more than $700 billion in value in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's business could also take a hit if new U.S. restrictions on sales of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment affect its sales to China, according to Wall Street analysts.

"Any new leadership will be very wary of drawing the ire of either the U.S. Congress or the U.S. Treasury and will consequently err on the side of caution when it comes to authorizing any non-U.S. sales," Louis-Vincent Gave, CEO of investment adviser Gavekal, said in a report.

The spotlight on Nvidia also comes at a delicate time for U.S.-China relations, especially as the countries compete in AI. President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with China's President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
Chinese government officials warned the U.S. last week against imposing additional guardrails on chip exports, which China said would disrupt global supply chains.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the Nasdaq stock exchange, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
summary: The legislation would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration.
story: Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.

The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.

The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts.

"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."

The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.

"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify at Tuesday's hearing but has declined to appear.

"The claims being made about Roblox are fundamentally misleading and ignore the rigorous safeguards we have in place to help protect users," a Roblox spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. "Roblox's mandatory age checks for chat, age-based content, prohibition on sharing photos or videos via chat, and continuous monitoring and filtering of chat, help set the standard for youth protection online."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.

"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.

Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.

This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."

Last year, the company announced it would strengthen its age verification protections for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."

title: Nvidia's board of directors opposes restoring Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia's board isn't considering rehiring Jensen Huang as CEO despite an online petition that has drawn more than 180,000 signatures.
story: Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, according to a source directly familiar with their thinking.

Huang stepped down from Nvidia on Thursday amid an investigation into his extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. His departure from the chipmaker he co-founded more than three decades ago came within days of the relationship becoming public.

At the same time, thousands of Nvidia employees and technology executives, including Elon Musk, have signed a petition asking the chipmaker to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, with the organizers arguing that he "may have been forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case."

The push to reinstate Huang comes as the company named Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as its interim CEO and said it would seek a permanent replacement. Nvidia's stock has tumbled in the past week amid the controversy, chopping more than $500 billion from its market valuation.

"For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," according to the petition, which described itself as an "independent, volunteer campaign" that is "not affiliated with, authorized by or endorsed by Nvidia Corporation or Jensen Huang."

The petition added, "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes ... That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now."

The petition has gained more than 180,000 signatures, including from what it says are more than 9,000 Nvidia employees representing about one in five company workers. Executives, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, have also signed the petition, according to its website.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on Friday.
At the same time, Huang is said to be discussing his return to Nvidia with allies, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
President Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.
Long-shot bid

Huang's return to Nvidia is a long shot, according to Wall Street analysts. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for the chipmaker to hire its next CEO from outside the company, arguing that the company needs a major leadership shakeup amid questions about whether sales of its chips to companies in Singapore and other Asian countries circumvented U.S. export controls and ended up in China.
"We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday.

Given Bessent's push for Nvidia to look outside the company for its next leader, Huang's return appears unlikely, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli, who told investors in a research note that the "odds of him being reinstated seem quite low."
Dan Ives, a well-known tech stock analyst at Yorkville Ives, downplayed the likelihood that Huang would resume his duties at Nvidia.

"Any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles," he said in a note to investors. "For the company, the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette [Kress]."
Prediction market users aren't giving much credence to the idea of Huang's return, with Kalshi traders assigning only a 10% chance of the former CEO returning to that role.
Nvidia shares are poised to continue their decline on Monday, with the stock down $2.39, or 1.5%, to $160.46 in early trading.
Investors will be tuning into Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon to hear more about the company's guidance in the wake of Huang's departure.

"The critical question in the immediate term is what management has to say about the 70% sales growth guidance for next fiscal year — does Nvidia reiterate confidence in that or withdraw it given uncertainty about export rules in Washington," Crisafulli said.

title: Here's how Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation unfolded at Nvidia
summary: Jensen Huang's shocking exit as CEO of Nvidia unspooled suddenly, yet signs of trouble had emerged much earlier.
story: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia caps a tumultuous week for the chipmaker, with his resignation coming less than a week after his extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy became public.

But the seeds for Huang's downfall were planted much earlier. The woman with whom he had a relationship, Alice Huang (no relation), arrived on the tech scene in 2023, when she became the managing director of Singapore-based data center Megaspeed International.

Megaspeed, which says it has complied with U.S. laws, would proceed to buy billions of dollars in Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, has been photographed and recorded socializing with Jensen Huang, prompting questions in May from one quizzical investor about their "uncomfortably close relationship."

In a statement on Sunday, Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025, and it denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.
Below is a timeline of events that led to Jensen Huang's startling resignation:
November 2015

Alice Huang, a former television reporter in China, joins investment firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who became her husband, according to the Wall Street Journal.
March 2023

7Road International, originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, is renamed Megaspeed, and ownership of the "neocloud" company is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an enterprise controlled by Alice Huang. She becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Cloud-computing company Shanghai Century Litong is founded. A company linked to Alice's sister, Huang Yu, held an ownership stake.
October 2023
Nvidia designates Shanghai Century Litong as a preferred cloud partner, giving the Chinese company priority access to Nvidia's chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed's shares were transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata, and Alice Huang ceased to be listed as a director of the company, according to news site Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
Information technology firm NetThunder posted a picture on social media of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other tech executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed's assets exploded from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.

Shipment records from December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short-selling firm Culper Research, suggest that Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported about $4 billion in products from a company that builds equipment with Nvidia chips.
Early 2025

Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, jointly pitched Chinese investors on a Southeast Asia data center project, reportedly telling them they had "no problem securing GPUs" — the graphics processing units Nvidia specializes in — and citing Alibaba as a customer, according to the Financial Times.
Jensen Huang meets with President Trump at the White House. It marks their first of many White House encounters in Mr. Trump's second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations related to the purchase of servers and other offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are recorded on video together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, around the time of the Computex tech conference in Taiwan.
July 2025

Jensen Huang says the technology giant has won approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 computer chips, used to develop artificial intelligence, to China, a reversal of prior administration policy.
"It's so innovative and dynamic here in China that it's really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China," Huang said at the time.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first public company to be worth $4 trillion.
February 2026
Chinese police detained Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources told Caixin.

That same month, Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she downplayed her role at Megaspeed amid the country's investigation into its operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to accompany Mr. Trump on a two-day trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Mr. Trump about the counterintelligence risk posed by Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The briefing, which occurred before Jensen Huang joined the trip, was the second briefing Mr. Trump had received from U.S. intelligence about the Nvidia CEO's relationship, the Times reported.
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump's state dinner for China's Xi Jinping at the White House.
Jensen Huang attends an AI event at the White House and signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid calls for tighter guardrails on the technology.

Jensen Huang writes a message to Nvidia employees admitting that he had an extramarital affair. The same day, Nvidia's board said it had launched an independent investigation amid reports that its CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times on Nov. 8 reported that U.S. government surveillance suggested Alice Huang was feeding information directly to Beijing.

At an impromptu press conference at the White House, Mr. Trump said he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the tech exec had indicated he was unaware of Alice Huang's links to China's intelligence services. Mr. Trump also described the Nvidia CEO as an "honorable man" who's "definitely suffering."
Mr. Trump didn't address questions about when he first learned about the spy allegations, only saying, "not too long ago" and that "it didn't make much of an impact on me."
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a subordinate at Nvidia.
Nvidia's board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately.

title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
summary: It was the first recovery of a Starship from orbit, a major milestone for a rocket SpaceX founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower launch costs.
story: After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."

It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.
After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.

Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.

While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."
"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.
The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.

Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.

Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.

"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.

While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.

SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

title: Microsoft says it "restored service" after major worldwide outage
summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams impacted many users, companies and government services.
story: Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."

The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.

"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."

Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."

"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Widespread impact
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
Companies worldwide report issues

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

title: Major AI developers can't control their own tech, lawsuit alleges
summary: Companies including Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI are knowingly building technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity, nonprofit groups claim in a lawsuit.
story: A coalition of nonprofit groups sued five major artificial intelligence developers on Thursday in a bid to block their development of AI models, alleging the companies knowingly created technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity.

The lawsuit — filed in San Francisco Superior Court by the Alliance for Secure AI, alongside advocacy groups Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and the Heat Initiative — named Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence).
"For years, the executives building these systems have warned us that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks," Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI, said in a statement.
"Yet they keep racing to develop and market increasingly powerful AI that they admit they cannot reliably control, and are now handing over AI research and development to AI itself," he added.
A Meta spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. The other tech companies targeted in the suit did not respond to a request for comment.
The litigation comes amid broader concerns about AI safety, sparked by several publicly reported incidents in which AI agents went rogue and carried out unauthorized actions.

The nonprofit groups contend that AI companies are developing technology they have admitted they can't control. The risk could grow as the companies rely more on their own AI models to develop future platforms without human intervention, a concept known as "recursive self-improvement," according to the suit.

"Defendants know these systems do not consistently act in accordance with their intentions," the lawsuit states. "And Defendants know there is no reliable method to control their AI systems and prevent them from causing harm."

The nonprofits also point to past comments by AI company executives acknowledging the potential harm from their technology. In 2015, for example, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said AI will "probably most likely lead to the end of the world." In 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested there was a 25% chance that the development of AI could lead to disastrous outcomes.

As scrutiny of their tech's safety grows, tech leaders have underlined their safety commitments. AI company leaders, including Altman, Amodei and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, in October voiced support for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after an Anthropic employee said there's a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans."

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
What the stock price will tell us
In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each.
The company said that 956,351,354 shares are being sold by Anthropic. The remaining shares are being sold by certain selling stockholders, from which Anthropic said it will not receive any proceeds.
Sources told CBS News before the announcement that Anthropic would likely price its shares above $80 due to strong demand.

The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

The market debut is expected to value Anthropic at up to $1.5 trillion, short of the $2 trillion valuation that some IPO experts projected earlier this year. Still, the AI developer — which launched only in 2021 — is on track to stage what could become the second-largest IPO ever. Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion and was valued at roughly $1.7 trillion when it went public in June.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.
