title: Trump expected to press Xi on Americans detained in China
summary: President Trump is expected to again press Chinese President Xi Jinping to release two Americans wrongfully detained in China when the leaders meet, their families say.
story: President Trump is expected to again press Chinese President Xi Jinping to release two Americans wrongfully detained in China when the leaders meet, their families say, as Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

Mr. Trump previously raised the detention of American scholar Youlin Chen with Xi during a meeting in Beijing in May, and confirmed discussing detained Americans with the Chinese leader again during his September visit to Washington. The leaders' upcoming bilateral meeting would mark the third time Mr. Trump has raised Chen's case and the second time he is expected to raise that of Min Zin, another American scholar who was detained in June.

Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, or APEC. He is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday, ahead of a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The families of the detained Americans say they have been assured Mr. Trump intends to raise the cases, though it remains unclear whether the issue will ultimately figure in his discussions with Xi, which are expected to cover a range of trade and national security matters.

Asked whether the president would raise the cases with Xi, the White House pointed to remarks he made earlier this month, when he said he discussed detained Americans with Xi "a lot" and cited the administration's record of freeing Americans. The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Sylvia Zin, whose husband Min Zin has been detained for nearly six months, said he is being held in solitary confinement at an undisclosed location, without access to legal counsel. She said the family recently learned he had been hospitalized last month for severe dehydration following a stomach illness and that the facility where he is being held has no heat.
"My worry for my husband's health and wellbeing increases with each passing day," she said.

"I am grateful for the President's commitment in continuing to raise my husband's wrongful detention, yet again," Sylvia Zin said. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays."

The other American, Youlin Chen, has been detained in China since November 2024. He faces espionage charges stemming from U.S. government-funded research on detecting North Korean nuclear tests. His family denies the allegations, noting that his work relied on publicly available data and was conducted in collaboration with Chinese scientists.
His wife, Yufang Rong, said she has also received assurances that Mr. Trump intends to raise his case directly with Xi.

"I've been assured that President Trump remains firmly committed to securing Youlin's freedom and that he intends to raise Youlin's case with President Xi at both the APEC meeting and, if needed, the G20," she told CBS News.
The next G20 summit is scheduled for December at the president's golf resort in Doral, Florida. Xi is expected to attend, although Beijing has not confirmed his participation.

Min Zin is a naturalized American citizen who fled his native Myanmar during the pro-democracy movement of the 1980s. He was detained by Chinese authorities on June 3 after traveling from Thailand to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference at the invitation of a Chinese professor. He runs a think tank that studies China's role in neighboring Myanmar, and his organization previously received U.S. government funding — which may have been a factor in attracting the scrutiny of Chinese intelligence authorities, U.S. officials have said.
Sylvia Zin previously told CBS News she believes he was lured to China and arrested on false charges. The State Department formally designated him as wrongfully detained in August.

Min Zin is being held by China's Ministry of State Security under a system known as Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location, or RSDL, which human rights groups describe as a form of secret detention. U.S. consular officials have been permitted brief, closely monitored monthly visits with him at a nearby hotel, according to his wife, but his family has not been allowed to see or speak directly with him.

Chinese authorities have accused Min Zin of activities endangering national security, including suspected espionage, allegations his family vehemently denies. Beijing has rejected the U.S. government's wrongful detention designation, maintaining that its authorities are acting in accordance with Chinese law.

The administration has repeatedly touted its record of bringing detained Americans home, including teacher Marc Fogel and ballet dancer Ksenia Karelina from Russia, and academic Dennis Coyle from Afghanistan. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said more than 100 detained Americans have been freed during Mr. Trump's second term.

Most recently, Mr. Trump said he personally appealed to Putin to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, the last American formally designated as wrongfully detained in Russia, who was freed in October without a prisoner swap. There are roughly 20 Americans imprisoned in Russia, and some of them are under review for potential designation by Rubio as wrongfully detained. Mr. Trump and Putin are also expected to meet one-on-one in China on Thursday.
But despite the president's personal interventions, neither of the two Americans held in China has been released.

Their cases have prompted scrutiny of the risks facing Americans traveling to China. In October, the State Department reinstated a "D" risk indicator on its China travel advisory, warning that Americans face a serious risk of wrongful detention there. The designation, also applied to six other countries including Russia, North Korea, Iran and Afghanistan, had been removed from China's advisory in November 2024 following a prisoner exchange. China's overall travel advisory remains at Level 2, with the State Department advising Americans to exercise increased caution.

Eric Lebson of Global Reach, an advocate for the detained Americans, said the administration is considering raising China's overall advisory to Level 3, which would advise Americans to reconsider travel. Such a move would be separate from the wrongful detention designation and could significantly affect academic exchanges, business travel and international conferences in China, Lebson said.

"It is uncharacteristic of the Chinese government to not engage on resolving matters of this type after two discussions about them at the presidential level," Lebson said, suggesting there may be disagreements within the Chinese government over how to handle the cases.

The potential push to secure the Americans' release comes as senior Trump administration officials have publicly disagreed over how aggressively to confront Beijing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, have pressed for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced American technology, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has resisted some of those measures, warning they could jeopardize relations with Beijing.

The disagreement has centered on efforts to prevent sensitive Nvidia chips from reaching China through third countries. Bessent publicly criticized the Commerce Department for delaying restrictions, while Mr. Trump defended Lutnick on Monday, saying he understood the concern that tougher measures could provoke a confrontation with Beijing. The president has at times favored a more accommodating approach to China, even as he has reportedly authorized tighter export controls.

title: 5 EU nations make plans to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda
summary: Five European nations have reached an agreement with Rwanda to deport failed asylum seekers to the African nation, but it's far from a done deal.
story: London — Five European Union countries have announced a plan to establish a deportation center in Rwanda next year to which they hope to send migrants whose asylum requests they have rejected.

The plan has echoes of President Trump's controversial initiative to deport migrants to third countries to which they have no links, and an effort by a previous British government that failed to clear legal hurdles. It is an attempt by the five European nations to address widespread concerns about mass-migration that have fueled political change across the continent, but it is far from guaranteed to succeed, or even to get off the ground.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have reached an agreement in principle with Rwanda to open a so-called "return hub" in the landlocked African nation in 2027. Unlike the U.S. program, the plan would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in Europe and subsequently been placed under a deportation order.

Rather than being returned to their countries of origin, some migrants would instead be transferred to Rwanda, where they would have the option of staying or returning to their home countries. The plan is intended to provide the European nations an alternative for cases in which deportation to a migrant's country of origin is not possible, either because those countries will not accept them, or due to circumstances that could endanger the migrant if they return.
Many European governments have sought to reduce the number of migrants entering their countries, or already present without permission, in the face of mounting political pressure from voters.

As an example of the kind of statistics fueling that public concern, there were some 230,000 foreign nationals in Germany at the end of 2025 who were legally required to leave the country, according to the Die Welt newspaper, yet government figures show fewer than 23,000 deportations were carried out during the year.

"If people without the right to remain in the EU cannot be removed from the country, our entire asylum system becomes absurd," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said this week. "If the state sets limits, then these must be respected."

According to a statement from the Netherlands government, migrants deported to Rwanda under the proposed program would initially be accommodated in an "open, temporary facility." If they choose to remain in Rwanda, they will "have access to education, the labor market, healthcare and the legal system."

"For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system, a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said during a news conference on Monday.
"Under this partnership, Rwanda would provide a second chance to people who no longer have the legal right to remain in the partner countries," Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said.
Legal and logistical hurdles
But some big questions remain unanswered about how the proposed deportation program might work in practice.

"The countries will need to negotiate the detailed arrangements with Rwanda, including who would be eligible for transfer, what legal status and rights they would have in Rwanda, how the facilities would operate, who would pay for them, and how the authorities would monitor people's treatment after transfer," Dr. Peter W. Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, told CBS News.

"A big open question is what Rwanda will receive as part of the deal, such as financial payments, as was the case with the U.K.-Rwanda agreement," he said, referring to a similar plan the former Conservative U.K. government embraced, but failed to get past a challenge in Britain's Supreme Court.
The new Labour Party government scrapped the policy completely in July 2024.
There are important differences between the British and European proposals, however.

"The U.K.'s Rwanda scheme was designed to transfer asylum seekers to Rwanda for their asylum claims to be decided there," Walsh said, whereas the European proposal "is intended for people who have already been determined to have no right to remain in the participating countries, rather than people awaiting an initial asylum decision."

"This distinction may avoid some of the specific legal problems that affected the U.K. scheme, particularly concerns about whether Rwanda's asylum system could reliably assess claims for international protection," he said.

Another significant difference, Walsh said, is the EU has adopted legislation explicitly allowing member states to establish migrant return hubs outside the bloc, providing a clearer legal framework for the European proposal.
"However, this does not mean that transfers to Rwanda would automatically be lawful," he cautioned.
The U.K. Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal based on concerns that asylum seekers transferred to Rwanda could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution or other serious harm.

"The European countries would also need to address concerns about safety, individual rights, and the treatment of people transferred to Rwanda — especially to ensure that people were not sent on to countries where they could be at risk of serious harm," Walsh said. "The existence of an agreement with Rwanda would not, by itself, settle these questions."
Would the program deter illegal migration?
Even as a proposal, the plan has drawn criticism from humanitarian organizations questioning not only its potential legality, but its likely effectiveness as a deterrent to unauthorized migration.
The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) told CBS News it was "deeply concerned and disappointed" by the announcement.

"While European states have the right to return individuals who do not have a legal right to stay, sending people to a third country with which they have no connection is not the answer," said Céline Mias, the organization's EU director. "Instead of fixing existing EU asylum and return systems, Member States are creating a costly new mechanism and calling it innovative."
The organization said its research also showed "that restrictive migration policies fail to deter people from migrating, while carrying severe consequences for human lives."

Rwanda has long been criticized for its human rights record. In a statement this week, the rights group Amnesty International said "sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights."

The participating governments have said the return hub will be developed in accordance with EU and international law, including human rights obligations, and that relevant national agencies were already working with the European Commission and international migration organizations to ensure compliance.
Whether the countries will be able to begin deportations under the program next year, or ever, however, remains uncertain.

"The proposed timetable is ambitious," Walsh told CBS News. "It is possible that a small pilot could begin in 2027, particularly if the participating countries initially limit transfers to a relatively small group."

"Even if the first transfers take place next year, that would not necessarily demonstrate that return hubs could make a substantial difference to the overall number of people leaving Europe," he added. "And the question of scale will be key to the plan's hoped-for deterrent effect."

title: Inside China's race to get humanoid robot helpers into our homes
summary: China is racing to make humanoid robot helpers common home appliances, and one industry insider says they have an "edge globally."
story: Wuhan, China — In the large lobby of a three story building in Wuhan, China, a child-size yellow robot greets visitors with a dance. It sways along to traditional Chinese music while robots twice the size stand on either side of the stage, beating loud drums to the rhythm. The little robot then moves on to another dance, bopping along to a pop tune that makes people smile and laugh.
The small humanoid robot's agility makes it look almost lifelike. Then it stops, and the crowd is ushered on to see the real wonders inside the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center.

On the top floor, more than 100 computer science and engineering graduates toil at individual work stations wearing gloves and outfits equipped with motion and tactile sensors, while cameras record their every movement.
One pours water into a jug; another places cutlery and chopsticks into a container. The graduate at the next table unscrews a flashlight and removes the battery, then replaces it.

All the movements are done slowly, meticulously and repeated over and over again, with the actions recorded as valuable data from the cameras and sensors that can be used to train the company's humanoid robots.
"It was fun at first," said 22-year-old intern Mei. "It gets a little boring in the middle. But it's such a proud moment when we get the model trained."

Mei is one of nearly 1 million engineering graduates China's universities are estimated to be churning out every year. The U.S., by comparison, sends about 140,000 young engineers into the job market annually.
Another graduate sits with a remote control in his hand and a humanoid robot next to him. As he moves his hand, the robot mimics his motions.

"Right now I'm capturing the motion of pouring water into a cup. We're training this action and gathering data for the model. It's controlled by this hand controller. It moves exactly how the hand moves," he explains. "We need to run this hundreds or thousands of times. We have only completed 500 iterations so far."

At the G20 summit in September, Elon Musk made a bold statement, declaring that within 10 years, "there will be well over a billion humanoid robots, and productivity of a robot will be five-times that of a human."
The world's richest man may believe robots will replace human productivity within a decade, but many in China take a different view.

"Our main goal is for these robots to serve humans in household and industrial settings," Prof. Jiyin Cao, who runs the Hubei robotics center, told CBS News, clearly oozing pride over the work they are doing. "We train them to carry out tasks for industrial applications. This is why we train these robots — to help them integrate better into human life."

China is under enormous pressure to make that happen. The country has an aging, shrinking population. It's one of the fastest demographic shifts playing out anywhere in the world, and it is lending urgency to efforts to get humanoid robots into labor-intensive sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, retail and healthcare.

"I believe future robots will be deployed across all industries. They will work in factory workshops, homes, nuclear energy sites, provide elderly care services, and serve as our personal assistants," Cao told CBS News. "They can help us with all these things."
Training the humanoids, however, takes an enormous amount of time, especially for more complex tasks.
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Cao laughed off any suggestion that most people could have humanoid helpers in their homes anytime soon.

"It still requires extensive training and learning," he said. "Home environments are unstructured, far from simple. Early robots mostly perform actions in simple, fixed, structured settings. But every household is unique, making home environments highly complex. It could be three to five years away before one is in our home. But it could also take 10 years."

The timescale may be up for debate, but China is working at breakneck speed and on a monumental scale to bring robots into the mainstream consumer world — and to ensure it is Chinese companies developing and making them.
"China has the world's strongest industrial manufacturing system and a full supply chain for upstream and downstream robotics products," Cao said. "That is our greatest edge globally."

title: China's Xi greets Trump at airport ahead of planned summit with Putin
summary: President Trump arrived Wednesday in China, where the Kremlin said he had an informal meeting with Vladimir Putin.
story: President Trump arrived in China on Wednesday after starting a multiday Asia swing in the Philippines. He's scheduled to meet in Shenzhen, a hub of China's tech industry, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit on Thursday.
Mr. Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying such a meeting "may not be possible" but the president is "prepared" for one.
Xi greeted Mr. Trump on a red carpet as he walked off Air Force One in Shenzhen.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Mr. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting Wednesday ahead of the planned trilateral summit. Peskov also said Putin had already held a meeting with Xi, during which they discussed the war in Ukraine. Mr. Trump and Putin may also discuss Ukraine, Peskov said.
Putin mentioned his recent discussions in Moscow with Mr. Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during his meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Peskov said.

"The three leaders have a lot to discuss, given the unstable situation in the world," Putin's senior aide Yury Ushakov told reporters in Shenzhen, according to Russian state broadcaster Vesti. He did not confirm the plan for an initial bilateral meeting between Putin and Mr. Trump on Wednesday, but said they might meet during a formal dinner.
It "will not be a single event," Ushakov said of the possibility of Trump-Putin encounters on Wednesday. "It will take place both standing, on the steps, and while seated."

In Manila, Mr. Trump visited the Malacañang Presidential Palace on Wednesday and met with his Philippine counterpart, Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., before his flight to China. In a public bilateral meeting, the two leaders lauded the U.S.-Philippine relationship, which Mr. Trump called "one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific." The U.S. president suggested the two countries could cooperate further on technology, energy and defense.

In a banquet luncheon before departing for China, Mr. Trump announced that he and Marcos "just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, and it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that. And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly, and it's a magnificent deal for both."
Later, in a social media post, Mr. Trump said the deal "will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of Energy."

A day earlier, after landing in the Philippine capital of Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia-Pacific region. The president described the relationship with the Quad — made up of the U.S., Australia, India and Japan — as "very special."
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korea's Kim in China. After arriving in the Philippines, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia board of directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

title: 2,000-year-old bog woman was beheaded in possible ritual killing
summary: The "Ballymacombs More Woman," whose body lay in a Northern Ireland bog for 2,000 years, was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," researchers say.
story: London — An investigation into the death of a young Iron Age woman whose remains were preserved in a Northern Ireland bog for more than 2,000 years has found that she was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," when she was between 15 and 22 years old.

The enquiry into the remains known as the "Ballymacombs More Woman," discovered in a peat bog in central Northern Ireland in October 2023, determined that she was decapitated from behind, most likely with a bladed weapon.

"While the precise circumstances surrounding her death remain unknown, the evidence suggested that she may form part of a wider tradition of ritualized killing and sacrifice," said the Ulster Museum, which hosted a coroner's investigation into the two-millennia-old killing. It said the woman's death appeared similar to others documented among  Iron Age bodies discovered in bogs across northwest Europe.
The More Woman's body dates from between 343 to 1 B.C., from the prehistoric Iron Age period.

"Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare," Hannah Crowdy, head of curatorial for Northern Ireland's National Museums, told CBS News partner network BBC News. "She's the first of her kind in Northern Ireland."

"This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious," Crowdy added. "There's been a really intensive period of research … To honor her, it's important to tell her story and bring that to the fore."

The team that carried out what the Ulster Museum called a "unique public event modelled on a modern coroner's investigation into the remains" used scientific mapping techniques, 3D imaging and analyses of bone, hair, skin and nails to gain evidence of the woman's age, health, diet, physical condition and the injuries that led to her death.

Niamh Baker, the Ulster Museum's curator of archaeology, told the BBC that an osteoarchaeologist — someone who studies archaeological human bones —   reviewed the remains and found cut marks on the woman's neck.
"It would appear she was intentionally decapitated in the bog," said Baker. "No skull was recovered with further investigation."

"There are examples of some Iron Age remains in the Republic of Ireland that are male that similarly met violent deaths and some of those are thought to be associated with kingship and sovereignty," said Baker. "Was she a female sovereign? Or it may be that it was related to an agricultural or weather issue at the time."
Residents of the nearby town of Balleghy have named the woman Aine.

"We feel that Aine is one of our own," said Séamus Mac an Fhirléighinn, from the town's historical society, who attended the coroner's investigation."This is her inquest. She needed her people, her family there with her to act on her behalf as advocates."
"Local people are very interested," he said. "We wanted to know who this person was, how she died, how she lived."

title: Man with ax destroys $60M U.S. military plane, prosecutors say
summary: Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is charged in the U.S. with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport.
story: An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man's supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States' involvement in Middle East conflicts.

An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.

O'Corrain isn't in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn't been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.

The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won't fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.

O'Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends "a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated."

An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O'Corrain's friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.'s war with Iran and support for Israel's war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.

"An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel's genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.

O'Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport's grounds, prosecutors said.

He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," James Barnacle, the head of the FBI's New York office, said in a statement.

O'Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport's perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.

He used the crew's hammocks to cover the plane's windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.

O'Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O'Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would've risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O'Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.

Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane's exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O'Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.

Shannon Airport, which was used by President Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: American soldier accused of spying in U.S. custody after U.K. arrest
summary: Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."
story: A United States Army soldier arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia has been taken into the custody of the U.S. military, British and American officials said Tuesday.

A U.S. official previously identified the suspect as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior human resources officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Tyner, 41, joined the Army in 2008 and has been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a news release that U.S. authorities will continue the investigation. The suspect is expected to be charged soon.

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said.

The soldier is suspected of violating the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 to obtain or disclose protected information and to assist a foreign intelligence service. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia. Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."

He was arrested by the the London Metropolitan Police during a sting operation in Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, on November 10. The operation involved the Met Police's Counter Terrorism Policing Unit, the U.S. military and the FBI.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday.
Officials have carried out further searches in Gloucestershire, the county where Gloucester is located, related to the investigation, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow last week that Russia had "nothing to do with" the soldier's detention.

U.K. police said the arrest is not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations." The unit is investigating a recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base where U.S. troops and aircraft are stationed. The U.S. military removed its bombers from that base after the security incident.

Five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national were arrested in late September. Last week, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at the site. One suspect is in custody in New York, and the other two are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: U.S. identifies remains of 6 soldiers killed in Korean War, including teens
summary: The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of U.S. soldiers killed in the Korean War.
story: Six soldiers who died in the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been accounted for decades after their deaths, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Monday.

The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of those killed in the Korean War. When a soldier is marked as accounted for, they receive a burial with full military honors.

U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman was a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division. Thurman, 18, was a forward observer near Waegwan, South Korea, when his post came under heavy attack, according to the agency, and was last seen trying to evacuate a shell-shocked officer from the area while under heavy enemy fire.
Afterward, Thurman was reported missing in action. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were declared unrecoverable two years later, in January 1956.

The agency said that a set of remains, designated X-5814 Tanggok, was recovered by the Quartermaster Graves Registration Company near Kumhwa-dong, South Korea, in October 1952. The remains were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. In November 2022, the agency disinterred the remains. Analysis allowed the agency's scientists to identify the remains as Thurman's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 18, 2026.

U.S. Army 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert was a member of B Battery, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, who was reported missing during the battle of the Ch'ongch'on River in North Korea, according to the agency. Witness statements allowed the Army to determine that Gilbert, 23, had been taken as a prisoner of war by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army and died from battlefield wounds in a POW camp on Jan. 31, 1951.

After the war, a recovered set of remains was returned to U.S. custody as part of a 1954 exchange known as Operation Glory, the agency said. The remains could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. They were disinterred on July 1, 2024, and sent to the agency's laboratory. Analysis, circumstantial and historical evidence allowed the agency to identify the remains as Gilbert's. His remains were marked as accounted for on June 4, 2026.

U.S. Army Cpl. William R. Laughlin Jr. was a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, attached to the 31st Regimental Combat Team, according to the agency. Laughlin, 21, was among the U.S. soldiers ambushed by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army at the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea.

The ambush sparked a 17-day battle in frigid weather. Each side took thousands of casualties. U.S. and United Nations forces eventually retreated south toward the supply base of Hagaru-ri. Laughlin could not be located after the battle and was reported missing in action on Dec. 2, 1950. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953.

A pair of remains returned during Operation Glory were connected to an isolated burial east of the Chosin Reservoir. They could not be identified and were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The agency disinterred the remains in July 2022 and used modern forensic techniques at its laboratory to identify them as Laughlin's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on Sept. 28, 2026.

U.S. Army Sgt. Joseph A. Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, was last seen during an ambush near Inje in South Korea. Platzkoester, 28, was part of a convoy doing counteroffensive clearing operations at the time, the agency said. The convoy encountered an enemy roadblock. While his battalion pushed through, Platzkoester could not be found after the fight and was reported missing in action.
The area was searched, but Platzkoester's remains were not found. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953, and his remains were declared nonrecoverable in January 1956.

In 1951, the 148th Quartermaster Graves Registration Company found a set of remains that could not be identified. They were interred as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. In November 2023, the set of remains was disinterred and sent to the agency's laboratory, where analysis identified them as Platzkoester's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 29, 2026. A photo of Platzkoester was not available.

U.S. Army Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, was assigned to Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, and was reported missing in action during a road march near Taewol Village in South Korea, according to the agency. The agency said it was able to account for him on May 5, 2026. Information about how his remains were found and identified was not available. A photo was not shared by the agency.

The other teen soldier, U.S. Army Cpl. Richard N. Lennox, 18, was accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025, the agency said. He was a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division reported missing in action after his unit was attacked by enemy forces near Sachang-ni, North Korea, on Nov. 28, 1950. He was captured and marched to a prisoner-of-war camp in Changsong, where he died in October 1951.

Lennox's remains were among those handed over during Operation Glory, the agency said. They could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The remains were disinterred on June 13, 2016. The agency analyzed the remains and said that Lennox had been accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025. A photo of Lennox was not available.

Each missing soldier's name was engraved on the Walls of the Missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Now that they have been accounted for, rosettes will be placed alongside their names.

More information about each soldier, including how they were identified, may be shared after their families are briefed by the agency. The agency told CBS News in 2024 that history, diplomacy and science all come into each investigation. First, researchers start with archival records. Investigators then search for surviving witnesses and clues. Once the potential location of a set of remains is identified, a recovery mission is sent to bring those remains to the agency's laboratory.

At the lab, scientists use dental evidence and other records to study the remains. For soldiers who disappeared during the Korean War, experts can use tuberculosis skin test results taken before someone shipped out. The remains also undergo X-rays, DNA analysis and isotope analysis. Finally, a reference sample of DNA from a family member is compared to the remains. The process can take decades, the agency told CBS News.

About 7,500 Americans are still unaccounted for from the Korean War, the agency says. Efforts to bring home fallen soldiers from the conflict are complicated by relations with North Korea: While the agency operates in 46 countries, North Korea is an outlier. Sometimes, war dead are recovered during exchanges like Operation Glory.

title: Ukraine says underground gas pipeline used to mount sneak attack
summary: Ukraine says troops spent weeks crawling through an old underground gas pipeline to get behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack.
story: Ukrainian soldiers spent weeks navigating a decommissioned, underground Soviet-era gas pipeline to sneak behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack on Russian troops this autumn as part of an operation to prevent the invading forces from reaching the eastern city of Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian unit involved.

The operation forced the soldiers to get past barricades laid by Russian forces — including the bodies of fallen troops —   and involved close-quarters combat inside the roughly three-foot-wide pipeline, Ukraine's military said.

"Operation Veles" was carried out by members of the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps in the Kharkiv region within the last couple of months, according to a series of posts by the unit on social media. The unit said troops crawled and were pulled on wheeled carts some nine miles through the underground pipeline before emerging behind Russian positions.

The operation was part of a broader Ukrainian effort, more than four and a half years into Russia's full-scale invasion, to prevent the invading forces from advancing toward the front-line city of Kupiansk.

The unit's social media posts quoted soldiers saying they engaged in close combat with grenades and small arms inside the pipe, where the cramped space came with pooled freezing water and traces of natural gas lingering years after the pipeline was decommissioned. Some Ukrainian forces spent as long as a month underground during the operation, the Khartiia Corps said.

"They used electric winches to move through the pipe, and transported ammunition and equipment on small wheelbarrows," the unit said in one post. It called the conditions "extremely harsh," and noted that the troops "constantly moving on their knees caused injuries, and dirt clogged the mechanisms of their weapons and caused malfunctions."

Russian troops had laid obstacles in some sections of the pipeline, with Ukrainian soldiers saying that some of those barricades included the bodies of other Russian soldiers. The claims by the Ukrainian forces about the battle have not been independently verified by CBS News.
Russian authorities have acknowledged the operation, referring to a Ukrainian raid.

The Khartiia Corps has not confirmed any Ukrainian casualties, but at least one report on the battle, by Britain's Telegraph newspaper, mentioned Ukrainian forces recovering the body of a fallen comrade from inside an underground gas pipeline.

The pipeline offered a way for Ukrainian forces to conceal their movements in one of the most heavily monitored sectors of the nearly 1,000-mile front line that stretches from the far north to the far south of eastern Ukraine.

Both sides have sought to exploit underground infrastructure to evade increasingly sophisticated aerial surveillance in a conflict shaped by drone warfare. In September 2025, Russian forces similarly attempted to use sections of underground pipeline to move troops closer to Ukrainian positions around the northern outskirts of Kupiansk without being detected by drones.

Military analysts say operations like the underground pipeline assault highlight how the widespread use of drones in Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, and Ukraine's defense, have transformed modern warfare. Both sides rely heavily on surveillance and attack drones to find and strike troops and hardware moving in the open.
As a result, even short movements above ground can expose soldiers to near real-time observation and attack.

While underground operations present their own dangers, including limited ventilation, restricted movement, navigational challenges and the risk of entrapment, soldiers involved in the Ukrainian mission suggested the hazards were outweighed by the dangers posed above ground, where they could have been spotted by Russian drones.
"It's damp, it's dark, it reeks. There are corpses lying around, but I felt safer there," one Khartiia Corps member, using the callsign "Sgt. Santa," was quoted as saying in a post by the unit.

The operation came ahead of what could prove a critical juncture in the war. President Trump, who campaigned on ending the war quickly, has pushed hard for Ukraine and Russia to agree to a peace deal. Kyiv and its European allies fear, however, that the White House appears to be offering Vladimir Putin and Russia too much — including the prospect of major energy deals, with no significant concessions in return,  while putting pressure on Ukraine to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Ukraine says the operation in the gas pipeline helped stop Russian forces from gaining more ground near Kupiansk, a city that Ukrainian forces recaptured from Russia's invading troops in 2022.

title: Pope Leo calls for "less controversy, less war, less division"
summary: The Catholic Church's first U.S.-born leader, returning from a major Latin America tour, spoke about American unity, his health, and the prospect of married priests.
story: Rome — Speaking to reporters on his return trip to Rome after an extensive tour of Latin America, Pope Leo XIV called for less political polarization in the United States following the recent midterm elections.

"I would like to see a greater capacity for dialogue, building bridges, reconciliation, less controversy, less war, less division," the Chicago-born leader of the Catholic Church told reporters. "I know this is also a dream, but I know it is possible, so we shall see."

Leo, who confirmed earlier this month that he had voted in the 2026 midterms and was proud to "exercise my right" to do so, said it was the duty of all American citizens to participate in elections. He spoke on the flight back to Italy about his American identity, calling himself "a gringo in many ways."
"My deep faith in democracy, of democratic participation, is also part of being a North American," he said.
The pontiff said being American was also likely why he had been forthcoming about his recent health issues.
"Not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well"

"When I speak in general, I am very direct. I say things as they are," he told reporters. "The issue of my health and the fact of openly speaking about it … it's not so typical in many countries and cultures. In U.S. society, it is a bit more of a common attitude."
"I'm not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well," he said, crediting his doctors, prayers and personal determination for his recovery, calling stamina "one of the gifts the Lord gave me."

Leo underwent surgery in October after doctors discovered a lung tumor and diagnosed him with cancer. His medical team said the cancer was confined to a lobe of one lung that was removed, and that no further treatment was necessary. The tumor was discovered during a routine annual medical examination.
"The initial news was a surprise," the pope said. "I had no symptoms and felt fine."

Leo, who set off on the trip to Latin America just 24 days after his operation, said he had decided to proceed quickly with the surgery because he was determined to stick to the plans for his Latin American tour. He said the diagnosis did not change his agenda, or his priorities.
Asked whether he had signed a conditional resignation letter in the event of permanent incapacity, as previous popes have done, Leo said he had not.
"For now, I don't see the need," he said.
Pope doesn't rule out married priests
Leo also addressed one of the most divisive issues in the Catholic Church on the return flight —   the ordination of married men to the priesthood.

He acknowledged that allowing married priests could help address severe shortages in remote regions such as the Amazon, but cautioned that the issue was "complicated" and could create division within the church.
"It's a solution which, in certain areas of the church, can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance, of that concept," he said.
Leo did not completely rule out the possibility, but made it sound unlikely any time soon.
"It may be in the future that some things will change. However, for right now, what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together," he said.
The pope also joked with reporters about being hit in the face with a flying rosary during his final mass in Lima.
"The affection of Peruvians —   including that person who, with great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary — these are things one carries in one's heart, perhaps in one's eye," he quipped.

title: Scientist fired after 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial
summary: The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition, an investigation found.
story: A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.

Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.

"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."

Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
"Unusual and dangerous"
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.

"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science. "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."

The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui, a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.

title: Dead racehorse found in dumpster days after prestigious race
summary: The dead body of So You Are was found in a waste facility less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.
story: The dead body of Melbourne Cup horse So You Are was found in a waste facility in Sydney less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.

The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported Tuesday that racing stewards were investigating after a construction worker saw a dead horse in a dumpster at a licensed waste center and posted a video on Facebook.

Trainer Bjorn Baker had released a statement Monday saying So You Are died following a severe bout of colic. The 5-year-old gelding was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but couldn't be saved.
Baker posted an update Tuesday after discovering So You Are hadn't been properly buried.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in a statement. "He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred," he added. "My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."
So You Are placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup on Nov. 3, with Point of Law winning the 166th running of the 2-mile classic.
REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr. Jonathan Lumsden issued a statement saying So You Are had been "humanely euthanized under anesthesia" after receiving emergency treatment.

"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said. "What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."
Lumsden said he was working with the service provider and the state's horse racing authority, Racing NSW, to establish what went wrong and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.

"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," he said. "We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week."
Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the landfill, told national broadcaster ABC the horse's body was moved to a permitted area of the site.

"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson told ABC. "The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons. In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."
"These images are distressing"
Racing NSW said So You Are was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when the video was recorded.

"These images are distressing for all involved and for all of us who care deeply about our horses," Racing NSW said in a statement. "The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect."

The state's racing regulator said under industry guidelines — now under review — a licensed landfill was the preferred option for animals that have been euthanized because of the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," the statement continued. "If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."
Australian politician Emma Hurst called the news "absolutely heartbreaking," but not surprising, ABC reported.

"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said. "To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament."

title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub
summary: Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence hub.
story: Manila, Philippines — Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub just north of the country's capital of Manila.

In the opening salvo for Pax Silica, a U.S. State Department-led international initiative to secure non-Chinese supply chains for high-tech manufacturing, a more than 4,000-acre manufacturing hub is planned to be built in the Philippines.
Protesters in Manila on Monday held signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or a devil, and signs calling on the public to reject the Pax Silica initiative.
Critics argue the proposed industrial hub will displace farming communities and the Indigenous Aeta tribe, harm the country's water supply and represent U.S. imperialism over the Philippines.
"They have been grabbing our lands. They have been grabbing our economy. … Pax Silica is just for the U.S. It's not for us," said Maninging Vilog, a teacher and advocate for Aeta communities.

"If you look at the farmers, what do they care about AI? The people selling water … selling cigarettes, the people who drive buses. What do they care about AI?" said Kaiser Cortina, a 20-year-old protester.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also a subject of the protests this week, supports the hub. He said in October he is "terribly excited" about the project's economic benefits, framing it as a "grand opportunity" for the country to move up the "value chain" by shifting into advanced manufacturing and research, according to PhilStar Global.
Marcos' administration has claimed the project could create 100,000 to 130,000 jobs.

A proposed 4,000-acre artificial intelligence hub north of Manila is drawing opposition ahead of President Trump’s visit to the Philippines.The project is part of Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative aimed at reducing reliance on China for critical technology supply chains.… pic.twitter.com/9BQJFClqL8

Over 25 countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative since it was announced by the U.S. State Department in December 2025, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Japan and India. The Philippines joined the initiative in April, leading the U.S. and the Philippines to announce plans for a manufacturing hub.

A State Department spokesman said that the Philippines proposed the site of the hub, and that it is up to them to decide under its own laws and timetable, whether and how to proceed. They added that the U.S. remains committed to their set goal to create skilled manufacturing jobs in the Philippines and a more reliable supply chain for both countries.

The U.S. has raised concerns for years about supply chains for the hardware that powers AI, including worries that China could get access to advanced chips. The issue has drawn new attention in recent weeks, amid revelations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose company was under investigation for smuggling chips. (The company has denied chip smuggling.)

Pax Silica participants signed a declaration on Sunday that sets out a "common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin" artificial intelligence supply chains.

U.S. and Filipino officials have said there aren't expected to be any big announcements about Pax Silica this week during Mr. Trump's visit during the ASEAN summit in Manila. The U.S. president is expected to meet with Marcos on Wednesday before flying to China.
CBS News has reached out to the State Department for comment.

Antonio Tinio, a member of the Philippine House of Representatives, said there aren't any specific votes on Pax Silica planned in the country's legislature, and claimed "it's far from certain" that the Pax Silica hub will start construction and be successful.
And he added that the critiques of the Manila hub mirror the anti-AI data center sentiment in the U.S.

"The opposition to AI data centers is global. … That was one of the big issues in your election. It's a big issue. There's a lot of opposition throughout Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia, and also in the Philippines," Tinio said.

title: Ella Langley dominates CMA Awards with major wins as Taylor Swift makes stunning return to stage
summary: Ella Langley dominates the CMAs as she wins big while Taylor Swift makes her return after decade-long absence.
story: Fresh off winning Entertainer, Album, and Female Vocalist of the Year, the "Choosin’ Texas" hitmaker reflects on her career-defining night backstage at Bridgestone Arena.
The 60th annual Country Music Association Awards took place live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Wednesday night.
Ella Langley dominated the awards ceremony, as the winner of entertainer of the year, the biggest award of the night.
While accepting the award, she joked that the crowd must be sick of her already, getting a laugh from those in the room.
"This isn't real life," she said while accepting the award. "Thank you, Jesus, I'm at a loss for words," she added, before saying, "This has been the most special night."
Langley won album of the year for her album, "Dandelion." (Michael Buckner/Billboard via Getty Images)
As she swept all the categories she was nominated in, Lainey Wilson brought out a bedazzled broom for her, telling her she knew she had it prepared as she knew Langley was going to sweep the show.

Langley also won music video of the year before the broadcast. "Choosin' Texas" was named as the music video of the year winner during Good Morning America Wednesday morning. The record-breaking hit also won single of the year and song of the year.
WATCH: Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert and the 'Choosin' Texas' team pose with their CMA Awards

Later in the show, Langley got teary-eyed as she accepted the award for album of the year, for her album, "Dandelion," noting it took two years to make. She was speechless while accepting the award and received a standing ovation from the audience.
Langley joked the audience must be sick of her after winning entertainer of the year. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)
"I’m at a loss for words. I don’t know what to say," she said in her speech. "I love country music and I love what I do."
Her wins also resulted in two wins for Miranda Lambert, who is credited as a producer on the song.
Langley continued her winning streak later on in the show when she took home the award for female vocalist of the year, beating out Lambert, Musgraves, Moroney and Wilson for the honor.

"I have so much love and respect for every single person and every single woman in this category," she said while accepting the award. "This is what I have lived and breathed not only just the past seven years that I moved to Nashville, but genuinely my whole entire life. I haven’t wanted to do another thing. There wasn’t anything on my heart. I never had a plan B. I was never gonna have a plan b. If I was still playing cover gigs with a tip jar out in front of me for four hours I’d still be doing this."
Langley won female vocalist of the year. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

Rising star Langley led the pack with 9 nominations, tying Lainey Wilson and Lambert's all-time record for the most nods by a female artist in a single year. Her win for single of the year left Taylor Swift going home empty-handed tonight, which didn't stop Taylor Swift from cheering for her as she went up to accept the award.
Swift made her big return to the CMA Awards – after last attending in 2016. Her single, "I Knew It, I Knew You," is nominated for single of the year.
The singer took the stage to perform at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years, starting her performance with her nominated song, before transitioning into one of her classic hits, "Our Song."
Lambert also had a moment on stage with Kacey Musgraves, when the two sang their hit duet, "Horses and Divorces," from Musgraves' latest album, "Middle of Nowhere."
Taylor Swift and Ella Langley both have big nights at the 2026 CMA Awards. (Getty Images)
The song references the rumored feud between the two singers, with them patching things up earlier this year.
Zach Top honored veteran and military families, bringing one on stage and surprising them with the return of their son from service.

In addition to her performance with Musgraves, Lambert took the stage once again with Langley to sing their song, "Snakeskin Boots" for the first time on television. The two matched in their versions of brown dresses with snakeskin print and fringe as they commanded the stage during their performance.
Lambert and Langley sang their song together on stage. (Michael Buckner/Billboard via Getty Images)

Brooks & Dunn won vocal duo of the year for the 17th time in a row at this year’s award show. In addition, the duo also received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award, which was presented to them by Swift.
Prior to Swift handing them the award, Luke Bryan took to the stage alongside Brothers Osborne, HARDY, Marcus King and Halestorm to pay tribute to the iconic duo.
WATCH: Miranda Lambert poses with her CMA Awards following her wins

Little Big Town announced Chris Stapleton as the winner of male vocalist of the year. The musician took the stage earlier in the evening with both Mumford & Sons to sing "Here" and Stephen Wilson Jr. to sing, "I’m a Song."
Chris Stapleton won male vocalist of the year at the CMA Awards. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)
During his speech he encouraged fans to follow their dreams, and dedicated the award to his mother, who died last year around this time.
"She always told me that I could be whatever I wanted to be, and turns out that was true," he said.

Lady A introduced Tim McGraw to the stage to perform, "Don’t Take the Girl" for the first time on the CMA stage, as he is one of the Country Music Hall of Fame inductees this year. It was an intimate performance with the majority of the stage lights turned off save for a few spotlights behind him.
Musgraves and Lambert performed "Horses and Divorces" at the award show. (Frank Micelotta/The Walt Disney Company via Getty Images)
Wilson returned to host the event for the third consecutive time, her second solo. Wilson is also nominated for entertainer of the year, which she won in 2023 and 2025.
She also took to the stage during the show to perform her hit song, "Just A Woman."

Megan Moroney blew fans away while strumming on her pink guitar as she sang "Beautiful Things" into her pink microphone. During her performance, fans surrounding the stage held up pink roses, while everyone in the arena swayed to the beat as with their flashlights lighting up the crowd.
Moroney sang into a pink microphone as she strummed a pink guitar. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

Tucker Wetmore got the crowd pumped with his performance of "Who Told You That," encouraging the crowd to get up and dance. While singing, he enthusiastically played the piano which was surrounded by a circle of fire on the stage.

The show began with a tribute to Dolly Parton. Parton was one of the most decorated figures in CMA Awards history, earning 45 nominations and winning 10 trophies over her career, including entertainer of the year in 1978, two female vocalist of the year awards, and the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award in 2016.
Wilson performing during the show. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)
Beyond her wins, she also helped define the telecast itself, famously co-hosting the ceremony in 1988 and returning in 2019 to co-host alongside Carrie Underwood and Reba McEntire.
'GOD HAS BEEN SO GOOD TO ME': ELLA LANGLEY REACTS TO INCREDIBLE NINE CMA AWARDS NOMINATIONS
Parton died on August 25, 2026, at age 80 in Nashville following a brief, private battle with cancer, roughly a year and a half after the passing of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean.
Dolly Parton was honored at the 2026 CMA Awards on Wednesday night. (Getty Images)

title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in picking Robert Pattinson as James Bond
summary: Jeff Bezos says Robert Pattinson's fame initially worked against him in the James Bond casting until old-fashioned screen tests made it obvious.
story: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said the team was ‘slightly biased a little against’ Robert Pattinson because of his fame before screen tests made it ‘so obvious.’
When it came to naming Robert Pattinson the next James Bond, Jeff Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in the selection process.

During an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference Tuesday, the Amazon founder opened up about the casting process and said the team initially considered choosing a lesser-known actor.

"Yes, I was heavily involved. We ran a really tight process, and we made the final decision on Friday. We down selected. There were a big group initially. We down selected to five finalists," Bezos said, according to The Associated Press.
ROBERT PATTINSON’S JAMES BOND CASTING COULD BRING 'DARKER,' 'MOODIER' TWIST AS FANS CRAVE CLASSIC 007: EXPERT
Jeff Bezos was "heavily involved" in Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond. (Getty Images)

"And then we did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists, and it was — it was really interesting, you know? Full costume, real sets, other actors with them. We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists. And then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all those screen tests and reviewing all that."
While Bezos said all the other actors were "extraordinarily talented," there was something about Pattinson.
WATCH: Jeff Bezos was ‘heavily involved’ in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond
ROBERT PATTINSON IS THE NEW JAMES BOND; CAN HE BECOME THE HERO THE WEST NEEDS?
"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performances," Bezos said.

"And it was kind of immediately undebated. Denis, the director, we all sort of gravitated. ... By the way, initially, I would say we were slightly biased a little against him just because he’s already so famous. We sort of thought maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown. But in the screening test, it was so obvious. He is James Bond."
Robert Pattinson will portray the next James Bond.  (Stephane Cardinale/Corbis)
The news of Pattinson's casting was announced Monday.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said in a statement.

story: 2025 ACM Awards host Reba McEntire wore a black suit while she posed for a group photo on the red carpet. Her boyfriend, Rex Linn, stood back while his leading lady had her moment.
Glen Powell is cracking beers and throwing on cowboy boots in his upcoming comedy, "The Comeback King."

The first trailer, which debuted Nov. 18, offered fans a glimpse of Powell as Aubrey King, a country music superstar whose career comes crashing down after a public breakup with his pop star girlfriend Missy, played by "Outer Banks" star Madelyn Cline.
King discovers Missy is cheating on him, but she goes on to make a breakup anthem that makes it seem like he was unfaithful.

The comedy features appearances from some of country music's biggest names, including Reba McEntire, Miranda Lambert, Jelly Roll, Brad Paisley, Chris Stapleton, Luke Bryan and Shaboozey. In one memorable trailer moment, McEntire's character confronts Powell after he accidentally punches her during an altercation.

The first trailer for "The Comeback King," starring Glen Powell, was released Nov. 18. (Michael Tran/AFP via Getty Images)
