title: Healthy runner suffers sudden stroke at 27 as doctors discover possible cause
summary: Patrick Mascoli was running 40 miles a week when a stroke struck at 27. Doctors found a patent foramen ovale that likely sent a clot to his brain.
story: Patrick Mascoli, an engineer and fitness enthusiast, shares the story of the sudden stroke that sidelined him, and the possible cause that doctors uncovered.
As stroke rates continue to rise among young adults, one Boston man is sharing his experience of a life-threatening event at just 27 years old.

Patrick Mascoli, an engineer and fitness enthusiast, was regularly running 40 miles a week at the time of his medical emergency. Beyond a history of migraines, there were no obvious symptoms or warning signs, he shared with Fox News Digital.
On a Sunday in July 2024, Mascoli went for a 10-mile run and headed to the gym for a lifting session. As he was changing alone in the locker room, something felt suddenly wrong.
STROKES NEARLY DOUBLE AMONG ADULTS UNDER A CERTAIN AGE IN DISTURBING TREND
"It just felt like a bomb went off my head," he shared with Fox News Digital. "The right side of my brain just felt like a severe burning sensation, a lot of pain. And that came out of nowhere."
At first, Mascoli assumed it was related to blood pressure-related fainting episodes he’d had when he was younger, but then his vision grew blurrier and the pain intensified.
Patrick Mascoli, pictured at left with his father after his life-threatening stroke at just 27 years old in 2024, ran in the Chicago Marathon (right) in October 2026. (Patrick Mascoli)
"This wasn’t something I had ever experienced before," he said.
When Mascoli tried to stand up and step forward, his leg moved to the right instead, sending him into the wall.

"No matter what I was telling my body to do, it just wasn’t working," he said. "My legs just went in completely opposite directions of the way that I wanted them to. And my vision was a complete swirling mess."
WHAT TO DO IF SOMEONE IS HAVING A STROKE, AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALED DEBATE-NIGHT FEARS
Mascoli managed to text his sister before collapsing again. As his sister drove to the gym, he lay on the floor, repeatedly vomiting, unable to control his legs and struggling to see.
Stroke briefly crossed his mind, he said, but his age and fitness level made him dismiss it.
"I thought a stroke was something that happens to someone who is elderly or has other pre-existing conditions," Mascoli said. "And in my mind, I’m like, ‘I don’t fit that.’"

In October 2026, Mascoli completed the Chicago Marathon as part of Team Abbott, the company that made his heart implant. He is pictured at right with his girlfriend, Christine Bonarrigo. (Patrick Mascoli)
When his sister arrived, she found Mascoli on the bathroom floor of the gym, drenched in sweat, and called 911.

First responders initially suspected dehydration because Mascoli was young, appeared healthy and had just run in the heat. He received IV fluids, but there was no improvement, he shared. Clinicians also treated him for suspected vertigo, but that didn’t relieve the symptoms.
EVEN OCCASIONAL MARIJUANA USE LINKED TO HIGHER STROKE RISK, STUDY FINDS
Clinicians at Boston Medical Center later identified the stroke on a CT scan and confirmed it with an MRI, according to Mascoli.
The next morning, Mascoli’s head pain had subsided, but he still had significant movement problems, particularly on his right side, which he described as "completely useless."
"No matter what I was telling my body to do, it just wasn’t working."
He spent a few days in the hospital, during which he slowly began walking again with the use of a walker.
The diagnosis left Mascoli fearful about his future. "It was very jarring and terrifying," he said.
Searching for answers
Once the stroke was identified, Mascoli’s care team investigated possible causes. He underwent extensive blood testing for clotting disorders and other conditions, without clear answers.
A heart ultrasound using tiny bubbles injected into a vein revealed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) — an opening between the heart’s upper chambers that normally closes shortly after birth.

"In most people, it closes shortly after birth – but in others, it does not shut completely," Dr. Dheeraj Khurana, chief of cardiology at Episcopal Health Services in New York, told Fox News Digital. Khurana did not treat Mascoli.
"In rare cases, a blood clot passes through this opening, travels to the brain and causes a stroke," Khurana said.
Mascoli’s doctors considered the opening the likely route by which a clot reached his brain.
Mascoli is pictured with the entire Abbott running team prior to the Chicago Marathon. (Patrick Mascoli)
Most people with the opening experience no related health problems, according to the American Stroke Association.

In younger stroke patients who lack common risk factors and whose initial tests reveal no clear cause, doctors may look for a PFO using an ultrasound of the heart called an echocardiogram, Khurana said.
SILENT HEART THREAT FOUND IN ADULTS UNDER 30 WITH NO KNOWN CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE
Mascoli does have a lingering uncertainty about why a clot formed in the first place.
"I had none of the genetic predispositions to it. I had no clear physical issues that were causing it. So that is a little bit of a mystery," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
About a month after the stroke, Mascoli underwent a catheter procedure to close the opening in his heart, using an Abbott device that resembled a mesh, double-sided umbrella.
He said his cardiologist’s reassurance that the suspected pathway had been addressed helped ease his fears.

Although his mobility has improved with therapy, Mascoli said he still has lingering difficulty with fine motor skills. "I was very hard on myself, and I still get mad if my hands are shaking and my writing looks bad."
Source of motivation
Returning to running brought its own anxiety. Before the stroke, Mascoli said he would head out for miles without tracking his distance, but afterward, he worried about getting stranded.
"I need to know how far I’m going because I don’t want to be too far away and have something happen," he recalled thinking.
During his recovery, Mascoli’s girlfriend gave him a fitness watch and encouraged him to start racing.
"It was something that kept me motivated, because I knew it was helping me both physically and mentally," he said.

Anyone experiencing sudden loss of balance, vision changes, face drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking should call 911 immediately, regardless of age or fitness level, according to the American Stroke Association. (iStock)
In October 2026, Mascoli completed the Chicago Marathon as part of Team Abbott, representing the company that made his heart implant.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
After finishing, he listened to an emotional voice message from his sister, who had helped rescue him at the gym.
"She was the one who saved me, so it meant a lot to me," he said.

Factors that may raise stroke risk in younger adults include high blood pressure, smoking, unhealthy cholesterol levels, clotting disorders, certain heart conditions and tears in the arteries supplying the brain. (iStock)

To others who have experienced health emergencies, Mascoli urged them to be patient with themselves and to not let the traumatic event define them, emphasizing that recovery looks different for everyone.
"Just take as many steps as you can," he said. "It might not be running a marathon. It doesn’t need to be this big thing."
Risks, symptoms and prevention

Factors that may raise stroke risk in younger adults include high blood pressure, smoking, unhealthy cholesterol levels, clotting disorders, certain heart conditions and tears in the arteries supplying the brain, Khurana said.

"Younger adults with stroke may experience dizziness, altered mental status, vomiting and headaches, which they can easily mistake for exhaustion, especially after exercise or migraine," he told Fox News Digital.
"I had none of the genetic predispositions to it. I had no clear physical issues that were causing it."
"Other common symptoms include visual disturbances, speech problems, weakness, lethargy or seizures."
Dr. Sean Levchuck, chair of pediatric cardiology at St. Francis Hospital & Heart Center in New York, shared some general best practices for young adults to prevent a first stroke.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Young, active adults should stay active and exercise. Following strenuous activity, fluid replacement is necessary," he advised.
The cardiologist also recommends avoiding smoking and tobacco products.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Anyone experiencing sudden loss of balance, vision changes, face drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking should call 911 immediately, regardless of age or fitness level, according to the American Stroke Association.

title: Highly contagious bird flu detected in Wisconsin as officials euthanize infected flock
summary: Wisconsin officials euthanized a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County after confirming a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in the birds.
story: Wisconsin officials confirmed a highly contagious bird flu outbreak in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County, prompting the depopulation of affected birds and renewed warnings to livestock owners.

A highly contagious strain of bird flu has struck a backyard poultry flock in Wisconsin, prompting officials to euthanize the birds amid ongoing concerns about the spread of the potentially deadly disease.
The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) confirmed Thursday a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County.
Officials did not specify how the flock became infected.
DATCP said all birds on the property were euthanized and will not enter the food system.
H5N1 BIRD FLU CONFIRMED IN AUSTRALIA FOR THE FIRST TIME, MEANING VIRUS HAS NOW REACHED EVERY CONTINENT

Wisconsin agriculture officials confirmed an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County, prompting the depopulation of birds on the affected property. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
HPAI, a highly contagious virus that is often fatal to domestic poultry, has circulated among wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021, according to DATCP.
The disease is caused by influenza type A viruses and can vary in severity depending on the strain and affected species.
The virus can spread through contact with infected birds, wild birds or their droppings, as well as contaminated equipment or clothing worn by people working with the animals, according to DATCP.
JD VANCE INSTALLS CUSTOM CHICKEN COOP AT NAVAL OBSERVATORY AND WILL PERSONALLY CARE FOR BIRDS

A highly contagious strain of bird flu was detected in a backyard poultry flock in Wisconsin, according to the state's Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection. (Bernadett Szabo/Reuters)
When HPAI is confirmed in a backyard poultry flock, officials may establish a 10-kilometer surveillance zone, though surrounding poultry premises would not face movement restrictions.

DATCP urged livestock owners to take precautions to protect their flocks and herds, including washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals and separating new additions for at least 30 days.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Wisconsin officials confirmed a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in Rusk County, where birds on the affected property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. (Tiksa Negeri/Reuters)
The agency also recommended that poultry owners keep their birds indoors when possible.

title: Republicans hold lone Alaska House seat despite losing Senate, governor races
summary: Rep. Nick Begich won re-election to Alaska's lone House seat after ranked-choice tabulation, a rare Republican bright spot in a Democratic wave.
story: ‘Fox News @ Night’ anchor Trace Gallagher reports on Democrat Mary Peltola defeating GOP nominee Dan Sullivan in the Alaska U.S. Senate race, flipping the ninth GOP-held seat.
Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, won re-election to Alaska’s lone House seat Wednesday, surviving a Democratic wave that flipped both the Senate seat and the governor’s mansion.

Begich, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated independent challenger Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher backed by the Alaska Democratic Party, following the state’s ranked-choice voting tabulation.

Begich’s victory, called at 9:27 p.m. ET on Wednesday – more than two weeks after Election Day – stood in sharp contrast to the rest of Alaska’s top-of-the-ticket results, where voters handed Democrats major breakthroughs despite Trump winning the state by 13% in 2024.
HUNDREDS OF SUBPOENAS FLY IN DOJ’S ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE AS DEMOCRAT PELTOLA DECLARED WINNER IN ALASKA
Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, continues to show political strength in the state that has flipped Democratic in this midterm election cycle. (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The race was among the final House contests called nationally after the Nov. 3 general election, offering a rare bright spot for Republicans in a midterm cycle that saw Democrats seize control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats thus far hold a 257-172 majority in the House, having flipped 46 seats to just three for Republicans. There are three races that remain too close to call.

"This process requires engagement, and the perspectives brought forward during the campaign added value for Alaskans as they made important decisions about their vote in this race," Begich said in a statement after his victory.
Hill, who campaigned on lowering costs, curbing big money in politics and pushing back against billionaires, said he called Begich to concede and congratulate him.
"I wished him well as he continues representing Alaska in Congress, because all Alaskans have a stake in his success," Hill said in a statement.
ALASKA DEM PELTOLA DEFEATS SULLIVAN, FLIPPING 9TH GOP SENATE SEAT AFTER 'DECOY DAN' UPROAR

One day before Begich’s race was called, Democrat Mary Peltola unseated second-term Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. Peltola — who previously represented Alaska in the U.S. House before losing to Begich in 2024 — became the first Alaska native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state in nearly two decades. Her victory cemented a 56-44 Democratic Senate majority, the party's largest since 2009.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola wrote on X.

Democrats also secured the Alaska governor’s office for the first time in nearly 30 years, with Democrat Jonathan S. Kreiss-Tomkins winning the open-seat race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

Throughout the House campaign, Begich pitched himself as an effective advocate aligned with Trump’s push to expand oil, gas and resource development in Alaska. But the final stretch of the race was overshadowed by controversy surrounding Democrat Eric Hafner, a perennial candidate with no ties to Alaska who is currently serving a sentence in a federal prison in New York following a 2022 conviction for threatening to kill judges, police officers and others.
PELTOLA SAYS ALASKA ‘VOTED FOR CHANGE’ IN SENATE RACE

Hafner, whose state election booklet biography made no mention of his incarceration, captured nearly 8% of the first-round vote. In the closing weeks of the race, Hill’s campaign distributed stickers and yard signs branding Hafner a "fake ‘Democrat,’" while state party officials spent thousands of dollars on text messages to clarify that Hill was the party’s endorsed candidate after mysterious, unsourced texts circulated promoting Hafner.

Hafner’s mother, Carol "Kitty" Hafner — who also lacks ties to Alaska and finished sixth in the state's August Senate primary — dismissed claims that her son was recruited as a spoiler, writing in an email to The Associated Press that his runs have been "entirely independent of any influencers" and adding, "Tell President Trump to Pardon Eric Hafner!"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Controversy over alleged ballot spoilers also marked the Senate race, where independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan Jr. drew suspicion due to sharing a name with the Republican incumbent. title: China blocks Bloomberg reporter from Trump-Putin-Xi meeting over question to Trump
summary: Chinese officials barred Bloomberg's Annmarie Hordern from the meeting of President Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin after her earlier question.
story: A historic trilateral meeting takes place as President Donald Trump holds talks with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, China, to address key global issues. Fox News' Bill Melugin delivers updates from Shenzhen, while American Strategy Group president Brian Kennedy joins to analyze the geopolitical significance of these high-stakes discussions.

Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin after she asked a question during an earlier bilateral session.

The clash over press access unfolded on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China, where the three leaders gathered for their first-ever three-way meeting to discuss nuclear arms control, trade and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Despite a push from the White House to get her admitted, Chinese officials refused to budge on barring Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern from the room.
Hordern was blocked after she called out a question to Trump during his earlier one-on-one meeting with Xi: "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?"
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

A second reporter also started to ask a question during the bilateral session but was shushed by Chinese officials. Beijing subsequently passed along a message to the U.S. travel pool warning that yelling questions is considered "extremely rude" and that journalists would be pulled from the room if they did so.

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity surrounding the issue, said Chinese officials insisted Hordern not be allowed into the trilateral meeting even as the White House advocated for her inclusion.

President Donald Trump, left, speaks during a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Andres Martinez Casares/Pool Photo via AP)
TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

The dispute over press rules stood out alongside the friendly tone Trump sought to project toward both leaders during the summit. Trump praised his friendship with Xi, who greeted Air Force One on the tarmac Wednesday with a one-armed hug and called Putin "my friend" ahead of a separate 40-minute sit-down.
Tensions over artificial intelligence, however, still hung over the meetings.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump's ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped give China access to Nvidia's advanced computer chips used to develop AI models. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.
Fox News’ Kaitlin Sprague and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Democrats could enter congressional majority in a government shutdown
summary: House Republicans on Capitol Hill worry Democrats' post-midterm clout could trigger another government shutdown ahead of the Dec. 11 funding deadline.
story: Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen floated using a government shutdown threat to end the war in Iran during an interview on Thursday.
There's nonzero chance Democrats could kick off their newfound dominance on Capitol Hill with another government shutdown.

Several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they were worried about Democrats in both chambers making unreasonable and highly partisan demands ahead of the Dec. 11, 2026, federal funding deadline, potentially paralyzing the U.S. government until a deal could be reached.
"I’m concerned," Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. "I would say it is on my threat button, as a SEAL, it’s a five-meter target."
Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., suggested Democrats' recent midterm victories would give them the confidence to allow a shutdown to happen.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS DODGED A FALL SHUTDOWN, BUT THE REAL FIGHT LOOMS

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., sued President Donald Trump and his administration for the president's mail-in balloting executive order. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"I’m very worried about it. Unfortunately, the Democrat tactics of shutting down the government worked for them politically, so I’m afraid they’re going to go back to their winning playbook," he said.
SCHUMER, JEFFRIES SIDESTEP QUESTIONS ON NUKING FILIBUSTER, LAUNCHING ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER BLUE WAVE

Congress opted to delay the government funding fight until after the midterm elections, passing a simple extension of fiscal year (FY) 2026 spending levels called a continuing resolution (CR) from the beginning of FY 2027 on Oct. 1 through Dec. 11.
Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital expressed varying levels of optimism about whether they could hash out a budget for FY 2027 before the end of the year.
SENATE REPUBLICANS PLAN 54-DAY BLITZ TO PUSH TRUMP'S AGENDA BEFORE DEMOCRATS SEIZE POWER
"What we should get done is move every appropriation's bill we can," said Rep. Mark Messmer, R-Ind.
Asked about whether he's concerned about a shutdown, he said, "That's up to the Democrats in the Senate."
Most people who spoke with Fox News Digital said they believe another CR extending early into 2028 is the most likely path, which would give Democrats more control over writing it.
Rep. Mike Haridopolos leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on June 10, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
But for Democrats, unsurprisingly, Republicans are to blame.
CHRIS VAN HOLLEN FLOATS USING GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN THREAT TO FORCE TRUMP TO END IRAN WAR

"I wanted to finish the bills by the end of the year. We had the opportunity to do that, and the Republican side of the Senate has held out," Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said.
DeLauro said last week she wanted to see a short-term CR extending only as far as March.
MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS

She suggested, however, that the Iran war could be a sticking point for Democrats down the line, telling reporters, "I can just say that we're not going to be doing billions of dollars for a war of choice."
Senate Democrats are pushing for guardrails on funding for the Iran war, and Republicans are already worried that they’ll shutter the government if they don’t get what they want.

"That is playing with fire for sure," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told Fox News Digital. "It's one thing to pound your chest and talk about it. It's another thing to put America's military men and women in jeopardy."

U.S. House Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro talks to reporters following a House Democratic caucus meeting at the Capitol Sept. 29, 2025, in Washington. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

A trio of Senate Democrats, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., are pushing an amendment to a forthcoming bill that would stymie funds from helping the war effort, something that Republicans largely won’t support.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is running to topple Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., as Democratic leader, is supportive of the effort.
"For starters, we need a clear amendment that says we can't spend money on offensive operations because we do need to end the war, but we also need to bring down costs now," Van Hollen said.

title: Trump's historic summit with Xi, Putin marks diplomatic milestone, but breakthroughs remain elusive
summary: Donald Trump declares the U.S., China and Russia are "really making history" as nuclear arms reduction and an end to the Ukraine war anchor the summit.
story: The leaders of the United States, Russia and China gathered in Shenzhen for historic three-way talks, emphasizing the importance of continued diplomacy and maintaining open dialogue despite longstanding differences.

President Donald Trump joined the leaders of China and Russia Thursday for an unprecedented three-way summit, marking a historic moment in global diplomacy as the three powers discussed nuclear arms reductions, the war in Ukraine and global security without announcing a major breakthrough.

The unprecedented three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin underscored the leaders' commitment to continued diplomacy, with Trump emphasizing the importance of maintaining dialogue among rival nuclear powers.

Trump left the trilateral meeting, which lasted more than an hour, around 5 a.m. ET and headed to the airport. He is not expected to deliver public remarks before flying back to Washington, Fox News reported.
"We are really making history," Trump declared during the meeting in Shenzhen, China, as he sought to cast the gathering itself as a diplomatic achievement.
CHINA WATCHDOG WARNS TRUMP FACES ‘2-ON-1’ SHOWDOWN WITH XI, PUTIN AS TAIWAN RISKS MOUNT
The three leaders are meeting on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China from November 18–19. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
The three leaders sat down at a roundtable just after 3 a.m. ET, roughly two hours behind schedule.
Trump argued that bringing the three leaders together offered an opportunity to address issues that had long divided their countries.
"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump said. "But no problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them."
"Together we are choosing a different course," he added.
Ahead of the summit, Trump told Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich that he wanted to meet with Xi and Putin together "because they work together, they have a relationship."
Trump argued that previous U.S. policies had helped bring Moscow and Beijing closer together, despite their historically strained relationship.
"They were natural enemies, but because of Obama, not Biden, it was Obama before he drove them together because of energy," Trump said.

Russia and China had a fractured relationship for decades following their split in the 1960s, but energy ties deepened through a major 2014 gas deal signed during Obama's presidency after roughly a decade of negotiations.

President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Xi, who hosted the gathering, called the meeting a "groundbreaking move" and stressed the responsibility of the three powers to maintain global stability. However, no substantial breakthroughs were immediately announced.
"Our positive interaction is not optional, but a must," Xi said through a translator, arguing that the countries must work together to confront global challenges and preserve international peace.

Putin similarly emphasized the countries' shared responsibility for international security, pointing to their status as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council before turning to one of the summit's most pressing issues: the war in Ukraine.
KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including, obviously, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said through a translator.
The Russian president confirmed that Ukraine had been a focus of his earlier bilateral meeting with Trump, saying the discussion took place at the American president's initiative.
UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Mandel NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)
Trump also addressed the conflict directly, saying he believed both sides wanted to bring the fighting to an end.
"I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."
The historic summit followed separate meetings between Trump and the two leaders. Trump met with Putin for approximately 40 minutes before holding a meeting with Xi that lasted more than an hour.
The president also raised the possibility of broader nuclear arms reductions while acknowledging the difficulty of persuading nuclear-armed nations to surrender their weapons.
"It's a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them," Trump said.
KIM JONG UN'S NUCLEAR BUILDUP SPARKS 'SERIOUS CONCERN' AHEAD OF TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT
President Xi Jinping listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation. (Andres Martinez Casares - Pool/Getty Images)

Trump said ahead of the trilateral meeting that the leaders would discuss nuclear proliferation, including Iran, and indicated he would propose ways to protect national sovereignty from international organizations, singling out the International Criminal Court.

Trump held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and Xi earlier in the day, first meeting with the Russian leader at the APEC summit site before traveling to Kylin Villa, a government-owned lakeside resort, for talks with the Chinese president.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SANCTIONS SITTING PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT FOR 'ABUSES OF POWER'

Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands as leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Sergei BOBYLYOV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Trump said his meeting with Putin helped "set the stage" for the trilateral talks and expressed hope that cooperation with China could help end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

"The dialogue between President Putin and President Trump, which the entire world is watching closely, is crucial both to resolving the conflict in Ukraine and to advancing relations between Russia and the United States, including economic cooperation," Special Envoy to the Russian President Kirill Dmitriev told Fox News Digital.

"Both presidents are committed to finding a peaceful solution to the Ukraine conflict. There are, of course, forces in Europe and elsewhere seeking to derail this process, but the importance of this dialogue cannot be overstated," Dmitriev added.

Prior to his meeting with Xi, Trump identified Iran as an area of potential cooperation with Beijing, emphasizing the importance of keeping energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and preventing Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL

Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump ride an escalator ahead of the plenary session during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. "We both feel that very strongly on both points."
TRUMP KICKS OFF HIGH-STAKES ASIA TRIP WITH XI, PUTIN MEETINGS LOOMING ON WORLD STAGE
World leaders pose for a "family photo" during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Speaking on China's own turf amid a fierce technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing, Trump asserted American dominance in artificial intelligence, declaring the U.S. the world leader in "superintelligence" and claiming Americans invented the technology.
"Americans invented. We just invented [superintelligence], and it is unleashing extraordinary prosperity and growth for people all around the globe," Trump said.

Trump described superintelligence as the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution, acknowledging that the technology has "some bad elements" that must be carefully managed while rejecting international efforts to regulate it.
TRUMP CANNOT DETER XI AND PUTIN’S NUCLEAR GOALS WITH A STRATEGY DESIGNED FOR JUST ONE

President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Photo by Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The competition over advanced technology also surfaced in a tense moment involving the press, when a Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after questioning Trump about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an earlier bilateral session.

The reporter had asked Trump, "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?" Chinese officials blocked her access to the trilateral talks despite efforts by White House officials to have her reinstated, according to a White House pool report.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Supreme Court urged to defang ‘criminal trap’ that has sent Trump officials to prison
summary: Peter Navarro asks the Supreme Court to overturn his contempt of Congress convictions, arguing willfulness could make such prosecutions harder to prove.
story: Abhi Kambli, Navarro's attorney, says a ruling in his favor could curb the 'weaponization' of congressional subpoenas by making contempt convictions harder to secure.

A Trump administration official who served four months in federal prison for defying a congressional subpoena is asking the Supreme Court to overturn his convictions in a case that could raise the bar for criminally prosecuting others who refuse to comply with Congress’s demands.

Peter Navarro, who was a senior trade advisor to President Donald Trump during his first administration, filed a petition with the Supreme Court last month. Navarro currently serves in the Trump administration as senior counselor for trade and manufacturing. He was convicted in 2023 on two counts of contempt of Congress stemming from his refusal to provide testimony and documents to the Democratic-led House Jan. 6 committee on the grounds that he believed he was barred by executive privilege.
If the justices take the case, they could make it harder to convict someone for defying a congressional subpoena by requiring proof that the person knew they were breaking the law.
JUDGE TOSSES CASE AGAINST EX-FBI OFFICIALS ACCUSED OF LYING TO CONGRESS ABOUT HUNTER BIDEN INVESTIGATION

Peter Navarro, White House senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, during a television interview at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Monday, July 7, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Before Navarro’s trial, U. S. District Judge Amit Mehta ruled in August 2023 that he had failed to establish that Trump invoked executive privilege for the subpoena, barring him from relying on that claim as a defense. After serving his sentence, Navarro appealed his conviction to the U. S. Court of Appeals for the D. C. Circuit, which ruled that a person violates federal law by refusing to comply with a subpoena "even if he subjectively and mistakenly believed his default was lawful. "
The three-judge panel ruled that only the president can invoke executive privilege under Article II, and Trump never granted Navarro protection.

"Dr. Navarro claimed executive privilege before even seeing the subpoena and refused to turn over documents, appear for his deposition, or engage with the Select Committee’s efforts to accommodate his privilege claim," the court wrote.
"A court, in other words, cannot simply take a defendant at his word that the President invoked privilege because doing so would impermissibly tangle separation-of-powers lines."

But Abhishek Kambli, counsel for Navarro, argued the D.C. Circuit misinterpreted the statute, pointing to United States v. Murdock, a 1933 Supreme Court ruling that a taxpayer’s sincere but mistaken belief that the Constitution protected his refusal to answer investigators’ questions mattered in determining whether he acted "willfully."

"We absolutely believe that we are correct on the law on this, because Congress chose to use the word willful when it put this statute together, and there's no reason to believe that willful applies any differently in this context than it has in just about every other one, but it would have the added effect of toning down lawfare and weaponization if we were to succeed," Kambli told Fox News Digital.

The House voted to hold Navarro in contempt for failing to comply with a subpoena, but Kambli argued the Jan. 6 committee bypassed the negotiations traditionally used to resolve disputes involving executive branch officials.
WHITE HOUSE LAWYER'S HARDBALL WARNING TO DEMS HAS LEGAL EXPERTS ON BOTH SIDES QUESTIONING ONE KEY THREAT

U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House Office Building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"When it comes to executive branch officials, there was an accommodation process where they would negotiate terms of the appearance of the witness that's an executive branch official, and then determined whether executive privilege applies or not," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "What happened with the J-6 committee is that they short-circuited a lot of that and sent people straight to getting prosecuted and indicted."
Kambli said a Supreme Court ruling in Navarro's favor could help "tone down the weaponization that could potentially occur" once Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

"What would happen is that if we were to win and the correct mental state is required to prove someone violated this law and get convicted and sent to jail, you would have fewer prosecutions for contempt of Congress because they're going to be much harder to prove," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "And what will happen is that there's less of an opportunity to wield a congressional subpoena in a weaponized manner rather than just through a legitimate legislative purpose, which Congress is limited to traditionally."

Navarro’s lawyers filed the petition a week before Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., called for an investigation of alleged Trump administration corruption, saying cases targeting those who "enabled" the president could send a "deterrence message" to young people considering administration jobs.

Following Democrats’ wins in the 2026 midterm elections, lawmakers took to social media to vow investigations into Trump officials, with House Oversight Committee ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., posting on X, "LAWYER UP." However, Republicans still control both chambers of Congress until Democrats take control in January 2027.

"We can't keep this up where people are utilizing lawfare and other weaponization tactics to harm their political opponents, so we think that this petition would protect everyone in the long term and allow our politics to be better, because we're not constantly trying to utilize congressional subpoenas as a way to indict people," Kambli told Fox News Digital.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Steve Bannon speaks at the National Conservatism Conference in Washington D.C., Sept. 3, 2025. (Photo by Dominic Gwinn / Middle East Images via AFP)

Mike Davis, a conservative lawyer and founder and president of the Article III Project, which filed an amicus brief supporting the petition, said the Supreme Court must take this case up to end "lawfare."

"Democrats weaponized Congress to throw Peter Navarro in prison for standing up for President Trump’s executive privilege in good faith," Davis said. "The D.C. Circuit then ruled that good faith is no defense to contempt of Congress, and that turns every congressional subpoena into a criminal trap. It tears up more than two centuries of negotiation between the co-equal branches."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The petition from Navarro comes after the Supreme Court vacated the ruling against Steve Bannon. The former Trump White House strategist served four months in federal prison in 2024 after being convicted of two counts of contempt of Congress for defying a subpoena from the House Jan. 6 committee. In April 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit’s decision in his case and sent it back for further proceedings following the Justice Department's motion to dismiss his indictment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Trump's China trip: Historic Xi-Putin talks, 'superintelligence' boast and other top moments
summary: President Donald Trump declared the U.S. the world leader in "superintelligence" at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, staking a tech claim amid the AI rivalry.
story: President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit featured an elaborate welcome, warm exchanges with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and a declaration of American technological dominance on Chinese soil.

The gathering in Shenzhen culminated in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, with nuclear arms reductions and the war in Ukraine among the issues on the table.
Here are some of the standout moments from Trump's visit.
XI BREAKS PROTOCOL TO PERSONALLY WELCOME TRUMP AHEAD OF HISTORIC TRILATERAL SUMMIT AND MORE TOP HEADLINES
Trump touts US 'superintelligence' on China's turf
Trump declared the United States the world leader in "superintelligence" during remarks at the summit Thursday, making the assertion in one of China's major technology hubs.
"The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution," Trump told APEC leaders.
The remarks came as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors.
Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic three-way talks

Trump joined Xi and Putin for the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia just after 3 a.m. ET, calling the gathering an opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons and address global conflicts.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth," Trump said.
The president also said he had held extensive discussions with Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China November 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
"I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."

Trump also raised preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons and said he would propose ways for the three countries to protect their sovereignty from the International Criminal Court, which he accused of exceeding its jurisdiction.

A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking Trump during his bilateral with Xi whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been "disloyal to the United States," according to White House pool reports. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was considered extremely rude and that reporters could be removed for doing so, despite White House efforts to secure the Bloomberg reporter's access.
Xi rolls out red carpet for Trump
Xi personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen Wednesday, meeting the president at the foot of the aircraft stairs in an elaborate welcome.
The two exchanged greetings before standing together for the American and Chinese national anthems. A military flyover followed, with five jets leaving trails of colored smoke overhead.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
Trump later praised the reception as a display of "great respect."

U.S. President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by President of the People's Republic of China Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. Trump is visiting China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping November 18–19. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin greet each other before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)
Trump strikes warm tone with Xi, Putin
Trump offered warm words for both Xi and Putin during the summit, praising his personal relationship with the Chinese leader and referring to the Russian president as a "friend."

title: Trump's massive DC triumphal arch project dealt another blow by federal judge
summary: A federal judge extended her order blocking construction of President Donald Trump's triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., putting the project on hold until at least Dec. 3.
story: A federal judge extended the construction halt on President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., until at least Dec. 3, prompting criticism from the White House amid ongoing legal challenges.

President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington in Washington, D.C., was dealt another blow Wednesday when a federal judge extended an order blocking construction until at least early December.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her initial Nov. 5 temporary restraining order blocking construction of the arch for another 14 days, delaying progress on the structure until at least Dec. 3.
The extension comes as Chutkan's original order was set to expire Thursday.
The judge said the extension would give her additional time to consider lawsuits filed by the District of Columbia and Virginia seeking a longer-term injunction against the project.
MULTIPLE KENNEDY FAMILY MEMBERS SEEK TO JOIN LEGAL BATTLE AGAINST TRUMP'S TRIUMPHAL ARCH

President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., faces another legal setback after a federal judge extended an order blocking construction until at least Dec. 3. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

The order marks the latest setback for one of the president's major projects in the nation's capital. Inspired by Paris' Arc de Triomphe, the proposed monument would stand near the Memorial Bridge, which connects Arlington National Cemetery to Washington, D.C.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, the White House criticized the order, saying the project was being undercut by an "activist district court."
"The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said.
"We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds," he added.
EXCAVATION SET TO BEGIN ON TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 250-FOOT TRIUMPHAL ARCH AMID LEGAL BATTLE
Above is the updated rendering of the proposed United States Triumphal Arch, showing the 250-foot monument without the four lion statues that appeared in earlier designs. (Harrison Design)
Chutkan issued the temporary restraining order earlier this month just hours after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the project.
The approval had cleared the way for construction to begin before the court intervened.
Trump has previously said the triumphal arch would be converted into a military complex capable of rapidly deploying large numbers of drones, with snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas.
He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition."
The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

A view of Columbia Island, the site of President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)
Last week, nine members of the Kennedy family also sought to stop the project, saying it would obstruct views and cast shadows over their relatives' grave sites at Arlington National Cemetery.
Reuters contributed to this report.

title: 'You will regret it': Angry resident confronts Democratic mayor during chaotic council meeting
summary: Video captured a California immigration activist threatening to reveal Mayor Kevin McCarty's home address at a Sacramento City Council meeting after becoming angry with city policies.
story: A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos after a resident confronted Mayor Kevin McCarty, threatened his political career and attempted to publicly reveal his home address, prompting officials to cut her microphone and recess the meeting. (City of Sacramento via YouTube)

A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos Tuesday after an angry resident threatened the Democratic mayor's political career and attempted to publicly reveal his home address, prompting officials to cut her microphone and temporarily recess the meeting.

Video from Tuesday's City Council livestream reviewed by Fox News Digital showed a woman confronting Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty during the public comment portion of the meeting, warning that protesters would continue disrupting city business if officials failed to address their concerns.
"If you do not vote in our interest again, you will regret it," the woman said. "We protest. We stop things. We shut things down, Kevin. And careers."
The woman then suggested that McCarty's political career had run its course.
MEMPHIS CITY COUNCIL DEVOLVES INTO CHAOS AFTER DATA CENTER MORATORIUM VOTE POSTPONED

A woman warned Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty that he would "regret it" if city officials continued voting against protesters' interests during a heated City Council meeting. (Sacramento City Council livestream)
"It's time for your f---ing career to end," she said, before raising the possibility of his retirement.
As council officials repeatedly attempted to restore order, someone in the audience also urged the angry woman to show decorum.
"F--- your decorum," she responded.
The confrontation escalated further when the woman threatened to disclose the mayor's home address.
"I do not give a f--- about your privacy," she shouted. "Do you want everyone to know your address? Because now I know your address."
Her microphone appeared to be cut as she began reciting what she claimed was the mayor's address, and a council official warned her against disclosing private information.
'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING

A Sacramento City Council meeting descended into chaos on Nov. 17 after a resident confronted Mayor Kevin McCarty and attempted to publicly disclose what she claimed was his home address. (Sacramento City Council livestream)
As shouting erupted in the council chambers, officials called a recess and council members left the dais.
Approximately 20 minutes later, council members returned and resumed public comment. No audience members were removed, The Sacramento Bee reported.

According to the newspaper, the confrontation with the woman, identified by the outlet as a local immigration activist, unfolded amid ongoing tensions over the city's immigration enforcement policies and its cooperation with federal authorities.

Earlier in the meeting, McCarty announced that the council would postpone consideration of a $3.7 million Department of Homeland Security grant agreement amid questions about potential data-sharing provisions.

Tuesday's incident marked the fifth time this year that Sacramento City Council members had recessed a meeting because of audience disruptions, according to The Sacramento Bee. The repeated confrontations have largely stemmed from activists' concerns about immigration enforcement and the city's sanctuary policies, the outlet reported.
DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty faced a heated confrontation during a City Council meeting Tuesday after a resident threatened his political career and attempted to reveal his home address. (Sacramento City Council livestream)
The mayor's office declined to comment on the incident to Fox News Digital.

This week's outburst comes months after Fox News Digital reported that a live microphone captured McCarty and Vice Mayor Karina Talamantes discussing whether disruptive protesters could be barred from future council meetings.

"We should go over this disruptions thing, because if we want to ban somebody in the future, like to take them out, we have to point out specifically," Talamantes was heard saying during the July meeting.
"I know, but the city attorney said we can't do that," McCarty responded.

The woman who confronted McCarty on Tuesday also appeared during the July meeting, when she shouted at the mayor, "Kevin, listen to me. Stop being an a--hole, dude. Listen to your f---ing constituents."
Following the July incident, McCarty told Fox News Digital that council leaders were responsible for ensuring public meetings remained accessible and orderly.

title: Dozens of Army soldiers sign up for unique reenlistment incentive to play Grand Theft Auto VI
summary: The U.S. Army offered Fort Stewart soldiers four-day passes to play "Grand Theft Auto VI" as a reenlistment perk, and 43 of 130 eligible troops took it.
story: Fox News contributors Ben Domenech and Joe Concha discuss the release of the new ‘Grand Theft Auto’ video game and parents' responsibility to monitor household video game consumption during 'Fox & Friends Weekend.'
The U.S. Army turned to one of the year’s most anticipated video games to get soldiers at Fort Stewart, Georgia, talking about reenlisting.
The offer was a four-day pass to play "Grand Theft Auto VI" when it launches Thursday.
The Army said 43 of the 130 eligible soldiers in the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion chose the perk when they reenlisted for two to six more years, Task & Purpose first reported.
NBA PLAYER PREDICTS AMERICAN ATHLETES' PERFORMANCES WILL DIP IN NOVEMBER WHILE THEY PLAY GTA
A poster for the Grand Theft Auto VI video game, which will be released Nov. 19, 2026, is displayed at a GameStop store Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in Colma, Calif. (Jeff Chiu/AP Photo)

"I’m all campaign. I’m all about the heist," Sgt. Jamire Smith, a combat engineer who signed up for six more years in the Army and took the four-day pass, told Task & Purpose. "I think I have a good 24 hours to waste on it."

Smith said he had been close to leaving the Army before leaders in his company and battalion showed him they still needed his skills. He qualified for a roughly $60,000 reenlistment bonus after training to drive heavy breaching vehicles, the outlet reported.
US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT
A sign at the entrance of Fort Stewart in Georgia Aug. 6, 2025. (Mike Stewart)

The battalion offered the pass from Aug. 1 through Nov. 14. The Army said the time off came on top of standard reenlistment incentives, which can include cash bonuses or a choice of duty station depending on a soldier’s eligibility and the Army’s needs.

Staff Sgt. Brittany Wolfer, the battalion’s career counselor, called the perk an "eye grabber." She pitched it to her commander after hearing Sgt. Maj. Celeste R. Spencer, a senior Army career counselor, float the idea on TikTok.

Wolfer said the battalion had gone about eight months without a career counselor before she arrived, and she wanted soldiers nearing a decision about reenlisting to know whom to talk to about their options.
Ads for "Grand Theft Auto VI" in New York City ahead of the game's release. (Richard B. Levine)
The commander had played "Grand Theft Auto 2" and backed the idea, Wolfer told the outlet. Wolfer, a gamer herself, went to basic training the same week "Grand Theft Auto V" came out.

Staff Sgt. Floyd Maxwell, a network systems and communications specialist, signed up for three more years. He told the outlet his father, who died a few months ago, had encouraged him to make a career of the Army. He said the battalion had also given him a sense of family.

"The excitement from this incentive has sparked positive conversations amongst Soldiers to discuss the continuation of their service in the Army," the Army said in a statement. The service said it recognized the 3rd Infantry Division as its top division for retention in 2025.
MIAMI HEAT FINALLY UNVEIL 'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI'-THEMED JERSEYS AND SOCIAL MEDIA IS LOVING THEM
Army barracks in Fort Stewart, . (Stephen Morton/Getty Images)

The game has an Army connection of its own. One of its main characters, Jason Duval, served in the Army before going to work for drug runners in the Florida Keys, according to Rockstar Games. Wolfer had a suggestion for the studio, too. She wants it to put Rocky the Bulldog, the 3rd Infantry Division’s mascot, in the game.
"Grand Theft Auto VI" had already brought in an estimated $1.65 billion from more than 17 million preorders by Wednesday, Forbes reported, citing market research firm Sensor Tower.
MIAMI HEAT UNVEIL VICE CITY COURT FOR 'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI'-THEMED CLASH WITH MILWAUKEE BUCKS
A billboard for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI" is pictured above Hollywood Boulevard Nov. 4, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/AP Photo)
Hours before the U.S. launch, PlayStation warned that a network disruption could make it difficult for some players to launch games or access online features.
Its status page showed the issue was resolved by 2:30 p.m. ET, Axios reported. Rockstar says the game unlocks at midnight local time Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

title: Mullin defends TSA shoes-on policy after congressman calls classified briefing ‘very concerning’
summary: Markwayne Mullin defended the TSA shoe removal policy at a House Homeland Security hearing, telling Rep. Eli Crane the change never put anyone at risk.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended TSA’s shoes-on policy after Rep. Eli Crane said a classified inspector general briefing raised serious concerns.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended letting travelers keep their shoes on at airport checkpoints Wednesday after an Arizona congressman pressed him on why the TSA policy remains in place despite a classified watchdog review.
"We have never put anyone at risk at all," Mullin told Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz., at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing.
Mullin said the department evaluates screening technology daily and that he had personally met with DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari in a secure facility.
"In fact, we addressed three of the four concerns," Mullin said. He said the fourth, in his view, had nothing to do with security.
TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS
Travelers wait in line at a TSA checkpoint at John F. Kennedy International Airport  in New York on May 22, 2026. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Mullin gave no specifics about what DHS had done to address the three concerns or what the fourth involved.
Crane said he had received a classified briefing from the inspector general and called it "very concerning." He asked Mullin to discuss the matter privately.
The exchange put renewed scrutiny on a July 2025 decision by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to end routine shoe removal at TSA checkpoints nationwide.
Travelers move through a TSA security checkpoint at an airport. (iStock)

Noem said at the time that advances in screening technology would allow the agency to speed up lines while maintaining security. TSA officers could still ask travelers to remove their shoes for additional screening.
Within weeks of the change, the inspector general sent DHS and TSA leaders a formal warning about a screening weakness, according to questions entered into the Senate record in July.

Secretary Markwayne Mullin testifies before the House Committee on Homeland Security during a hearing on the department's Fiscal 2027 budget, in Washington, June 3, 2026. (Cliff Owen/AP Photo)

The watchdog issued its final classified report on Nov. 1, 2025. In a March memo reviewed by CBS News, Cuffari said his office was still waiting for the agencies’ formal response after the 90-day deadline had passed.

The Senate record also shows that Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., asked TSA in April to reverse the policy until the screening weakness was addressed. In a May response cited by Cantwell, then-acting TSA Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill said "current intelligence and risk assessments indicate no direct, credible threats related to shoes."

Mullin’s testimony Wednesday left open whether the inspector general had signed off on the steps DHS says it took.

title: Hundreds of subpoenas fly in DOJ’s ‘Decoy Dan’ probe as Democrat Peltola declared winner in Alaska
summary: The DOJ has issued 200 subpoenas in a multi-state criminal probe tied to "Decoy" Dan J. Sullivan's Alaska Senate run, per a law enforcement source.
story: Reacting to a New York Times article, Senator Dan Sullivan details serious allegations of a long-term secret scheme run by Peltola campaign aides. Sullivan expresses strong outrage over reports of focus groups laughing at Alaskans and circulating rumors of hush money, calling on voters to reject what he describes as the most outrageous election cheating scandal in Alaska history.

EXCLUSIVE: The Justice Department has issued more than 200 subpoenas in its criminal investigation into Dan J. Sullivan — "Decoy Dan" — who ran against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, Fox News Digital has learned.

News of the scope of the sprawling criminal probe comes after Democrat Mary Peltola was officially declared the winner of the four-way general election on Tuesday night — two weeks after Election Day. She won 144,302 votes to the incumbent Sullivan's 131,844. A GOP candidate named Gerald Heikes won 6,105 votes, while so-called "Decoy Dan" won 4,760 votes as a non-party affiliated candidate.

A law enforcement source says the criminal case is continuing, and that Peltola being named the winner doesn't change anything from an investigative standpoint. The DOJ's investigation spans multiple states, and there are multiple criminal targets in the case, the source said.
Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, stands in the Senate Subway of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on June 17, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg)
A second source familiar with the investigation confirmed that more than 200 subpoenas have been issued.

Allegations have swirled that Democrats searched for a person with the name Dan Sullivan to run against the incumbent senator of the same name in order to confuse voters and potentially spoil the Republicans' chances of reelection.
TRUMP ADMIN PUTS ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' CONSPIRATORS ON NOTICE IN ALASKA ELECTION SPOILER PROBE
High-profile Democrat attorney Marc Elias, whose law firm represents the Peltola campaign, is among those who received a criminal target letter from the DOJ earlier this month.

The controversy exploded just days before the midterm election day on Nov. 3, 2026, when The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and political operatives outside of Alaska participated in what they called the "ballot composition project," with the goal of recruiting a second Dan Sullivan to enter the race.
MARY PELTOLA TRASHES NEW YORK TIMES REPORT ON DAN SULLIVAN PLOT, CALLING IT A 'DISTRACTION'
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have denied any wrongdoing.
Dan J. Sullivan, who filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)

"Decoy Dan" is a retired teacher from the tiny southeastern Alaskan island town of Petersburg, who had virtually no presence on the campaign trail — even his neighbors reported never seeing campaign materials from him. His campaign raised $35,556.
Peltola, a former state lawmaker, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She was unseated in 2024 by Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska.

Alaska election officials initially moved to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot amid allegations that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters or siphon support from the senator. The candidate denied wrongdoing, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he could remain on the ballot.
The DOJ sued in October to mitigate any "misleading" impact of the newcomer Sullivan.
PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE
Then-Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, smiles in a photo. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump called for Peltola to drop out of the race, and blasted the Democratic Party over the alleged scheme.

"You had the Democrat Party headed up by Elias, their lawyer, who was a bad guy, very bad guy — should go to jail, in my opinion," Trump said on "Fox & Friends" on Election Day. "But you had the Democrat Party look all over Alaska for somebody named Sullivan."

Neither Peltola nor Sullivan's campaigns returned comment requests — and neither did the DSCC. The White House deferred Fox News Digital to the president's earlier comments on the case.

title: Jeffries brushes off opposition from far-left Dems who voted no: 'We’re going to work together'

story: House Democrats are prepared to govern with a robust 260-member majority in the next Congress. The caucus pledges to unite its members, reject MAGA extremism and dramatically lower the high cost of living for everyday Americans.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., brushed off opposition from far-left Democrats during Wednesday's caucus vote, which overwhelmingly nominated him to become the next House speaker.
Speaking after the vote, Jeffries said he expects the incoming Democratic majority to "work together."

FOLLOW THE LEADER: DEMOCRATS FACE PARTY BATTLE AS DIVISIONS DEEPEN
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is poised to become the next House speaker after his nomination by fellow Democrats for the job. (Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)

‘SQUAD’ MEMBER ANNOUNCES ‘MAJORITY PRIORITIES’ INCLUDING REPARATIONS, ABOLISHING ICE AFTER BLUE WAVE
When asked about the dissenting votes, Jeffries said the caucus' election results spoke for themselves.

WHOOPI GOLDBERG LECTURES DEMOCRATS OVER INFIGHTING ABOUT LEADERSHIP, WARNS 'GET YOUR STUFF TOGETHER'

Darializa Avila Chevalier, U.S. Democratic House candidate for New York, speaks at a Get Out The Vote rally at Kings Theater in Brooklyn, N.Y., June 18, 2026, ahead of the state's primary election on June 23. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Jeffries emphasized that the incoming Congress' primary focus should be to "fight MAGA extremism, not each other."
PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP
"To fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people," he added. "And that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on Jan. 3."
Rep.-elect Frederick D. Haynes III, who will succeed Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, explained that he woke up unexpectedly ill Wednesday morning and was unable to vote.

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

title: Protesters heckle Trump's ex-Border Patrol chief offstage after Dem governor condemns College Republican event
summary: Protesters shouted "Immigrants are welcome here" as Gregory Bovino was escorted offstage at Rutgers College Republicans event Mikie Sherrill called "wrong."
story: Video shows protesters heckling former Border Patrol chief Gregory Bovino off the stage at a Rutgers College Republicans event.

Protesters heckled former Trump Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino off stage during a Monday night speech at Rutgers University, hours after New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill called the Rutgers College Republicans’ decision to host him "wrong" and urged the club to reconsider.

Bovino previously criticized Sherrill online, accusing her of prioritizing illegal immigrants over New Jersey residents. After returning to the stage, he called her "Sugar Pop Sherrill" and "Kim Jong Sherrill." Speaking to reporters afterward, he said she wanted to "trounce this freedom of speech," described the "Kim Jong Sherrill" label as "very fitting" and called the governor a "totalitarian." He also told Blaze News that Sherrill had timed her social media comments to "foment violence" against conservatives.

At Monday night’s Rutgers College Republicans event, protesters began shouting within minutes of Bovino taking the stage. Rutgers police escorted him offstage and ordered the hecklers to leave or face arrest, according to local reports. Bovino returned about ten minutes later to resume his remarks and answer questions. Hundreds of protesters also gathered outside.
30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS
Attendees at Greg Bovino's talk at Rutgers shout him down and heckle the former border patrol commander off stage. (FreedomNews.TV)

"What’s so crazy is that you all allowed a Nazi to be here," a protester yelled as the heckling began. Another shouted, "Your fascist death cult is failing!" Video from inside the event captured chants of "Get out of New Jersey!" and "Immigrants are welcome here!" Outside, hundreds of protesters carried images of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed by federal agents in Minneapolis.

Before Bovino’s Monday appearance, Rutgers told Fox News Digital it was committed to protecting freedom of expression and maintaining campus security. The university also said hosting a student-organized event did not constitute an endorsement of the speaker or his views. Rutgers had not responded to Fox News Digital's follow-up request for comment about the disruption by publication.

Hours before Bovino’s speech, Sherrill said in a social media post that she was "deeply disappointed" by the Rutgers College Republicans’ invitation, adding, "Giving him a platform is the wrong decision."

Sherrill said that if the club went ahead with the event, she would ensure the state worked with Rutgers to protect "the safety of everyone and the rights enshrined in our Constitution," and she urged attendees to question Bovino about his record.
SHERRILL COMMITS $20.2M TO DEPORTATION DEFENSE WHILE CONDEMNING RUTGERS OVER BORDER PATROL SPEAKER
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is seen. (Getty Images)
Fox News Digital contacted Sherrill's team for comment on the disruption at Bovino’s event but received no response before publication.

Bovino served as Trump's commander-at-large of the U.S. Border Patrol and oversaw immigration enforcement and deportation operations, including Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis. He was removed from command in January following the shootings of Good and Pretti and retired from the Border Patrol in March.

During the Rutgers College Republicans event, a student asked Bovino about the deaths of Good and Pretti. He clarified that his earlier comment about going "harder" referred to mass deportation operations, not the shootings of Good or Pretti.
