title: 16 Ecuadorian fishermen sue US government, allege drone attack destroyed their boat near the Galápagos
summary: Ecuadorian fishermen allege U.S. drones struck their boat in the Pacific Ocean near the Galápagos, forcing the crew to jump overboard, a lawsuit says.
story: A Sunday strike against a low-profile vessel that intelligence showed was participating in "narco-trafficking," killing two people on board, according to U.S. Southern Command. (Credit: U.S. SOUTHCOM)

More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen have sued the federal government, alleging they were wrongly targeted in a drone strike that destroyed their boat in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year as part of the Trump administration’s broader campaign against vessels suspected of drug trafficking.
The 16 fishermen aboard La Negra Francisca Duarte II say drones launched from a U.S. vessel struck their boat March 17, 2026, as they headed home from a two-week fishing trip near the Galápagos.

The strike set the boat ablaze, forcing the crew to jump overboard and escape in lifeboats, according to a lawsuit filed Monday in federal court in Pennsylvania. All 16 survived, but two suffered serious burns. One man’s leg was burned to the bone, the lawsuit says.

The fishermen’s lawyers say the crew had no ties to drug cartels or terrorist groups and posed no imminent threat when U.S. drones struck their vessel, which they say had been cleared by Ecuadorian authorities hours earlier.

This still image from Sept. 19, 2026, shows the moment before a projectile hits a vessel in the Caribbean the U.S. military alleged was involved in drug trafficking. (US Southern Command/Handout via Reuters)
US MILITARY LAUNCHES FIRST AUTONOMOUS WARFARE COMMAND TO DEPLOY UNMANNED SYSTEMS ACROSS LATIN AMERICA

After their boat was destroyed, the fishermen sailed toward a blue vessel, which the lawsuit identified as a U.S. ship. Some personnel wore U.S. Coast Guard vests, the suit says. They allegedly zip-tied the uninjured men, hooded them and forced them to stand barefoot on the hot metal deck with no food and little water.

One injured fisherman was taken below deck for treatment, where U.S. personnel allegedly told him they had carried out the drone strike and laughed about destroying the boat, according to the lawsuit.

The fishermen were held until the next day before they were put on an El Salvadoran ship that took them back to El Salvador, where they were held at a migrant center in "deplorable conditions" until the end of March.

Demonstrators gather to protest against the deportation of immigrants to El Salvador outside the Permanent Mission of El Salvador to the United Nations on April 24, 2025, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN
The Department of War and the U.S. Coast Guard have denied knowing about or being involved in the March 17 attack on La Negra Francisca Duarte II.
U.S. Southern Command declined to comment, citing its policy of not issuing statements on pending or ongoing litigation.
A suspected drug-trafficking vessel erupts in flames following a U.S. military strike in the Eastern Pacific on June 18, 2026. (U.S. Southern Command)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The lawsuit argues that the Trump administration’s strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific violate federal and international law because they have been carried out outside an armed conflict. It adds that even if an armed conflict existed, the attacks could constitute war crimes under the Geneva Conventions.
The plaintiffs are seeking compensatory and other financial damages to be determined at trial, plus an injunction ordering the U.S. to end similar boat attacks.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: CodePink co-founder's $55M foundation reinstated in California amid grant questions
summary: Medea Benjamin's Arc of Justice foundation regained California charitable registration after missed filings, but it stays on probation through August 2029.
story: CodePink activists ignore questions from Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani on their intentions ahead of Capitol Hill foreign influence hearing.

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin’s $54.6 million family foundation has been reinstated as a California charity after years of missed financial filings, although questions linger over $2.7 million in grants it reported paying in 2024, the year its registration was suspended.

The foundation, Arc of Justice, has poured $24.6 million into protest groups, legal advocacy organizations and progressive nonprofits over more than two decades, a previous Fox News Digital investigation found. The 2024 payouts included $350,000 to CodePink, according to the foundation’s 2024 federal tax return.

Years of missed filings prompted regulators in California to revoke the foundation's charitable registration in January 2025 after more than a year of suspension for repeatedly failing to submit required annual reports or respond to regulatory notices.
State regulators restored it in September, placing the foundation on three years probation.
$54M CODEPINK-LINKED FOUNDATION SHUT DOWN IN CALIFORNIA POPS UP AT RAMSHACKLE MIAMI HOME

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin protests before former special counsel Robert Hur testifies at a House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., March 12, 2024. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Under California regulations, organizations with suspended or revoked charitable registrations are prohibited from distributing or spending charitable assets without the attorney general’s prior written approval, according to Title 11, Section 345(b) of to the California Code of Regulations.
Fox News Digital asked the California Attorney General’s Office whether the foundation needed or received approval to distribute those grants.
"While the organization was suspended from activity in California, our office received no information regarding the organization’s out-of-state activities," the office said.
The office added that "a California registration revocation does not apply to grants outside California by a foreign nonprofit doing business in other states."
Arc of Justice is a California-incorporated nonprofit, and its charitable registration was suspended during 2024 before being revoked in January 2025.
The attorney general’s office did not directly address whether the foundation’s grants required or received written approval.
The foundation’s attorney, David Levitt, also did not answer Fox News Digital’s questions about whether the foundation obtained approval for the payments.

A Miami property previously listed as the address of a newly incorporated Arc of Justice nonprofit, left, and CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin holding a "China is not our enemy" sign during a Capitol Hill protest in Washington, D.C., on June 4, 2024, right. (AJ Skuy for Fox News Digital; Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Regulators approved its reinstatement petition Sept. 9 after it submitted five years of overdue reports covering 2020 through 2024 and paid $1,800 in fees and penalties, according to the petition and state records.
Levitt previously said that foundation leaders mistakenly believed a planned relocation to Florida had ended its California reporting obligations.

"The Foundation's failure to comply with the Registry's registration and reporting requirements resulted from an administrative misunderstanding concerning the Foundation's state of registration," Levitt wrote in its reinstatement petition.

Fox News Digital previously reported that a new Florida nonprofit using the Arc of Justice name had been incorporated at the Miami home of Benjamin’s longtime partner, Tighe Barry, after California revoked the foundation’s charitable registration.

Levitt previously said the Florida corporation was created as a "placeholder" while the foundation considered relocating. He said the move was never completed, the California corporation was never formally dissolved and no assets were transferred.
LAWMAKERS RAISE ALARM OVER NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S $278M NETWORK SPREADING CCP PROPAGANDA IN THE U.S.

Medea Benjamin, who led the California-based Arc of Justice foundation and co-founded CodePink, holds a "Let Gaza Live" sign as she is removed by U.S. Capitol Police after interrupting a House Armed Services Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on April 30, 2024. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Arc of Justice, a private grant-making foundation, was formerly known as The Benjamin Fund, Inc.

Benjamin's father, Alvin Benjamin, a prominent Long Island real estate developer who founded The Benjamin Companies in the early 1960s, provided some of the foundation's earliest documented financial backing.

The foundation’s assets grew from $39.63 million at the end of 2020 to $54.64 million at the end of 2024, fueled in part by investment gains even as it distributed millions of dollars annually in grants, federal tax returns reviewed by Fox News Digital show.

A review of its complete IRS filing history found it distributed nearly 1,500 grants totaling about $24.6 million to organizations involved in anti-war activism, progressive policy, legal advocacy and campaigns involving immigration enforcement, China, Cuba and the Israel-Hamas war.
CodePink co-founders Medea Benjamin, left, and Jodie Evans stand in a hallway wearing the group’s signature pink shirts. (Michael Dorgan)

CodePink was Arc of Justice's largest activist beneficiary. The foundation began funding CodePink in 2009 and provided grants to the organization in 15 tax years through 2024, totaling nearly $3.2 million, according to IRS filings.

Benjamin co-founded CodePink with Jodie Evans, the wife of Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham. Benjamin remains one of the group's most visible members, frequently leading protests and interrupting congressional hearings.

Founded in 2002 with the aim of preventing the Iraq War, CodePink has grown into one of the country’s most visible anti-war protest groups, and its activists are easily recognizable in hot pink T-shirts and often wear keffiyehs.
In September, Benjamin was escorted from a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing on alleged foreign malign influence after protesting during the proceedings.
On Nov. 10, Benjamin clashed with Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., near an elevator bank at the Capitol over Israel and the Iran war.

CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin speaks with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., as Tighe Barry, Jodie Evans and other activists gather inside the Rayburn House Office Building on Nov. 11, 2026. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

The following day, Veterans Day, Benjamin and fellow CodePink activists confronted Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., inside the Rayburn House Office Building, pressing him over U.S. military cooperation with Israel. Evans also attended the group’s Taxpayer Uprising Capitol Hill lobbying event.

In October, CodePink organized a China tour promoting the country’s revolutionary history, infrastructure and socialist development. During the trip, Benjamin posted a video praising public safety, pointing to unattended bicycles and umbrellas as examples of belongings people could leave without fear of theft, Fox News Digital previously reported.

The group has also participated in nationwide No Kings protests, opposed ICE enforcement actions, organized anti-Israel rallies and campaigned against U.S. policy toward China, Cuba and Iran. Earlier this year, CodePink led a delegation to Cuba that included Twitch political streamer Hasan Piker.

Since 2009, the foundation and its predecessor, The Benjamin Fund, also directed about $2.05 million to Global Exchange, the anti-war and social justice advocacy group Benjamin co-founded with her former husband, Kevin Danaher. The group has long campaigned against U.S. military intervention and economic sanctions.

Arc of Justice also provided about $2.24 million to Grassroots International, which funds grassroots social movements around the world; $1.61 million to Social Good Fund, which helps charitable projects raise money and manage their operations; about $1.29 million to the Center for Constitutional Rights, a legal advocacy organization; and about $114,000 to Alliance for Global Justice, an activist nonprofit.

Other recipients since 2009 included World Beyond War, which received about $492,000; the Institute for Policy Studies, roughly $255,000; and Jewish Voice for Peace, about $124,000. The foundation also gave $110,000 to Grassroots Global Justice and about $90,000 to the Center for Popular Democracy.
IRS filings also show the foundation provided about $65,500 to Democracy Now!, where Benjamin has frequently appeared as a guest, since 2009.

title: Recent service outages not state-sponsored attacks, DNI Jay Clayton testifies
summary: DNI Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee recent U.S. service outages stem from maintenance, not a coordinated state-sponsored attack.
story: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton outlines national security threats including terrorism and Iranian plotting, saying recent cyber service disruptions are not state-sponsored attacks, nor are they related.

Recent service outages across U.S. systems stem from routine technical and maintenance issues – not a coordinated foreign cyberattack, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday, even as he warned lawmakers that "superintelligence" is rapidly escalating the speed and sophistication of future cyber threats.

"Based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, " Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee's "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" hearing. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

Clayton acknowledged public concern over the timing of the recent outages, telling the panel that the American people are right to ask questions, but intelligence reviews point away from foreign interference.
THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia testify during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years after 9/11" on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 18, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty Images)

"We have no indication that these events are related," Clayton said in response to persistent questioning from Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y. "But let me answer something that the American people should know, which is the speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially, which means legacy systems that were old six months ago or a year are a lot older."
The intelligence community remains on alert and continues to monitor for any malicious cyber activity targeting U.S. networks or law enforcement partners, Clayton said in his opening statement.

"After doing a great deal of due diligence inside the government with the private sector, with people in the private sector whose job is cybersecurity, we have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton reiterated in the question and answer session of the hearing. "We also have no indication that they're a result of a state-sponsored malign actor."
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

Beyond the immediate outages, the intelligence chief warned lawmakers that rapid advancements in artificial intelligence – also referred to as "superintelligence" – are fundamentally altering the digital battlefield and raising the stakes for homeland defense.

"Let me note that superintelligence is reshaping the cybersecurity landscape, " Clayton said. "It is sharply increasing speed, scale, and sophistication of offensive and defensive cyber operations. And it's not just cyber. This goes to national security. It goes to the battlefield and it goes to commerce. Superintelligence is changing the way we do business, the way we fight wars and the way we combat terrorism every day."
GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATORS FIND AI PLATFORMS PRODUCE TERROR PLOT PLANS IN UNDERCOVER OP

During his opening remarks, Clayton outlined a broader heightened threat environment 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks. While declining to discuss classified intelligence in an open setting, he noted that full briefings have been provided to the Gang of Eight and congressional intelligence committees.
Among the primary threats highlighted in his testimony:

Iranian plotting: Clayton said threats from Iran – both inside the United States and targeting Americans abroad – have "substantially increased," underscoring a commitment to detecting and deterring lethal plots.Terrorism: While post-9/11 counterterrorism efforts have degraded the capabilities of major groups, Clayton warned of persistent threats from individuals inspired by ISIS and al-Qaeda, as well as networks exploited by adversarial nations.

Terrorism: While post-9/11 counterterrorism efforts have degraded the capabilities of major groups, Clayton warned of persistent threats from individuals inspired by ISIS and al-Qaeda, as well as networks exploited by adversarial nations.

Surveillance authorities: Clayton urged Congress not to let Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) expire, calling it the "single most indispensable tool" for early warnings on foreign threats to the homeland and U.S. troops.

"No other program can replicate the speed and effectiveness of FISA 702," Clayton said. "Letting it expire would simply be a mistake."

title: Florida eyes poaching NYPD officers after Mamdani dismantles elite unit
summary: Sen. Ashley Moody invites NYPD Strategic Response Group officers to Florida after Zohran Mamdani announced the counterterrorism unit's disbandment.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was pressed on why he is not retraining NYPD officers on de-escalation instead of sending an unarmed civilian unit to handle protests.

Florida’s former top law enforcement officer issued a call for members of an NYPD counterterrorism unit to relocate to the Sunshine State as many New Yorkers already have, after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Councilman Chi Ossé announced the disbandment of the specialized unit.

Mamdani and Ossé, D-Brooklyn, announced this week that the Strategic Response Group (SRG) will be dissolved in alignment with a key campaign promise by the mayor, as critics, including former NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton, who created the unit, warn it will make the nation’s largest city more dangerous.
"Florida is always looking for well-qualified new officers," Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., said in reaction to the news.
MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE
"The Sunshine State welcomes members of the NYPD Strategic Response Group to join our mission of protecting Florida communities," said Moody, who was previously the state’s attorney general.
NYPD officers who accept the invitation would add to the nearly 376,000 New Yorkers who relocated to Florida between 2019 and 2023, according to figures reported by New York's WPIX-11 News.
Miami-Dade County Commissioner Roberto Gonzalez, a Republican, also issued a call for disillusioned NYPD officers to relocate.
"In Florida, it’s always our priority to back the brave men and women that wear the badge. Miami-Dade [Sheriff’s Office] is the best in the country. NYPD’s finest: We’re hiring," he said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, and Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, R-Fla., for further comment but did not receive an immediate response.

The invitations come months after another Florida law enforcement leader rented Times Square advertising space to draw NYPD officers southward after Mamdani defeated former Gov. Andrew Cuomo, D-N. Y., and activist Curtis Sliwa in the 2025 mayoral election.
Volusia County Sheriff Michael Chitwood — who hails from Philadelphia — publicly encouraged NYPD officers to come to Daytona Beach.
"Dear NYPD, Sunny Florida is waiting," read one of the billboards from the Volusia County Sheriff’s Foundation. The displays in Times Square included a QR code for officers to apply on the spot.
"Serve a community that appreciates you," it went on.
"You’re going to get support here, and you’re going to have a tremendous quality of life," Chitwood told Fox’s Orlando affiliate.
MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES
Chi Ossé, a New York City Council member, speaks at a campaign rally for mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani at United Palace in New York City on Oct. 13, 2025. (Christian Monterrosa/Bloomberg)

On Monday, Mamdani said in a video announcing the end of the SRG that counterterrorism and protest response should have separate enforcement entities, while Ossé added that the government has a responsibility to protect constitutional rights and "keep communities safe."
"Those priorities are not in conflict," Ossé said, as the two announced a replacement agency within the mayor’s office called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD).
MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS
The CDDD will be staffed with unarmed civilians without arrest powers who will seek to engage in dialogue with protesters while reserving the right to call in uniformed police if necessary.
The two referenced their own prior arrests, remarking deadpan, "We both know something about that," when laying out how officers can still respond to arrest people involved in "civil disobedience."

Ossé was arrested in April while protesting the scheduled eviction of a constituent, while then-Assemblyman Mamdani was arrested in 2023 during a traffic-blocking protest outside the Brooklyn home of Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Fox News Digital reached out to the NYPD and Mamdani’s office for comment.

Mamdani's office responded by sharing a transcript of his news conference on the SRG. At one point, Mamdani said, "The point here is looking for de-escalation, looking for engagement and dialogue, and that being a constant both in advance and during. And when you're asking about — as the march continues, if you have a sense that this march is transforming into something else, then it's not for civilians to be on the front lines of that."
Some fellow Democrats also criticized Mamdani for the decision.

New York City Councilman James Gennaro, D-Queens, said on X that transferring the SRG’s responsibilities to the new division the mayor described raised concerns about whether the NYPD will be able to "maintain the specialized training and experience to respond to volatile and potentially violent situations."
"It also raises concerns about the city’s ability to respond to large-scale events and major incidents, including active-shooter attacks," Gennaro said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani listens to reporters' questions during a press conference at Athens Square Park on Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. The appearance came a day after Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced plans to disband the department's Strategic Response Group. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Former NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton, who served under Mayors Rudy Giuliani and Bill de Blasio, said the city can reorganize the NYPD but not "reorganize away the threats that require" the SRG’s specialized response.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As the commissioner who created the 600-officer Strategic Response Group and the 500-officer Counterterrorism Critical Response Command, I know why we built them — and what they were meant to do," Bratton said on X after publishing an op-ed on the matter in the New York Post.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Americans misled on Social Security for decades as clock counts down on benefits, explosive report reveals
summary: Sen. Ron Johnson says Americans are being scammed by Social Security, calling the program a legal Ponzi scheme that is hurtling toward insolvency by 2032.
story: Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., Senate Budget Committee chair, claims that Social Security is nothing more than a "Legal Ponzi Scheme." (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican is sounding the alarm that Americans are being "scammed" by the government’s handling of Social Security, and warned that it’s too late to change the trajectory of the decades-old safety net.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., claimed in a new report called "Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme," that the federal government has been duping Americans on what really happens with taxpayer money that flows into the program.

As Social Security hurtles toward insolvency — meaning the fund will run out of money and be unable to pay 100% of scheduled benefits on time — Johnson warned in the report first obtained by Fox News Digital that "once a Ponzi scheme begins to collapse, it can’t be fixed."
AMERICA’S RETIREMENT SYSTEM IS BROKEN. TRUMP MAY HAVE FOUND A BOLD FIX

"It can only be liquidated, with late investors often receiving only pennies on the dollar for their end-of-scheme investments," Johnson said. "Their only hope is that an underlying financial entity can provide a backstop to limit their losses."

Johnson’s report projected that by 2032, when Social Security is expected to become insolvent, there will be a roughly $511 billion Social Security shortfall, equal to roughly 21% of the projected $2.4 trillion total federal deficit that year.

The main thrust of Johnson’s report, which he wrote himself, is that Americans have been convinced that Social Security and the portion that comes from their paychecks that fund it, known as the Federal Insurance Contributions Act — the percentage deducted from a person’s paycheck that helps fund Social Security and Medicare — is a retirement account that grows over time.
CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100

Johnson, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee for another two months, countered that Americans’ tax dollars aren’t in a "lock box" designed to flourish, but instead that 6.2% from every person’s paycheck goes to pay for other peoples’ benefits.
"People often say, ‘Don’t touch Social Security, that’s my money,’" Johnson wrote. "Actually, it’s not."
"Your money was spent to pay current beneficiaries or fund other government programs as soon as it was collected from your paycheck."

"Your future benefits will be paid with the money collected from your sons and daughters working at that time, plus money borrowed from the public now that Social Security is running deficits," he continued.
Johnson blamed decisions from Congress in the past, like not investing surpluses in the program into stocks or promising increasingly expensive benefits with few workers in the workforce.
GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

Johnson acknowledged that "Social Security cannot be fundamentally fixed as a retirement investment fund because it never was one," and noted that under current law, once the program’s trust fund is depleted, which is estimated to hit in 2032, benefits will be reduced.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The solution: "repeal that portion of the law that reduces Social Security benefits and quit scaring seniors."
"We should then roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem — our massive debt and deficits," Johnson wrote.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Jeffries survives Dem vote to secure speaker position as progressive resistance clouds his chances
summary: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker despite progressive backlash, setting up a January vote that could test party unity.
story: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries tells Fox News that he is going to speak to every member ahead of leadership elections to rally support to be selected as Speaker of the House.

House Democrats selected Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as their nominee for speaker of the House in the 120th Congress following the party's sweeping midterm victories, a senior House Democratic staffer confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Despite growing opposition from progressives over his leadership and ties to the Democratic establishment, Jeffries survived the secret-ballot vote on Wednesday in a "landslide," according to the staffer, advancing him as the party's nominee to lead the majority in the new Congress. Only 11 Democrats voted against his speaker nomination.
The New York lawmaker must now win a full House vote in January to secure the position.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)
SENATE DEM CHALLENGING SEN CHUCK SCHUMER FOR LEADERSHIP POST BACKS HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR HOUSE SPEAKER

Jeffries ran unopposed for the nomination, although recent reports indicated Democratic congressional offices had been inundated with calls from frustrated voters urging lawmakers to select an alternative candidate.

After he cleared the vote, the committee room where the incoming class of Democratic members, made up of re-elected and newly elected caucus members, erupted in cheering and clapping immediately following the vote.
"It was a blowout number," Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., told Fox News Digital after the vote.

The Democratic leader has faced criticism from progressive members of his party over his support for Israel and his ties to corporate political action committees, which critics argue reflect the priorities of the Democratic establishment rather than the party's progressive base.

Rep.-elect Don Leonard, D-Ohio, who flipped a district carried by Trump in 2024, told local media that he would be "shopping for a new leader" if Jeffries did not commit to changing his position on Israel.

When asked by Fox News Digital if he voted against Jeffries on Wednesday, Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., a new member of the progressive caucus, declined to comment. After the vote count was reported, it was confirmed that Hamawy voted against Jeffries’ nomination.

Rep. elects Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-NY., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, PA, and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., joined Hamawy in opposing Jeffries.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks with reporters as he walks to his office after a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 27, 2026. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)
FOLLOW THE LEADER: DEMOCRATS FACE PARTY BATTLE AS DIVISIONS DEEPEN

Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., told Fox News Digital that the members who voted against them were "unfair" as they had never seen his abilities as a legislator, minority leader and let alone Speaker of the House.
Jackson added that these new representatives probably voted against Jeffries because they were following what their constituents wanted them to do.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that these new representatives are members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), not the Democratic Party, and have their own independent legislative agenda outside that of the establishment.

After the vote, the coalition who voted against Jeffries released a statement claiming that they opposed Jeffries' nomination because the minority leader does not represent the agenda they believe in, which includes abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Medicare-for-all.

Democrats are preparing to use their new majority in January to immediately launch investigations, challenge President Donald Trump's policies through legislative oversight and hold congressional hearings. If Jeffries advances to speaker, he will lead that effort.
Despite the opposition, Jeffries has maintained support from prominent Democratic leaders, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who publicly backed his bid for the speakership.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., talk on the House floor on Jan. 6, 2023. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Jeffries' nomination does not guarantee that he will become speaker when the new Congress convenes in January. The New York Democrat must still secure enough votes from the full House to win the position, but with the overwhelming victory on Wednesday, the path to speakership appears clearcut.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The looming vote could test whether progressive dissatisfaction with Jeffries' leadership translates into opposition on Capitol Hill or remains largely confined to grassroots activists.

The controversy also raises questions about whether incoming Democrats who campaigned against the party's establishment will ultimately support its chosen leader or demand policy concessions in exchange for their votes.
During the secret ballot session on Wednesday morning, Democrats selected Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to become the party's next caucus chair.

title: Government investigators find AI platforms produce terror plot plans in undercover op
summary: GAO investigators bypassed AI safeguards on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok, obtaining feasible plans for terrorist attacks in under 12 hours of testing.
story: Government Accountability Office official Kevin Walsh described investigators using AI technology to plan an attack on the homeland. (Courtesy: Government Accountability Office)

Federal investigators successfully bypassed safety safeguards on four major artificial intelligence platforms, obtaining detailed plans for potentially deadly terrorist attacks in less than 12 hours, according to a government watchdog report released Wednesday.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok each generated information that could help carry out attacks targeting crowded locations or the nation's electrical grid during undercover testing conducted in spring 2026.

Two platforms produced plans involving improvised explosive devices intended to cause mass casualties, while the other two outlined attacks on electrical infrastructure designed to inflict economic damage.

The AI-generated responses included potential targets, locations, timing and attack methods. Although all four platforms initially activated safeguards to block or remove harmful content, investigators ultimately circumvented those protections.
CHINESE AI MODEL INVESTIGATED AFTER RESEARCHER SAYS IT PROVIDED INSTRUCTIONS FOR BIOWEAPONS, ASSASSINATIONS
A finger taps the Grok app icon on a smartphone screen in this illustration photo taken on September 17, 2026. (Photo Illustration by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

GAO investigators also consulted experts and conducted real-world checks to assess the plans, finding that the information provided by all four platforms was sufficiently feasible to assist someone planning an attack.
"The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors," the GAO warned, citing growing risks to national and economic security.
The companies behind the platforms — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and SpaceXAI — said they were continuing to improve their safety measures, while some raised concerns about the testing.
BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS

Anthropic acknowledged that determined users could bypass AI safeguards and said it took the findings seriously, but questioned aspects of the GAO's methodology and said it could not independently verify the results.

Google noted that investigators tested earlier versions of its models, saying, "We continue to improve our models." OpenAI welcomed the opportunity to respond to the findings and acknowledged "the work that remains," while SpaceXAI said it "continues to work diligently" to strengthen safety with each model release.
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Monday, Nov. 10, 2025. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The report, requested by Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., comes amid growing scrutiny of AI's potential misuse and renewed calls for stronger safeguards against national security threats.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical," Hassan said in a statement Wednesday. "If Congress does not act, it is a question of when – not if – a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack."

title: Far-left groups cheer Mamdani for disbanding elite NYPD protest team
summary: Groups in Neville Roy Singham's network, including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, celebrate Zohran Mamdani's move to dissolve the NYPD's SRG unit.
story: ‘The Five’ co-hosts comment on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s move to disband the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group. Panelists criticize Mamdani’s decision to replace the tactical police unit with civilian-led conflict resolution teams.

Far-left radical groups, including some within tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham’s pro-CCP network, are cheering New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s decision to dissolve an elite NYPD unit responsible for handling protests.

After Mamdani announced Monday morning that he would disband the elite police department's Strategic Response Group, applause came in rapid succession from nonprofit organizations that regularly mobilize protests of ICE, Israel, capitalism and America in general.
"The mass movement has won the disbanding of NYPD’s Strategic Response Group — but the fight continues," the Party for Socialism and Liberation posted to X following the announcement.
MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani listens to reporters' questions during a press conference at Athens Square Park on Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. The appearance came a day after Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced plans to disband the department's Strategic Response Group. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"For everyone who has been kettled, beaten, pepper-sprayed or dragged onto a bus by the SRG, this is a real victory. But it was not handed down from City Hall. It was won by a mass movement that refused to let a campaign promise die quietly. The work of turning this victory into lasting change for working people is just beginning," the post added.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is part of a protest network of activist groups tied to Singham, a Shanghai-based tech tycoon married to far-left CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans. A Fox News Digital analysis found that Singham funneled $278 million into six nonprofits, including $22.4 million to the People's Forum, the Manhattan organizing hub that works closely with the Party for Socialism and Liberation on protests.
SHANGHAI-BASED TYCOON NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S 'SQUAD,' BERNIE SANDERS DONATIONS RESURFACE

Fox News Digital has witnessed protest foot soldiers and field marshals from the Party for Socialism and Liberation enter and leave the People's Forum headquarters on W. 37th Street, their signs, wagons and loudspeakers in tow.

David Chung, organizing director at The People’s Forum, left, prepares for an anti-war demonstration in Union Square in New York City. Tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, right, attends The Red Party in New York City on Feb. 14, 2018. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital; Mark Sagliocco/Getty Images)

The Party for Socialism and Liberation also shares leadership with Singham-funded groups. Claudia De la Cruz, a 2024 presidential candidate for the Party for Socialism and Liberation leader, was on the People's Forum's founding board alongside Evans.

Longtime organizer Brian Becker, a self-described communist, helped build the People's Forum into a base for the Party for Socialism and Liberation and the ANSWER Coalition, and his son, Ben Becker, is editor-in-chief of the Singham-funded BreakThrough News, which also shares a home at the People’s Forum headquarters on W. 37th Street.
SINGHAM-BACKED, PRO-CHINA GROUP DROPS HUGE SUM ON MANHATTAN HQ AS FEDS PROBE SHADOWY NETWORK
By early morning, self-declared Marxist influencer and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker weighed in, saying he was "glad" the unit had been disbanded.

At 11:16 a.m., Piker posted a response to Mamdani’s message, skipping capitalizations as he wrote: "one of the hardest problems for NYC mayor is police reform. The SRG is a ‘counter terrorism’ unit that has primarily been deployed on protestors. glad the mayor is moving on this promise to disband."
HASAN PIKER NAMES PRO-CCP TYCOON SINGHAM AS FINANCIER OF 'POLITICAL MOVEMENTS' DESPITE NONPROFIT VENEER

By the afternoon, at 2:55 p.m., Nerdeen Kiswani, an anti-Israel activist who founded the organization Within Our Lifetime, responded to the announcement by calling for consequences for NYPD officers who subdued protests, while saying the disbanding is "overdue and welcome news" in a post on X.

Within Our Lifetime co-founder Nerdeen Kiswani speaks during a "Nakba 78" anti-Israel protest in Washington Square Park on May 15, 2026, in New York City, as demonstrators carrying Palestinian flags and Hamas flags gather behind her. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

"The settlement gave us a way to challenge the NYPD when it violated protesters’ rights, and officers violated it anyway," Kiswani wrote. "The limits Mamdani announced today give us more specific rules to point to when we challenge police conduct. We’ll see whether the NYPD actually follows them when we’re back in the streets, especially when we’re protesting something the people in power would rather we stay quiet about."

Mamdani previously joined Kiswani in an anti-Israel protest, where calls to "globalize the intifada" rang out from the protesters in the crowd. Within Our Lifetime is not a registered nonprofit, so its tax filings and funding aren’t available to the public. Fox News Digital hasn’t identified any direct ties to the Singham network aside from joining member groups in demonstrations.

Mamdani’s announcement fulfilled a campaign promise he made to disband the group. While the Party for Socialism and Liberation says "the mass movement has won," it’s unclear whether the organization had any impact on the mayor’s decision.
MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS
Hasan Piker speaks at a press conference during day two of Web Summit Vancouver 2026 at Vancouver Convention Centre in Vancouver, Canada. (Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani told reporters in a news conference announcing the changes. "We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation."
Former NYPD officers weighed in on Mamdani’s decision, saying the move would empower criminals and promote anarchy.
POLICE GROUPS CONDEMN MAMDANI OVER AXING ELITE NYPD UNIT

"I think it’s one more step towards emboldening the criminals, emboldening the anarchists and emboldening the terrorists," said James Gagliano, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and Fox News contributor who spent years working alongside the NYPD.
Protesters and counter-protesters gathered inside Washington Square Park in New York, New York, on Friday afternoon. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani told reporters in a news conference announcing the changes. "We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation."

title: Fake vacation rental sites use live chat to steal your data
summary: Fortra researchers say fake vacation rental sites use live customer support chats to trick travelers into handing over credit card details this holiday.
story: Travel expert and advisor Bobby Laurie explains when Europe's ETIAS travel authorization system is expected to launch, how the application process will work and what travelers should know about potential scams taking place right now.

You're booking a vacation rental for the holidays when a message appears saying there's a problem with your reservation. Before you can figure out what's wrong, a customer support chat opens and offers to help. You're told your credit card won't be charged, but you'll need to enter the number to complete a security check. Sounds helpful, right? That's exactly what scammers want you to think.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered fake vacation rental sites that look remarkably similar to legitimate booking platforms. Some even include live customer support chats designed to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. With Thanksgiving travel approaching, it's worth knowing how these scams work before you book your next trip.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
Scammers copy legitimate vacation rental listings, complete with property photos, prices and reviews, to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. (Yuliya Taba/Getty Images)
Fake vacation rental sites are getting harder to spot

Researchers with Fortra's Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) team recently identified fraudulent travel-booking websites that impersonate popular vacation rental platforms. The scammers copy legitimate property listings and surround them with details you'd expect to see on a real booking site. You might recognize the familiar layout or see reviews that make a property seem trustworthy. The photos may even come from an actual vacation rental.

One example uncovered by researchers showed listings for an apartment and a house. Both appeared to be legitimate properties available for booking. Someone searching for a holiday rental could easily spend more time comparing the accommodations than questioning the website itself. That's the problem. A professional-looking listing tells you very little about who's actually running the website. Fortra says its researchers identified and remediated examples of these phishing sites. The company did not report how many travelers may have fallen for the scams or whether money was stolen.
Fake booking messages make travelers think something went wrong

The scammers also know that travel plans can be stressful, especially around the holidays. If you've already arranged transportation and suddenly see a warning about your accommodations, you're probably going to want answers.
Researchers found fraudulent booking pages displaying messages such as:
"Your reservation is unconfirmed.""Complete verification to continue.""Your payment has not been processed.""Your booking will be canceled.""Special pricing is available for a limited time."
"Your reservation is unconfirmed."
"Complete verification to continue."
"Your payment has not been processed."
"Your booking will be canceled."
"Special pricing is available for a limited time."

In one case, a fake booking page told visitors their reservation was still unconfirmed. To finish the process, they needed to complete what the website called a mandatory verification step. The page reassured them that there would be no additional charge. But the next screen asked for personal information, including contact details that scammers could potentially use for future phishing attacks. Researchers also identified a separate website impersonating a major lodging platform. Its login page used recognizable branding and familiar sign-in options to encourage visitors to submit account information. That creates another risk. If you use the same password for multiple services, giving it to a fake booking website could put those other accounts in danger.
Fake customer support chats make the scam more convincing

The live chat feature is what makes this scam particularly concerning. In a separate case, Fortra's researchers discovered a fraudulent travel-booking page with a credit card payment form and a live support chat. When visitors expressed concerns, the chat responded and described the card request as a routine security check. It even reassured visitors that their cards wouldn't be charged. Now consider how often you've used an online customer support chat to straighten out a billing problem. You explain what's happening, someone responds and you follow their instructions. Most of the time, that experience is perfectly legitimate.

Scammers are borrowing that familiar interaction to make their websites seem more trustworthy. The chat's reassurance was designed to encourage visitors to submit payment details. The researchers did not say whether a real person or an automated system operated the chat. Either way, the conversation was part of the fraudulent booking process. And that's an important reminder. Just because someone responds to your questions in real time doesn't mean you're dealing with the company you think you're dealing with.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

A fake customer support chat reassures travelers that their credit cards won't be charged while directing them to enter payment information for a supposed reservation verification. (Fortra Intelligence and Research Experts)
Tips to protect yourself from fake vacation rental sites

Before you enter your credit card information or book a place to stay, take a moment to make sure you're dealing with a legitimate website. A little extra checking now could save you from losing money or having your personal information stolen.

If you're using Airbnb, Vrbo or another rental platform, open its official app or enter the website address yourself. Don't rely on links in unexpected emails or text messages, even when they mention a reservation you recognize. Be cautious with sponsored search results as well. Scammers sometimes pay for advertisements that lead to fraudulent websites. If you're unsure about a booking message, go back to your account through the official platform and look for it there.

A fake website may use a familiar company logo while hiding behind a completely unrelated web address. Scammers also add extra words to brand names to make fraudulent domains appear legitimate. Check the address before signing in or entering your credit card number. Remember that a padlock symbol doesn't guarantee a website is safe. It only indicates that the connection is encrypted.

Found a rental you really like? Search for the address separately and see whether the property appears on another reputable booking website. Compare the details and pay attention to prices that seem unusually low. You can also reverse-search the listing photos to see where else they're being used. However, finding matching photos doesn't automatically prove the listing is legitimate. Scammers often steal pictures from real properties. Take a few minutes to read reviews from previous guests. If something about the listing doesn't add up, contact the booking platform directly.

If a message claims your reservation will be canceled unless you act immediately, check your booking through the official website or app. A legitimate reservation problem may require attention, but that doesn't mean you should trust a link that arrived unexpectedly. If the warning doesn't appear in your account, contact customer support using the information published on the company's official website.

Be especially careful if a host asks you to visit another website to complete payment. The same goes for unexpected requests to move the conversation to WhatsApp or another messaging service. Airbnb warns that paying outside its platform can leave guests without AirCover protection. Vrbo also requires bookings and payments to follow its authorized process. Some legitimate properties may collect certain disclosed charges separately. If that happens, confirm the payment instructions through the official booking platform before sending money.

Strong antivirus software that includes malicious website and phishing protection can help warn you about known fraudulent booking pages. Some security programs can also detect suspicious links before you enter sensitive information. Keep your browser updated as well, since updates often include important security fixes. Of course, newly created scam websites may escape detection. Security software helps, but you still need to check where you're entering your information. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Credit cards generally offer stronger protections for disputing fraudulent charges than many other payment methods. That's especially useful when you're paying for an expensive vacation rental. Be suspicious if someone insists on a wire transfer or wants payment through cryptocurrency. Gift card requests are another major warning sign. Once money is sent using these methods, recovering it can be difficult. Even when paying by credit card, make sure you're using the actual booking platform.
32 TRAVEL ESSENTIALS THAT HELP PROTECT YOU AND YOUR BELONGINGS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON

Fraudulent vacation rental booking pages tell travelers their reservation remains unconfirmed and ask them to provide personal information to complete a mandatory verification process. (Halfpoint/iStock/Getty Images)

Some legitimate vacation rentals require identification. However, that doesn't mean you should upload your driver's license or other sensitive documents to an unfamiliar website. If you're asked to complete an unexpected verification process, confirm it through your official reservation. Also, never share a one-time security code with someone contacting you through a support chat or message. That code could give a scammer access to your account.

A password manager can help you recognize a suspicious login page. If the website address doesn't match the saved address for your account, the password manager generally won't autofill your credentials. That doesn't automatically prove the site is fraudulent, but it's a good reason to check the address more carefully. Use unique passwords for your booking accounts and enable two-factor authentication. Passkeys are another good option when a service supports them.
What to do if you've entered information on a fake rental website
If you think you've shared personal or financial information with a scammer, act quickly. Here's what to do based on the information you provided.

Contact your credit card company. If you entered your card details, call the number on the back of your card or contact your issuer through its official app. Explain what happened and ask whether your card should be replaced. Review recent transactions and dispute any unauthorized charges. Don't wait for a fraudulent charge to appear before reporting your card information as compromised.Change your passwords. If you entered login credentials, go directly to the legitimate booking website and change your password. Update any other accounts where you used the same password. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if you haven't already and check for unfamiliar account activity.Monitor your identity and financial accounts. Watch your bank statements and credit card transactions for suspicious activity. If you shared sensitive identity information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance. If your Social Security number was exposed, consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts in your name.Report the fraudulent website. Notify the legitimate rental company being impersonated. You can also report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Save screenshots of suspicious messages and payment confirmations in case you need them for a fraud investigation or dispute.Make sure you have a real reservation. If you've been dealing with a fraudulent booking website, you may not have an actual reservation. Sign in to the legitimate booking platform to verify your stay. If you can't find your reservation, contact customer support directly. You don't want to arrive at your destination and discover you have nowhere to stay.

Contact your credit card company. If you entered your card details, call the number on the back of your card or contact your issuer through its official app. Explain what happened and ask whether your card should be replaced. Review recent transactions and dispute any unauthorized charges. Don't wait for a fraudulent charge to appear before reporting your card information as compromised.

Change your passwords. If you entered login credentials, go directly to the legitimate booking website and change your password. Update any other accounts where you used the same password. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if you haven't already and check for unfamiliar account activity.

Monitor your identity and financial accounts. Watch your bank statements and credit card transactions for suspicious activity. If you shared sensitive identity information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance. If your Social Security number was exposed, consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts in your name.

Report the fraudulent website. Notify the legitimate rental company being impersonated. You can also report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Save screenshots of suspicious messages and payment confirmations in case you need them for a fraud investigation or dispute.

Make sure you have a real reservation. If you've been dealing with a fraudulent booking website, you may not have an actual reservation. Sign in to the legitimate booking platform to verify your stay. If you can't find your reservation, contact customer support directly. You don't want to arrive at your destination and discover you have nowhere to stay.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think the live chat feature makes this scam especially troubling. We're so used to turning to customer support when something goes wrong that we tend to trust the person offering to help. And that's exactly the reaction these scammers are hoping for. I wouldn't assume a booking website is legitimate simply because someone in a chat window tells me everything is fine. My advice? If you're asked to enter your credit card information to fix an unexpected reservation problem, stop and check with the booking company directly. I know that's frustrating when you're trying to get your holiday plans settled. But I'd rather spend a few extra minutes verifying a reservation than find out later that a scammer has my credit card number.

Have you ever had a vacation rental reservation suddenly require additional payment or verification? Did you trust the request, or did something make you suspicious? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI data centers could consume more water than Americans drink in a year by 2030, says CEO working on solution
summary: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck says AI data centers could drink as much water as Americans by 2030 unless direct chip cooling and water recycling catch on.
story: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck says that under current trends, data centers in the U.S. could consume as much water as the American public drinks yearly by 2030. Beck’s company is developing more sustainable cooling solutions for data center chips.

Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck, whose company is working on sustainable solutions to ecological problems like AI data centers’ robust water consumption, said that without reform, AI data centers could wind up consuming more water than Americans drink every year.

"Ninety-five percent of the data centers today use a lot of water," he told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We estimate that by 2030, with the old technologies in the U.S., we will use as much water to cool data centers as Americans are using for drinking needs."
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
Beck argued that this phenomenon is "not sustainable," and laid out the technologies his company is working on in an effort to reduce data centers’ water consumption.
Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck (Fox News)

"Behind AI there's water in every step of the process. You need water to produce the chips, to power the chips and to cool the chips. And for the last four or five years, the chips generation that we were using were just cooled with air," he told Fox News Digital.
However, with the increasing complexity of chips to match an ever-building demand for computer power, air conditioning alone is no longer sufficient to cool chips in data centers, Beck explained.

"You need something that's way stronger. Water is 30 times better at extracting heat than air from the chips. So that's why many of those new data centers are moving toward direct chip water cooling, which ultimately is bringing cold water on top of the chip," he said.

Direct water cooling, he explained, has the dual benefits of increasing efficiency and sustainability, because the water used to cool the chips can be recycled and used on every chip in a given data center.
Racks of graphics processing units (GPUs) with a closed-loop liquid cooling system are seen inside an operational Microsoft data center. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)

"So you end up in a place where you have a data center that is much more powerful [than] using no water, using less power, and ultimately not having an impact on natural resources and in communities around us, which is one of the unlocks that people are pushing back so much against right now," he said.
ONE INDUSTRY FACES MULTI-TRILLION-DOLLAR RECKONING AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION RESHUFFLE
On Nov. 4, voters across the U.S. elected lawmakers and executives who ran on campaigns to limit the number of data centers.

In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa upset incumbent Republican Greg Abbott. Voters who ticked the box for Hinojosa did so after she campaigned heavily on instituting a data center moratorium, a fact that Beck took note of.
THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO
Gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa speaks during a campaign event in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Most of the data centers that were installed in Texas or anywhere else in the country or in the world, for that matter, were using a lot of water, a lot of power. And that's created a lot of backlash from the communities, which is rightfully so," Beck told Fox News Digital.
Beck noted that while Texas is one of the most economically strong states in the union, it is also one of the most water-stressed.

"It's a bad combination," he said. "Obviously, high growth, great news; no water, less good news. So we've looked at those technological solutions on how do you bring higher growth, more data processing while using much less water."
Beck added that the technologies Ecolab is developing will exclusively be used in new-build data centers, while the political pushback is surrounding the existing, more resource-demanding projects.
Direct cooling allows for what is known as a closed loop system, a method that is far more sustainable and requires less water than previous iterations of water-cooling methods.
Ecolab, Beck explained, has found a way to recycle water not only in the chip cooling process, but in chip fabrication as well, a process that necessitates extremely pure water.
An employee works in the cleanroom at X-FAB, a chip manufacturer in Erfurt, Germany, on June 23, 2026. (Martin Schutt/picture alliance via Getty Images)
"The so-called fabs, they use huge amounts of water, which is very specialized water because it needs to be ultra pure," Beck explained.

"And that, to be recycled, is even way harder than in a data center. But even there, at Ecolab we found solutions to not only get the highest purity of water to get the most advanced chips, but we can reuse that water as well in ways that are water neutral," he said.
Beck also put in context just how pure the water for chip fabrication needs to be.
"The purity is a million times more pure than what you would inject in your blood if it's a drug. So super high quality, super high purity of water at the end," he said.

"So the way we do it, in short, is ultimately at every step of the process we try to extract the water from that process step. We treat, we purify that water, we bring it back to an ultra-pure water level, and we bring back to the process. And the very special thing that we have at Ecolab, within that water you have some trace materials that we call connected water," he said.

"So we understand the quality of the water throughout the process within the fab or the data center, for that matter, that we know exactly the quality of that water to make sure that the chips are perfectly produced. And we know what we need to do in order to re-treat that water so that it can be reused afterwards. And you end up with better chips, lower cost, and most importantly, water neutral," Beck said.

title: What to know about Ring Drone Cam, which can patrol your home for $250
summary: Ring's Drone Cam flies room to room with AI navigation, 2K video and a $249.99 price, but it still awaits FCC authorization before it can ship in the U.S.
story: Ring's $250 Drone Cam uses AI to fly through your home, investigate security alerts and stream live video. Kurt "Cyberguy" Knutsson breaks down what to expect from the new technology.

Ever leave the house and suddenly wonder whether you closed the back door? You pull up your security camera, but it only shows the driveway. Not much help when you want to see what's happening inside. Well, Ring thinks it has an answer. And this one actually flies. Amazon-owned Ring has unveiled the Ring Drone Cam, a tiny $249.99 indoor security camera that flies from room to room. It can investigate security alerts, check specific areas of your home and send live video directly to your phone.

Earlier this month, the company announced the new drone as part of its new Ring Robotics lineup. And thanks to artificial intelligence, it can navigate your home without someone steering it around. We also talked in depth about this new technology on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast," including what a flying camera could mean for home security. But before you get too excited about having your own miniature security patrol, there are some things worth knowing.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI ROBOT MAY STOP YOUR DOG FROM BARKING WHILE YOU'RE GONE
A mock-up shows how the Ring app lets you view live footage from the Drone Cam and send it to specific locations inside your home. (Ring)
How Ring Drone Cam flies around your home

Traditional home security cameras have one obvious limitation. They only show what's in front of them. Ring wants to change that. The Ring Drone Cam uses a system called AI Pilot to learn the layout of your home. During the initial setup, you carry the drone through your space while it creates a digital floor plan. From there, the system identifies rooms and suggests places worth checking. For example, maybe you want to see whether a window is open. Or perhaps your security system detects movement near the back door. You can save those locations in the Ring app. Then, when you want a closer look, the drone can fly there automatically. You can also create customized routes and schedule patrols with a compatible Ring subscription.

The drone can work with connected Ring cameras and security sensors. If a linked device triggers an alert, Ring Drone Cam can automatically fly to a previously selected location to investigate. According to Ring's official announcement, AI Pilot combines cameras with onboard sensors and cloud processing to navigate around obstacles. So, instead of wondering what triggered an alert, you could actually see what's happening in another part of the house.
Ring Drone Cam records 2K video as it flies

The Ring Drone Cam weighs approximately 5.8 ounces and packs quite a bit of technology into its compact design. It records video at 1920 by 1920 resolution, which Ring describes as 2K. The camera has a 148-degree field of view and can rotate to capture a 360-degree view of a room. You can watch live footage through the Ring app. And if something happens at night, the drone has two built-in LED spotlights that illuminate dark areas. Unlike some traditional security cameras, it doesn't use infrared night vision. The drone also makes noise while flying. That's intentional. Ring says the audible propellers help people know when the camera is moving around.

The drone has no microphone or speaker, so you cannot hear what's happening or talk to someone through it. There's also no built-in siren. And although it can move independently, it doesn't stay airborne indefinitely. Ring advertises up to eight minutes of flight time on a fully charged battery under controlled conditions. When the flight ends or the battery runs low, the drone returns to its charging dock.
The Ring Drone Cam features enclosed propellers, a 2K camera and built-in lights to help it navigate and capture video indoors. (Ring)
The man behind Ring has been working on this for years

If this concept sounds familiar, there's a good reason. Ring originally announced a flying indoor security camera called the Always Home Cam back in September 2020. It was an ambitious idea at the time. Instead of installing cameras throughout your house, you could use one device to check different rooms. Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff explained the thinking behind that original concept. In his September 2020 announcement, Siminoff wrote: "We wanted to create one camera that could give users the flexibility of every viewpoint they want around the home." However, bringing that concept to a broad consumer launch took much longer than expected.

More than six years later, Ring is returning to the idea with a new product called Ring Drone Cam. This version uses AI to map your home, navigate around obstacles and fly to specific locations through the Ring app. In the company's November 2026 announcement, Siminoff explained what customers had been asking for. "For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn't reach." The new drone reflects that feedback. Ring announced the original Always Home Cam at $249.99 in 2020. The new Ring Drone Cam carries that same advertised price in 2026. So, despite years of development and the addition of AI navigation, the announced price hasn't changed. That's pretty remarkable for a product with this kind of technology.
WHAT A SMART FIREWALL DOES AND WHY IT MATTERS ON HOME WI-FI
Can Ring Drone Cam really navigate around everything?

Ring says its AI Pilot system can recognize obstacles and adjust its flight path as it moves. However, certain surfaces can make navigation more difficult. According to Ring's official product information, highly reflective floors, large mirrors and transparent glass can interfere with navigation. Rooms with plain walls and few visual details may also create challenges.

The drone is limited to single-floor operation at launch, although Ring plans to support multiple floors in the future. It also requires Wi-Fi and a suitable location for its charging dock. Ring recommends an upload speed of at least 5 Mbps for optimal performance and 10 Mbps for 2K video quality.
What about privacy with a flying camera inside your house?

Ring says it has built several privacy protections into the device. Ring says the new Drone Cam only records while flying. When it returns to its docking station, the camera stops recording and the device powers down. A visible indicator and audible propellers help let people know when the drone is operating. The company also says recordings will receive protection through its new Throw Away the Key encryption system, known as TAKE. According to Ring's privacy documentation, the company retains video encryption keys for up to 24 hours to support enabled features. It then deletes its copies of those keys, leaving customers with control of the keys needed to access their recordings.

However, TAKE differs from traditional end-to-end encryption because it allows Ring to process video for certain connected features during that initial period. There's another consideration. AI Pilot uses cloud processing as part of its navigation system. So, anyone thinking about buying one should understand how Ring handles the home's digital map and what information gets processed remotely. And if you share your home with someone else, it's worth discussing whether they're comfortable with a flying camera operating indoors.
Ring's new Drone Cam hovers above its charging dock, ready to fly through your home and investigate security alerts. (Ring)
What Ring Drone Cam costs beyond the $250 price

Here's something else to keep in mind before deciding whether this little drone belongs in your home. The advertised price is $249.99. That includes the drone and its charging dock. However, some features require a compatible Ring subscription. For example, you need a subscription to schedule automatic patrols. You'll also need a compatible plan if you want to save recordings in the cloud and review them later.

Without a subscription, you can still use Live View to check what's happening. But if you want the drone to maintain a video history, there will be an additional recurring cost. Ring says eligible plans can provide up to 180 days of cloud video history, depending on the subscription and settings. And there's one more thing to consider. The drone relies on its battery for flight. With a maximum advertised flight time of eight minutes, you'll need to allow time for recharging between patrols. That makes it better suited for checking specific areas than watching your entire house continuously.
FLOCK CEO, TECH RIVALS CALLED TO TESTIFY BEFORE SENATORS OVER AI CAMERA PRIVACY CONCERNS
When can you buy a Ring Drone Cam?

Ring says the Drone Cam is scheduled to begin shipping in the U.S. on January 27, 2027. The announced price is $249.99. However, the company still needs authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

So far, Ring says the device has not received the required FCC authorization and cannot legally be offered for sale or lease until that approval arrives. For now, you can sign up for product availability updates through Ring's official website at ring.com/products/drone-cam. And if you're wondering whether it will actually fly around your house as smoothly as it does in promotional videos, that's something we'll have to evaluate when the product becomes available.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to say, I love the idea of a security camera that can actually fly through your home. If I'm away and something triggers an alert, I'd much rather send a camera to check it out than wonder what's happening beyond the view of my existing cameras. And at $250, Ring has certainly priced this to get people's attention. What I'm curious about is how well it actually flies through a home. Can it navigate doorways and avoid obstacles reliably? And then there's the privacy question. I'd want to know exactly how Ring handles the map of my home and who can access the footage. I'm looking forward to seeing this technology in action.
We also talked about it in depth on my podcast, The CyberGuy Report at cyberguy.com/podcast. Check it out and subscribe for more conversations about the latest technology changing our lives.

Would you let an AI-powered drone fly through your house to keep an eye on things, or would a camera that can roam from room to room feel like too much surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: States put speed-limiting devices in reckless drivers' cars
summary: Virginia's GPS speed limiter program is already active for reckless driving offenders, but early users report glitches that apply wrong speed limits.
story: A LifeSafer GPS-powered speed limiter displays a 35 mph limit and helps prevent the driver from accelerating beyond the posted speed limit. (LifeSafer ISA)

We've all seen it. You're driving down the highway when someone flies past you at a ridiculous speed. Maybe they're weaving through traffic while everyone else tries to stay out of their way. Now, states are turning to speed-limiting devices that could stop some of the most dangerous drivers from doing it again.

Virginia has already started installing GPS-powered devices in vehicles used by certain reckless-driving offenders. Washington, D.C., has a similar program, and more jurisdictions are exploring the technology. The idea sounds promising. Instead of simply telling someone to slow down, the device can actually restrict how fast their car accelerates.

However, there's a catch. Some drivers using these systems have reported GPS glitches that mistakenly apply the speed limits of nearby roads. And that raises a question worth asking. What happens when your car refuses to accelerate because its GPS thinks you're somewhere else?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
