title: MICHAEL RUIZ: What is a dirty bomb? Explosive terror threat explained
summary: Iran's reported dirty bomb exploration puts new focus on a threat experts say could shut down a city and displace families even without mass casualties.
story: Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., discusses the longstanding threat of a nuclear Iran while pressing DNI Jay Clayton on the dirty bomb threat in the U.S.

While no dirty bomb is known to have been successfully detonated in a terror attack, a reported Iranian effort to explore such an option has placed a new spotlight on long-standing fears of one — even as experts say the disruption could spread farther than the blast.
A dirty bomb is an explosive designed to spread radioactive material — but not in the way an atomic bomb like those dropped in World War II would.

"Anything involving radiation sounds frightening, but there’s a big difference between a dirty bomb and a nuclear weapon," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory special agent who at one point served as the Jackson Field Office's weapons of mass destruction coordinator.
Dirty bombs use a conventional blast to spread radioactive dust or a similar contaminant.
US REMOVES RADIOACTIVE CANCER-TREATMENT MATERIAL FROM CENTRAL AMERICAN COUNTRY OVER 'DIRTY BOMB' RISK

Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia testify during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years after 9/11" on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 18, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

"The initial blast may pose the greatest immediate danger, but the contamination, fear and disruption afterward could be significant," Pack told Fox News Digital. "A dirty bomb doesn’t have to kill thousands of people to terrorize millions."
An attack could certainly be deadly. It would also shut down significant portions of a targeted city, he said, displacing families and businesses.

They're also risky to build, according to Pack. Bomb makers are at risk of exposing themselves to the same radioactive material they plan on using against the public, it's difficult to ensure the contaminants are dispersed in the explosion, and the terrorist would need to procure something to disperse to begin with.

"Just because somebody puts radioactive material with an explosive doesn’t mean they’re going to contaminate half a city," he said. "But even a relatively small incident could create tremendous fear, evacuations and disruption. That’s why we take these threats seriously."

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi immediately rejected the allegations of a dirty bomb plot in a post on X, invoking Iran's history as a victim of chemical warfare. (Askin Kiyagan/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

The radioactive materials to make them can be gathered without the ability to produce nuclear power or weapons, according to Paul Mauro, a retired NYPD inspector and Fox News contributor. One potential source is medical waste, he said, such as byproducts of certain cancer treatments.
"That's why they call it dirty," he said. "It's waste."

The greatest danger of a dirty bomb is the blast itself, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but radioactive material can spread and quietly cause dangerous health problems for people who unknowingly breathe it in.

"The radioactive materials used in a dirty bomb would probably not create enough radiation exposure to cause immediate serious illness, except to people who are very close to the blast site," according to the CDC.
The west front of the U.S. Capitol Building is seen at daybreak on Oct. 1, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (J. David Ake/Getty Images)
Police departments are equipped with devices that can detect radiation, Mauro said — which are sensitive enough to flag medical radiation in a passing ambulance.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

CNN reported earlier this week that U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing potential plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological device or chemical weapon, although sources described the effort as Iran exploring options rather than plotting an attack.

The issue came up again at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing Wednesday morning involving testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia.
IRGC OPERATIVE LANDS ON FBI’S MOST WANTED TERRORISTS LIST OVER ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL FORMER TRUMP ADVISOR
Christopher Raia, deputy director of the FBI, speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Clayton acknowledged that the threat of a dirty bomb attack has existed for years, but officials said they haven't seen evidence of an imminent plot.

"In the aftermath of September 11, 2001, there is heightened concern that terrorists may try to smuggle nuclear or radiological materials into the United States," the United States Government Accountability Office warned in a 2006 report. "These materials could be used to produce either an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, known as a dirty bomb."
The GAO report cited a failed attack in Russia's capital in the mid-1990s as an example of the "capability and willingness" of terrorists to resort to such weapons of mass destruction.
Chechen separatists had placed a canister packed with cesium-137 and dynamite in a Moscow park, but it wasn't detonated.

The report included a summary of Department of Energy plans in place to scan for and detect sources of radiation that could be linked to terror plots or weapons smuggling and even locate material washed away in the wake of a natural disaster like Hurricane Katrina.
Now, the source of potential threats is believed to be Iran or its proxy militia group, Hezbollah.
"The best dirty bomb response is the one that you never hear about," said Pack, the retired FBI agent. "Because somebody stopped the plot before a bomb ever made it onto our streets."

Radiation has no taste or smell, according to the CDC.

If you find yourself in the midst of a suspected dirty bomb attack, the CDC warns that you should cover your mouth and nose and try not to breathe it in. If you aren't already indoors, seek shelter. Remove your clothes and seal them in a bag, then shower up, making sure to thoroughly wash your hair to remove any potential contaminants. Indoors, close doors and windows and turn off fans that bring in outside air.

"The good news is that it can be cleaned up," Mauro said of the dispersed material. "It would be expensive, time-consuming, a nightmare, sure."

title: Susan Smith prosecutor fears her release would put her in grieving father’s face ‘every day’
summary: Prosecutor Tommy Pope says Susan Smith would "love the attention" on social media if freed, putting her in ex-husband David Smith's face every day.
story: Tommy Pope, the prosecutor who tried Susan Smith’s murder case, tells Fox News Digital he fears her release would put her in her grieving ex-husband’s face "every day" through social media attention as she seeks parole.
The prosecutor who put Susan Smith behind bars fears she would embrace social media attention if released on parole, putting her in the face of her slain sons’ grieving father "every day."

Susan Smith was convicted of two counts of murder in 1995 and sentenced to life in prison. While she was handed a life sentence, state law at the time allowed her to be considered for parole after serving 30 years. She will face a seven-person parole board in Columbia, South Carolina, on Thursday morning, who will decide if she will be let out of prison.

Smith strapped her two young sons into her car and let it roll into a lake, killing them in what prosecutors argued was a bid to win back a former lover who did not want children. She was sentenced to life in prison.
SUSAN SMITH'S EX-HUSBAND WANTS HER ‘IN PRISON UNTIL SHE DIES’ AFTER KILLING SONS IN ALLEGED BID TO WIN LOVER
Susan Smith is escorted from a building in handcuffs. Smith was convicted in 1995 of murdering her two young sons, Michael and Alex. (Brooks Kraft LLC/Sygma via Getty Images)

The two children, 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alexander, were killed on Oct. 25, 1994. She initially gave police a false account, alleging that a Black man had carjacked her and taken her two children. Her husband believed the story, and the couple appeared together on national television pleading for the return of their kids.

Rep. Tommy Pope, who is currently the speaker pro tempore for the South Carolina House of Representatives, prosecuted Smith and told Fox News Digital that if released, the convicted murderer would get on social media and "love the attention."
CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE

"I think the difficulty is ... but I think the difficulty if Susan was out, she would be on social media," Pope said. "She would love the attention. It would be in David's face every day, and all he has ever talked about is justice for Michael and Alex."

"[David Smith is] very good about not being vindictive towards Susan from a biblical standpoint. He says he's forgiven her. But he just thinks that justice ought to be served for those boys, and I fully agree," he added.
CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON

Susan Smith wipes away a tear during a parole hearing on Nov. 20, 2024, in Columbia, South Carolina. It was the first parole hearing for Smith, who killed her two sons in 1994. She appeared at the hearing via video. (The Island Packet/Getty Images)
Pope said he believes Susan Smith, when she killed the children, wasn't sorry for killing them and said the jury intended on giving her an actual life sentence, not to be released on parole.

title: Hotel workers' skills put to the test at 36th Annual Housekeeping Olympics in Las Vegas
summary: Hotel workers from across the country gathered in Las Vegas for the 36th annual Housekeeping Olympics, turning everyday duties into a series of fast-paced competitions.
story: Hotel housekeepers traded their daily routines for a shot at gold in Las Vegas. A first-time team from South Dakota swept the competition, bringing home the championship at the 36th annual Housekeeping Olympics.
LAS VEGAS – Hotel workers put their housekeeping skills to the test earlier this week in Las Vegas at the 36th annual International Sanitary Supply Association (ISSA) Housekeeping Olympics.

Ten teams competed Monday at Michelob ULTRA Arena at Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino in eight events that turned routine cleaning duties into fast-paced challenges testing speed, precision and teamwork.
The competition is organized by the ISSA, which is a global trade association for the cleaning industry.

Michael Patterson, executive director of the Indoor Environmental Healthcare & Hospitality Association, a division of ISSA, said the competition began 36 years ago to recognize housekeeping employees and give them an event of their own.
F1 LEGEND RICCARDO PATRESE TALKS ABOUT F1'S FIRST FAILED ATTEMPT AT RACING IN LAS VEGAS: ‘IT WAS A CAR PARK’
Ten teams of hospitality workers competed at the Mandalay Bay Hotel's Michelob ULTRA Arena in Las Vegas. (Amalia Roy)
"The housekeepers are always the unsung heroes, whether they're in hospitality or whether they're in health care," Patterson said.

The contests included a two-minute bed-making challenge, a mop relay, a vacuum cleaner race and a pad toss. A new triathlon-style event combined glass cleaning, a stain section and a paper towel toss.

Some of the loudest cheers came during the spirit dance competition. Judges watched as teams danced choreographed performances complete with dazzling costumes and complete sets. Many teams leaned into the themes of their hotels and the glamour of the Las Vegas Strip.
The two-minute bed-making race was one of eight events of the night. (Amalia Roy)
Team Luxor took the floor first in mummy costumes inspired by the ancient Egyptian theme of the Luxor Hotel and Casino.
The team's choreographer told Fox News she wanted to keep the routine accessible to everyone.
"We wanted moves that everybody can do," she said.
The dance competition was the final event of the night. (Amalia Roy)
When the final scores were tallied, a team of South Dakota hotel workers competing for the first time took home the championship.
US WARNS AMERICANS IN KEY LOCATIONS TO ‘KEEP A LOW PROFILE’ AHAD OF CROWDED HOLIDAY TRAVEL

LIV Hospitality finished first overall, followed by Excalibur Hotel in second place and Mandalay Bay in third, according to the company's announcement. The South Dakota team also won the mop relay and toilet paper toss.

The victory capped LIV Hospitality's statewide Road to Vegas Housekeeping Championship Series. The company held regional competitions before hosting a final at The Box Elder Events Center. Top competitors earned spots on the team that traveled to Las Vegas.

Rather than representing one hotel, the team brought together employees from multiple properties across South Dakota. They competed against workers from Las Vegas resorts including Bellagio, The Cosmopolitan, Luxor and MGM Grand.

"We went to Las Vegas proud to represent South Dakota. Coming home as the overall champions makes this incredibly special," Kayti Ratigan, LIV Hospitality's chief of operations, said in the company's announcement.

"Our team competed against some of the best hospitality professionals in the industry, and they showed exactly what we already knew: There is tremendous talent, pride and professionalism right here in South Dakota," Ratigan said.
LIV Hospitality's Linen Legends won first place all-around in its ISSA Housekeeping Olympics debut. (Amalia Roy)

For LIV Hospitality team member Adrianna Young Bear, making it to Las Vegas was an achievement in itself. She said she had followed the competition for years before her team finally got the opportunity to participate.
"I've been following the housekeeping competition for years. We finally made it here," Young Bear said. "This was a long journey for us to get here, and we finally did."

Young Bear said seasonal tourism can make it difficult to recruit and retain hospitality workers in South Dakota. She said the competition gave the group an opportunity to recognize the contributions of those employees.
"We are the backbone to every local town across the United States, across the world," Young Bear said.
SKYDIVING INJURY LEAVES 24-YEAR-OLD TOURIST STRANDED IN AUSTRALIA ON MEDICAL NO-FLY LIST
The vacuum competition had competitors race to clean a small patch of carpet the fastest. (Amalia Roy)

Over the years, the competition has also attracted attention beyond the hospitality industry. ISSA estimated that the 2025 event generated more than 50 million views and 750,000 social media engagements.

In August 2026, the competition made its ESPN8: The Ocho debut at ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex at Walt Disney World Resort as part of the network's celebration of unconventional sports and competitions.

A member of the Bellagio team said the event gave employees a chance to celebrate their work with colleagues from other hotels. The team practiced weekly for months, increasing rehearsals in the final weeks before the competition.
"It's an amazing experience for everybody to be able to see the hard work all the team members do on a daily basis," the team member said. "It's just for fun here, but they do this every day."

title: Obama-era homeless policy fueled crisis it promised to end, expert says as Trump admin makes striking reversal
summary: Homeless services veteran Michele Steeb says LA’s funding cutoff offers a chance to restore accountability after years of alleged mismanagement.
story: In an interview with Fox News Digital, homeless services veteran Michele Steeb says rising homelessness despite increased spending exposes deep flaws in the Housing First approach.

The Trump administration’s decision to permanently cut federal funding to Los Angeles’ scandal-plagued homeless agency marks a stunning reversal of an Obama-era policy that one expert said produced massive failures.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, homeless services veteran Michele Steeb broke down Tuesday’s announcement from the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that it is severing ties with the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA).

Steeb said the Housing First model adopted by LAHSA, which provides housing unconditionally without requiring individuals to pursue sobriety or mental health treatment, was championed by former President Barack Obama.

HUD’S HOMELESSNESS REFORMS PUT HUMAN LIVES AHEAD OF HOUSING BUREAUCRACYShe argued the model discouraged recovery by allowing people to remain in subsidized housing indefinitely, leaving fewer available units for others seeking permanent housing.

"So, back in 2013, when they instituted this, President Obama promised that this very different approach would end homelessness in a decade. And a decade later, we were at an almost 35% increase with no accountability," Steeb said, referring to the national homeless population.
Former President Barack Obama championed Housing First, an approach Michele Steeb argues failed to deliver on its promise to end homelessness. (Getty Images/File)
The program ultimately "eliminates purpose from individuals," Steeb said. "They're given housing for life without any requirements."
Earlier this year, Obama called Los Angeles' homelessness crisis a moral "atrocity," arguing that homelessness programs must pair assistance with accountability.
"We should recognize that the average person doesn’t want to have to navigate around a tent city in the middle of downtown," Obama said. "That’s a losing political strategy."
EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKID ROW

California, which adopted the model statewide, offers a particularly striking example of what Steeb views as its shortcomings. Despite significant government investment, homelessness has continued to climb rather than move toward the promised goal of ending it.
Steeb said homelessness in California surged 40% between 2016 and 2025, even as federal spending on homelessness increased at least 200% under the Housing First approach instituted in 2013.
The situation has been particularly stark in Los Angeles, where homelessness climbed between 60% and 70% over the past five years despite LAHSA receiving more than $1 billion in federal funding.

Homelessness climbed despite billions in spending, fueling calls from expert Michele Steeb for greater accountability and treatment requirements. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images/File)
LA HOMELESSNESS FRAUD CASES EXPOSE DEEPER PROBLEM THAN STOLEN MILLIONS, OVERSIGHT HAWK WARNS
Steeb said, despite the mounting evidence of failure, defenders of the system continued to blame the homelessness crisis on insufficient funding.
"It's a shame to me that the system, what I often call the homeless industrial complex, is trying to defend it," she said.
"It just has failed so massively. So, there's no excuses except that it was the wrong approach."

Los Angeles County will take over the embattled homeless agency’s responsibilities, though Michele Steeb questions how much the transition will improve services. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images/File)

Steeb said HUD's settlement represents an effort by the Trump administration to restore accountability to homeless services after LAHSA became embroiled in allegations of fraud and financial mismanagement.
The agency's funding will soon be transferred to Los Angeles County, according to officials.
Although Steeb acknowledged the county has its own problems, she hopes the transition could improve a system she believes has failed to address the crisis.

"I'm hopeful. … I think it's better than LAHSA, but I don't think it's going to be that much better," Steeb said.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Wife and daughter arrested after DNA IDs man whose severed head was found in trash bag
summary: Mary Fitzmaurice allegedly kept collecting her father's Social Security and pension benefits after his death, telling relatives he was still alive.
story: Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo explains how DNA identified a man whose severed head was found by a dog walker in 2022 and how investigators linked his wife and daughter to the case. Credit: Placer County Sheriff's Office
A California woman and her daughter were arrested more than four years after a woman walking her dog found a man's severed head in a trash bag, authorities said.

The Placer County Sheriff’s Office identified the man as Paul Wesley Fitzmaurice Jr., 73, who had never been reported missing. Authorities said his wife and daughter had told relatives the victim was still alive.
His daughter, 45-year-old Mary Fitzmaurice, and his wife, 75-year-old Georgia "Gwenn" Fitzmaurice, were booked into the South Placer Jail on Tuesday, officials said in a news release.
Mary was booked on suspicion of murder and Gwenn on suspicion of being an accessory.
DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

Georgia "Gwenn" Fitzmaurice, left, was booked on suspicion of being an accessory, and Mary Fitzmaurice was booked on suspicion of murder, the Placer County Sheriff’s Office said. (Placer County Sheriff's Office)

The women "kept up the facade to family and friends that Paul was still alive," Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo said at a news conference Wednesday. He said they continued receiving Fitzmaurice’s Social Security benefits and California public pension after his death.
Woo said the women told some of Fitzmaurice’s estranged relatives "he was being a recluse, and he would disappear for days at a time."
They claimed he "would come back to the house every week or so and stay for a couple of days," Woo said.
In its news release, the sheriff’s office alleged Mary killed her father and the two women "conspired to dispose of his remains."
A forensic illustration depicts the man investigators later identified through DNA as Paul Wesley Fitzmaurice Jr., 73. (Othram Inc.)

At Wednesday’s news conference, Placer County District Attorney Morgan Gire said prosecutors expected to file a murder charge against Mary Fitzmaurice by the end of the day and were weighing additional charges related to the killing and the collection of Fitzmaurice’s benefits.
Asked whether money was a motive, Woo said, "There’s still a lot of investigative work to be done, and I would be speculating on motive at this point."
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS

The Mosquito Fire was burning in the Foresthill area when a dog walker found a severed head in September 2022, Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo said. The discovery was made away from the fire. (Josh Edelson/AFP via Getty Images)
The dog walker found the bag on Sept. 28, 2022, in the Todd Valley area of Foresthill while the Mosquito Fire was burning nearby. Woo said the discovery drew little attention at the time.
"The people that didn’t forget about this case is the residents of Foresthill and our cold case detectives," Woo said.

The remains were too decomposed for investigators to identify the man. Forensic experts at California State University, Chico, helped produce an artist’s rendering, but it yielded no match in missing-person cases. A search of the national law enforcement DNA database also came up empty.

In January 2024, detectives sent a DNA sample to Othram Labs, which used forensic genetic genealogy to find possible distant relatives. With the FBI’s help, investigators traced the family tree and obtained a DNA sample from an out-of-state relative that helped confirm Fitzmaurice’s identity.
GIRL KNOWN AS 'CHELSEA JANE DOE' ID'D 26 YEARS AFTER MUTILATED BODY FOUND HUNDREDS OF MILES FROM HOME STATE
Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo speaks at a Nov. 18, 2026, news conference announcing a break in the 2022 Foresthill cold case. (Placer County Sheriff's Office)
Othram said in a news release that Fitzmaurice’s identification marked the 94th publicly announced case in California in which investigators used its technology to identify someone.
The sheriff’s office said in its release that investigators believe Mary killed her father at the family’s Citrus Heights home, which detectives searched Tuesday with help from the FBI.
When asked at the briefing where Fitzmaurice was killed, Woo said, "With evidence that we gathered and collected yesterday, we’ll hopefully determine that."

Woo said the rest of Fitzmaurice’s remains have yet to be found.
"We did not find any remains at the residence yesterday," he said.

title: Former Penn State frat brother indicted by federal grand jury in cocaine trafficking scheme
summary: Prosecutors say Agostino Abbatiello supplied cocaine to Penn State's Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon fraternities, where pledges packaged drugs as initiation.
story: From FIT's fentanyl poisoning to Penn State's cocaine ring, campus drug scares reveal how organized crime networks are targeting college students, Paul Mauro warns.
The alleged leader of a cocaine-trafficking ring at Penn State University has been indicted on drug distribution charges by a federal grand jury, adding to the state charges he is already facing.

Agostino Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was a "major supplier" of cocaine to at least two separate fraternities — Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon — at the university in State College, Pennsylvania, between January 2023 and December 2024, according to federal prosecutors.

Abbatiello, a former Sigma Chi member, frequently drove to Philadelphia and New York to buy cocaine before bringing his hauls back to campus and enlisting his fellow fraternity brothers and pledges to package the drugs for resale, according to federal and state authorities.
He'd allegedly return with as much as a kilogram each time, which factors heavily into the sheer number of charges he's facing.

Agostino Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was charged on Nov. 18, 2026, by a federal grand jury with one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distribution of cocaine. He is accused of leading a drug ring at Penn State from 2023 to 2024. (Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office)
PENN STATE COCAINE RING SUSPECT’S ATTORNEY WARNS OF ‘FOOLISH’ MOVE IN ALLEGED FRAT DRUG OPERATION

Abbatiello, who graduated in spring 2024, now faces one count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and six counts of distribution of cocaine; these charges could land him in prison for the rest of his life if he's convicted.

"College should be a marketplace of ideas and not illegal drugs," said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania in a statement. "Our office will continue working with the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s office, and with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and hold accountable those who profit from illegal drug activity in our communities."

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican and former York County district attorney, announced state charges against Abbatiello and his alleged co-conspirators in August following a joint investigation. In all, 14 people were charged at the state level.
Agostino Abbatiello arrives at Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pa., Sept. 2, 2026. (Kamil Krzaczynski for Fox News Digital)
PENN STATE FRAT COCAINE BUST BLOWS LID OFF WIDER STIMULANT SCOURGE HITTING COLLEGE CAMPUSES — AND BEYOND
Thomas Robinson, who Pennsylvania authorities said made regular trips to Philadelphia and New York to buy cocaine with Abbatiello, has not been indicted in federal court.
Another state defendant was Robinson's father, Paul Robinson, who state prosecutors said tried to conceal evidence in the case, including a safe containing drugs and cash.
Sunday described Abbatiello as "the top rung of the ladder for a high-level drug trafficking ring." Robinson was a "rung below that on the ladder," he added.

Agostino Abbatiello and Thomas Robinson are accused of being the main suppliers of cocaine for a massive distribution ring where 14 people were charged. (Getty Images: Rolf Vennenbernd/picture alliance; Attorney General Dave Sunday's Office)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

When he announced the state charges in August, Sunday said the cocaine was sold among Penn State students, often at parties. Investigators also found that packaging the drugs was used as an initiation ritual for fraternity pledges.
"We found a pattern of events that showed cutting and bagging cocaine was for some pledges an indoctrination into the Delta Upsilon and Sigma Chi fraternities," Sunday said.

A variety of different agencies have investigated the case, including Homeland Security Investigations, the State College Police Department and a narcotics unit within the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office.

title: Russian national accused of surveilling US tech company
summary: Russian national Igor D'iu was indicted for allegedly stalking Silicon Valley tech employees with tracking devices and fake IDs, the FBI says.
story: A Russian flag flies above the Russian Embassy in Berlin, Germany. (Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A grand jury indicted Russian national Igor D’iu on Wednesday on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking, and fraud in connection with identification documents in connection to alleged espionage of a U.S. company in Silicon Valley.

"Igor D’iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major U.S. technology company, using physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence," Roman Rozhavsky, Assistant Director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.

D'iu was arrested in October after allegedly being recruited by co-conspirators through the messaging platform Telegram to clandestinely target employees of a Silicon Valley defense and technology company.
FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL

D’iu's co-conspirators, who provided him with instructions, equipment, and financial support, told him his espionage was for "the Motherland," explaining that the company he was spying on was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine, according to an arrest affidavit.

A Patriot system received by Ukraine is seen on the Day of Ukrainian Air Force on August 4, 2024, in Unspecified, Ukraine. At the event for the Day of Ukrainian Air Force with the participation of President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyi, the first General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcons received by Ukraine were demonstrated. (Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

"Russia may rely on covert operatives and criminal intermediaries as it attempts to gain an edge in its war against Ukraine, but those tactics do not place its government or its collaborators beyond the reach of the law. This arrest should serve as a warning to anyone looking to undermine U.S. interests or threaten our national security: No matter where you are or who you’re working for, justice will find you," Rozhavsky added.

D'iu is accused of entering the U.S. illegally, traveling from Istanbul, Turkey to Mexico City, Mexico in June, at which point his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who was able to smuggle him across the border.

The operative was then instructed to surveil employees of the company at a Paolo Alto, California coffee shop, even directing him to attempt to remotely access information from employees' laptop computers at the cafe, according to the affidavit.
The Russian national engaged in sweeping surveillance activities, including searching for employee addresses and even following a female employee for 30 miles.
Aerial photograph looking northeast over downtown Palo Alto, California, with University Avenue running through the heart of the commercial district. (iStock via Getty Images)

"The employee attempted to evade D’iu by making irregular turns, taking back roads, and entering a grocery store parking lot. D’iu allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle. Fearing for her safety, the employee called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department’s Mission Station. D’iu allegedly abandoned his pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. Investigators also obtained evidence that D’iu had followed other company employees on preceding days," a Department of Justice statement about the indictment read.

"The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies," Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General M. Scott Proctor said in a statement.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow, and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of U.S. sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation. We will use every tool at our disposal to find, prosecute, and punish such conduct, wherever and whenever it happens," Proctor concluded.
D'iu faces up to 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines if convicted on all charges. He is next set to appear in federal court on Nov. 21.

China's President Xi Jinping stands as President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press via AP)

title: Charlotte wants Iryna Zarutska murder lawsuit tossed, says it can’t be held responsible
summary: Charlotte argues governmental immunity shields its transit policing decisions as it asks a judge to toss Iryna Zarutska's family's wrongful-death lawsuit.
story: U.S. Attorney of North Carolina's Western District Russ Ferguson discusses the case against the man accused of killing Iryna Zarutska on a North Carolina train after he was deemed incompetent to stand trial on ‘The Story.’

The city of Charlotte is asking a judge to throw out a wrongful-death lawsuit filed by Iryna Zarutska's family over security failures they say left her unprotected aboard the city's light-rail system, arguing many of those decisions are protected by governmental immunity.

Zarutska's murder drew national attention after surveillance video showed Decarlos Brown Jr. seated behind her aboard a Lynx Blue Line train before he is accused of stabbing her in the neck about four minutes after she boarded. The 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee had just left work at a local pizzeria.

Her family alleges Charlotte failed to adequately police and secure the light-rail system. The city now argues decisions involving transit policing, crime prevention, security contractors and public safety are government functions shielded from liability under North Carolina law.
PROSECUTORS SAY CHARLOTTE TRAIN STABBING CASE WON'T BE DISMISSED REGARDLESS OF COMPETENCY RULING

Charlotte's new filing also acknowledges there was no private security guard inside Zarutska's train car when she was killed, that Brown apparently boarded without presenting a ticket or pass and that the light-rail system operates without turnstiles or fare gates.
Iryna Zarutska curls up in fear as a man looms over her during a deadly attack on a Charlotte, N.C. light rail train. (NewsNation via Charlotte Area Transit System)
But the city denies those circumstances caused Zarutska's death, arguing Brown acted on his own and that the attack could not have been predicted based on previous crime across the transit system.
DEATH OF GREAT-GRANDMOTHER BRUTALLY KILLED ON TRAIN TRIGGERS FEDERAL ACTION
Zarutska's family sued Charlotte and its private transit security contractor, Professional Police Services, or PSS, in August, alleging security failures left riders vulnerable to violent crime.
Charlotte responded Monday with a 34-page filing asking a Mecklenburg County Superior Court judge to throw out the claims against the city.
MURAL HONORING MURDERED UKRAINIAN REFUGEE IRYNA ZARUTSKA TAKEN DOWN IN PROVIDENCE AFTER LOCAL OUTRAGE

Zarutska's family anticipated that defense in its lawsuit, arguing Charlotte waived immunity and that operating a light-rail system that charges fares amounts to a proprietary rather than governmental function.

The family's complaint alleges stronger fare enforcement, physical barriers and adequate security could have prevented Brown from boarding the train or carrying out the attack.

It cites findings from the North Carolina state auditor showing Charlotte and the Charlotte Area Transit System (CATS) planned to spend about $2.23 million on safety and security equipment in 2025 but spent about $470,000, leaving roughly $1.76 million unspent and some planned security work unfinished.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Tyler Robinson defense wants testing on bullet fragments paused in assassination of Charlie Kirk
summary: Tyler Robinson's lawyers want Utah ballistics testing paused as prosecutors push FBI virtual comparison microscopy on Charlie Kirk's autopsy fragments.
story: Finn reports on the upcoming court proceedings, the timeline leading up to the trial and the latest developments in the high-profile case surrounding Kirk's assassination.

Attorneys for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin Tyler Robinson are asking a Utah judge to put additional ballistics testing on pause as prosecutors attempt to conclusively link bullet fragments recovered at autopsy to the suspected murder weapon, which some experts call unnecessary and even prosecutors admit isn't central to their case.

The Utah County Attorney's Office has asked the judge to deny the motion, countering that the testing they are seeking will not consume the evidence or prevent Robinson's experts from having a look at it once the government is done — and that they have more compelling evidence to introduce at trial.

"There is no reason to believe the bullet fragments contain exculpatory evidence," Deputy Utah County Attorney Ryan McBride alleged in an opposition to the defense motion. "To the contrary, all the evidence points to the inculpatory value of the fragments."
TYLER ROBINSON JUDGE UNSEALS ATF REPORT IN ASSASSINATION OF CHARLIE KIRK

Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, listens during a preliminary hearing at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

Robinson has allegedly admitted to the shooting, he wrote. Three unspent cartridges in the rifle were consistent with the gunshot fired at Kirk. The bullet fragments were consistent with the suspected murder weapon, although they have not been conclusively identified to it. And police recovered video evidence and a Dremel tool consistent with etchings made on brass casings recovered in the rifle at the scene.

While the fragment testing, known as virtual comparison microscopy (VCM), won't destroy the evidence, it is expected to physically alter or even damage it, according to court filings. "Petals" from the fragments may be folded out of the way as investigators look for rifling markings on the underlying surface, according to prosecutors. The fragments may be cleaned, at least in a small area. And lead fragments may be cleaned or scraped. There is a risk that pieces break off during the process.
TYLER ROBINSON'S DEFENSE TEAM FIGHTS TO SEAL EVIDENCE AND PUNISH PROSECUTORS IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION

Bullet fragments are shown on a screen during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

Robinson's lawyers want the VCM testing placed on hold until they have a chance to examine and photograph the same evidence — or an order allowing a defense expert to observe the testing in person or via a video recording, something the FBI does not allow for a number of reasons, including contamination and national security concerns.
They argued that prior ATF testing already damaged the evidence, and the next round of testing could result in further harm.
CHARLIE KIRK JUDGE DENIES TYLER ROBINSON'S ATTEMPT TO HAVE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY REMOVED

Samantha Karner, a firearm and tool mark examiner for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, holds a model of a bullet while she testifies during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

"The ATF couldn’t conclusively connect the bullet fragment to the recovered rifle, but it couldn’t rule out the rifle either," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory agent who has been following the case. "That’s an important distinction, and it helps explain why prosecutors want the FBI to take another look."

He explained that VCM is a more advanced process than simply looking at the fragments under a microscope, a more traditional method. Even so, there's no guarantee that examiners will find a more conclusive link between the fragments and the suspected murder weapon.
CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY COMES FACE TO FACE WITH ACCUSED ASSASSIN FOR FIRST TIME
"If the markings are too damaged or simply aren’t there anymore, even the best technology can’t bring them back," Pack told Fox News Digital.

Robinson is accused of shooting Kirk at Utah Valley University during a Turning Point USA public speaking event on Sept. 10, 2025. During Kirk's autopsy, investigators recovered a bullet jacket fragment and four lead fragments from his body, according to prosecutors.

An image that shows ammunition, including a casing engraved with the words "TEST SHOT" is displayed during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)
CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

"If the bullet fragment is again altered to the point where no independent comparison is possible, then the degree of prejudice to the defendant is severe," Robinson's lawyers wrote to the court. "The defense will be unable to independently verify conclusions, cross-examination will be unfairly limited, and the jury will hear unchallengeable expert testimony."

Bernard Zapor, a former ATF special agent in charge and faculty associate at Arizona State University, said those concerns may be overblown. The fragments were already documented meticulously during the ATF's initial examination, he said, with photographs, data and images available to the defense through discovery. If the fragments are damaged during additional testing, it may not change much, since the initial testing was inconclusive — which he said is not unusual in shootings involving similar caliber weapons.
TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT RULING AS EVIDENCE DISMANTLES CHARLIE KIRK CONSPIRACY CLAIMS

Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

"This is all distracting from the purpose of getting information to the jury so they can come to a conclusion, one way or the other," he told Fox News Digital. "This case is solid. You don’t want to do anything to disrupt it."
Robinson's lawyers previously flagged in court that they intend to challenge the ATF's findings and methodology.

title: US infrastructure crumbles as adversaries power up – leaving Americans dangerously exposed: cyber expert
summary: A wave of tech failures highlights weaknesses in America’s aging infrastructure that adversaries could exploit with increasingly accessible cyberattack tools, experts warn.
story: Charles Tango, chief strategy officer at cybersecurity company Hydden, discussed how aging U.S. infrastructure could leave critical systems vulnerable to attacks by foreign adversaries.

A string of technology failures that left flights grounded and disrupted workplace software and banking systems is renewing concerns about weaknesses in America's critical systems foreign adversaries could exploit, according to experts.

Cybersecurity professionals warn that U.S. adversaries are closely watching how the country responds to such failures for weaknesses they could exploit. A disruptive cyberattack doesn’t necessarily require sophisticated tactics, they say, and America’s foes already have the capabilities to carry one out.
The National Security Agency on Tuesday experienced disruptions to internal systems during scheduled maintenance, though officials said its critical national security functions remained operational.

Apple joined the wave of tech companies experiencing problems on Tuesday impacting services including the App Store, Apple Music and iCloud sign-ins. The tech giant attributed the disruptions to an internal update, saying many systems have since been restored.
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK
The Three Mile Island Nuclear power plant is seen at sunset in Middletown, Pennsylvania. (Reuters/Shannon Stapleton)
One day earlier, a technology failure forced United Airlines to delay departing flights by over 90 minutes. There was no indication of a cybersecurity issue.

The latest disruptions followed Friday's nationwide ground stop triggered by the Federal Aviation Administration, which lasted over four hours, the longest in 25 years, creating travel disruptions that took airlines days to resolve.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on "Fox News Sunday" there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, stating that investigators are examining if faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the hours-long ground stop.

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. "But we're open, if we see something else, we're gonna continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement."
According to The Wall Street Journal, FAA radio sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and possibly Amarillo, Texas, overloaded the communications system used by air-traffic controllers.
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
Planes wait on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport in New York on Nov. 13, 2026. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)
Meanwhile, a Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday lasted for nearly 24 hours before service was restored Friday morning.
Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the issue was the result of a previously undetected software defect, increased traffic and reduced server capacity.
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
Also on Friday, Workday — whose human resources and payroll software is used by millions of Americans — experienced a widespread outage.
"Workday is currently unavailable," a message for users said. "We are experiencing a service interruption. Your service will be restored as quickly as possible."
PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT
On Monday, customers of several large banks — among them Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo — reported problems accessing online banking services.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 13, 2026. (Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images)
Chase acknowledged that some transactions were experiencing delays but noted that customers continued to have full access to their accounts and funds.
BILL GATES SOUNDS ALARM ON AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS, WARNS OF 'NEGATIVE SURPRISES' WITHIN A YEAR

While officials have said there is no indication Friday’s ground stop was caused by a foreign cyberattack, U.S. adversaries have the capability to deliberately disrupt American infrastructure, Charles Tango, chief strategy officer at cybersecurity company Hydden, told Fox News Digital.
He said any of America's adversaries have the capability to deliberately cause a disruption to the nation's infrastructure, and warned it's easier to pull off than many think.

"It does not take a lot of sophistication these days to cause this type of attack, especially with the advent of AI, it's made security attacks much easier and much cheaper, but absolutely other countries like China would have immense capability of impacting our environments," Tango said. "They've spent a lot of time and a lot of effort trying to compromise our critical infrastructure."

"Not all warfare needs to be kinetic these days. A cyber warfare can be very effective. We've seen that with Russia and Ukraine. We should be very mindful of the capacities that our adversaries have when it comes to cyber capability. Many of them specialize on offensive cyber capabilities, and that's what we should be focusing on," Tango said.
"Other countries like China would have immense capability of impacting our environments. And we've seen that recently with organizations like Volt Typhoon," he added.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES

Tango said aging systems, some within U.S. critical infrastructure, create vulnerabilities that capable adversaries can exploit, pointing to how a small equipment problem triggered a widespread disruption.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
A Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday lasted for nearly 24 hours before service was restored Friday morning. (Cesc Maymo)

"What we saw here is that one very small incident led to a widespread outage. That's because a lot of these systems are old. They've been around for a while. We haven't invested in upgrading them. And that's not just for the FAA. That's across critical infrastructure," Tango said.
SEND US A TIP
"I mean, the world is watching how we respond to this, and certainly our adversaries are watching this very, very closely," he added.
HACKERS COULD ALREADY BE INSIDE AMERICAN UTILITIES, CYBER EXPERTS WARN OF 'TROJAN HORSE' THREAT

The threat from foreign adversaries extends well past aviation. In 2024, federal cybersecurity agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon had compromised U.S. energy providers and other critical infrastructure organizations. Officials assessed the group was positioning itself to be able to disrupt essential services during a conflict or major crisis with the U.S.

Michael Balboni, a former New York homeland security adviser who also served as a New York Power Authority trustee and is currently president of Adelphi University, told Fox News Digital that reports of foreign adversaries accessing American power grids have long concerned officials.

"We had reports and information that, in fact, adversaries were in the grids across the country," Balboni told Fox News Digital. "And that, again, had been there for years. The question becomes, what is their capability?"

title: Major drug kingpin ‘The Kraken’ captured in California after yearslong hunt
summary: Alleged Guatemalan cocaine kingpin Axel Montejo Saenz, known as "Kraken," was arrested in San Diego after agents seized over 5,500 kilograms of cocaine, authorities said.
story: Dana Perino reports on former President Donald Trump's initiative to combat drug cartels in Ecuador. The U.S. is providing military and intelligence assistance to the South American nation, which is grappling with significant drug-related violence and has become a major cocaine exporter. This joint effort reflects a broader strategy to reassert U.S. influence and target transnational criminal groups, aiming for enhanced security in the region.
An alleged Guatemalan cocaine kingpin known as "Kraken" has been arrested in San Diego, and federal officials are offering up to $10 million for information that could lead to his conviction.
Axel Bladimir Montejo Saenz, 40, is accused of helping run a cocaine trafficking network with ties to narcoterrorist cartels.
Agents seized more than 5,500 kilograms of cocaine and $3.7 million linked to him during a yearslong investigation, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California.

The State Department also announced a separate reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Walfre Donaldo Calderon-Calderon, 44, known as "El Teniente Jr." Prosecutors say he leads a drug trafficking operation in northwestern Guatemala near the Mexican border.
EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY'

Montejo Saenz pleaded not guilty Nov. 9 in federal court in San Diego. Members of the Homeland Security Task Force arrested him on charges that he conspired to distribute cocaine bound for the United States and to distribute cocaine aboard a vessel. He faces up to life in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors allege the operation moved cocaine through at least six countries, including Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala and Mexico, and continued through November 2018. The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Montejo Saenz and the Los Huistas drug trafficking organization in 2022.

title: Pentagon detains senior US Army officer accused of spying for Russians after UK arrest
summary: Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was handed to U.S. military authorities after British counterterrorism police arrested him on suspicion of spying for Russia.
story: Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on a senior U.S. Army officer detained in Britain over suspected Russian espionage. Authorities are searching two locations as U.S. officials warn about insider threats.

A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday, days after British counterterrorism police arrested him on suspicion of violating national security laws.

Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England, on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
British authorities previously said the allegations involved Russia, which the Kremlin denied any connection to.
SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA
A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday. (Sarah Crabill/Getty Images, File)
The Associated Press, citing a U.S. official, reported that Tyner had not provided information to Russia.
Tyner's transfer followed consultations between British prosecutors, the U.K. attorney general's office and U.S. authorities, according to London's Metropolitan Police.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators referred the case to the Crown Prosecution Service, which consulted the attorney general's office and U.S. authorities before transferring the investigation.
RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES
Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested by British authorities Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England. (Jacob King/PA Images via Getty Images, File)

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the officer was in custody following a joint espionage investigation involving the FBI's Philadelphia field office, its London legal attaché office, British counterterrorism police, MI5, U.K. defense counterintelligence officials and U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk. That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase," Patel said.
FBI Director Kash Patel said Tyner was in custody following a joint espionage investigation. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commander of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, warned service members against violating their oath to defend the Constitution.
"This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution," Stinchon said.
Tyner was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday. (J. David Ake/Getty Images, File)
Tyner, who previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar, served as a senior human resources officer with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester.
The British-led multinational force, which includes personnel from 20 nations, is designed to respond rapidly to military crises and operations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP. (Sputnik/Sergey Guneev/Kremlin via Reuters, File)
"This arrest does not concern us in any way," Peskov said Nov. 11. "We don’t know what it’s connected to. We have nothing to do with this."

British police said Tyner's arrest was unrelated to other ongoing counterterrorism investigations.

According to a Nov. 13 statement from the U.S. Army, Tyner entered active-duty service in January 2008 and deployed to Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017, and Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020.

title: Man legally named Captain America charged with murder after allegedly giving victim’s girlfriend chilling note
summary: A man legally named Captain America allegedly gave a woman a note saying her boyfriend was dead and demanding her money. Police later found the boyfriend dead inside a home.
story: Captain C. America is charged with murder after allegedly handing his co-worker’s girlfriend a note saying her boyfriend was dead and demanding money. She escaped, and police found Khanh Dinh dead in Peoria, Illinois, prosecutors say.
An Illinois woman giving her boyfriend’s co-worker a ride escaped after he allegedly handed her a chilling note saying her boyfriend was dead and demanding all her money.
Police then went to check on her boyfriend and found his body inside a Peoria home.
The passenger, Captain C. America, 34, was charged with first-degree murder in the death of Khanh Dinh, 63, according to Peoria County State’s Attorney Jodi M. Hoos’ office.
COWORKER ACCUSED OF SLASHING WOMAN’S THROAT DURING RIDE HOME, VICTIM ESCAPED MOVING CAR: POLICE

Captain C. America, right, was charged with first-degree murder in the death of Khanh Dinh, 63. The Peoria neighborhood where police found Dinh dead is pictured at left. (Google Maps/Tazewell County Sheriff's Office)
The encounter unfolded Friday, Nov. 13, when the woman was driving America, whom she knew because he worked with Dinh, prosecutors said.
"While in the car, the defendant handed her a note that said her boyfriend was dead and demanded all of her money," Hoos’ office said.
SUSPECT IN CUSTODY FOR ALLEGED MURDER OF COLLEGE STUDENT AFTER POLICE RELEASED EERIE SURVEILLANCE PHOTOS
The North Sheridan Road area in Peoria, Illinois, where police found 63-year-old Khanh Dinh dead during a welfare check Nov. 13, 2026. (Google Maps)
The woman managed to get away and call police in neighboring Tazewell County. Officers tracked down America and took him into custody shortly afterward, prosecutors said.
When officers removed him from a squad car, they found the note the woman had described.
GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD’S PARTNER, KEN URKER, FOUND DEAD INSIDE HIS LOUISIANA HOME: SHERIFF
A Peoria Police Department patrol vehicle is pictured in this file image. (Peoria Police Department Facebook)
The woman's account led Peoria officers to a home on North Sheridan Road, where they arrived for a welfare check at about 7:14 p.m., police said.
Inside, they found Dinh dead. A preliminary autopsy indicated he died from blunt-force head trauma, according to prosecutors.
Hoos’ office announced the murder charge Monday. Authorities have not publicly identified a motive in statements released about the case.

America, whose full legal name is Captain Cautious America, was previously known as Mark Anderson. He changed his name about a decade ago because he hoped to run for political office and wanted to stand out on the ballot, according to The Peoria Journal Star.
America remains in the Tazewell County Jail, where Peoria police said he was being held on unrelated charges. A Nov. 14 jail booking entry lists an unlawful restraint charge.

title: California sheriff's deputy, special officer put on leave after 5-second conversation with ICE agents
summary: Two California sheriff's department employees are on administrative leave after video captured a five-second ICE exchange outside a county jail.
story: The exchange happened shortly before ICE agents detained a man hiding in a public courtyard, authorities said. (Credit: Orange County Sheriff’s Department)

Two California sheriff's department employees have been placed on administrative leave pending an investigation after a five-second conversation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers outside a county jail.
The Orange County Sheriff's Department announced Friday that surveillance video captured the Oct. 31 exchange outside the Intake Release Center.
A deputy and a sheriff’s special officer (SSO) were seen leaving the facility, approaching an SUV and "appearing to have a five-second conversation" with ICE officers, the department said.
Moments after the sheriff's deputy and security officer walked away, a second vehicle arrived.
EXCLUSIVE: LA ICE DIRECTOR REVEALS OFFICERS FOLLOWED HOME, HARASSED AS POLICE FAIL TO HELP IN SANCTUARY CITY

The Orange County Sheriff's Department put a deputy and jail officer on leave pending an investigation after video footage showed them having a five-second exchange with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers moments before a man hiding in a public courtyard was detained. (Orange County Sheriff's Department)
The ICE officers exited both vehicles and entered a public courtyard outside the visitor's entrance.
There, they detained a man who appeared to be hiding, according to the sheriff's department. Authorities did not release the man's name or why he was detained.
NEW MAINE LAW LIMITS POLICE COOPERATION WITH FEDERAL IMMIGRATION OFFICIALS

The sheriff's department has opened an internal investigation into the incident, which raises questions regarding compliance with California's Values Act (SB 54), a state law that strictly limits how local law enforcement can assist federal immigration authorities.
Orange County Sheriff Don Barnes said his agency takes public safety and state compliance seriously.
MARYLAND SHERIFF TORCHES DEMOCRATS OVER LAW HE SAYS PUTS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FIRST
Video released by the Orange County Sheriff's Department shows a man being detained by immigration authorities outside a county jail on Oct. 31. (Orange County Sheriff's Department)
"I will fully cooperate with ICE to the extent the law allows to prevent serious criminal offenders from returning to the communities they have preyed upon," Barnes said in a statement.
"Personnel acting outside the law and Department policy will be held appropriately accountable.

"We will enforce state and local laws equally, without bias, and without concern for anyone’s citizenship," he added. "I want the community to continue to feel safe in calling for assistance, reporting crime and visiting the jail regardless of their immigration status."

"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country."
"Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country, including in California," the statement added.

Local law enforcement worked with DHS, including helping to make 40,000 arrests in Florida and a two-week operation in West Virginia that resulted in the arrest of over 650 illegal aliens, the agency said.

title: Veteran pilot: Congress must act to update 'archaic' FAA tech that is 'putting Americans in danger'
summary: Retired Air Force pilot Buzz Patterson warns the FAA ground stop will happen again, blaming "tribal" politics for delaying a $50 billion modernization.
story: With holiday travel looming, retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson warns that 30 years of lawmakers ‘kicking the can’ have left pilots and passengers ‘in danger’ due to outdated tech, as evidenced by the FAA's recent nationwide ground stop.

Friday's historic FAA ground stop will not be the last, a retired Air Force veteran and commercial pilot warns, unless Congress takes action and provides funds for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to update what he calls a "broken" and "archaic" system that is "putting Americans in danger."

"It's time for both parties to step up and say our AT system is degraded, it's old," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson, who carried the nuclear football for former President Bill Clinton and is a retired 16-year Delta Air Lines pilot, told Fox News Digital in an interview this week.

"We're putting Americans in danger when they get into an airplane, and we're putting the air crews in danger when they get into an airplane, if we continue to fly under archaic system, and that's what we're doing right now, it's archaic."
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP
Too many administrations from both parties have "kicked the can" down the road on the complex and pricy overhaul, according to Patterson.

"We've dug a big hole here, and we're trying to dig out of it," he said. "It's not going to take place overnight. It's going to be a long, grinding, devoted effort, and I think it's time for our politicians to get on board and fix it."
TRUMP'S $50B AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL OVERHAUL FACES GOP PUSHBACK AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Patterson, who just moved to Nevada and bought a new home he is renovating, said the $50 billion cost now laid bare by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy this weekend is akin to buying a home and immediately renovating it: Double down for the long-term benefits, if not savings.

"Our technology, I mean, we're still using floppy disks, for God's sakes, in some of our facilities," Patterson lamented. "Last time I was in a tower, they were still using paper scripts to show what airplanes were supposed to taxi next. This should all be automated ... I mean, this should be easy-peasy, and we've made it so difficult."

"We have way, way too much traffic to have an antiquated 1970s technology trying to drive our airplanes around the skies," he added, noting he "can't tell you the number of traffic avoidance calls I've gotten from ATC over the years that if I had not heard them, I probably would have hit somebody, or they would have hit me: so, it's essential."

Patterson, who now flies frequently as a commercial passenger himself, stressed that aviation safety transcends party lines and urged Washington to abandon what he called "tribal" politics to pass comprehensive modernization funding.

"It should be bipartisan, because I think if only one party pushes it, tries to push it through, it's not going to have success," he said. "I don't care what your political affiliation is: If you want to fly safely in our country, regardless of where you're going, or who you are, then you should be able to. And right now I think it's become tribal, where Democrats don't want to do anything that supports Trump or the FAA, and Trump's trying to get some stuff done."
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS
Even President Donald Trump is "late" to conduct the overdue modernization, but he is also facing congressional gridlock, too, Patterson lamented.
"He's late, granted, he's late, but every other president's been late too – and so Duffy asking for $50 billion, I understand that is probably too little, too late, but it's a start."

While praising the dedication of current air traffic controllers and flight crews, Patterson warned that human skill can only compensate for technological limitations for so long. He noted that pilots still rely heavily on traditional voice radio relays rather than seamless, automated cockpit-to-ground data and weather integration, recalling numerous midair traffic avoidance calls from controllers over his career that prevented potential collisions.
BUTTIGIEG TRASHES DUFFY’S GROUND STOP RESPONSE, BUT HIS DOT FAILURES DOOM HIS 2028 BID
Patterson said weather radar, FAA and ATC can all be upgraded to improve airline safety, noting the recent Learjet 60 crash in Florida.

"You don't fly through that stuff, you just don't," Patterson said of the Learjet 60 crash that featured pilots seeking a direct route through a thunderstorm. "If you do, you're going realize why you don't, because it's going to bang the crap out of you if you get through it. And in this, in this case, they didn't get through it."
FLORIDA PLANE CRASH INVESTIGATORS SAY WEATHER CONDITIONS A 'MAJOR FOCUS,' PLANE MAY HAVE STARTED TO BREAK UP
Communications, weather radar, routers and copper to fiber optic wiring upgrades all go hand-in-hand for safety, according to Patterson.

"There is an interconnectivity between the National Weather Service and the FAA," he said. "There's an interconnectivity there that could be had if we upgrade our ATC capabilities, and we can somehow connect.

"And it shouldn't be too hard to connect the National Weather Service directly to the cockpit, and I think that's where we're going to have to go, and I think that's necessary. And it's also not ironic that the same day ATC went down, the National Weather Service went down. I'm not saying it was a coordinated activity. I'm just saying that is the basis of our aviation system.

"And if we don't have the most advanced air traffic control technology and the most advanced weather technology, then we, as the world's superpower, we have failed dramatically, and I think that's where we are."
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK
With peak holiday travel approaching, Patterson warned that systemic meltdowns will continue to disrupt the flying public until Washington commits to a sustained, multiyear overhaul.

"I'm going to say this won't be the last one; it's going happen again," Patterson said of the nationwide ground stop. "It's probably going happen on Thanksgiving Eve or Christmas Eve, and people are going to wonder why it's happening, and I'm going tell you why it's happening: It's because our infrastructure is broken, and our ATC needs help, and the FAA needs help."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think Sean Duffy is doing a phenomenal job," he concluded. "He's done more as a DOT guy than anybody that I can possibly remember since I started flying, and I think that what we're seeing right now is decades of neglect on the part of both parties. I mean, I'm not going to absolve Republicans either, because I'm looking at this as a pilot and as an American with a family, and I want to be able to fly my family safely around the country, and I don't feel safe putting my family on an airplane right now until we figure this out."

title: Criminal past of Illinois ethanol plant bomb scare suspect includes multiple felonies, 2 prison stints
summary: Andrew Kozak, the BioUrja worker accused in the Peoria bomb threat, has a criminal past spanning four Nebraska counties, Fox News Digital reports.
story: FBI Special Agent in Charge Ryan Presley commends law enforcement partners after a credible explosive device is found in Peoria. Presley urges the public to report suspicious behavior to help defend the homeland.

An Illinois ethanol plant worker with a lengthy criminal past was federally indicted Tuesday after prosecutors said he emailed a threat claiming explosive devices had been placed at the facility where he worked.
A federal grand jury indicted Andrew M. Kozak on Tuesday on charges of threats regarding explosives and interstate communications of a threat.
Prosecutors allege Kozak emailed BioUrja Renewables on Friday indicating that explosive devices had been placed at the company's Peoria facility.
LIVE EXPLOSIVE DEVICE FOUND NEAR HOMELAND SECURITY OFFICE IN CLEVELAND, FORCING MASS EVACUATIONS
The email threatened to damage and destroy a building and other property "by means of fire and an explosive," according to the indictment.
Federal investigators swarmed a sprawling Illinois ethanol plant that spans 44½ football fields. (FBI Springfield Office)

NBC Chicago previously reported that Kozak, 41, of Chillicothe, had worked at BioUrja for about 10 months and allegedly planted the explosive device before sending the threat, citing federal law enforcement sources.
The indictment does not accuse Kozak of physically planting the explosive device found at the facility.

During a news conference Tuesday, federal officials declined to say who built or planted the explosive device, how many devices were involved or how powerful the device was. They also would not say whether anyone else may have been involved.
FBI Springfield Special Agent in Charge Ryan Presley said most bomb threats investigated by law enforcement are ultimately deemed not credible.
Andrew Kozak, as seen in a booking photo, has ben charged with making a bomb threat at the place of his employment, BioUrja ethanol plant, in Peoria, Illinois. (Courtesy Peoria Police Department)
"But in this instance, it was," Presley said. "Had it not been for the swift action of the responders and the bomb technicians, this incident could have had a very different outcome."
Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said about 2,500 homes were evacuated as authorities responded to the threat.

Kozak returned to BioUrja for work Monday morning and was taken into custody when he arrived, NBC Chicago reported, citing federal sources. FBI agents also executed a search warrant at his Chillicothe home, according to the outlet.
Kozak has a criminal past that includes several burglary-related felony convictions across four Nebraska counties and two stints in state prison, records reviewed by Fox News Digital show.
Andrew Kozak, 41, was federally indicted Tuesday on charges stemming from an emailed threat involving explosive devices at the BioUrja Renewables plant in Peoria, Illinois. (Andrew Kozak/LinkedIn)
Kozak's criminal history stretches back two decades.
Court and corrections records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Kozak was convicted of multiple burglary-related felonies across Platte, Polk, Nance and Colfax counties in Nebraska.
In Platte County, Kozak pleaded no contest to three felony burglary charges after initially facing seven burglary counts and one attempted burglary charge.
A judge found him guilty and determined Kozak was "not a fit and proper person" for probation before sentencing him to three to five years in prison.
Kozak was also convicted in two Polk County felony burglary cases. One court record identifies Osceola High School, while another shows Kozak was ordered to pay restitution to Osceola Public Schools.
In Nance County, Kozak was convicted of attempted felony burglary and sentenced to 20 months to five years in prison.
MASSIVE CHEMICAL FIRE ERUPTS AT ELECTRICAL TRANSFORMER PLANT IN MISSISSIPPI, FORCING EVACUATION

The BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, where authorities discovered an explosive device Friday, prompting a one-mile evacuation and a federal investigation. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Nebraska corrections records show Kozak was released on discretionary parole in August 2008.

He later returned to state prison on a separate Colfax County burglary conviction carrying a three-to-five-year sentence. Kozak was released on discretionary parole in October 2014, and his parole expired in May 2015.
CAR LOADED WITH EXPLOSIVES SLAMS INTO LAVISH PORTLAND SOCIAL CLUB, BOMB SQUAD STILL PULLING OUT LIVE DEVICES
The investigation began Friday afternoon when workers at BioUrja reported receiving a bomb threat. About an hour later, authorities located a suspicious package near the facility.
The device was deemed a credible threat, triggering the evacuation of homes and businesses within a one-mile radius.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
"I can just tell you it was deemed a credible threat," Dixon said Saturday. "There's an extensive criminal investigation going on."
Authorities warned that BioUrja houses large quantities of ethanol and other highly combustible materials, raising concerns about the potential consequences of an ignition.
Bomb technicians rendered the device safe, and authorities searched the facility without finding additional suspicious devices. The evacuation order was lifted Saturday after nearly a full day.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
No injuries were reported.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
NBC Chicago reported that Peoria County Jail records listed Kozak as being held on an FBI hold Monday. He no longer appeared in the county's online inmate search Tuesday morning.
SEND US A TIP
Fox News Digital requested Kozak's booking photograph and records from the Peoria County Sheriff's Office and asked whether he had been transferred from the jail.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Fox News Digital also reached out to BioUrja Renewables for comment and information about Kozak's reported employment, and to the ATF for information about the explosive device.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Authorities have not publicly established a motive.
