title: Israeli shepherds report suspected 'agricultural terror' targeting livestock
summary: An official source says dozens of animal poisoning cases have emerged in the West Bank, with contaminated cisterns and food bait found across grazing areas.
story: In the highly contested West Bank, Israeli officials received reports regarding animal poisonings across grazing areas. The incidents are being viewed as ‘acts of terror’ by Palestinian militants.  (Video: Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL.)

A series of suspected animal poisonings has raised concerns among Israeli security officials, farmers and regional leaders about the growing threat to agricultural communities. Farmers say the attacks have resulted in significant livestock losses and warn that poisoned food and water sources could also endanger other animals and nearby residents.

An Israeli source told Fox News Digital that military officials are taking reports of animal poisoning on Jewish-owned farms in the West Bank, known more commonly in Israel as Judea and Samaria, describing the incidents as "agricultural terror."

The trend gained attention following an investigation by The Press Service of Israel (TPS-IL) that identified a cluster of poisoning incidents at farms across the Binyamin region over the past 12 months.
CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND

A herd of goats grazes at an Israeli farm near the West Bank in July 2026. Local Israeli agricultural workers say Palestinian militants have carried out a series of poisoning attacks against their livestock since November 2025. (Yoav Dudkevitch/TPS-IL)
In a TPS-IL video, an Israeli farmer alleged that poisonings took place with substances placed within food such as dates and pita bread.

"We have two populations with warm blood," the source said, referring to Israelis and Palestinians in the contested region. "Sometimes this manifests as verbal or physical violence, attacks, arson, property damage and, among other things, agricultural terrorism involving harm to animals."

The source added that, "Lately, we have been receiving more and more reports of attempts by Palestinians to poison animals. We are talking about dozens of cases as we have seen in recent weeks … We act against terror. For instance, if we receive intelligence or information that a Palestinian intends to poison someone or has done so in the past, we will act to detain him, of course."

The source advised farmers to remain in approved grazing areas, mark livestock as instructed and file a complaint for every incident to the relevant authorities, noting that animal poisoning is considered a cruel act.
VANCE’S MIDTERM BLAME GAME HITS SNAG AS TRUMP’S OWN ISRAEL AMBASSADOR DISPUTES KEY CLAIM

An Israeli shepherd looks at a dead goat from his herd that he says was poisoned by Palestinian militants. Local shepherds report a series of livestock poisoning attacks in the area since November 2025. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

Evyatar Karo, one of the leaders of the farming movement whose Metzudat David farm is located in the Binyamin region north of Jerusalem, has been among the hardest hit by the poisonings. He told Fox News Digital that the incidents began in Nov. 2025. Karo said he went out to the pasture, as he did every day, and spotted one of his goats lying on the ground, gasping for air and drooling. He then saw another goat in the same condition.
"Suddenly, we found dates scattered about — strange, because they weren't natural; they had a blue substance inside," he said.
Karo said he mixed veterinary medication with water and administered it to the goats in an attempt to prevent the toxin from spreading through their bodies. One goat survived, but four died.
A poisoned diet was found near an area where Israeli farmers and shepherds take goats and sheep to graze. Palestinian militants are blamed for poisoning Israeli livestock. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

"We brought in the Nature and Parks Authority to investigate the matter. The poison is lethal. If the carcass of an animal that died from this substance is left in the field, it poses a danger to other animals that might eat it. It works like a chain that can affect other wildlife," he told Fox News Digital.
ISRAEL’S E1 PLAN EXPLAINED: THE JERUSALEM-AREA CORRIDOR SPARKING INTERNATIONAL BACKLASH
Karo claimed that one of the poisons used was Lannate, a broad-spectrum carbamate insecticide commonly used by farmers, but said it was being deployed in highly concentrated form.
"We lost 25 animals. It’s a terrible thing. The animals just die in your hands. They scream and cry. You can see them choking — it’s a horrible substance," he said.
Karo said police had opened an investigation, but he feared the incidents could escalate.

"It’s not just me, either — it involves a whole network, a lot of places. It occurred in Gush Etzion and Shiloh, including incidents involving poisoned water cisterns," he said. "We are speaking of organized Palestinian squads. They see where we take our animals and spread the poison there. It starts with animal lives, but eventually they can hurt people."
An Israeli shepherd checks a well for poison in July 2026. The poisonings are being blamed by Israeli farmers and shepherds on Palestinian militants. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

TPS-IL recorded further suspected poisoning incidents in January and February 2026, followed by several additional cases. Among them were the discovery of contaminated water in approximately 10 cisterns near Alon Road, close to al-Mughayyir, on May 5; an incident at Shlisha Farm on June 7, in which two sheep were killed and around 15 others fell ill; and the discovery of poisoned food bait near Tel Talpiot, close to Gush Shiloh, in July. In the latter case, two guard dogs died within minutes, and a goat reportedly also died.

But the Palestinians are also accusing the Israeli settlers of taking revenge against their livestock. The official Palestinian Authority news agency, WAFA, reported last Thursday that 13 sheep died, and several others suffered poisoning after an alleged attack by "Israeli colonists" west of al-Auja, north of Jericho.

Sheep owner Suleiman Mleihat told WAFA that dozens of "Israeli settlers" sprayed toxic substances on an area where his flock was grazing. He added that a veterinarian had examined the animals and determined that poisoning caused the deaths.
Mleihat said his sheep are kept on a farm on the outskirts of the area, which is frequented daily by local Israelis and security forces.

While they are often grouped under the term "Hilltop Youth" — a label associated with individuals who establish outposts in volatile areas near Palestinian communities, sometimes leading to violent clashes — most residents of Judea and Samaria reject the name.

Yisrael Ganz, governor of the Binyamin region and chairman of the Yesha Council, an umbrella organization representing Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria, warned that anyone willing to poison a goat could eventually target local residents.
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER
An Israeli farm in the West Bank in July 2026. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

"It could be a child tomorrow who sees the dates on the ground and eats them. Think about a shepherd who takes his children out into the area. If they’re able to poison our water sources, they could hurt thousands of people," Ganz told Fox News Digital. "They killed goats, dogs and cows, and we are sure we will be the next targets. It could happen today, with the same dates left near a playground or daycare.

"The terrorists will have no more mercy for humans than they do for goats," he continued. "When someone kills goats to terrorize the shepherd, they can kill the shepherd, too. When someone says he wants to kill you and has found a way to do so, you have to worry that one day he will succeed. We don’t have to wait for that."

An Israeli farmer points to blue powder on the ground of a farm in the West Bank in July 2026. The substance is connected to a broader wave of incidents, which began in November 2025, when Israeli farmers reported their livestock being targeted and killed amid ongoing tensions with Palestinians. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

Ganz cited 16 incidents but said the increasing frequency was his greatest concern. Recently, he said, incidents had occurred almost every week. "When they see that they are succeeding, they improve their techniques," he said.
Ganz said dozens of body cameras funded by donors had been distributed to shepherds as an immediate response, but stressed that this could not replace action by the authorities.
He said addressing the incidents was a top priority, warning that if poison reached water sources serving Jerusalem or other parts of Judea and Samaria, it could result in a major attack.

Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) told Fox News Digital that the Civil Administration takes reports of suspected poisoning involving grazing areas, water sources or animals very seriously and works to investigate every case brought to its attention.

Through its Agriculture Unit, the Civil Administration maintains ongoing cooperation and communication with relevant authorities and their professional counterparts to ensure a safe environment for animals in Judea and Samaria and address agricultural and animal-related needs.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A flock of sheep on an Israeli farm near the West Bank in July 2026. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

"Upon receiving a report, the unit's professional personnel conduct field inspections, collect findings and evidence, and, when necessary, take samples of the suspected substance and submit them for testing at specialized laboratories, including the Ministry of Agriculture's laboratories in Beit Dagan, in order to determine the circumstances of the incident and establish a professional assessment of the situation. Based on the findings and identified needs, the unit coordinates assistance, including the provision of medicines, food and water," COGAT said.

"The potential effects of toxic substances on soil, water sources and the environment depend, among other factors, on the type of substance, its concentration and the characteristics of the affected area. Therefore, each case is assessed individually. The Civil Administration attaches great importance to environmental protection in Judea and Samaria and acts within its authority to identify and address environmental hazards," it added.
COGAT emphasized that investigating these incidents and taking action against those responsible falls under the jurisdiction of the Israel Police.
Fox News Digital contacted the Israel Police but did not receive a response before publication.
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Bukele gets hero’s welcome from afar as thousands rally in Haiti after gang crackdown
summary: Thousands marched in Haiti to thank Nayib Bukele for sending troops to battle violent gangs, prompting an emotional response from the Salvadoran president.
story: Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele says his troops will rescue four missing technicians by force if Haitian gangs refuse to hand them over. (Reuters.)
Thousands of people in Haiti took to the streets Tuesday in a show of support for Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele deploying troops to the country to combat violent armed gangs.
The demonstration unfolded as Haiti's Minister of Justice and Public Security, Patrick Pélissier, prepared to travel to San Salvador to discuss anti-gang strategies and ongoing troop cooperation.
The president reflected on the moment in a post on X, sharing a video capturing a sea of people chanting, dancing and cheering in celebration.
"I never expected anything like this. I hear you loud and clear. I love you too. We will triumph. God will give us victory," Bukele said.
BUKELE WARNS HAITIAN GANG LEADERS THAT HIS FORCES WILL 'FINISH' THEM AS HE DID IN EL SALVADOR

Demonstrators gather during a rally to express support for Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Salvadoran troops involved in efforts to combat gangs in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Nov. 17, 2026. (Reuters/Fildor Pq Egeder)
According to Reuters, some demonstrators carried signs reading "Long live Bukele" and "Down with the gangs," while others voiced their support for the Salvadoran leader.
"Only a week of operation, we can see the path to change in Haiti. We say thank you to Bukele for all the help he gives us," demonstrator Claudy Mayas said.
Another demonstrator said Bukele was providing Haitians with the one thing they had been waiting years for.
"Four years ago, I could not go to Champs de Mars. I couldn't go to the south of Haiti," a demonstrator, also identified as Claude, said.
"We don’t ask much of the government. We don’t ask for jobs. We need only security."
ROBOT DOGS MOUNTED WITH RIFLES DEPLOYED IN ANTI-GANG STADIUM OPERATION IN HAITI
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele told Haitian supporters "We will triumph" after thousands rallied to thank him for sending troops to fight gangs. (Alex Pena/Anadolu via Getty Images/File)

Just two weeks ago, Bukele backed an operation involving devastating airstrikes that destroyed the headquarters of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti's most powerful criminal gangs. The home of its leader, Lanmò San Jou, was also targeted in the operation, Bukele previously said.
The direct military action marked a dramatic escalation in Haiti's fight against years of severe gang violence and insecurity.

Bukele joined the mission after four Salvadoran members of the U.N.-backed anti-gang force went missing in a suspected gang ambush near Port-au-Prince on Oct. 18. At the time, Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti.
EL SALVADOR-BACKED AIR ASSAULT DESTROYS HAITI GANG HEADQUARTERS AMID SEARCH FOR MISSING TROOPS
A demonstrator carries a Salvadoran flag during a rally to express support for El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele, in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Nov. 17, 2026.  (Reut3ers/Fildor Pq Egeder)
While residents paraded through the streets in celebration, U.N. officials issued a statement Tuesday reminding leaders that anti-gang operations must prioritize civilian protection.
"Security forces must strictly limit the use of lethal force to situations where it is unavoidable to protect life from an imminent threat and as a last resort," the agency said.
According to the U.N., armed gangs control an estimated 80% to 90% of Haiti's capital and are expanding into surrounding regions.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Between January and October 2026 alone, the U.N. documented nearly 4,600 people killed, alongside the wider displacement of nearly 1.5 million people.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Iran warns Bahrain monarchy its survival is at risk amid push to 'evict' US Fifth Fleet
summary: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Bahrain's monarchy its survival is in doubt as drones and missiles hit the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet home.
story: Iran’s attacks on Bahrain threaten key US naval hub, raise stakes for American forces, says Iran expert.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned Wednesday that Bahrain's monarchy faces an existential threat as Iranian drones and missiles targeted U.S. military installations in the Gulf kingdom.

Tehran's warning came amid renewed attacks on Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, and a regional expert warned of Iran's decades-long efforts to destabilize the island nation and assert territorial claims.

"This is a regime that has tried to inflame tensions there for quite literally several decades and has claims to the island nation as well," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
BAHRAIN INTERCEPTS IRANIAN DRONES TARGETING US RADAR AFTER 2-MONTH LULL IN GULF STRIKES
Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa (Benoit Tessier/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
"The Islamic Republic is also trying to use military force to evict the United States from the region," he added.

In a warning directed at Bahrain's ruling Al Khalifa family, IRGC Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi accused the monarchy of cooperating with military action against Iran, relying on U.S. protection and challenging Shiite religious authority.

"Colluding in the aggression against Islamic Iran, living inside the American security bubble, and encroaching on the authority of the Shiite religious leadership are three fundamental mistakes being made by the Al Khalifa regime," Mohebbi wrote on X.
IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi, left, and President Donald Trump. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters; Bonnie Cash/Pool/Sipa USA/Reuters)
"If it persists in them, its survival under the new regional security order will be in doubt," he warned.
"A word to the wise is enough."
Mohebbi's threat also followed a Bahraini crackdown on Shiite religious leaders.

On Monday, a criminal court sentenced dozens of Shiite clerics to life in prison on terrorism-related charges after prosecutors accused them of collaborating with Iran and plotting to undermine the government.

Bahrain's Public Prosecution agency said investigators uncovered communications between some defendants and Iranian authorities, including the IRGC, and accused the clerics of supporting terrorism and sabotage aimed at overthrowing the monarchy.
"The Islamic Republic has a panoply of gripes against Bahrain as well as against the ruling royal family of that country," Taleblu said.
"Some are sectarian, some are political, some are strategic, and some, again, have to do with the U.S. force presence in the region," the expert explained.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
Fox News' Jennifer Griffin reported that Iran appeared to hit the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, but no casualties were reported. (Fox News)
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, a critical hub for American naval operations across the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters.

The latest regional escalation follows repeated Iranian drone attacks targeting American military equipment in Bahrain, including a U.S. radar installation Tehran claimed to have targeted for the third time in less than a week. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said the attacks were intercepted.
Bahrain also reported intercepting Iranian attacks early Wednesday, a day after the IRGC claimed to have struck a base used by American forces.

"The regime is also looking for places close to its territory where it can land blows against the U.S.—as well as against the order that has allowed the U.S. to be in the region for quite some time—and to be able to do so on the cheap," Taleblu said.
IRAN ESCALATES IN HORMUZ, CLAIMS STRIKE ON OMANI ISLAND IT SAYS 'ENEMY' USES FOR US MILITARY OPS

Smoke rises after an Iranian drone was intercepted over the Bahrain Financial Harbour towers, which houses the Israeli embassy, amid the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, in Manama, Bahrain, March 6, 2026. Picture taken on a mobile phone. (Stringer/Reuters)
"They want to be able to generate pain against the U.S. more broadly in the region and do so in places that have already been hit."
Taleblu also said Iran's strategy is designed not only to damage American military assets but to increase pressure on Bahrain's monarchy to reconsider hosting U.S. forces.

"They've done this to limit the space for the U.S. to actually operate from the region and try to create tougher political conditions for the ruling family in that country to keep that U.S. force presence there."
He warned that the growing missile and drone threat could force Washington to reassess its long-term military presence in the Persian Gulf.

"Now that the war is out of the shadows and the weapons being used are missiles and drones, the future of the U.S. footprint in the region will be based on whether America can afford to build and defend bases so close to an adversary's territory under fire," Taleblu said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The test case as to what the U.S. does with the Fifth Fleet in Bahrain, and with the radars in that country, could actually be a harbinger of what the future of the U.S. footprint in the CENTCOM AOR — and in particular, the Persian Gulf region — looks like post-war with Iran," he added.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Muslims poised to outnumber Christians globally by 2035 amid demographic shifts
summary: Pew Research Center study projects Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, driven by higher fertility rates and younger populations.
story: A Pew Research Center analysis reveals that higher birth rates and a younger population will soon make Islam the world’s largest faith.
People practicing the Islamic faith are poised to outnumber Christians globally by 2035, becoming the world's largest religion, according to a new study released by the Pew Research Center.
The detailed report attributes the shift primarily to higher fertility rates and younger populations among Muslims, who are growing at a faster rate than other major faiths.

"Around the world, we find that Muslims tend to have more children than non-Muslims, [and] they tend to be younger as a result of having more children in the past," Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett told Fox News Digital.
WHY PEOPLE REALLY STOPPED HAVING KIDS: NEW STUDY UNCOVERS THE SURPRISING REASONS FAMILIES ARE SHRINKING
Muslims take part in Friday Prayers at a mosque. (Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images)

Muslims have the highest fertility rate at 3.1 children per woman, followed by Christians at 2.5, according to the study. Between 2020 and 2025, Muslim women gave birth to 252 million babies, more than women of any other religion and compared to 208 million born to Christian mothers.

If trends continue, the United States will also undergo a major religious shift. While Christians currently account for roughly 62% to 64% of U. S. adults, that share is expected to fall below 50% by 2065.
POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT'
By 2070, Christians are projected to make up less than half of the U. S. population, while religiously unaffiliated individuals, known as "nones," will rise to about 41%.
"The Muslim population in the U. S. is growing faster than the Christian population, but Christians vastly outnumber Muslims in the U. S., and that's not going to change," Hackett said.

By 2070, the Muslim population in the U. S. is expected to increase to nearly 4%, making Muslims the third-largest group in the country behind Christians and the religiously unaffiliated, surpassing the U.S. Jewish population.

Globally, the demographic center of major faiths is also moving. By 2070, Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia, which currently has the largest Muslim population of any country.

Muslims pray in Mecca, one of Islam's holiest sites in Saudi Arabia and Christians praying inside the Vatican City. A Pew Research report released Wednesday said Muslims are poised to outnumber Christians globally by 2035. (Reuters)
POPE LEO XIV TO VISIT FASTEST-GROWING CATHOLIC CONTINENT DURING 4-NATION AFRICA TRIP

Meanwhile, the presence of Christianity is shifting southward. By 2070, more than half of the world's Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo is projected to surpass the U.S. as the country with the single greatest number of Christians.

A century ago, most of the world's Christians lived in Europe, Hackett noted. However, Europe's population is now growing slowly and expected to shrink in the coming decades, while Africa's population expands rapidly.

"Europe's population has been growing slowly, and Africa's population has been growing very quickly," Hackett said. "In the coming decades, Europe's population is expected to shrink, [while] Africa's population is going to expand a lot."
Other religious demographics are shifting as well. The global Jewish population is expected to become increasingly concentrated, with 62% living in Israel by 2070, up from 46% in 2020.
AGE OF FIRST-TIME MOTHERS HITS RECORD HIGH IN BLUE STATES AS BIRTH RATES KEEP FALLING
In addition, the global Muslim population is projected to exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, compared to just under 3 billion Christians, according to Pew.

Overall, Muslims and Christians are the only major religious groups projected to keep pace with the world's overall population growth, which is expected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070. Christians are projected to grow by 30% and Muslims by 80%.
GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM
Beyond organized religions, many countries continue to see a surge in "nones," those with no religious affiliation, atheists or agnostics.

While China holds a massive proportion of the world's religiously unaffiliated, its population decline will offset growth elsewhere, Hackett said. Excluding China, the global population of "nones" is projected to grow by more than 180 million by 2070.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The religiously unaffiliated already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Irish activist indicted in US over alleged destruction of $60M military plane
summary: United States prosecutors say Daithi O'Corrain spent months planning the Shannon Airport attack that left a $60 million C-130H Hercules beyond repair
story: Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas joins 'America Reports' to discuss how federal prosecutors charged an anti-Israel activist after a $60 million U.S. Air Force warplane was destroyed and deemed a total loss in New York.

An Irish anti-Israel activist was indicted in the United States after allegedly destroying a $60 million American military aircraft at an airport in Ireland, leaving the plane damaged beyond repair after what prosecutors described as months of meticulous planning.

Federal prosecutors announced the indictment Tuesday, seven months after Daithi O'Corrain, 48, allegedly breached the security perimeter at Shannon Airport in western Ireland and broke into an unoccupied U.S. Air National Guard C-130H Hercules aircraft.

Prosecutors said O'Corrain then spent hours damaging the aircraft, cutting critical wiring and hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit instruments, puncturing air ducts and pinching shut the aircraft's liquid oxygen line.
2 FOREIGN NATIONALS BREACH UK BASE HOUSING KEY US, NATO INTEL HUB AMID $556M EXPANSION

Left: Smashed cockpit instruments inside a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft allegedly destroyed at Shannon Airport in Ireland April 11, 2026. Right: A separate U.S. Air Force C-130 Hercules aircraft at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, March 18, 2026. (U.S. Department of Justice; Leon Neal/Getty Images  )
The damage was so extensive it rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the $60 million plane will never return to active flight status, according to federal authorities.

Photographs released by federal prosecutors show extensive damage inside the aircraft, including smashed cockpit instruments, severed wiring and damaged equipment. Other images show tools allegedly used in the attack and O'Corrain standing on the aircraft's roof before his arrest.

According to the indictment, O'Corrain spent months researching the aircraft's construction, acquiring tools and gallium, a metal capable of corroding aluminum, and using a flight-tracking app to monitor military aircraft. He also researched previous attacks on U.S. military planes at Shannon Airport and searched for locations where he could breach the airport's security perimeter.

O'Corrain, who also goes by the name David Curran and is from County Cork in southern Ireland, was charged with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. said the attack was meticulously planned and jeopardized critical military operations.

"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism. The defendant allegedly spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict," Barnacle said.
"The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to pursue anyone who targets U.S. military assets, regardless of where those attacks occur."

Severed wiring and damaged components inside a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft after an alleged attack at Shannon Airport in Ireland April 11, 2026, according to federal prosecutors. (Department of Justice)
US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM

It remains unclear whether the United States has formally requested O'Corrain's extradition from Ireland. The Justice Department, Irish Department of Justice and Irish prosecutors did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment before publication.

The C-130 Hercules is a four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft used to carry troops, equipment and supplies, including into remote areas with short, rough runways. First introduced in the 1950s, it remains in service today, while the C-130H variant involved in the Shannon Airport incident dates to the 1970s. The aircraft was parked on a taxiway and was due to depart for another country on a U.S. military assignment, according to the indictment.
The indictment outlined how the alleged attack unfolded.

O'Corrain allegedly breached Shannon Airport's security perimeter at approximately 4:40 a.m. on April 11 before crossing the airfield and breaking through the aircraft's rear crew door. Once inside, he barricaded himself using tools and supplies he had brought with him. He also covered the aircraft's windows with the flight crew's hammocks, except for the cockpit windows, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said he demonstrated detailed knowledge of the aircraft's critical components and how to destroy them while protecting himself. They warned that the aircraft could have been rocked by a massive explosion had O'Corrain cut through its liquid oxygen line instead of pinching it shut.
Five hours later, the flight crew returned to prepare for departure and spotted O'Corrain through a cockpit window, prompting them to alert airport security.

O'Corrain allegedly climbed through a roof hatch and continued damaging the aircraft, striking its exterior with an axe and pouring unidentified substances and placing objects, including ball bearings, into its fuel tanks. Video circulating online at the time appeared to show a man in dark clothing walking along the wing of the aircraft near the engines and fuselage.
Irish police arrived shortly afterward and arrested him.
"These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said.

Daithi O'Corrain is seen on the exterior of a U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft at Shannon Airport in Ireland on April 11, 2026, before his arrest, according to federal prosecutors. (Department of Justice)
O'Corrain is also facing criminal charges in Ireland over the same incident. He was initially denied bail before securing his release through the Irish High Court, according to RTÉ.

Irish prosecutors have since moved to bring the case to trial, with O'Corrain facing charges, including criminal damage to the aircraft and interference with airport operations. He is scheduled to appear in court again in January.
O'Corrain has drawn support from pro-Palestinian activists in Ireland.

An online fundraiser describes him as an independent peace activist and portrays the incident as an act of resistance against the U.S. military's presence in Ireland and American support for Israel. The campaign features a raised fist gripping a hammer — imagery associated with labor and revolutionary movements — superimposed over a photograph of the aircraft.

"An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.

A U.S. military C-130H Hercules aircraft (left) and smashed cockpit instruments (right) after an alleged attack by Irish activist Daithi O'Corrain at Shannon Airport in Ireland April 11, 2026. (Department of Justice)
Shannon Airport, which has long served as a transit hub for U.S. military aircraft, was also used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September.

The alleged attack followed three other security breaches at Shannon Airport in 2025, according to the indictment. In May, three people were arrested after driving a van through the airport's perimeter fence. Weeks later, three others breached the airfield and sprayed a U.S. military aircraft with paint, temporarily grounding it.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In November 2025, three more people drove a van through the airport's security perimeter and entered a restricted area near a U.S. military C-40 aircraft before being intercepted by security personnel.
Unlike those earlier incidents, the April attack allegedly resulted in the permanent loss of a U.S. military aircraft, with O'Corrain now facing prosecution in two countries.

title: Japan scrambles fighter jets after Russian aircraft breach airspace amid rising Pacific tensions
summary: Suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Okinoshima, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned of instability at the Quad Leaders Summit.
story: More than 13,000 troops and dozens of ships, submarines and aircraft take part in Russian naval drills across the Sea of Japan, Sea of Okhotsk and Northwest Pacific. (Credit: East2West)

Japan scrambled fighter jets early Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace, prompting a rapid military response ahead of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's warning of rising global instability during the Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila.

Hours later, President Donald Trump had also joined Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the summit, where the leaders voiced opposition to actions threatening regional peace and stability.

"We strongly oppose any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability," the leaders said in a joint statement later released by the White House.
TRUMP KICKS OFF HIGH-STAKES ASIA TRIP WITH XI, PUTIN MEETINGS LOOMING ON WORLD STAGE
Japan scrambled fighter jets after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace, prompting a rapid military response. (Aviation-images.com/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
On Wednesday, two U.S. military officials confirmed to Fox News that the aircraft carrier USS George Washington was departing the Middle East for the Pacific.

Sen. Mazie Hirono, D-Hawaii, questioned acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao Tuesday about the lack of aircraft carriers in the Pacific, noting that three carrier strike groups had been deployed to the Middle East.
"There are none in the Indo-Pacific area when we are looking at China, not to mention North Korea and especially what China may have in mind," Hirono said.
"See, this is stretching and stressing our resources. You can't take away the strike group out of the Indo-Pacific."

The Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima, an island in southwestern Japan's Fukuoka Prefecture, at about 4:07 a.m. local time Nov. 17, according to Japan's Defense Ministry.
Fighter jets from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force's Western Air Defense Force were scrambled to issue warnings and take other measures, the ministry said in a statement posted on X.
The first suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace at approximately 4:07 a.m. and remained for three minutes.
A second aircraft entered the same area at approximately 4:09 a.m. and departed three minutes later.
THREE MANILA MOMENTS THAT GIVE TRUMP MOMENTUM GOING INTO TALKS WITH CHINA

U.S. President Donald Trump, second from right, poses for photos with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, left; Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, second left; and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as they take part in a meeting of the Quad group at the Solaire Resort on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in Manila Nov. 17, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
Japan's Defense Ministry said the aircraft traveled through the Tsushima Strait and passed between Japan's Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before continuing into the Pacific Ocean.

"In response, the Self-Defense Forces scrambled fighter jets from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s Western Air Defense Force to issue notifications and warnings and take other measures," the Ministry of Defense said.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tokyo lodged a strong protest with Moscow and demanded measures to prevent further airspace violations.
The incidents "not only constitute a grave infringement upon Japan’s sovereignty but also pose a threat to our security. They are entirely unacceptable," Koizumi said.
This came as Takaichi warned of growing instability in the international order and promised a bigger role for Japan in maintaining regional security.
CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks during a news conference at the prime minister's office in Tokyo Oct. 21, 2025. (Eugene Hoshiko)
"While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play a more proactive role," Takaichi said during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila.
Takaichi emphasized Japan's commitment to maintaining an international order based on freedom, openness and the rule of law while strengthening cooperation with Southeast Asian nations.
"Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific," Trump had also said ahead of the Quad meeting.

The leaders had expressed "grave concerns" about economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions, and outlined plans for a joint military exercise involving maritime patrol aircraft in 2027.
KIM JONG UN'S NUCLEAR BUILDUP SPARKS 'SERIOUS CONCERN' AHEAD OF TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT
An F-35C stealth jet sits on the deck of the USS Carl Vinson in the Western Pacific, south of Japan. (Reuters/Tim Kelly)
The airspace incursion comes amid broader security concerns across the Indo-Pacific, where Japan and its regional partners have increasingly monitored Russian and Chinese military activity.

On Tuesday, South Korea’s air force also scrambled fighter jets as multiple Russian military aircraft had entered the country’s air defense identification zone, according to the Ministry of National Defense.
Otherwise, Japan's relations with Moscow have deteriorated since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, with Tokyo joining Western allies in imposing sanctions on the Kremlin.

The two countries are also locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over islands north of Japan's northernmost main island of Hokkaido. Russia administers the islands, which Japan claims as its Northern Territories.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Japan previously scrambled fighter jets in 2024 after a Russian military patrol aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Hokkaido three times.

title: US races to build bunkers across Middle East as Iranian strikes threaten American troops
summary: The U.S. Army is hiring contractors to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon amid Iranian missile and drone attacks.
story: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst has the latest on the escalation of the US-Iran conflict after the US military intercepted Iranian strikes headed toward a base in Bahrain on 'America Reports.'

The U.S. Army is racing to hire contractors to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon to protect American and coalition troops from deadly missile and drone attacks, according to a government procurement notice posted Friday.
The move comes amid escalating violence in the Middle East, where Iranian attacks on U.S. military installations have killed at least 23 American service members since war broke out in late February.
On Tuesday, Iran also claimed responsibility for another strike on a U.S. military base in Bahrain, its third attack there in five days.
BAHRAIN INTERCEPTS IRANIAN DRONES TARGETING US RADAR AFTER 2-MONTH LULL IN GULF STRIKES
Smoke rises after an Iranian strike on a U.S. Navy 5th Fleet installation in Bahrain in April. (Stringer/Anadolu via Getty Images, File)
Kuwaiti air defenses also intercepted incoming drones as Israeli forces launched new strikes in eastern and southern Lebanon.
The Army plans to build 10 bunkers in Israel, five in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon, replacing makeshift shelters made from shipping containers.

"Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace nonstandard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized, precast, reinforced concrete Indirect Fire bunkers," the Army said in the notice.

"The objective is to safeguard U.S. and coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility," the notice added.
PENTAGON JUMPS FROM $225M TO $55B ON DRONES AS CHEAP ATTACKS OVERWHELM US DEFENSES

A U.S. Army carry team moves a flagged-draped transfer case containing the remains of Capt. Cody A. Khork at Dover Air Force Base, March 7, in Dover, Del. Six soldiers from the 103rd Sustainment Command were killed in action by an Iranian drone strike on March 1 in Port Shuabia, Kuwait, during "Operation Epic Fury." (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images, File)
The effort also follows a series of Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf.
A March drone strike on a U.S. Army command post at Kuwait's Port of Shuaiba killed six American service members, with reports saying the facility lacked adequate protection against aerial attacks.
President Donald Trump said Nov. 16 that defensive measures had been effective across the region.

"Iran has fired between 8,000-9,000 One-way Attack Drones. Only 2 of them got through, resulting in U.S. fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Likewise, Iran has fired about 2,000 Ballistic Missiles. Only 1 out of the 2,0000 got through, and caused U.S. fatalities (Jordan)," he wrote on Truth Social.
US CARRIES OUT SELF-DEFENSE STRIKE ON IRGC MISSILE LAUNCH SITE ON QESHM ISLAND

"Translation: 99.99% of Iranian missiles and drones have been shot down or, in any event, not caused U.S. deaths. [U.S. Central Command] defensive measures have been historically effective. No one in the World has the ability to do so well. All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes ‘report,’" he added.
The 17 bunkers will be built at five military installations: one in Israel and two each in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon, the notice said.
The Army is withholding the sites' locations for security reasons, saying names and coordinates will be provided only to eligible contractors once the formal solicitation is issued.
Each bunker will have three precast, reinforced concrete sections, steel entrance doors shielded by concrete barriers and sandbag-reinforced exterior walls.
Each roof will be covered with at least 18 inches of layered sandbags to protect against incoming fire.
US PULLS PERSONNEL FROM SAUDI ARABIA AS KINGDOM COMES UNDER HOUTHI FIRE
Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid International Airport after Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Oct. 8. (Reuters)
Contractors will have 45 days to finish construction after receiving a task order, while bidders will have just three days to submit quotes.

"Due to extreme operational urgency (soldiers currently at risk using non-standard containerized shelters), the subsequent solicitation is anticipated to have an expedited 3-day quote turnaround window," the Army said.
The Army is looking for construction and engineering firms that can deploy to Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Contractors must respond by Nov. 25, and specify whether they can work in all three countries or only certain locations.

The Army is looking for "qualified, capable, and licensed construction and engineering firms with immediate cross-border and local mobilization capabilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the State of Israel, and the Republic of Lebanon," the notice said.
The Pentagon and Army did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Kim Jong Un's nuclear buildup sparks 'serious concern' ahead of Trump-Xi-Putin summit
summary: IAEA chief Rafael Grossi warned Kim Jong Un's North Korean uranium enrichment expansion at Yongbyon is complete, calling it a serious concern.
story: Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to react to President Donald Trump revealing that North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un may join his upcoming summit in China with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. Schmitt also discusses the national security implications of the alleged Nvidia spy scandal.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is accelerating his nuclear program, expanding a uranium enrichment facility that can produce plutonium for nuclear weapons, the United Nations' nuclear watchdog warned Wednesday, calling Pyongyang's growing program a "cause for serious concern."

International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi said the latest construction at the Yongbyon nuclear complex began in mid-September and was externally complete by late October, raising fresh alarms about North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material.

"The ongoing expansion of the DPRK's uranium enrichment programme remains a cause for serious concern," Grossi said in remarks to the IAEA's board of governors in Vienna, referring to North Korea by its official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
Grossi warned against strikes like the one on Bushehr nuclear plant in Iran. (Abdul Saboor / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

The warning came as President Donald Trump prepared to meet President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, for an unprecedented three-way summit expected to address nuclear arms negotiations and other global security concerns.

Trump had also floated the possibility of meeting Kim during his trip to China, potentially opening another diplomatic channel with the North Korean dictator as Pyongyang continues to reject demands that it abandon its nuclear arsenal.
TRUMP CANNOT DETER XI AND PUTIN’S NUCLEAR GOALS WITH A STRATEGY DESIGNED FOR JUST ONE

North Korea, whose leader Kim Jong Un is shown left, conducted missile launches just days ahead of a visit by President Donald Trump to South Korea. (China Daily via Reuters/Korea News Service via AP; Ahn Young-joon/AP; Alex Brandon/AP)
As he departed the White House on Monday, Trump told reporters that denuclearization would be among the issues discussed with world leaders.
"We're going to talk about denuclearization – tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said.
The president also raised the possibility of Kim joining the diplomatic discussions, although no meeting with the North Korean leader has been confirmed.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump told reporters. Trump also said he believed there was an opportunity for progress.
"So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot," he added.
TRUMP TEASES POTENTIAL KIM JONG UN MEETING LATER THIS YEAR
Putin, Xi and Kim (Getty Images)

The possibility of a meeting gained attention after Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin could meet Kim if the North Korean leader traveled to China for the summit, according to Reuters.
Trump said Tuesday that Kim would like to meet with him, adding, "We'll see what happens."
North Korea has repeatedly rejected calls to dismantle its nuclear weapons program, even as international monitors report continued construction and activity at key nuclear facilities.

Grossi said the IAEA had previously reported ongoing enrichment operations at Yongbyon and Kangson, construction of an additional enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of further expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material.
"Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026," Grossi said.
The agency also observed indications that Yongbyon's 5-megawatt reactor, which can produce plutonium for nuclear weapons, likely will continue to operate in its seventh irradiation cycle.
A separate light-water reactor at the complex resumed operations at the end of April following a shutdown, according to the agency.
NORTH KOREA MISSILE COULD PUT GUAM IN RANGE AS KIM REBUFFS TRUMP OUTREACH: EXPERT
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un spoke during the Ninth Congress of the ruling Workers’ Party in Pyongyang on Feb. 23, 2026. (Korean Central News Agency via REUTERS)
"The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," Grossi said.
The IAEA has not had inspectors inside North Korea since 2009, when Pyongyang expelled them.

The agency now relies primarily on satellite imagery and other publicly available information to monitor nuclear developments, limiting its ability to independently verify activity inside the facilities.

North Korea carried out its first nuclear weapons test in 2006 and five additional tests through 2017, prompting successive rounds of U.N. Security Council sanctions targeting its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.

In September, IAEA member states also expressed "growing concern" over increased nuclear activity in North Korea, while Kim's sister, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the pressure and said North Korea's status as a nuclear-armed country was "absolute" while calling those who continued to seek its denuclearization "idiots."
TRUMP REVEALS EXACT NUMBER OF NORTH KOREA'S NUCLEAR WEAPONS

North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un poses with US President Donald Trump north of the Military Demarcation Line that divides North and South Korea, in the Joint Security Area (JSA) of Panmunjom in the Demilitarized zone (DMZ) on June 30, 2019. (BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP via Getty Images)

Kim has also indicated that future talks with Washington would depend on the United States abandoning its demand for denuclearization and instead negotiating with North Korea as a nuclear-armed state.
The two leaders met in Singapore in 2018, when they signed a broad statement committing to work toward the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula.
Their second summit, in Hanoi in 2019, ended without an agreement after negotiations broke down over North Korea's nuclear facilities and demands for sanctions relief.
Trump and Kim met again in June 2019 at the Demilitarized Zone separating North and South Korea, where Trump briefly crossed into North Korean territory.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Those meetings also failed to secure a verifiable agreement to dismantle North Korea's nuclear weapons program.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: China watchdog warns Trump faces ‘2-on-1’ showdown with Xi, Putin as Taiwan risks mount
summary: President Donald Trump faces a "two versus one" dynamic with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, who arrive as a team eyeing Taiwan and Ukraine gains.
story: U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.

President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.

"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES

President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)

The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)

The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress, detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.

Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.

"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.

Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.

Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.

"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.

Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Responding to concerns about Taiwan, a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.

"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americans. And as President Trump has said: much has been, and will be, accomplished, between the two leaders," the official said.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People’s Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation."

"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," the official added.
The Chinese Embassy rejected outside involvement in Taiwan's future, reiterating Beijing's claim of sovereignty over the self-governing island.

"There is only one China in the world. Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory," the spokesperson said. "The Taiwan question is China's internal affair; how it is resolved is entirely a matter for the Chinese people themselves and brooks no interference from any external forces."
The spokesperson added that the U.S. should "exercise extra caution in handling the Taiwan question".
TRUMP’S TAIWAN ‘NEGOTIATING CHIP’ REMARK SPARKS ALARM OVER HOW FAR HE'D SHIFT US-CHINA POLICY

A procession of Taiwanese armed military vehicles patrols outside the Songshan Airport in the capital city following China’s announcement of the military exercise Joint Sword-2024B that encircles Taiwan, Oct. 14, 2024, in Taipei, Taiwan. (Daniel Ceng/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The commissioners also raised alarm about China's rapidly expanding capabilities beneath the ocean, warning that Beijing could threaten the communications infrastructure on which the United States and its allies depend.
Asked whether China could disrupt critical American communications during a conflict, Kuiken was unequivocal. "Simple answer is absolutely yes," he said.
"The Chinese have spent a long time studying the global communications network and they have absolutely developed the capabilities to sever undersea cables around the globe."
Kuiken said he was confident China had probably conducted exercises involving such operations, although he did not identify specific exercises during the interview.
Schriver pointed to China's advances in undersea warfare and ocean mapping as among the most concerning developments identified in the commission's research.

Officers and soldiers in the Chinese People's Liberation Army PLA Navy's guided-missile destroyer Nanning wave as the ship enters the waters of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region in south China, July 2, 2026. (Ji Peng/Xinhua via Getty Images)

He said the commission is urging Congress to strengthen protection of undersea communications cables through improved real-time threat detection, rapid repair capabilities and greater coordination with U.S. allies.
"So you need to be able to understand in real time when there's a threat to those communication cables," Schriver said.

The commission has separately warned that cables linking the United States with Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines are vulnerable to disruption, with damage potentially forcing communications onto slower and less direct routes.
The broader concern, Kuiken suggested, is the cumulative effect of China's sustained investment in science and technology at a time when American innovation faces growing competitive pressure.
"I think what we are seeing is that the Chinese are starting to turn science, engineering and artificial intelligence into economic strength, national security and global influence," he said.

The Chinese Embassy pushed back against framing undersea cable infrastructure as a security threat, arguing that doing so could undermine international connectivity. "Politicizing this issue and turning it into a security one will only disrupt normal international market rules, threaten global digital connectivity and cybersecurity, and serve no one’s interest," the spokesperson said.

"China always supports international cooperation on submarine cables under the principles of fairness, justice, equality and inclusiveness, and stands ready to work actively with the rest of the world to promote the building and protection of submarine cables and other global information infrastructure."

Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump visit the Temple of Heaven on May 14, 2026, in Beijing. (Brendan Smialowski/Pool/Getty Images)

For the two commissioners, those developments underscore the stakes of Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin: Washington faces not only an immediate diplomatic challenge but a longer-term competition with a Chinese leadership that is steadily building the capabilities to challenge American power.

title: Rare anti-government protests erupt in Iran over workers' deaths
summary: Hundreds of Iranians chanted "Death to the dictator!" in Abdanan after a bus crash killed 13 oil refinery employees, with at least seven people arrested.
story: Iranian protesters in the southern Iranian town of Abdanan chant 'death to the dictators!" during a protest after 13 oil refinery workers were killed in a road accident over the weekend. Credit: The Associated Press.

Hundreds of Iranians took to the streets chanting "Death to the dictator!" and other anti-government messages in the wake of a deadly bus crash over the weekend that killed 13 employees of an oil refinery company, reports said.

The rare display of anti-government anger unfolded Tuesday in Abdanan, a city in western Iran near the country's border with Iraq. Demonstrators called for the resignation of company officials blamed for the accident.

"Those who seek to exploit this incident to disrupt public order and inflame people’s emotions will be dealt with decisively," local prosecutor Amrollah Meysaei was quoted by Iran's Mizan news agency as saying, according to Radio Free Europe.

The outlet, citing Iran's Fars news agency, also reported that an estimated 1,000 people took part in the protests, making them the largest demonstrations since mass unrest swept across Iran at the beginning of this year. Some of the protesters reportedly tried to damage public property.
IRAN LAUNCHES DRONE ASSAULT ON KUWAIT AFTER US STRIKE ON IRGC MISSILE SITE
Protesters are seen marching through the streets of Abdanan, Iran, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (UGC via AP)
A video verified by The Associated Press showed protesters chanting "Death to the dictator!"
A video shared by HRANA, a rights group based outside Iran, also showed a crowd of protesters marching through the center of Abdanan, calling for accountability for the road accident.
The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights said at least seven people were arrested in Abdanan after Tuesday's protests.
Two were later released, including a 15-year-old boy, Hengaw said.
LEAKED IRAN REPORT FINDS RECORD PUBLIC ANGER AS REGIME FOCUSES ON HOLDING POWER
People gather during a protest on Jan. 8, 2026, in Tehran, Iran. (Getty Images)
In January, Iran witnessed some of the largest anti-government protests since the 1979 Islamic Revolution and Abdanan was a hotspot of unrest.
Security forces shot thousands of protesters in the streets and arrested thousands more during those demonstrations.
Iranians block a street while gathering during a protest in Tehran, Iran, on Jan. 9. (MAHSA / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

In late July, small protests broke out in the central city of Isfahan ahead of the public hanging of two protesters.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Protesters call for regime change in Iran following deadly crash that killed 13 oil and gas workers
summary: Hundreds take to the streets in western Iran after 13 oil workers are killed, with demonstrations escalating into political protests against Tehran's leadership.
story: Footage from western Iran shows demonstrators taking to the streets, chanting against the Islamic Republic and calling for the return of the Pahlavi monarchy after a crash killed 13 oil and gas workers.

Hundreds of protesters poured into the streets of western Iran on Tuesday following a deadly bus crash that killed 13 oil and gas workers, with demonstrations quickly escalating into anti-government chants with some protesters calling for the return of the Pahlavi monarchy.

The unrest erupted in Abdanan, a city in Iran's Ilam province near the Iraqi border, where residents initially gathered to demand accountability for Saturday's fatal accident before turning their anger toward the Islamic Republic's leadership.
Videos obtained by Fox News Digital showed large crowds marching through the streets, chanting "Death to the dictator!"
IRANIAN PROTESTER HANGED HOURS AFTER MARRYING HIS IMPRISONED FIANCÉE OVER JAIL PHONE LINE
In this photo obtained by The Associated Press, protesters chant slogans during an anti-government protest in Tehran, Iran, Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026. (UGC via AP)

Iranian-American journalist and foreign policy analyst Lisa Daftari said the demonstrations underscore the deeper political tensions facing Tehran. "Abdanan is a reminder that the Islamic Republic sits on top of a dormant volcano," Daftari told Fox News Digital. "These uprisings start with different catalysts, and in this case it was a local grievance, but they always arrive at the same conclusion."
"The slogans we hear are ‘Death to the Dictator’ and ‘Javid Shah,’ not complaints about a policy. They are an indictment of the entire system, top to bottom," she said.
New reports Wednesday indicated that Iranian security forces arrested at least seven people, including a 15-year-old boy, during the unrest in Abdanan.

The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights said two detainees had been released, but the whereabouts of five others remained unknown. The Kurdistan Human Rights Network separately reported that security forces fired tear gas at demonstrators and that internet access was disrupted during the crackdown.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard-affiliated Fars news agency acknowledged the demonstrations, reporting that approximately 200 to 300 people initially gathered in Abdanan's Vali-e Asr Square before the crowd grew to roughly 1,000.

Fars reported that the slogans initially focused on the deadly accident but subsequently took on a political character. Police were deployed as protesters moved into surrounding streets, according to AFP's Nov. 17 report.
ONE GLARING ISSUE GOES UNADDRESSED IN UN CHIEF'S HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH IRAN'S PRESIDENT

Reza Pahlavi, the exiled crown prince of Iran, said the Islamic Republic is "crumbling" and called for a democratic transition following recent U.S. and Israeli military strikes. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)

The protests followed Saturday's overturning of a bus transporting workers from the Dehloran gas processing project. Thirteen people were killed and more than a dozen injured, according to Iranian media reports.

Euronews Persian reported on Nov. 17 that provincial traffic police identified driver negligence, irregularities involving the company's bus contract and inadequate road barriers as factors contributing to the accident. Prosecutors have announced legal proceedings against the company and provincial transportation officials, although responsibility has not been established in court.
Authorities warned against allowing the demonstrations to escalate.

"Individuals who seek to exploit this incident to disrupt public order or incite public sentiment will be dealt with firmly," Abdanan prosecutor Amrollah Misaie said, according to Iran's judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency, as quoted by AFP on Nov. 17.

Daftari, The Foreign Desk editor-in-chief, argued that the Iranian government's greatest challenge may ultimately come from within, regardless of its confrontation with Washington and Jerusalem. "Whatever happens in the military standoff with the United States and Israel, Tehran will still face its most serious adversary at home," she said.

She also pointed to the protesters' willingness to return to the streets following the deadly crackdown earlier this year, saying that "despite thousands being killed by the regime for protesting in January, we still see bravery on the part of the Iranian people to tell the world of their grievances and to stand up to their murderers."

At the United Nations' daily briefing on Tuesday, Fox News Digital asked the U.N. spokesperson whether the organization was monitoring the situation, particularly the actions of Iranian security forces on the ground. "Well, we're keeping an eye on the situation and we want to make sure that all peaceful protests are allowed to proceed without obstruction and without harassment of protesters," the spokesperson said and added, "Certainly our human rights colleagues will continue to monitor the situation as we've done in the past."
IRAN TURNS CITIZENS INTO INFORMANTS AS CHILLING CRACKDOWN SPREADS BEYOND ITS BORDERS
Hundreds of protesters swarm the streets as they march against the Iranian regime. (Simay Azadi)
The demonstrations carry particular significance because Abdanan was previously a flashpoint during Iran's nationwide anti-government protests earlier this year.
Reuters reported on Jan. 9 that it had verified footage showing demonstrators marching through the city during the broader uprising against the Islamic Republic.

The city also witnessed renewed tensions during mourning ceremonies for protesters killed in the January unrest. Reuters reported on Feb. 18 that witnesses and activists said security forces opened fire on hundreds of mourners gathered at a cemetery in Abdanan.

Iranian security forces are seen near a crowd during demonstrations amid ongoing unrest, according to images released by the Iranian opposition group National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI). (NCRI)
Tuesday's demonstrations mark another outbreak of public anger in a city with a recent history of confrontations with Iranian authorities.
