title: Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official over investigation of her political speech
summary: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz has suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.
story: WASHINGTON — A Democratic senator repeatedly targeted by the Trump administration for potential prosecution due to her political remarks is firing back at a Trump-appointed Justice Department official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her rhetoric about congressional oversight.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is one of five Democratic members of Congress who have been the subject of letters that the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, has posted on social media. In one of the letters, which have come under scrutiny from legal experts, Reitz suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight potentially acting as a “deterrence message” to people considering joining the Trump administration could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.

“I made those statements consistent with my basic right to freedom of speech, a right that every American enjoys under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” Slotkin wrote Wednesday in a letter to Reitz obtained by NBC News. “In addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility.”

“The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts,” she wrote. “As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

Slotkin went on to say that Reitz’s “public threats” violated Justice Department policy, and that his decision to publicly post the letter rather than providing it to her, her attorney or the Senate legal counsel “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Reitz, 39, previously worked as chief of staff for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and became U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas over the summer after placing fourth in the Republican primary for state attorney general.
Reitz also posted letters on X to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.
He told NBC News this week that he was “not interested in chilling free speech.”

Slotkin and five other sitting Democratic lawmakers were separately targeted by the Trump administration earlier this year over a video they posted to social media that sought to remind members of the military and intelligence communities that they should not obey unlawful orders. Allies of the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, tried to indict the six Democrats for their speech in that video, but federal grand jurors unanimously rejected the indictment attempt.

Slotkin’s attorney, Preet Bharara, had previously written a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche cautioning him against following President Donald Trump’s public instruction to look into Slotkin’s political speech, which he dubbed a “criminal act.”

Blanche has conceded that Slotkin’s words alone were “absolutely not a crime” and said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Slotkin wrote in her letter that Reitz appeared to be “seeking attention” for himself and the Justice Department, or was “unaware” of basic constitutional rights.

“Given all of this, your threats are frivolous and a violation of your ethical duties as an attorney,” she wrote. “I reserve all rights to take appropriate actions in the future as it relates to this sham investigation.”

title: House Democrats select Jeffries as leader, setting him up as the first Black speaker
summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York won his party’s nomination for speaker of the House, putting him on a glide path for election to the top job on the first day of the new Congress in January.
story: WASHINGTON — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries won House Democrats’ nomination for speaker Wednesday, putting him on track to be the first Black lawmaker elected to wield the gavel in January.

Jeffries was nominated in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote of 251-11, according to two sources in the room. It was a show of strength for Jeffries, who had faced grumbling from progressive members and activists calling for new and bolder leadership. But no challenger emerged.

Some of Jeffries’ allies had pushed for a vote by acclamation, which would not result in a tally. But Jeffries asked for a recorded vote to give his rank-and-file members an opportunity to voice their support or opposition — something he said the Democratic Caucus did when it returned Nancy Pelosi to the speaker’s office after the 2018 midterm elections amid calls for a new generation of leadership.

“The results of today’s election speak for themselves. We’re going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters when asked about the Democratic defectors. “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people. And that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on Jan. 3rd.”
After the vote, seven of the 11 Democrats who voted against Jeffries issued a joint statement explaining their position.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” wrote Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they said. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”

Jeffries was nominated by five colleagues representing the broad diversity of the Democratic Caucus: Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., Rep. Derek Tran, D-Calif., Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett, D-N.J., and former Majority Whip Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., one of Jeffries’ political mentors.
“This is a very surreal moment for me,” Clyburn, a veteran of the Civil Rights Movement and former chair of the Black Caucus, told reporters before the vote.
Jeffries, a 56-year-old Brooklyn native, former attorney and former state lawmaker, is now poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House.

He campaigned across the country in recent months and helped Democrats win what NBC News projects will be 259 seats — the largest majority in 35 years and well more than the 218 votes he will need to be elected speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

It means that Jeffries can afford roughly 40 Democratic defections that day and still be elected speaker. By contrast, in 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy had a razor-thin 222-212 majority; he managed to win the speaker’s gavel on the 15th ballot.
Last week, House Republicans elected Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., to be minority leader in the next Congress.

Like the speaker race, the other major Democratic leadership races are also uncontested. Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., was elected by her colleagues as majority leader, the No. 2 position. She will make history as the first woman in either chamber elected to that role.
Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., was elected majority whip, the No. 3 leader and party’s top vote counter. No Hispanic American lawmaker has ever climbed higher in the House.
Rep. Ted Lieu, another California Democrat, was elected as caucus chairman. He will make history as the first Asian American to hold that job.
And Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., was elected assistant speaker.

The only significant contested leadership race is for vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, where Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., a member of the Black Caucus, defeated Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Progressive Caucus.
Jeffries, a Pelosi protégé, had served as Democratic Caucus chairman before he was elevated to minority leader following House Democrats’ loss in the 2022 midterms.

He spent much of Tuesday holding meetings with the various factions of his massive new majority that he will need to unite to pass legislation on issues like affordability. He met separately with the leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the two moderate groups, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs.
After Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries told reporters that Democrats will be laser-focused on affordability and lowering the cost of living when they take control of Congress.
“The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic, and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable,” said Jeffries, flanked by his top lieutenants, Clark and Aguilar.

“And we’re committed to delivering, in a meaningful way, the type of change that the American people deserve,” he said, “so that everyone in this country can live an affordable life, a comfortable life, and a good life.”

title: Takeaways from the Trump-Xi-Putin summit and ‘GTA VI’ launches to rave reviews: Morning Rundown
summary: Trump touts his friendships with China’s Xi and Russia’s Putin at a historic three-way summit.
story: Trump touts his friendships with China’s Xi and Russia’s Putin at a historic three-way summit. Workers whose employers dropped GLP-1 coverage scramble to pay out-of-pocket costs. And the highly anticipated “GTA VI” goes on sale.
Here’s what to know today.
President Donald Trump has wrapped up historic three-way talks with the leaders of U.S. rivals, Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s  Xi Jinping.
This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

What these three men might decide has the potential to reverberate across the globe. But the spectacle of Trump’s meeting with Putin and Xi, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, may be what delivers the defining image.

Sitting around the table were three of the world’s most powerful leaders: The U.S. with its largest economy, Russia its biggest nuclear arsenal, and China its largest standing army and manufacturing sector. “We are really making history,” Trump said before the talks began.

Trump called Xi and Putin “friends,” but it was unclear what exactly had been accomplished during the 90-minute meeting. Still, comparisons have already been drawn with the Yalta Conference of 1945, in which President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin sat down to carve up the postwar world.

Trump focused on calling for new curbs on nuclear weapons, after the last remaining nuclear treaty between Washington and Moscow lapsed this year, and China, whose arsenal is smaller than that of the other two, has resisted calls to be involved in a new one.

The Russian leader said it was up to them to “strengthen the system of international law” (Russia has been accused of war crimes in Ukraine) as well as work on issues such as food and energy security. Xi meanwhile stuck to broader themes.

Post-summit identical statements released by China and Russia — but not yet the U.S. — also called for the three countries to increase their energy production and supply, which would fuel Russia’s oil-driven war economy.

As well as nuclear issues, the leaders said they would discuss Iran, economics and trade. But the optics of the meeting, the diplomatic ballet of three strongmen leaders operating in close quarters, was just as gripping to foreign policy observers.
Takeaways from the summit.
Follow the latest news and analysis on our liveblog.

In an exclusive interview with NBC News’ Richard Engel, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the U.S. and China could end the war in Ukraine if they “put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade” with Russia.

In an exclusive interview with NBC News’ Richard Engel, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the U.S. and China could end the war in Ukraine if they “put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade” with Russia.
Workers scramble as employers cut GLP-1s from health coverage

Workers signing up for next year’s health insurance plans might notice a glaring difference, as an increasing number of employers cut coverage for GLP-1s for weight loss. An industry survey shows the share of companies providing insurance coverage for the medication fell from 72% last year to 60% this year. Among the companies that have recently ended insurance coverage or will do so in 2026 are Starbucks, UPS, PepsiCo and Comcast, the parent company of NBC News.

Caitlin Mendoza, a Starbucks employee who has lost 60 pounds, said she faces a monthly bill of $299. Her doctor said the only way her insurance would cover the medication is if she developed diabetes. Doctors and advocates for patients who spoke to NBC News pointed out the double standard for patients with obesity, with one advocate saying “we just don’t see that happen to other people living with different conditions.”
Why it’s easier for employers to cut GLP-1 coverage.
‘Grand Theft Auto’ is back

The 13-year wait is over. “GTA VI” is live, welcoming gamers to Miami-inspired Vice City. As of Tuesday, the game had sold nearly 16 million copies, earning Rockstar Games more than 1.5 billion, one analysis found. And it has already garnered rave reviews, scoring 99/100 on Metacritic.

For the first time, players will be allowed to toggle between the perspectives of the game’s main characters, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Completing the game’s missions will likely take 50 hours, according to the publication Insider Gaming, though it’ll likely be closer to 200 hours if you want to achieve “platinum” status. And that doesn’t include time players can spend in the game’s world doing activities like working out, gambling, petting animals, robbing banks or jetskiing.
So, don’t be surprised if you don’t hear from your loved ones (or employees) today — or maybe for a few weeks.
Here’s what else to know about GTA VI, and follow our live blog for reactions and updates.
Elon Musk says he is ‘not MAGA’

Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million in contributions to Republican campaigns and allies of President Donald Trump in the lead-up to the midterm elections — but he’s “not MAGA,” he insisted. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO’s remarks were made while he was in China as part of Trump’s delegation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk said in an interview for the New York Times DealBook Summit. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” Musk also said he expected Democrat Gina Hinojosa to be “quite moderate” when she takes office as Texas governor. He also claimed to spend big on campaigns because “it’s good to have some balance of power.”

Apple AirPods Pro 3
